questions.stem: Ms. Alvarado teaches a kindergarten class. She notices that many of her five-year-old students struggle to sit through a 40-minute whole-group lesson and become restless and distracted. Considering typical early-childhood development, which adjustment would best support these students' learning?
options: Move the most distracted students to the back of the room to reduce disruption
Require students to remain seated longer to build their stamina for later grades
Replace all group instruction with independent worksheet packets
Break instruction into shorter segments with frequent movement and hands-on activities
questions.rationale: Young children have short attention spans and learn best through active, concrete, and varied experiences. Chunking instruction and adding movement aligns with developmentally appropriate practice.

questions.stem: Mr. Boateng, a 7th-grade science teacher, observes that his students are increasingly concerned with peer opinions and want opportunities to work with friends. According to developmental theory, which approach would best leverage this stage of adolescent development to support learning?
options: Prohibit all peer interaction to keep students focused on content
Incorporate structured collaborative group work with assigned roles
Assign seating randomly each day to prevent any friendships from forming
Have students complete all assignments individually and in silence
questions.rationale: Early adolescents are highly motivated by peer relationships. Structured cooperative learning channels this social orientation into productive academic engagement.

questions.stem: During a unit on fractions, Ms. Chen provides 4th-grade students with fraction tiles and paper circles to manipulate before introducing abstract fraction notation. Which principle of cognitive development best explains why this sequence is effective for these students?
options: Students at this age learn best through purely abstract reasoning before concrete examples
Concrete, hands-on experiences help build understanding that supports later abstract thinking
Students should memorize procedures first and develop understanding only afterward
Manipulatives should be avoided because they slow down content coverage
questions.rationale: Children in the concrete operational stage benefit from manipulating physical objects to build conceptual understanding before moving to abstract symbols, consistent with a concrete-to-abstract progression.

questions.stem: Mr. Delgado wants to apply the concept of the zone of proximal development when teaching a challenging poetry analysis to his 9th-grade English class. Which instructional move best reflects this concept?
options: Lecturing on the full analysis while students copy notes verbatim
Providing scaffolds such as guided questions and a worked example, then gradually removing them as students gain competence
Giving students only tasks they can already complete independently
Assigning the analysis with no support so students learn through struggle alone
questions.rationale: The zone of proximal development is the range of tasks a learner can accomplish with support but not yet independently. Effective teaching provides temporary scaffolding that is gradually withdrawn.

questions.stem: Ms. Fontaine notices that a 2nd-grade student, Marcus, can decode words accurately but reads very slowly and with little expression, which affects his comprehension. Which area of development should Ms. Fontaine most directly target to help Marcus?
options: Phonemic awareness through rhyming games
Spelling through weekly memorization lists
Reading fluency through repeated and guided oral reading
Handwriting through additional copying practice
questions.rationale: Marcus already decodes accurately, so his need is fluency: reading with appropriate speed, accuracy, and expression. Repeated and guided oral reading directly builds fluency, which supports comprehension.

questions.stem: A high school teacher, Mr. Iglesias, designs a project asking 11th-grade students to evaluate competing economic theories, justify a position with evidence, and anticipate counterarguments. A colleague questions whether this is developmentally appropriate. Which response best reflects an accurate understanding of adolescent cognitive development?
options: The task is inappropriate because adolescents cannot consider multiple perspectives at once
The task is appropriate because most adolescents are developing the capacity for abstract, hypothetical, and evaluative reasoning, though they still benefit from support
The task is appropriate only if students simply summarize each theory without forming a position
The task is inappropriate because abstract and hypothetical reasoning is beyond all high school students
questions.rationale: By adolescence, many students are developing formal operational thinking, enabling abstract, hypothetical, and evaluative reasoning. Such tasks are appropriate when paired with scaffolding, since development is uneven.

questions.stem: Ms. Park observes that her 6th-grade students are highly motivated when they can make choices about their learning and feel their work matters. To best support intrinsic motivation, which strategy should Ms. Park prioritize?
options: Providing meaningful choices and connecting tasks to students' interests and real-world relevance
Posting rankings of student grades publicly to encourage competition
Offering candy and prizes for every completed assignment
Removing all student choice to maintain consistent expectations
questions.rationale: Intrinsic motivation is fostered by autonomy, relevance, and a sense of competence. Offering meaningful choices and connecting tasks to students' interests supports this, whereas external rewards mainly drive extrinsic motivation.

questions.stem: Mr. Tran has a 3rd-grade student, Aisha, who gives up quickly when problems become difficult, saying, 'I'm just not smart at math.' Drawing on motivation research, which long-term approach would most effectively help Aisha persist?
options: Praising Aisha's effort and strategies and framing challenges as opportunities to grow her abilities
Praising Aisha's intelligence whenever she gets answers right
Giving Aisha only easy problems so she never experiences failure
Telling Aisha that some people are simply born good at math and others are not
questions.rationale: Process-focused praise that emphasizes effort and strategy fosters a growth mindset, helping students view ability as developable and persist through challenges, unlike praise for fixed intelligence.

questions.stem: Ms. Okafor wants her 8th-grade students to retain new vocabulary over time. Based on principles of how memory and learning work, which strategy is most effective?
options: Requiring students to copy each definition ten times in one sitting
Having students reread the word list silently several times the night before the test
Allowing students to study only the morning of the assessment
Using spaced practice and retrieval, such as low-stakes quizzes revisiting words over several weeks
questions.rationale: Spaced practice and retrieval practice produce more durable, long-term learning than massed rereading or cramming, which favor short-term recall only.

questions.stem: Ms. Ramirez has several English learners in her 5th-grade class who are at the beginning stages of English proficiency. Which strategy would best support their content learning during a science lesson?
options: Requiring the students to translate the entire textbook chapter independently
Using visuals, gestures, realia, and simplified language alongside content vocabulary
Excusing the students from the lesson until they learn more English
Speaking faster so students are exposed to more English
questions.rationale: Beginning English learners benefit from comprehensible input supported by visuals, gestures, and realia, which make content accessible while developing academic language.

questions.stem: Mr. Sullivan teaches a 10th-grade history class with students of varied reading levels. He wants all students to access the same key concepts from a complex primary source. Which approach best reflects differentiated instruction?
options: Giving every student the original text with no support and expecting the same output
Assigning the strongest readers the source and giving everyone else unrelated busywork
Providing tiered versions and supports such as annotated texts and graphic organizers while maintaining the same learning goal
Lowering expectations and skipping the primary source for struggling readers
questions.rationale: Differentiation adjusts how students access content while keeping the same essential learning goal. Tiered texts and supports allow all students to engage with key concepts.

questions.stem: Mr. Castillo notices that a gifted 6th-grade student, Lena, finishes assignments quickly and appears bored and disengaged. Which strategy would best meet Lena's learning needs?
options: Giving Lena more of the same worksheets to keep her busy
Providing curriculum compacting and extension tasks that increase depth and complexity
Withholding new content until the rest of the class catches up
Asking Lena to tutor classmates for the entire class period every day
questions.rationale: Gifted learners benefit from enrichment that adds depth, complexity, and challenge. Curriculum compacting lets students move past mastered material into more advanced tasks.

questions.stem: Ms. Faulkner suspects that one of her 2nd-grade students may have an undiagnosed learning disability based on persistent difficulty despite quality instruction and interventions. Within a Response to Intervention (RTI) framework, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ignore the difficulty since the student is still young and may catch up on his own
Immediately place the student in special education without documentation
Lower the student's grade-level expectations permanently without any intervention
Continue documenting data, increase the intensity of evidence-based interventions, and monitor progress before referral
questions.rationale: RTI is a tiered, data-driven process. Before special-education referral, teachers intensify evidence-based interventions and monitor progress, documenting the student's response to guide decisions.

questions.stem: Mr. Abara teaches a 7th-grade class with students who have diverse learning preferences and strengths. He wants to ensure all students can demonstrate mastery of a unit on ecosystems. Which assessment design best honors this diversity while maintaining the same standard?
options: Assessing only through a single timed multiple-choice test
Letting students choose any topic unrelated to ecosystems for their project
Requiring every student to write an identical five-paragraph essay only
Offering varied product options such as a model, a written report, or a recorded presentation, all assessed against the same criteria
questions.rationale: Allowing varied products judged by common criteria lets students demonstrate the same standard through different means, supporting diverse strengths without lowering rigor.

questions.stem: Ms. Lindqvist has a 1st-grade student, Diego, whose home language is Spanish and who is just beginning to learn English. Diego seems hesitant to participate aloud. Which approach best supports both his language development and his confidence?
options: Discouraging Diego from using any Spanish in the classroom
Providing low-anxiety opportunities such as partner talk, sentence stems, and time to rehearse before sharing
Avoiding calling on Diego at all so he is never uncomfortable
Calling on Diego frequently to answer complex questions in front of the class
questions.rationale: Beginning English learners benefit from low-anxiety, supported speaking opportunities like partner talk and sentence stems that build language and confidence gradually.

questions.stem: A high school teacher, Ms. Pereira, learns that a student in her class uses a wheelchair and that some lab stations are inaccessible. What is the teacher's most appropriate response to support equitable access?
options: Rearrange or adapt lab stations and procedures so the student can fully participate
Tell the student to find a way to manage on his own
Ask the student to simply observe while classmates complete the labs
Exempt the student from all lab activities for the semester
questions.rationale: Equitable access requires adapting the physical environment and procedures so students with disabilities can participate fully in learning experiences.

questions.stem: Mr. Holloway is planning a 5th-grade lesson. He begins by identifying what students should know and be able to do based on the relevant Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills (TEKS). Why is starting with the TEKS objective the appropriate first step in planning?
options: Because clear, standards-based objectives guide the selection of aligned instruction and assessment
Because activities should be chosen before deciding on learning goals
Because objectives are unnecessary as long as students stay busy
Because the textbook sequence should always determine the objective
questions.rationale: Effective planning is goal-driven: clear, TEKS-aligned objectives direct the choice of instructional activities and assessments so that all components target the intended learning.

questions.stem: Ms. Reyes writes the following learning objective for her 8th-grade math class: 'Students will solve multi-step equations involving variables on both sides.' Which feature makes this a strong, measurable objective?
options: It specifies an observable, measurable skill students will demonstrate
It lists the activities the teacher will perform during the lesson
It describes a vague feeling students should have about math
It focuses on how long the lesson will last
questions.rationale: A strong objective states an observable, measurable student outcome, which makes it possible to plan aligned instruction and assess whether the goal was met.

questions.stem: Mr. Schwartz wants his 10th-grade students to move beyond recalling facts about World War II to analyzing causes and evaluating decisions. Using a hierarchy of cognitive demand, which set of objectives best reflects this higher-order goal?
options: Analyze the factors leading to the war and evaluate the effectiveness of specific strategic decisions
Copy a timeline of events from the textbook
Memorize the names of all wartime leaders
List the dates of major battles and define key terms
questions.rationale: Higher-order objectives target analysis and evaluation rather than mere recall. Asking students to analyze causes and evaluate decisions engages higher levels of cognitive demand.

questions.stem: Ms. Donovan has set a clear TEKS-aligned objective for a 6th-grade reading lesson. As she plans the activities, what is the most important consideration to ensure instructional alignment?
options: Choosing learning activities and assessments that directly develop and measure the stated objective
Picking activities based solely on which require the least preparation
Using whatever activity the class did last week to save planning time
Selecting the most entertaining activity regardless of the objective
questions.rationale: Instructional alignment means that activities and assessments directly support and measure the stated objective. Alignment ensures students practice and are evaluated on the intended learning.

questions.stem: Ms. Yamamoto reviews her 4th-grade science TEKS, which asks students to 'plan and conduct simple investigations and analyze results.' She had planned a lesson where students only watch the teacher perform a demonstration and copy conclusions. What is the most significant instructional problem, and the best fix?
options: The problem is the lesson is too long; she should shorten the demonstration
The standard is wrong and should be ignored in favor of the demonstration
There is no problem; watching a demonstration fully meets the standard
The lesson is misaligned because students must actively plan and conduct investigations; she should redesign it so students do the investigating
questions.rationale: The TEKS requires students to plan, conduct, and analyze investigations themselves. A teacher-only demonstration does not have students perform these processes, so the lesson must be redesigned for active student investigation.

questions.stem: Ms. Cardenas is designing a problem-based learning unit for 11th-grade environmental science. She wants the unit to promote deep, transferable learning rather than surface coverage. Which design choice best supports this aim?
options: Assigning a series of disconnected worksheets on separate topics
Having students memorize definitions for a comprehensive vocabulary test
Covering as many isolated topics as possible in the available time
Centering the unit on an authentic, complex problem that requires students to apply and integrate concepts to develop a solution
questions.rationale: Deep, transferable learning is fostered by authentic, complex problems that require students to integrate and apply concepts, rather than by surface coverage of disconnected facts.

questions.stem: Mr. Fitzgerald is selecting instructional resources for a 3rd-grade lesson aligned to a specific TEKS objective. Which is the most important criterion when choosing a resource?
options: Whether the resource was the easiest to find online
Whether the resource directly supports the lesson's objective and is appropriate for the students
Whether the resource is the newest one available
Whether the resource is the longest and most detailed
questions.rationale: Resources should be chosen primarily for their alignment with the learning objective and appropriateness for the learners, not for novelty, length, or convenience.

questions.stem: Ms. Ibrahim plans a lesson in which students first watch a short modeling segment, then practice with teacher guidance, and finally work independently. Which instructional framework does this sequence reflect, and why is it effective?
options: Pure lecture, because students absorb information passively
Random grouping, because it varies who students sit near
Gradual release of responsibility, because it moves students from modeled to guided to independent practice, building competence
Unstructured discovery, because students receive no support
questions.rationale: The 'I do, we do, you do' gradual release of responsibility model transfers responsibility from teacher to student through modeling, guided practice, and independent application, supporting skill development.

questions.stem: During a 5th-grade math lesson, Ms. Lawson pauses to have students solve a problem on individual whiteboards and hold them up so she can quickly see who understands. What type of assessment is she using, and what is its main purpose?
options: Formative assessment to monitor understanding and adjust instruction in the moment
Standardized assessment to compare schools
Diagnostic assessment given only at the start of the year
Summative assessment to assign final grades
questions.rationale: Formative assessment occurs during learning to gather evidence of understanding and inform immediate instructional adjustments. Whiteboard checks are a quick formative technique.

questions.stem: Ms. Okonkwo administers a brief quiz at the start of a 6th-grade unit to find out what students already know and what misconceptions they hold. How should she best use these results?
options: Share each student's score publicly to motivate the class
Use the information to adjust her instructional plans and target identified gaps and misconceptions
Record them as the students' first major grade of the unit
File the results away without reviewing them
questions.rationale: Pre-assessment data should inform planning. Identifying prior knowledge and misconceptions allows the teacher to tailor instruction to students' actual needs.

questions.stem: Mr. Lindgren wants to give his 8th-grade students feedback that helps them improve their writing. Which type of feedback is most effective for promoting learning?
options: A note that simply says the essay was wrong
Specific, descriptive feedback that identifies strengths and gives actionable steps for improvement
A single letter grade with no comments
Only general praise such as 'good job' on every paper
questions.rationale: Effective feedback is specific, descriptive, and actionable, telling students what they did well and how to improve, which supports continued learning more than grades or vague praise.

questions.stem: Ms. Beaumont wants her 11th-grade students to become more self-regulated learners by taking ownership of their progress. Which assessment practice most directly develops students' metacognition and self-assessment skills?
options: Teaching students to use criteria and reflection tools to evaluate their own work and set improvement goals
Allowing only the teacher to judge the quality of any work
Comparing each student publicly to the highest performer in the class
Keeping all assessment data hidden from students
questions.rationale: Self-regulation and metacognition grow when students evaluate their own work against clear criteria, reflect on their learning, and set goals, shifting ownership of progress to the learner.

questions.stem: Ms. Alvarado, a first-grade teacher, wants her students to feel that every contribution they make during class discussions is valued. Which of the following actions would BEST help her create a classroom climate of mutual respect and emotional safety?
options: Praising the most academically advanced students as models for the rest of the class
Calling only on students who raise their hands quickly so the pace stays brisk
Establishing a clear norm that all responses are received without ridicule and acknowledging each student's effort
Correcting incorrect answers immediately and publicly so misunderstandings are not repeated
questions.rationale: A positive, supportive climate depends on emotional safety. When students know their contributions will be received respectfully and their effort acknowledged, they are more willing to participate and take intellectual risks.

questions.stem: Mr. Boateng teaches a diverse ninth-grade English class. He wants the physical arrangement and materials in his room to communicate that all students belong and that excellence is expected of everyone. Which strategy MOST clearly reflects a commitment to equity and high expectations?
options: Keeping wall space blank to minimize visual distractions for all learners
Seating students in fixed rows by their most recent test scores
Posting only the work of the highest-scoring students to inspire others
Displaying student work and posting culturally varied texts and authors that represent the class's diversity
questions.rationale: An equitable, high-expectation environment affirms students' identities and signals that all learners can achieve. Displaying varied student work and diverse texts communicates belonging and excellence for everyone.

questions.stem: During the first week of school, Ms. Carrillo notices that her sixth-grade students do not yet know one another well and seem hesitant to work together. Which approach would BEST foster a sense of community and positive peer relationships?
options: Allowing students to sit only with friends they already know
Assigning individual seatwork until students mature enough to cooperate
Using structured team-building activities and cooperative tasks that require positive interdependence
Postponing all group work until the end of the grading period
questions.rationale: Intentional community-building and cooperative tasks structured for positive interdependence help students build relationships and learn to collaborate, strengthening classroom climate.

questions.stem: Mr. Delgado wants his fourth graders to take ownership of their learning environment. Which of the following BEST promotes student self-direction and shared responsibility for the classroom climate?
options: Reminding students daily that the teacher is in charge of all decisions
Posting a detailed list of rules he created and enforcing them strictly
Involving students in collaboratively developing class norms and classroom jobs
Rewarding compliant behavior with extra recess each Friday
questions.rationale: When students help create norms and take on meaningful roles, they develop ownership, self-direction, and a shared sense of responsibility for the classroom community.

questions.stem: Ms. Whitfield, a high school chemistry teacher, communicates her belief that every student can succeed by setting challenging goals and providing the support needed to reach them. This practice MOST directly reflects which principle of an effective learning environment?
options: Lowering standards so all students can pass easily
Allowing students to opt out of difficult tasks to reduce frustration
Maintaining high expectations paired with appropriate scaffolding for all students
Reserving challenging work for students identified as gifted
questions.rationale: Conveying high expectations while providing the scaffolding students need to meet them communicates that all learners are capable and supports both equity and excellence.

questions.stem: Mr. Okafor, a seventh-grade math teacher, finds that the transition from whole-group instruction to small-group work each day wastes nearly ten minutes as students mill around and ask repeated questions. Which strategy would MOST effectively reduce lost instructional time during this transition?
options: Reducing the amount of small-group work to avoid the transition entirely
Assigning extra homework as a consequence whenever transitions run long
Waiting silently at the front until all students are quiet before giving directions
Teaching, rehearsing, and posting a clear routine for the transition and signaling it consistently
questions.rationale: Efficient transitions come from explicitly taught, rehearsed, and consistently signaled routines. Once students know exactly what to do, transitions become quick and predictable, maximizing instructional time.

questions.stem: Ms. Ferraro notices that several students in her tenth-grade history class frequently disengage during long lectures, putting their heads down or talking quietly. To increase engagement and reduce off-task behavior, which instructional adjustment would be MOST appropriate?
options: Incorporating frequent opportunities for active participation, such as paired discussion and quick writes
Moving the most disengaged students to seats directly in front of her desk
Lowering the difficulty of the material so students do not lose interest
Lengthening the lecture so students have more time to absorb the content
questions.rationale: Off-task behavior during passive lectures is often a sign of low engagement. Building in frequent active participation gives students meaningful involvement, which sustains attention and reduces misbehavior.

questions.stem: On the first day of school, Mr. Sandoval establishes procedures for entering the room, sharpening pencils, and turning in work. He then has students practice each procedure and provides feedback. What is the PRIMARY purpose of teaching and rehearsing these procedures so early?
options: To demonstrate that the teacher has authority over the class
To create predictable routines that prevent disruptions and maximize time for learning
To give students something to do until the real curriculum begins
To identify which students are likely to become behavior problems
questions.rationale: Establishing and rehearsing procedures early creates predictable routines that minimize confusion and disruption, allowing more time and attention to be devoted to learning throughout the year.

questions.stem: During independent work, Ms. Trinh, a fifth-grade teacher, notices a student, Marcus, quietly tapping his pencil and looking out the window instead of working. Marcus is not disturbing others. Which teacher response BEST reflects effective, low-intrusion behavior management?
options: Sending Marcus to the office for failing to complete his work
Using a nonverbal cue or quiet proximity to redirect Marcus while keeping the lesson flowing
Stopping the class to point out that Marcus is off task
Ignoring the behavior entirely since it is not disruptive
questions.rationale: Effective managers use the least intrusive intervention that works. A nonverbal cue or proximity redirects the student privately without interrupting instruction or embarrassing him, preserving both learning time and climate.

questions.stem: Mr. Patel wants to manage instructional time so that students are productively engaged from the moment they enter his eighth-grade science class. Which practice would BEST accomplish this goal?
options: Spending the first several minutes taking attendance before beginning any work
Beginning instruction only after all materials have been distributed one student at a time
Posting a brief warm-up or bell-ringer task that students begin immediately upon entering
Allowing free time at the start of class until everyone has settled
questions.rationale: A bell-ringer or warm-up task engages students immediately and protects the opening minutes of class, increasing time on task and signaling that learning begins right away.

questions.stem: Ms. Rourke teaches a kindergarten class and is introducing a new procedure for cleaning up centers. To ensure young students learn the procedure successfully, which sequence reflects BEST practice?
options: Explain the procedure once, then expect students to follow it independently
Post a written description of the procedure on the wall for students to read
Wait for students to make mistakes, then correct them as problems arise
Model the procedure, have students practice it with guidance and feedback, then reinforce it consistently
questions.rationale: Especially with young learners, procedures must be explicitly modeled, practiced with feedback, and consistently reinforced so they become automatic, predictable routines.

questions.stem: Mr. Estrada has established clear classroom expectations, but he notices that he often reacts to misbehavior only after it escalates. To shift toward a more proactive approach to classroom management, he should PRIMARILY focus on which of the following?
options: Waiting to see whether minor misbehavior resolves on its own before acting
Increasing the severity of consequences for repeated misbehavior
Removing students who misbehave so the rest of the class can learn
Monitoring the whole class continuously and intervening early with subtle cues before problems grow
questions.rationale: Proactive management relies on 'withitness': continuously scanning the room and addressing potential problems early with minimal interventions before they escalate, which preserves instruction and climate.

questions.stem: Ms. Nakamura wants to design a behavior management system for her third-grade class that builds students' capacity for self-regulation rather than relying solely on external control. Which approach BEST supports this goal?
options: Teaching students strategies to monitor their own behavior and reflect on choices, with guided support
Posting each student's daily behavior color for the whole class to see
Issuing immediate penalties for any rule violation without discussion
Awarding stickers for every instance of good behavior throughout the day
questions.rationale: Helping students learn to monitor and reflect on their own behavior develops self-regulation and internal responsibility, which is more durable than systems based only on external rewards or punishments.

questions.stem: Mr. Lindqvist teaches an eleventh-grade class with students from many cultural and linguistic backgrounds. He observes that a few students rarely participate in whole-class discussion, though they engage actively in small groups. He suspects cultural norms about speaking in large groups may be a factor. Which response BEST reflects a culturally responsive, equity-minded approach to classroom climate?
options: Requiring each student to contribute aloud in whole-group discussion to ensure fairness
Offering varied participation structures, such as small groups, written responses, and think-pair-share, so all students can engage in ways that affirm their strengths
Calling on the quiet students unexpectedly so they become accustomed to speaking up
Lowering his expectations for those students' verbal participation because of their backgrounds
questions.rationale: A culturally responsive teacher recognizes that students bring different norms and strengths and provides multiple avenues for meaningful participation. This maintains high expectations while honoring diversity, rather than forcing one mode or lowering expectations.

questions.stem: Ms. Adeyemi's ninth-grade class includes a student, Devon, whose disruptive outbursts have increased over several weeks. She has consistently applied her established consequences, but the behavior persists. Which action represents the MOST appropriate next step in addressing the ongoing behavior?
options: Looking for patterns and possible underlying causes of the behavior and collaborating with colleagues, support staff, and the family to address needs
Removing Devon from the class permanently to protect the learning of other students
Publicly warning Devon that further outbursts will result in failing the course
Increasing the severity of the same consequences each time the behavior recurs
questions.rationale: When established consequences are not changing a persistent behavior, an effective teacher investigates underlying causes and triggers and works collaboratively with support staff and the family to meet the student's needs, rather than simply escalating punishment.

questions.stem: Mr. Halverson is planning a project-based unit in which his sophomore students will work in groups, move around the room to access materials, and use shared technology. Anticipating the management challenges of this less-structured format, which planning decision would MOST effectively support a productive learning environment?
options: Keeping students in their seats for the whole unit to avoid movement-related disruptions
Establishing and teaching specific procedures for movement, material use, technology, and group collaboration before the project begins
Allowing the structure to emerge naturally as students discover what works during the project
Assigning individual rather than group work so that management is simpler
questions.rationale: Less-structured, active learning formats demand more, not fewer, procedures. Proactively establishing and teaching routines for movement, materials, technology, and collaboration prevents confusion and keeps students productively engaged.

questions.stem: Mr. Boateng wants to encourage more students to participate in whole-class discussions. Which questioning technique would most effectively increase the number and quality of student responses?
options: Answering his own questions when no one responds within two seconds
Asking a question, then providing several seconds of wait time before calling on a student
Calling on the first student who raises a hand to keep the pace brisk
Limiting discussion to yes-or-no questions so more students can answer
questions.rationale: Adequate wait time after posing a question gives students time to think, increasing participation rates and the depth of responses.

questions.stem: During a high school English lesson, Ms. Carrillo uses precise academic vocabulary such as 'theme,' 'tone,' and 'inference.' What is the primary instructional benefit of consistently modeling academic language?
options: It builds students' academic vocabulary and prepares them to communicate within the discipline
It allows the teacher to cover material more quickly
It ensures only advanced students can follow the lesson
It reduces the need for the teacher to give any examples
questions.rationale: Modeling discipline-specific academic language helps students acquire the vocabulary and discourse patterns needed to think and communicate like practitioners in the content area.

questions.stem: Mr. Delgado teaches a sixth-grade class that includes several emergent bilingual students. While leading a discussion, he asks a complex question and a student gives a partial answer in halting English. Which response best supports the student's communication and learning?
options: Telling the student to write the answer down later when there is more time
Calling on a fluent English speaker to give the 'right' answer instead
Affirming the idea, then using a follow-up prompt to help the student elaborate and supplying needed vocabulary
Quickly correcting the student's grammar before moving to the next question
questions.rationale: Validating the student's idea and scaffolding elaboration with prompts and vocabulary supports both content understanding and language development without discouraging participation.

questions.stem: During a unit on persuasive writing, Mr. Huang wants students to recognize when communication is unclear and to repair it themselves. Which strategy best develops students' metacommunicative awareness?
options: Providing a single model essay for students to copy the structure
Grading only the final draft so students focus on the product
Having students exchange drafts and ask clarifying questions, then revise based on where readers were confused
Reading all drafts aloud himself so students hear correct phrasing
questions.rationale: Peer questioning surfaces points of confusion and prompts students to clarify their own communication, building awareness of audience and effective expression.

questions.stem: Ms. Ibarra notices that when she lectures for long stretches, fourth-grade students stop responding to her questions and appear disengaged. Which adjustment best reflects effective communication that promotes active engagement?
options: Asking the same rhetorical questions without expecting answers
Continuing the lecture but raising her voice to regain attention
Assigning the reading as homework and skipping discussion entirely
Breaking the content into shorter segments interspersed with structured opportunities for students to discuss and respond
questions.rationale: Chunking content with frequent, structured interaction sustains attention and gives students active roles, making communication a two-way process.

questions.stem: Mr. Jiang leads a seventh-grade discussion in which one student dominates while others stay silent. He wants all students to engage in meaningful academic discourse. Which combination of strategies would most effectively restructure the discussion?
options: Allow the talkative student to continue since participation should be voluntary
Replace discussion with silent written responses to avoid the imbalance
Call only on students who have not spoken, regardless of whether they are prepared
Use a think-pair-share, assign discussion roles, and employ a talk move such as 'Can someone build on that idea?' to distribute participation
questions.rationale: Structured talk routines, roles, and talk moves equitably distribute participation and deepen discourse, ensuring all voices contribute rather than relying on one dominant student.

questions.stem: Ms. Knight is planning a high school chemistry lesson and wants her questioning to move students from recall toward analysis and evaluation. Which sequence of questions best reflects an intentional progression in cognitive demand?
options: Which answer is correct, A or B? Is water a liquid? Did the temperature rise?
What is the boiling point of water? What is the freezing point of water? What is the melting point of ice?
How would you redesign the experiment? Define a state change. What is the boiling point of water?
Define a state change. What evidence shows a state change occurred? How would you redesign the experiment to test a new variable, and what results would justify your conclusion?
questions.rationale: Effective questioning scaffolds from lower-order recall (define) toward higher-order analysis and evaluation (evaluate evidence, redesign, justify), building cognitive complexity in a logical sequence.

questions.stem: Mr. Lin wants his fifth-grade students to engage in critical thinking rather than simply recalling facts about ecosystems. Which task best promotes critical thinking?
options: Listing all the animals that live in a forest
Copying a labeled diagram of a food chain from the textbook
Memorizing the definitions of producer, consumer, and decomposer for a quiz
Predicting how a local ecosystem would change if a key predator were removed and justifying the prediction with evidence
questions.rationale: Critical thinking requires analysis, prediction, and evidence-based reasoning. Predicting consequences and justifying them engages higher-order thinking, unlike recall or copying.

questions.stem: Ms. Mbeki wants to design a problem-solving activity for her second-grade math class. Which task best engages students in authentic problem solving?
options: Reciting subtraction facts aloud as a class
Watching the teacher solve subtraction problems on the board
Completing 30 identical subtraction problems on a worksheet
Determining how to fairly share 24 crayons among groups of different sizes and explaining their strategy
questions.rationale: Authentic problem solving presents a meaningful, somewhat open situation requiring students to devise and explain a strategy, rather than apply a single rote procedure.

questions.stem: Mr. Novak wants students to take greater ownership of their learning during an inquiry unit. Which teacher action best promotes student self-directed inquiry?
options: Encouraging students to generate their own questions about the topic and design ways to investigate them
Providing students with the answers to all inquiry questions in advance
Requiring all students to follow one identical investigation step by step
Telling students exactly what conclusions they should reach
questions.rationale: Self-directed inquiry develops when students pose their own questions and plan investigations, fostering curiosity, autonomy, and higher-order thinking.

questions.stem: Ms. Ortega gives her ninth-grade history class a set of conflicting primary-source accounts of the same historical event. Her main instructional goal is to develop students' critical-thinking skills. Which task best aligns with this goal?
options: Having students choose the source they like best and explain why they enjoy it
Directing students to memorize the date and location of the event
Asking students to evaluate the reliability of each source and construct an evidence-based interpretation that accounts for the discrepancies
Having students summarize each source in their own words
questions.rationale: Evaluating source reliability and reconciling conflicting evidence requires analysis, evaluation, and synthesis—core critical-thinking processes—rather than summary or recall.

questions.stem: During a collaborative engineering challenge, Mr. Park's eighth-grade groups must build a bridge from limited materials. One group's first design collapses. Which teacher response best fosters problem solving and a productive disposition toward failure?
options: Prompting the group to analyze why the design failed and to use that analysis to revise their approach
Giving the group the correct design so they can finish on time
Lowering the group's grade for not succeeding on the first attempt
Reassigning the struggling students to other groups that are succeeding
questions.rationale: Treating failure as data for revision develops problem-solving skills and perseverance. Guiding analysis and iteration keeps cognitive ownership with students.

questions.stem: Ms. Quintero wants her tenth-grade students to connect a literature unit to real-world issues to deepen engagement and thinking. Which approach best achieves this aim?
options: Asking students to recall the sequence of plot events for a timeline
Assigning a vocabulary quiz on words from the novel
Requiring students to read each chapter aloud in turn
Having students analyze a contemporary social issue reflected in the novel's theme and propose a reasoned response supported by textual and current evidence
questions.rationale: Connecting themes to authentic contemporary issues and requiring evidence-based reasoning fosters relevance, transfer, and higher-order thinking.

questions.stem: Mr. Reyes plans a first-grade lesson and wants to encourage early critical thinking. A colleague suggests several questions. Which question is most likely to elicit critical thinking from young students?
options: How many characters are in the story?
Why do you think the character made that choice, and what might have happened if she had chosen differently?
What color is the apple in the story?
What is the title of the book?
questions.rationale: Open-ended 'why' and 'what if' questions prompt reasoning, justification, and consideration of alternatives, fostering critical thinking even in young learners.

questions.stem: Ms. Sandoval wants students to develop metacognitive skills during problem solving in her seventh-grade math class. Which strategy most directly builds metacognition?
options: Having students explain their reasoning, monitor their strategy, and reflect on what they would do differently next time
Rewarding only students who get the correct answer on the first try
Providing an answer key so students can check their final answers
Timing students to solve problems as quickly as possible
questions.rationale: Metacognition involves awareness and regulation of one's own thinking. Explaining reasoning, monitoring strategies, and reflecting directly cultivate these self-regulatory skills.

questions.stem: Mr. Tanaka designs a multi-week project-based learning unit on local water quality for his eleventh-grade environmental science class. To maximize critical thinking and problem solving, which design feature is most essential?
options: Grading primarily on the neatness of the final poster presentation
Specifying a single correct conclusion that all groups must reach
Limiting research to one assigned textbook chapter to keep the scope manageable
Framing an authentic, open-ended driving question that requires students to gather data, evaluate evidence, and propose justified solutions
questions.rationale: A genuine, open-ended driving question that requires data collection, evaluation, and justified solutions is the core of meaningful PBL and drives sustained critical thinking and problem solving.

questions.stem: Mr. Vargas wants to use technology to enhance a fourth-grade geography lesson. Which use of technology most meaningfully supports learning rather than simply replacing a traditional tool?
options: Showing a digital photo of the textbook page on the projector
Using an interactive mapping tool that lets students explore terrain, zoom into regions, and analyze geographic features
Asking students to type their answers instead of writing them by hand
Having students copy notes from a slideshow instead of from the board
questions.rationale: Technology enhances learning when it provides experiences not otherwise possible, such as interactive exploration and analysis, rather than digitally substituting for an existing task.

questions.stem: Ms. Zhao wants to integrate technology into a fifth-grade science unit on the water cycle. Which application best uses technology to deepen conceptual understanding?
options: Replacing the lab with a digital worksheet of fill-in-the-blank questions
Having students watch a 40-minute video while taking no notes
Projecting the lesson objectives on a screen at the start of class
Using an interactive simulation in which students manipulate variables such as temperature and observe effects on evaporation and condensation
questions.rationale: An interactive simulation lets students manipulate variables and observe results, supporting conceptual understanding through active exploration that would be difficult to replicate otherwise.

questions.stem: Mr. Abara has access to one classroom set of tablets for his diverse third-grade class, which includes students with varied reading levels. Which use of the tablets best supports differentiated instruction?
options: Allowing students to play unrelated games when their work is done
Using the tablets only as a reward for students who finish early
Assigning adaptive reading software that adjusts text difficulty and provides supports based on each student's level
Having all students complete the identical app activity at the same pace
questions.rationale: Adaptive software that adjusts difficulty and provides individualized supports leverages technology to meet diverse learning needs, a key benefit of instructional technology.

questions.stem: Ms. Becker plans to use a new educational app with her sixth-grade class. Which step should she take first to ensure the technology effectively supports her instructional goals?
options: Let students download any app they prefer for the assignment
Use the app only because the district purchased licenses for it
Introduce the app to students because it is popular and engaging
Evaluate whether the app aligns with the lesson objectives and the standards students must learn
questions.rationale: Technology should be selected to serve clear instructional purposes. Confirming alignment with objectives and standards ensures the tool enhances rather than distracts from learning.

questions.stem: Ms. Dunlap wants to integrate technology into an eighth-grade unit so that it transforms learning rather than merely substituting for traditional methods. Which project best represents a transformative use of technology?
options: Students type their essays in a word processor instead of writing them by hand
Students read the textbook on a tablet rather than in print
Students collaborate with a class in another country via video conferencing and a shared digital platform to co-author a research report comparing local environments
Students take the unit test online instead of on paper
questions.rationale: Transformative technology use creates learning experiences impossible without it, such as authentic global collaboration and co-creation, going well beyond substituting a digital tool for an analog one.

questions.stem: Mr. Goldberg wants his second-grade students to understand the criteria for a high-quality science journal entry before they begin. Which tool would best communicate clear expectations?
options: Letting students guess what a good entry looks like
Sharing a rubric or checklist that describes the criteria for a quality entry, ideally with a model example
Grading the entries strictly after they are submitted with no prior guidance
Telling students to 'just do their best' without further detail
questions.rationale: A rubric or checklist with a model makes success criteria transparent, helping students self-monitor and produce higher-quality work.

questions.stem: Ms. Jacobs is designing assessments for a unit and wants to ensure they are valid. Which consideration is most central to assessment validity?
options: The assessment is colorful and visually appealing
The assessment uses only multiple-choice questions
The assessment measures the knowledge and skills described in the learning objectives it is intended to assess
The assessment is the shortest possible length
questions.rationale: Validity concerns whether an assessment measures what it is intended to measure. Alignment between the assessment and the learning objectives is central to validity.

questions.stem: Mr. Kaur uses several formative checks throughout a tenth-grade math lesson. Beyond informing instruction, what is the most important way he should use the patterns he sees in the data over time?
options: To rank students from highest to lowest for display
To identify trends and adjust grouping, pacing, and intervention to meet students' evolving needs
To justify giving the whole class the same grade
To prove to administrators that he gives frequent quizzes
questions.rationale: Analyzing assessment data over time lets teachers identify trends and make responsive decisions about grouping, pacing, and intervention, the core purpose of ongoing assessment.

questions.stem: Ms. Lowery teaches a diverse eleventh-grade class that includes emergent bilingual students and students with learning disabilities. She wants to assess content mastery fairly and accurately for all learners. Which approach best supports valid and equitable assessment?
options: Lowering the content expectations for students who need accommodations
Giving every student the identical timed paper test to keep conditions uniform
Excluding struggling students' scores so class averages remain high
Providing appropriate accommodations and varied means for students to demonstrate mastery while keeping the assessed learning target constant
questions.rationale: Equitable, valid assessment provides accommodations and multiple means of demonstrating learning so results reflect content mastery rather than barriers, while holding the learning target constant for all.

questions.stem: Mr. Mensah notices that his feedback on essays, though detailed, does not seem to improve later student work. Which change is most likely to make his feedback lead to genuine improvement?
options: Giving feedback only on the final summative essay at the end of the unit
Replacing comments with only a numerical score for efficiency
Providing focused, actionable feedback and building in a structured opportunity for students to act on it through revision before the next graded task
Writing even longer comments on each essay
questions.rationale: Feedback drives improvement only when students have a structured chance to apply it. Pairing focused, actionable feedback with revision opportunities closes the feedback loop and produces growth.

questions.stem: During a conference, Mrs. Okafor expresses frustration that her son Daniel is 'always being singled out' and is failing math. She becomes visibly upset and raises her voice. What is the most professional and productive response from his teacher, Mr. Lin?
options: Defend his grading decisions firmly and explain that Daniel's grades are entirely the result of the student's own lack of effort
End the conference immediately and ask Mrs. Okafor to return when she can remain calm
Agree to raise Daniel's grade so that Mrs. Okafor will feel reassured and the conflict will be resolved
Calmly acknowledge her concern, listen actively to understand her perspective, and then collaboratively review Daniel's work and a plan to support him
questions.rationale: Maintaining professionalism with an upset parent means staying calm, listening actively to validate concerns, and shifting toward a collaborative, solution-focused discussion.

questions.stem: Ms. Patel wants to increase family involvement in her diverse seventh-grade classroom, but turnout at evening events has been low. Many parents work multiple jobs or evening shifts. Which approach best reflects an understanding of these families' circumstances?
options: Continue scheduling all events in the evening since that is the traditional time and families should make it a priority
Offer flexible involvement opportunities at varied times and through varied formats, including some that can be done from home or by phone
Assume that low turnout means these families are not interested in their children's education
Require parents to sign a contract committing to attend a minimum number of in-person events
questions.rationale: Effective teachers recognize the diverse circumstances of families and provide flexible, varied ways to be involved so all families can participate meaningfully.

questions.stem: A divorced parent, Mr. Reyes, who does not have primary physical custody, calls Ms. Bui requesting detailed information about his daughter's grades, attendance, and behavior. Court documents on file with the school grant joint legal custody but specify the mother as the custodial parent. What should Ms. Bui do?
options: Refuse to share any information because Mr. Reyes is not the custodial parent
Share the information freely, since both parents naturally have an equal right to all records
Verify the custody and records-access provisions with the front office or appropriate administrator before releasing information
Tell Mr. Reyes to obtain the information directly from his ex-wife to avoid getting involved
questions.rationale: Custody arrangements affect who may access student records. When details are unclear, the teacher should verify access rights through proper school channels rather than guessing.

questions.stem: Mr. Chambers wants to send home a weekly newsletter that genuinely strengthens the home-school connection. Which of the following content choices would most effectively support student learning at home?
options: A list of every student's current grade so parents can compare their child to classmates
A reminder that homework must be completed or students will lose recess
Photos of the highest-performing students of the week posted to motivate others
Specific descriptions of upcoming learning goals along with concrete, easy activities families can do at home to reinforce them
questions.rationale: Newsletters best support learning when they share upcoming goals and give families practical, accessible ways to extend learning at home.

questions.stem: Ms. Whitfield teaches in a community with several cultural and linguistic groups whose norms about education and authority differ from her own. A parent declines to question the teacher's decisions during a conference, deferring to her as the expert. The teacher wants the parent to be an active partner. What is the most culturally responsive interpretation and action?
options: Switch entirely to written communication because the parent is clearly uncomfortable speaking
Insist that the parent voice opinions immediately so the conference can be considered productive
Recognize that deference may reflect cultural respect for educators, and continue building trust while gently inviting input in ways that honor the family's communication style
Conclude that the parent is uninvolved and document a lack of cooperation in the student's file
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive teachers interpret family behaviors within cultural context and adapt their approach to invite participation in ways consistent with the family's values.

questions.stem: Before the school year begins, Mr. Sandoval plans a 'meet the teacher' communication to introduce himself to families. Which goal should most guide the content and tone of this first contact?
options: Explaining that he is very busy and prefers families contact him only in emergencies
Listing the consequences students will face for misbehavior so families know he is strict
Detailing his academic credentials to convince families he is qualified
Establishing a warm, welcoming, and positive first impression that signals partnership with families
questions.rationale: An initial contact with families should set a welcoming, positive tone that establishes the teacher as a partner and opens the door to ongoing communication.

questions.stem: Ms. Trang is a first-year teacher who feels uncertain about her classroom management. Which action best reflects a professional commitment to her own ongoing growth and development?
options: Avoid asking for help so colleagues will not think she is incompetent
Wait until her formal evaluation to learn what she needs to change
Seek out a mentor, observe experienced colleagues, and reflect on feedback to improve her practice
Assume management problems will resolve themselves once students get used to her
questions.rationale: Professional growth involves actively seeking support, learning from colleagues, and reflecting on feedback rather than waiting passively or hiding struggles.

questions.stem: Mr. Becker's school organizes teachers into professional learning communities (PLCs) that meet weekly to analyze student data and share instructional strategies. What is the primary benefit of this collaborative structure?
options: It allows administrators to monitor which teachers are underperforming
It enables teachers to learn from one another and collectively improve instruction and student outcomes
It reduces the amount of individual planning each teacher must do
It ensures all teachers deliver identical lessons in exactly the same way
questions.rationale: PLCs are collaborative structures whose central purpose is shared learning and continuous improvement of instruction to benefit students.

questions.stem: A veteran colleague, Mr. Hollis, frequently makes negative, sarcastic comments about students and their families in the teachers' lounge. Ms. Egan, a newer teacher, finds this troubling. Which response best reflects professional and ethical conduct?
options: Repeat the comments to other teachers to confirm whether they share the same views
Join in occasionally so she is accepted by the more experienced staff
Immediately report Mr. Hollis to the superintendent for disciplinary action
Decline to participate in the negative talk and maintain a respectful, professional attitude toward students and families
questions.rationale: Professional educators maintain respect for students and families and avoid participating in disparaging talk, modeling ethical conduct even when colleagues do not.

questions.stem: After receiving constructive feedback from her appraiser that her lessons need more differentiation, Ms. Nwosu wants to respond as a reflective professional. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Request a different appraiser who will give her a higher rating
Develop a concrete plan to incorporate differentiation strategies and seek resources or professional development to support that growth
Disregard the feedback because she believes her current methods work for most students
Add a single enrichment worksheet to one lesson so she can say she addressed the concern
questions.rationale: A reflective professional uses feedback to set growth goals and actively pursues development to improve practice for all students.

questions.stem: Mr. Okeke notices that a struggling colleague's students consistently lack foundational skills he expects them to have arrived with. He wants to address the issue in a way that strengthens the school as a whole. Which course of action best reflects collaborative professionalism?
options: Raise the concern privately and constructively, and propose using PLC or vertical-team meetings to align expectations and supports across grade levels
Complain to parents that the previous teacher failed to prepare the students
Lower his own expectations and standards to match what the students can currently do
Report the colleague to the principal as incompetent without speaking to the colleague
questions.rationale: Collaborative professionalism addresses systemic concerns through constructive dialogue and shared structures like vertical teaming, improving outcomes without blaming individuals.

questions.stem: While grading papers, Ms. Ferris notices that a quiet eight-year-old student has unexplained bruises and makes a comment suggesting he was hurt at home. Under Texas law, what must Ms. Ferris do?
options: Ask the student's parents directly whether they are abusing him
Report her suspicion of possible child abuse to the appropriate authorities within the legally required timeframe
Wait and observe the student for several weeks to gather more evidence before acting
Discuss the situation with other teachers to decide together whether it is serious enough to report
questions.rationale: Texas educators are mandatory reporters and must personally report suspected child abuse or neglect to the proper authorities within the legally required time, without needing proof.

questions.stem: Mr. Salazar wants to comply with the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) when handling student records. Which practice is consistent with FERPA?
options: Discussing a student's confidential academic records only with school officials who have a legitimate educational interest
Sharing a student's detailed academic struggles with another parent who asks about it
Posting students' grades on the classroom wall using their full names
Leaving graded tests in a stack for students to sort through and find their own using names
questions.rationale: FERPA protects the privacy of student education records and limits disclosure to those with a legitimate educational interest or with proper consent.

questions.stem: A parent emails Ms. Howard asking her to share a classmate's behavior records to prove that her own child was provoked in a conflict. The classmate's parents have not given consent. According to FERPA and professional ethics, how should Ms. Howard respond?
options: Decline to release the other student's protected records and address the parent's concern by discussing only her own child's situation
Share the records verbally rather than in writing, since FERPA only applies to written documents
Provide a summary of the other student's discipline history since it directly affects her child
Forward the email to the other student's parents so they can decide what to share
questions.rationale: FERPA prohibits disclosing one student's education records to another student's parent without consent; the teacher should help the requesting parent regarding her own child only.

questions.stem: The Texas Educators' Code of Ethics addresses educator conduct toward students. A teacher, Mr. Vance, has begun exchanging frequent personal text messages and private social media messages with a sixteen-year-old student about non-school matters. According to the Code of Ethics, this conduct is best described as:
options: Inappropriate, because it crosses professional boundaries and may constitute an improper relationship with a student
Acceptable, because the student is old enough to make her own decisions about communication
Acceptable, as long as the messages do not contain anything explicitly illegal
A private matter outside the scope of the Educators' Code of Ethics
questions.rationale: The Texas Educators' Code of Ethics requires educators to maintain appropriate professional boundaries; private, personal electronic communication with a student about non-school matters violates those boundaries.

questions.stem: Mr. Cho suspects that a student in his class, Lila, may have a learning disability that is affecting her reading. He wants to act in accordance with special education law and procedures. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Wait until Lila fails the year before involving anyone else
Document his observations and concerns, implement targeted interventions, and follow the district's referral process to request an evaluation
Independently diagnose Lila with a reading disability and create his own modified program
Tell Lila's parents she belongs in special education and should be removed from his class
questions.rationale: When a teacher suspects a disability, the proper course is to document concerns, provide interventions, and follow the district's referral and evaluation process under IDEA and Child Find.

questions.stem: Ms. Beaumont is using a classroom set of district-issued tablets. She is asked by a friend to install some paid educational software for personal home use using the school's licensed account. According to the Texas Educators' Code of Ethics, what should she do?
options: Install it, since it is educational software and therefore serves a good purpose
Decline, because using school-funded property, funds, or licenses for personal or unauthorized use is an ethics violation
Install it but reimburse the district later if anyone notices
Ask a student to install it so she is not personally responsible
questions.rationale: The Code of Ethics prohibits the misappropriation or unauthorized personal use of school property, funds, and resources, including licensed software.

questions.stem: During an Admission, Review, and Dismissal (ARD) committee meeting for a student with autism, the parents disagree with the team's proposed placement and decline to consent. The other team members feel the placement is appropriate. What is the most legally and ethically sound response by the committee?
options: Continue working toward consensus, document the disagreement, and inform parents of their procedural rights, including dispute-resolution options
Tell the parents that, by law, the school always has the final decision over placement
Remove the student from special education services until the parents agree to the placement
Implement the proposed placement immediately, since the majority of the committee agrees it is best
questions.rationale: Under IDEA, parents are essential ARD/IEP team members; when disagreement arises, the team should seek consensus, document it, and ensure parents are informed of their procedural safeguards and dispute-resolution options.

questions.stem: Mr. Tanaka discovers that a colleague has been quietly changing several students' answers on the state standardized test answer documents to boost the class's scores. The colleague asks Mr. Tanaka to keep it confidential 'to protect the team.' Under the Texas Educators' Code of Ethics, what is Mr. Tanaka's obligation?
options: Report the test-security violation through the appropriate channels, as the Code requires honesty and prohibits aiding in unethical conduct
Privately warn the colleague to stop but take no further action
Change a few of his own students' answers as well so suspicion is spread evenly
Keep the information confidential to preserve collegial loyalty and team morale
questions.rationale: The Code of Ethics requires honesty and integrity and prohibits falsifying or aiding in falsifying records and assessments; serious testing violations must be reported through proper channels.

questions.stem: Ms. Pruitt posts a photo on her public social media account from a weekend outing that includes a caption mocking 'the lazy parents' at her school and naming her campus. A parent sees it and complains. Which statement best reflects the professional and ethical considerations involved?
options: Only the content posted during school hours is subject to professional standards
Because it was posted on personal time and a personal account, it is entirely protected and raises no professional concern
Educators are expected to maintain professional conduct that does not disparage students, families, or the school, and such a post can violate professional standards even when made off duty
The post is acceptable as long as Ms. Pruitt deletes it before her next evaluation
questions.rationale: Educators are held to professional standards that extend to public conduct, including social media; publicly disparaging families and the school can violate professional and ethical expectations even off duty.

questions.stem: Ms. Alvarado teaches kindergarten and notices that her students learn the names of shapes best when they handle wooden blocks, trace shapes in sand, and sort objects by form. According to Jean Piaget's theory of cognitive development, this preference reflects which stage that most of her students are in?
options: Sensorimotor stage, in which object permanence is first developing
Formal operational stage, in which abstract reasoning dominates
Preoperational stage, in which children learn through concrete, hands-on experiences and symbols
Concrete operational stage, in which students master conservation and logical operations
questions.rationale: Children roughly ages 2-7 are in Piaget's preoperational stage, characterized by symbolic thinking and reliance on concrete, sensory, hands-on experiences rather than abstract reasoning.

questions.stem: Mr. Chen, a 4th-grade teacher, provides a math lesson where students work just slightly above their independent skill level with his guided support and prompts, gradually removing help as they gain confidence. This practice most directly applies Vygotsky's concept of the:
options: Multiple intelligences inventory
Zone of proximal development supported through scaffolding
Fixed intelligence quotient
Behaviorist reinforcement schedule
questions.rationale: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development describes the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with guidance; scaffolding is the temporary support that helps the learner bridge that gap.

questions.stem: During a high school biology unit, Ms. Okafor wants students to retain key vocabulary long-term. She spaces review of terms across several class periods and asks students to retrieve definitions from memory before re-teaching. Which principle of cognitive learning best explains why this approach improves retention?
options: Distributed practice and retrieval practice strengthen memory more than massed cramming
Egocentrism limits a learner's perspective-taking
Negative reinforcement removes an unpleasant stimulus to increase behavior
Operant extinction reduces an unwanted response over time
questions.rationale: Spacing review over time (distributed practice) and requiring active recall (retrieval practice) are well-supported cognitive strategies that produce stronger, more durable learning than massed review.

questions.stem: Ms. Rivera observes that her middle school students are highly concerned with peer acceptance, beginning to question authority, and forming a clearer sense of personal identity. According to Erik Erikson, these adolescents are primarily working through which psychosocial stage?
options: Initiative vs. guilt
Identity vs. role confusion
Integrity vs. despair
Trust vs. mistrust
questions.rationale: Erikson's adolescent stage, identity vs. role confusion, centers on developing a coherent sense of self, which often involves peer influence and questioning authority.

questions.stem: Mr. Solis teaches a 6th-grade science class and wants new content about ecosystems to connect to what students already know about their local park. He has students complete a chart linking new terms to prior experiences before reading the textbook. From a constructivist perspective, the primary instructional value of this activity is that it:
options: Ensures students memorize definitions through repetition
Provides extrinsic rewards that condition correct responses
Eliminates the need for differentiated instruction
Activates prior knowledge so learners can build new understanding onto existing schemas
questions.rationale: Constructivist theory holds that learners build new knowledge by connecting it to existing mental structures (schemas); activating prior knowledge supports meaningful integration of new content.

questions.stem: In a 1st-grade classroom, Ms. Tran notices that students can copy letters but struggle to hold a pencil with a mature grip and tire quickly when writing. Recognizing the role of physical development, the most appropriate instructional response is to:
options: Provide developmentally appropriate fine-motor activities and short, frequent writing practice
Conclude the students have a learning disability and refer them for evaluation
Require longer handwriting drills until students' hands strengthen
Move all writing instruction online to avoid handwriting entirely
questions.rationale: Young children's fine-motor skills are still developing; supporting them with appropriate fine-motor activities and brief, frequent practice matches their physical development rather than forcing prolonged drills.

questions.stem: Ms. Bell wants her 5th graders to move beyond simply recalling facts about the water cycle to analyzing how human activity disrupts it. To plan questions that target higher-order thinking on Bloom's revised taxonomy, she should design prompts that ask students to:
options: Match vocabulary terms to their pictures
List and define the stages of the water cycle in order
Recall the definition of evaporation from the textbook
Analyze and evaluate the effects of pollution on the water cycle and propose solutions
questions.rationale: Bloom's revised taxonomy places analyze, evaluate, and create at the higher levels; prompts asking students to analyze effects, evaluate impact, and propose solutions target higher-order thinking.

questions.stem: A high school English teacher, Mr. Nguyen, notices that intrinsically motivated students read more independently than those who read only for grades. To strengthen intrinsic motivation, which strategy is most aligned with self-determination theory?
options: Promising a pizza party only to the top reader
Posting a public ranking of students by pages read
Offering students meaningful choice in reading topics and opportunities to develop competence
Giving frequent pop quizzes with deductions for low scores
questions.rationale: Self-determination theory holds that intrinsic motivation grows when learners experience autonomy, competence, and relatedness; offering meaningful choice and chances to build competence supports these needs.

questions.stem: Ms. Flores plans a 3rd-grade lesson and wants to ensure students can focus and process new information without overwhelming their working memory. Which strategy best reduces cognitive load?
options: Requiring students to multitask between two new skills simultaneously
Breaking complex information into smaller, sequenced chunks with clear examples
Removing all visuals so students rely only on text
Presenting many new concepts at once to maximize coverage
questions.rationale: Working memory is limited; chunking complex content into smaller, sequenced parts with clear examples reduces cognitive load and supports processing.

questions.stem: Ms. Park has a 4th-grade class that includes English learners, gifted students, and a student with dyslexia. To meet this range of needs in a single lesson, the most appropriate first step is to:
options: Teach one lesson identically to all students to ensure fairness
Assign the gifted students to tutor everyone else during the lesson
Differentiate content, process, and product based on students' readiness, interests, and learning profiles
Group all struggling students separately and give them worksheets
questions.rationale: Differentiated instruction adapts content, process, and product according to students' readiness, interests, and learning profiles to meet diverse needs equitably.

questions.stem: Mr. Abara teaches social studies and has several recently arrived English learners at the beginning stage of English proficiency. To make a lesson on the U.S. branches of government comprehensible, the most effective strategy aligned with the ELPS is to:
options: Use visuals, graphic organizers, sentence stems, and native-language support to build comprehension
Provide grade-level text only and expect them to use a dictionary independently
Speak more loudly and slowly but keep the text and tasks unchanged
Exempt the English learners from the content until they are fluent
questions.rationale: The English Language Proficiency Standards call for linguistic accommodations such as visuals, graphic organizers, sentence stems, and primary-language support to make grade-level content comprehensible for English learners.
