questions.stem: Ms. Ito teaches a 9th-grade geometry class with a wide range of readiness levels. She offers a tiered assignment in which all students work toward the same standard but complete tasks at different levels of complexity. The primary purpose of tiering is to:
options: Reduce the standard for lower-readiness students
Provide appropriately challenging work for all students while addressing the same essential learning goal
Sort students permanently into ability tracks
Give faster students extra busywork while others finish
questions.rationale: Tiered assignments keep the essential learning goal constant while varying complexity, so each student is appropriately challenged on the same standard.

questions.stem: A 7th-grade teacher, Ms. Delgado, has a student with an IEP that specifies extended time and reduced-item assessments. Another student has a 504 plan for ADHD requiring preferential seating and chunked directions. The most accurate understanding of these documents is that:
options: Both are optional suggestions the teacher may choose to follow
The IEP accommodations are legally required, while the 504 plan is merely a courtesy
Both are legally mandated plans the teacher must implement to provide appropriate access
The teacher should apply the same accommodations to the whole class for fairness
questions.rationale: Both IEPs (under IDEA) and 504 plans (under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act) are legally binding documents that teachers must implement to ensure students receive appropriate access to learning.

questions.stem: Ms. Coleman wants to design lessons accessible to the widest range of learners from the start, rather than retrofitting accommodations later. She provides content in multiple formats (text, audio, video), offers several ways to demonstrate learning, and includes options that engage student interest. This approach is best described as:
options: Ability grouping
Behavior modification
Standardized testing
Universal Design for Learning (UDL)
questions.rationale: Universal Design for Learning provides multiple means of representation, action and expression, and engagement so instruction is accessible to all learners by design.

questions.stem: A gifted 8th grader, Priya, finishes assignments quickly and shows boredom. Her teacher, Mr. Lowe, wants to extend her learning meaningfully rather than just assign more problems. The most appropriate differentiation for a gifted learner is to:
options: Give her additional repetitive practice of mastered skills
Provide acceleration and enrichment through complex, open-ended tasks that deepen and extend learning
Make her grade other students' papers
Have her wait quietly until classmates finish
questions.rationale: Gifted learners benefit from acceleration and enrichment with complex, open-ended, intellectually challenging tasks that deepen understanding rather than from more repetition of mastered content.

questions.stem: Mr. Yates uses flexible grouping in his 6th-grade reading class, changing group composition based on the task and ongoing assessment data. Compared with fixed ability grouping, the chief advantage of flexible grouping is that it:
options: Guarantees every group produces identical results
Permanently labels students by their reading level
Allows groupings to shift with students' evolving needs and avoids fixed expectations
Eliminates the need to assess students
questions.rationale: Flexible grouping regroups students according to changing needs and assessment data, preventing the fixed labels and lowered expectations associated with static ability grouping.

questions.stem: A high school chemistry teacher, Ms. Banks, has a student who is deaf and uses an interpreter, along with several English learners. When planning a lab, the most inclusive approach to ensure all students access the content is to:
options: Rely solely on spoken lecture because the interpreter will handle everything
Combine clear visuals, written procedures, captioned media, and structured collaboration so multiple access points support all learners
Pair the deaf student only with the interpreter and exclude group work
Simplify the lab so much that the essential chemistry concepts are lost
questions.rationale: Providing multiple, redundant access points such as visuals, written procedures, captioned media, and structured collaboration ensures both a deaf student and English learners can access rigorous content without lowering the learning goal.

questions.stem: Ms. Quinn is planning a 3rd-grade unit. Before selecting activities, she identifies what students should know and be able to do by the end of the unit and how she will measure it, then designs lessons to reach those outcomes. This planning sequence reflects:
options: Random activity selection
Choosing activities students enjoy regardless of objectives
Backward design, starting with the end goals and assessments
Teaching to whatever is in the textbook chapter order
questions.rationale: Backward design begins with desired results and assessment evidence, then plans instruction to achieve those outcomes, ensuring alignment to standards.

questions.stem: Mr. Vance is designing a problem-based learning unit for 10th-grade environmental science in which students investigate a real local water-quality issue and propose solutions to the city. The greatest instructional strength of this approach is that it:
options: Guarantees that all students will reach identical conclusions
Minimizes the need for students to apply content knowledge
Removes the need to align tasks to the TEKS
Engages students in authentic, real-world application that develops critical thinking and transfer
questions.rationale: Problem-based learning engages students in authentic, real-world problems that require applying content, promoting critical thinking and the transfer of learning to new contexts.

questions.stem: Ms. Hahn plans a unit so that early lessons build foundational vocabulary and skills that later lessons require, sequencing content from simpler to more complex and connecting each lesson to the next. The primary instructional reason for this deliberate sequencing is to:
options: Make the unit longer to fill the calendar
Ensure students never revisit earlier concepts
Allow the teacher to skip formative assessment
Build a logical progression in which prerequisite knowledge scaffolds more advanced learning
questions.rationale: Logical sequencing from simple to complex ensures students acquire prerequisite knowledge and skills that scaffold subsequent, more advanced learning, supporting coherent understanding.

questions.stem: Ms. Bowen reviews a TEKS standard that requires 8th graders to 'analyze how an author develops the points of view of characters.' When designing instruction, she must ensure her lesson activities and assessment match the cognitive demand of the verb 'analyze.' The most aligned activity is to have students:
options: Copy the definition of point of view from a glossary
Recite a list of characters from the text
Examine textual evidence to explain how the author shapes contrasting character viewpoints
Color a picture of a favorite character
questions.rationale: Aligning to the standard means matching the cognitive demand of analyze; examining textual evidence to explain how the author develops contrasting viewpoints requires analysis rather than recall.

questions.stem: Ms. Long opens her 4th-grade math lesson by stating, 'By the end of today, you will be able to solve two-step word problems involving addition and subtraction, and I'll know you've got it when you can explain your steps.' Sharing the objective and success criteria at the start of a lesson primarily helps students by:
options: Clarifying the learning target and what success looks like so they can focus and self-monitor
Guaranteeing a perfect score for everyone
Replacing the need for any instruction
Keeping the lesson purpose hidden until the end
questions.rationale: Communicating clear objectives and success criteria orients students to the learning target and helps them monitor their own progress toward it.

questions.stem: Mr. Okafor wants to design a lesson that targets the highest level of Bloom's revised taxonomy. Which student task best reflects this goal?
options: Summarizing a chapter in their own words
Identifying the main characters in a story
Designing an original proposal for a new community park
Listing the causes of the American Revolution
questions.rationale: Creating something original—such as designing a proposal—represents the 'Create' level, the highest tier of Bloom's revised taxonomy.

questions.stem: During a 4th-grade math lesson, Ms. Tran notices that Diego can solve two-digit multiplication problems with her step-by-step prompts but cannot yet do so independently. Vygotsky would describe the gap between what Diego can do alone and what he can do with guidance as his:
options: Zone of proximal development
Fixed mindset
Schema
Equilibration
questions.rationale: The zone of proximal development (ZPD) is the range of tasks a learner cannot do alone but can accomplish with guidance from a more knowledgeable other.

questions.stem: Mr. Bellamy provides a partially completed graphic organizer, models the first paragraph aloud, and then gradually withdraws support as 7th-grade students draft their essays. This instructional approach is best described as:
options: Tracking
Norm-referenced grading
Scaffolding
Summative evaluation
questions.rationale: Providing temporary supports that are gradually removed as students gain competence is the defining feature of scaffolding, rooted in Vygotsky's theory.

questions.stem: In a 3rd-grade classroom, Mr. Lindqvist assigns reading passages at three different complexity levels on the same topic so all students engage with the same essential question. This is an example of differentiating by:
options: Assessment timing
Content
Grading scale
Classroom seating
questions.rationale: Adjusting the materials or information students access—such as varied-complexity passages on one topic—differentiates the content of instruction.

questions.stem: Mr. Adeyemi is planning a unit and writes the objective: 'Students will analyze how an author's word choice shapes tone in a persuasive editorial.' To design instruction that is genuinely aligned to this objective, his summative assessment should require students to:
options: Define the term 'tone' from a word bank
Examine an editorial and explain how specific words create its tone
Memorize a list of persuasive techniques for a matching quiz
Copy three persuasive editorials by hand
questions.rationale: Aligned assessment must match the cognitive demand of the objective; an 'analyze' objective requires students to examine text and explain how word choice produces tone.

questions.stem: Ms. Rourke notices that her 2nd graders learn new vocabulary best when she connects each word to a concept they already understand. This practice aligns most directly with which learning principle?
options: Teaching in strict isolation from context
Eliminating all student errors before practice
Operant conditioning through punishment
Building on prior knowledge to support new learning
questions.rationale: Connecting new information to existing knowledge helps learners construct meaning, a core constructivist principle and key to effective instruction.

questions.stem: Mr. Delgado plans to use a single end-of-semester exam to assign final grades and report mastery to parents. This assessment is primarily:
options: Formative, because it guides instruction
Diagnostic, because it precedes instruction
Summative, because it evaluates cumulative learning
Authentic, because it occurs in a real-world setting
questions.rationale: An exam that evaluates cumulative achievement at the end of instruction to assign grades is summative.

questions.stem: Ms. Whitfield gives 8th graders a rubric before they begin a research project and has them use it to evaluate a sample paper, then to assess their own drafts midway. Her primary instructional purpose for this sequence is to:
options: Ensure all students earn the same score
Make assessment criteria transparent so students can self-monitor and improve
Reduce the time she spends grading final papers
Replace teacher feedback entirely with peer grades
questions.rationale: Sharing rubrics and using them for self-assessment makes success criteria transparent, enabling students to monitor and improve their own work—an effective formative practice.

questions.stem: A teacher learns that one of her students has an Individualized Education Program (IEP) requiring extended time on tests. The teacher should view this accommodation primarily as a way to:
options: Lower the academic standards for that student
Provide equitable access so the student can demonstrate true learning
Give the student an unfair advantage
Avoid assessing the student altogether
questions.rationale: Accommodations remove barriers so students with disabilities can access content and demonstrate their actual knowledge without changing what is being measured.

questions.stem: Ms. Nguyen designs a 5th-grade science unit by first identifying the desired TEKS-based learning outcomes, then determining acceptable evidence of mastery, and finally planning daily activities. This planning model is best described as:
options: Spiral review
Inquiry by accident
Backward design
Direct instruction
questions.rationale: Beginning with outcomes, then evidence, then activities is the backward design model, which ensures activities and assessments serve clear learning goals.

questions.stem: Mr. Salazar praises specific effort and strategy use—'You kept trying different approaches until the proof worked'—rather than praising intelligence. According to Carol Dweck's research, this feedback is most likely to foster students':
options: Growth mindset
Egocentrism
Fixed mindset
Learned helplessness
questions.rationale: Praising effort and strategy, rather than fixed traits, cultivates a growth mindset—the belief that ability can develop through effort.

questions.stem: Ms. Beaumont wants real-time evidence of whether her 9th graders understood today's lesson on linear equations before they leave class. Which strategy best serves this purpose?
options: A cumulative final exam at semester's end
An exit ticket asking students to solve one problem and explain a step
A graded research paper due next month
A standardized state assessment in the spring
questions.rationale: An exit ticket gives immediate, low-stakes evidence of daily understanding, allowing the teacher to adjust the next lesson.

questions.stem: Mr. Iverson has a 7th-grade student who consistently finishes assignments early, asks probing questions, and seems disengaged during routine practice. The most appropriate differentiation strategy is to:
options: Assign the student additional copies of the same worksheets
Provide curriculum compacting and an extension task requiring deeper analysis
Move the student to a lower grade level
Have the student tutor peers during every class period
questions.rationale: Advanced learners benefit from compacting (skipping already-mastered material) and enrichment that extends learning to higher cognitive demands.

questions.stem: A well-written learning objective should specify the observable behavior students will demonstrate, the conditions, and the criteria for success. Which objective is best stated for instructional alignment?
options: Students will be exposed to poetry
Given a number line, students will correctly place 4 of 5 given fractions
Students will understand fractions
Students will learn about the water cycle
questions.rationale: A measurable objective names an observable action (place fractions), conditions (given a number line), and criteria (4 of 5), enabling clear assessment alignment.

questions.stem: Ms. Eklund plans a unit and intentionally offers students choices in how they demonstrate mastery—through a written report, an oral presentation, or a visual model. This reflects differentiation of:
options: Product
Seating chart
Attendance policy
Standards
questions.rationale: Allowing varied ways for students to show what they have learned differentiates the product of instruction while keeping the learning goal constant.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a star to students each time they complete homework on time, and over weeks homework completion increases. This use of reinforcement to increase a desired behavior is rooted in which theory?
options: Piaget's stage theory
Skinner's operant conditioning
Gardner's multiple intelligences
Vygotsky's sociocultural theory
questions.rationale: Increasing a behavior by following it with a rewarding consequence (positive reinforcement) is the core mechanism of Skinner's operant conditioning.

questions.stem: Mr. Haddad teaches a lesson in which students conduct an experiment, gather their own data, and form conclusions with minimal direct instruction. This student-centered, discovery-based approach is best categorized as:
options: Lecture-only instruction
Rote memorization
Standardized drilling
Inquiry-based learning
questions.rationale: Having students investigate, gather data, and construct conclusions is inquiry-based learning, a constructivist instructional model.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the clearest example of an authentic (performance-based) assessment?
options: A timed matching exercise of dates and events
Having students write and deliver a persuasive speech to a real audience
A true/false quiz on vocabulary definitions
A 50-item multiple-choice test on grammar rules
questions.rationale: Authentic assessment asks students to apply skills in realistic, meaningful tasks; writing and delivering a real speech demonstrates this application.

questions.stem: Mr. Donovan wants his lesson activities, his learning objective, and his assessment to all measure the same intended outcome. When these three components match one another, the lesson is said to have strong:
options: Bell-curve grading
Extrinsic motivation
Classroom proximity
Instructional alignment
questions.rationale: When objectives, instruction, and assessment all target the same learning outcome, the lesson demonstrates instructional alignment, which maximizes the validity of conclusions about learning.

questions.stem: Ms. Castro encourages her students to plan their approach to a problem, monitor their progress while solving it, and reflect on what worked afterward. She is fostering students':
options: Stranger anxiety
Reflexive responses
Metacognitive skills
Object permanence
questions.rationale: Planning, monitoring, and reflecting on one's own thinking are metacognitive processes that improve self-regulated learning.

questions.stem: A 3rd-grade student insists that because rain falls when she is sad, her sadness causes the rain. Piaget would attribute this reasoning to which characteristic of preoperational thought, and what should the teacher do?
options: Conservation; introduce abstract algebra
Formal operational logic; assign hypothetical debates
Transductive (cause-effect) reasoning; provide concrete experiences linking real causes and effects
Object permanence; play peekaboo games
questions.rationale: Reasoning from one specific event to another without true logical causation is transductive reasoning, typical of the preoperational stage; concrete, hands-on experiences help build accurate cause-effect understanding.

questions.stem: At the start of the school year, Ms. Alvarez, a 2nd-grade teacher, displays photographs of each student's family and invites students to share an item that represents their home culture. This practice most directly contributes to a positive classroom climate by:
options: Eliminating the need for classroom rules and procedures
Communicating that each student is valued and that diversity is an asset in the classroom
Reducing the amount of instructional planning the teacher must complete
Ensuring every student scores higher on standardized assessments
questions.rationale: Affirming students' identities and cultures signals that each learner is respected and that diversity enriches the community, which is central to an equitable, positive climate.

questions.stem: Mr. Boateng wants to establish high expectations for all students in his 9th-grade biology class. Which statement best reflects a belief that supports excellence for every learner?
options: "Students who struggle should be moved to an easier course as quickly as possible."
"I lower the difficulty of assignments so that no student ever feels frustrated."
"All of my students can master rigorous content when I provide appropriate support and scaffolding."
"Some students simply aren't cut out for science, so I focus my energy on the strongest ones."
questions.rationale: High expectations paired with appropriate support reflect the belief that all students are capable of rigorous learning, a foundation of an excellent, equitable classroom.

questions.stem: Ms. Cho, a 4th-grade teacher, posts a daily schedule and reviews it each morning. The primary management benefit of this routine is that it:
options: Guarantees students will earn higher grades on homework
Allows the teacher to skip teaching procedures for new activities
Provides predictability that helps students feel secure and transition smoothly
Replaces the need for the teacher to give directions during lessons
questions.rationale: A visible, reviewed schedule creates predictability, reducing anxiety and helping students manage transitions efficiently.

questions.stem: During the first week of school, a middle-school teacher explicitly teaches, models, and has students practice the procedure for turning in lab materials. This approach is most consistent with which classroom-management principle?
options: Procedures are unnecessary if rules are posted on the wall
Procedures should be enforced only after misbehavior occurs
Students learn procedures best by being corrected repeatedly
Clear procedures are most effective when taught and rehearsed proactively
questions.rationale: Effective managers teach and rehearse procedures before they are needed so routines run smoothly and minimize disruption.

questions.stem: Mr. Ferreira notices that several minutes are lost each period while students settle in. Which strategy would most efficiently maximize instructional time at the start of class?
options: Begin the lesson and re-teach later for students who were not ready
Wait silently at his desk until every student is quiet
Send late or unprepared students to the office
Post a brief warm-up task that students begin immediately upon entering
questions.rationale: A bell-ringer/warm-up routine engages students productively from the moment they enter, reclaiming transition time.

questions.stem: Ms. Delgado arranges desks in clusters and teaches students collaborative norms so they can support one another. This arrangement most directly fosters a classroom climate characterized by:
options: Strict individual competition among students
A sense of community and mutual responsibility for learning
Elimination of all whole-group instruction
Reduced teacher accountability for student outcomes
questions.rationale: Collaborative seating with taught norms builds community and shared responsibility, supporting a positive, cooperative climate.

questions.stem: Mr. Nguyen, a high-school teacher, finds that during independent work several students frequently go off task. Applying the concept of "withitness" and proximity, which action is most appropriate?
options: Assign extra homework to the whole class as a deterrent
Continue working at his desk and address problems only when they escalate
Stop the entire class and lecture everyone about staying on task
Circulate continuously through the room, scanning and quietly redirecting students near where issues arise
questions.rationale: Withitness and proximity control involve monitoring the whole room and intervening early and unobtrusively, preventing minor issues from escalating.

questions.stem: A 3rd-grade student, Priya, calls out answers without raising her hand, disrupting discussion. The teacher wants a response that corrects the behavior while preserving Priya's dignity and the lesson's momentum. The best first step is to:
options: Move Priya's desk to the hallway for the remainder of the lesson
Calmly and privately remind Priya of the hand-raising procedure and acknowledge her when she follows it
Ignore all of Priya's contributions for the rest of the day
Publicly reprimand Priya so other students learn the rule
questions.rationale: A low-key, private reminder that reinforces the expected procedure corrects behavior, preserves dignity, and maintains momentum, escalating only if needed.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that her questioning unintentionally calls on boys more often than girls during math discussions. To promote equity, the most appropriate action is to:
options: Assume the imbalance reflects genuine differences in ability
Call only on girls for the rest of the unit to compensate
Stop asking questions during math to avoid the imbalance
Use a systematic strategy, such as equity sticks or tracking, to distribute participation opportunities fairly
questions.rationale: Systematically distributing questions (e.g., randomized name draws or tracking) ensures equitable participation and high expectations for all students.

questions.stem: During a group project, two 8th-grade students begin arguing loudly. Applying a problem-solving, restorative approach to the conflict, the teacher should first:
options: Assign both students detention to end the disruption immediately
Calmly separate them, then guide each to express their perspective and work toward a mutually acceptable solution
Tell the class that group work will be canceled for everyone
Determine which student is at fault and discipline only that student
questions.rationale: A restorative, problem-solving response de-escalates, lets students be heard, and guides them to resolve the conflict, building social skills and a positive climate.

questions.stem: Mr. Okafor wants transitions between activities in his 5th-grade class to be smoother. Which combination of practices is most likely to minimize lost time during transitions?
options: Lengthening transitions so students have plenty of time to socialize
Giving spontaneous, varied directions so students stay flexible
Establishing consistent transition cues, giving advance warning, and having materials prepared in advance
Allowing students to decide when each transition begins
questions.rationale: Predictable cues, advance warnings, and pre-organized materials reduce confusion and wasted time during transitions.

questions.stem: A teacher observes that a normally cooperative high-school student, Marcus, has become withdrawn and occasionally disruptive over two weeks. Before applying consequences, the most appropriate professional response is to:
options: Publicly ask Marcus what is wrong during class
Apply the standard consequence ladder immediately for the disruptions
Privately check in with Marcus to understand possible underlying causes and offer support
Lower Marcus's participation grade to motivate better behavior
questions.rationale: A sudden behavior change may signal an underlying need; a private, supportive conversation seeks the cause before responding, reflecting care for the whole student.

questions.stem: Ms. Patel wants to keep students actively engaged during a whole-group review. Which technique best maximizes the number of students cognitively engaged at any moment?
options: Asking the class a question and accepting the first call-out
Using whole-class response methods such as individual whiteboards or response signals
Reviewing answers herself while students listen
Calling on volunteers who raise their hands
questions.rationale: Whole-class response systems require every student to think and respond simultaneously, increasing engagement and giving the teacher quick formative data.

questions.stem: A new student who is an emergent bilingual (English learner) joins a 4th-grade class mid-year. To create a welcoming, equitable climate, the teacher should:
options: Avoid calling on the student to prevent embarrassment
Reduce the rigor of all the student's assignments indefinitely
Assign a peer buddy, use visuals, and affirm the student's home language as an asset
Seat the student alone until their English improves
questions.rationale: Welcoming structures (peer support, visuals) and valuing the home language build belonging and maintain high expectations for the emergent bilingual student.

questions.stem: A teacher consistently catches students behaving well and names the specific behavior, e.g., "I appreciate how Group 3 cleaned up materials quickly and quietly." The primary management value of this practice is that it:
options: Reinforces desired behaviors and clarifies expectations for the whole class
Embarrasses other groups into compliance
Eliminates the need for any corrective feedback
Encourages students to compete for the teacher's praise
questions.rationale: Specific positive feedback reinforces the targeted behavior and models the expectation for everyone, strengthening a positive, well-managed environment.

questions.stem: During independent reading, a 6th-grade teacher notices that a small cluster of students near the window is repeatedly distracted by activity outside. Which proactive adjustment to the physical environment is most appropriate?
options: Assign the distracted students extra reading as a consequence
Remove independent reading from the schedule altogether
Allow those students to read in the hallway unsupervised
Rearrange seating or use a window covering to reduce the visual distraction
questions.rationale: Modifying the physical environment to limit distractions is a proactive management strategy that supports focus without punishing students.

questions.stem: Ms. Greene wants her behavior-management system to be effective and fair. Which feature is most essential for the system to support a positive climate?
options: Consistency and fairness in applying expectations and logical consequences to all students
Severe penalties reserved for repeat offenders only
Frequent public displays of who has lost privileges
Consequences that vary unpredictably so students stay cautious
questions.rationale: Consistent, fair application of expectations and logical consequences builds trust and predictability, essential to a positive climate.

questions.stem: A high-school teacher wants students to feel safe taking intellectual risks during discussions. Which classroom norm most directly supports this goal?
options: Discussion should be limited to the highest-achieving students
Only students who are certain of the correct answer should speak
Students who give wrong answers should be corrected sharply to prevent repetition
Mistakes are treated as valuable opportunities to learn, and all respectful ideas are welcomed
questions.rationale: Normalizing mistakes as learning opportunities and welcoming respectful contributions creates psychological safety, encouraging risk-taking and deeper engagement.

questions.stem: Mr. Halverson has implemented clear procedures, yet one student, Tyler, continues low-level disruptions that escalate when publicly corrected. Data show the disruptions cluster during long independent tasks. The most effective next step is to:
options: Move Tyler permanently to in-school suspension
Analyze the pattern, hypothesize the behavior's function, and adjust task design and private supports accordingly
Ignore the behavior entirely since procedures are already in place
Increase the severity of public consequences until the behavior stops
questions.rationale: When standard procedures are not working, examining the behavior's function and triggers (here, long independent tasks) and adjusting the environment and supports is the evidence-based, proactive response.

questions.stem: A 10th-grade teacher uses a token-reward system that initially boosted participation, but engagement has now dropped and students ask, "What do we get for this?" before any task. The best interpretation and response is that:
options: Over-reliance on extrinsic rewards may be undermining intrinsic motivation; the teacher should gradually shift toward relevance, autonomy, and mastery
The teacher should add public leaderboards to renew competition
The rewards were too small and should be made larger immediately
Students are simply unmotivated and the system should be abandoned with no replacement
questions.rationale: Extrinsic rewards can crowd out intrinsic motivation over time; shifting toward meaningful tasks, choice, and a focus on mastery rebuilds genuine engagement.

questions.stem: In a diverse 7th-grade classroom, a teacher notices that a few students make subtle dismissive comments about a classmate's accent during discussions. To uphold an equitable, respectful climate, the most effective long-term response is to:
options: Move the targeted student to a different class to avoid further incidents
Avoid drawing attention to the issue so it does not become a bigger problem
Tell the offending students privately to stop and consider the matter closed
Address the incident directly and also build ongoing structures, norms, and curriculum that affirm diversity and teach respectful discourse
questions.rationale: Effective equity work pairs an immediate, direct response with sustained climate-building (norms, curriculum, modeling) that affirms diversity and teaches respectful interaction.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher's class is generally orderly, but momentum stalls because she stops the whole lesson to address every minor off-task behavior, creating frequent interruptions. Drawing on principles of lesson flow and "overlapping," the most effective improvement is to:
options: Hand classroom management entirely over to a teaching aide
Continue stopping for each infraction to maintain strict control
Eliminate all rules so there is nothing minor to address
Develop the ability to manage minor issues unobtrusively while sustaining instruction, reserving full stops for significant disruptions
questions.rationale: Overlapping and maintaining lesson momentum mean handling minor issues with subtle cues while teaching continues, stopping only for serious disruptions, which preserves pacing and engagement.

questions.stem: During a fifth-grade discussion about a novel, Mr. Boone wants students to move beyond recalling plot events and instead analyze characters' motivations. Which type of question should he ask?
options: "How many characters appear in the story?"
"What is the title of the book?"
"Why do you think the main character chose to keep the secret?"
"What happened at the end of chapter five?"
questions.rationale: Higher-order questions that ask students to infer motivations promote analysis and critical thinking, the goal Mr. Boone has set.

questions.stem: A high school biology teacher wants to use technology to help students visualize cellular processes that are difficult to observe directly. Which use of technology BEST supports this instructional goal?
options: Having students copy notes from a slideshow projected on the board
Using an interactive 3D simulation that lets students manipulate and explore a cell
Showing a feature-length film unrelated to the cell unit
Requiring students to type their lab reports instead of handwriting them
questions.rationale: Technology is most effective when it enhances learning in ways traditional methods cannot. An interactive simulation lets students explore processes that cannot be directly observed.

questions.stem: A fourth-grade teacher poses a real-world problem: "Our class garden is producing too many tomatoes. What could we do with them?" She asks students to brainstorm and evaluate several solutions. This approach primarily develops students':
options: Handwriting fluency
Problem-solving and critical-thinking skills
Test-taking speed
Rote memorization skills
questions.rationale: Open-ended, real-world problems that require generating and evaluating solutions engage students in problem solving and critical thinking.

questions.stem: Before assigning students to research a topic online, Ms. Nguyen teaches them how to determine whether a website is credible. This lesson primarily promotes students':
options: Digital literacy and responsible use of technology
Ability to play educational games
Memorization of website addresses
Keyboarding speed
questions.rationale: Teaching students to evaluate online source credibility develops digital literacy and responsible, critical use of technology.

questions.stem: After grading a set of essays, Mr. Foster returns them with specific comments on what each student did well and one concrete suggestion for improvement. This type of feedback is MOST effective because it:
options: Focuses only on the final grade
Compares each student publicly to classmates
Is identical for every student
Is specific, balanced, and actionable for students
questions.rationale: Effective feedback is specific, timely, and gives students clear, actionable guidance for improvement while recognizing strengths.

questions.stem: Ms. Park, a kindergarten teacher, frequently uses visuals, gestures, and simple language paired with realia when giving instructions. These practices are especially important for supporting which group of learners?
options: Students who dislike group work
Students who already read fluently
Emergent bilingual (English learner) students
Students who finish work early
questions.rationale: Visuals, gestures, realia, and simplified language provide comprehensible input that supports emergent bilingual students' understanding.

questions.stem: In a sixth-grade class, Mr. Tran notices that a few students dominate discussions while others rarely speak. Which strategy would BEST ensure more equitable participation while maintaining a positive communication climate?
options: Calling only on the quiet students to balance things out
Reducing the number of discussions in class
Using structured turn-taking protocols such as think-pair-share before whole-group sharing
Letting the same volunteers answer to keep the discussion moving
questions.rationale: Structured protocols like think-pair-share give all students a chance to formulate and rehearse responses, promoting equitable participation without singling anyone out.

questions.stem: Ms. Holloway wants her tenth-grade chemistry students to design their own experiments to test a hypothesis about reaction rates. Which instructional approach BEST fosters higher-order thinking in this context?
options: Using inquiry-based learning where students plan, conduct, and analyze their own investigations
Having students memorize the lab procedure for a test
Demonstrating the experiment while students watch passively
Providing a step-by-step recipe lab with predetermined results
questions.rationale: Inquiry-based learning requires students to plan, investigate, and analyze, engaging them in higher-order scientific reasoning and problem solving.

questions.stem: Mr. Okafor plans to integrate tablets into his eighth-grade geography lessons. Which question should he ask FIRST to ensure the technology is used effectively?
options: "Which app looks the most entertaining?"
"How can I keep students busy for the whole period?"
"Which device is the newest model available?"
"How will this technology help students achieve the specific learning objective?"
questions.rationale: Effective technology integration begins with the learning objective; the tool should be selected because it advances a specific instructional goal.

questions.stem: A second-grade student, Mateo, gives a partially correct answer during a reading lesson. Which teacher response BEST promotes learning and maintains a supportive climate?
options: "You're on the right track. Can you tell me more about how you got that?"
"You should already know this by now."
Ignoring the answer and moving to another student
"That's wrong. Who else can answer?"
questions.rationale: Acknowledging the correct portion and prompting elaboration scaffolds the student toward a complete answer while preserving a safe, supportive climate.

questions.stem: Mr. Salinas uses a learning management system to post resources, collect assignments, and give feedback to his ninth graders. A student tells him she has no reliable internet at home. The MOST appropriate response is to:
options: Provide alternative ways to access materials and submit work, such as printed copies or extended time
Lower the student's grade for not participating online
Remove all online components for the entire class
Tell the student to use the LMS anyway
questions.rationale: Equitable technology use requires accommodating the digital divide by offering alternative access so all students can fully participate.

questions.stem: In a seventh-grade math class, Mr. Iverson regularly asks students to explain their reasoning aloud and to consider whether another student's method would also work. This practice MOST directly develops students':
options: Metacognition and the ability to reason about mathematical thinking
Neat handwriting
Ability to copy procedures exactly
Speed at computing answers
questions.rationale: Asking students to explain and compare reasoning builds metacognition and mathematical reasoning, central to critical thinking.

questions.stem: Mr. Adeyemi wants his fifth graders to collaborate on a shared digital document to co-write a story. Beyond writing skills, this activity BEST helps students develop:
options: Faster typing through competition
A preference for working without feedback
Collaboration and communication skills in a digital environment
The ability to work in isolation
questions.rationale: Collaborative digital tools build teamwork and communication skills while integrating technology meaningfully into instruction.

questions.stem: Ms. Whitfield introduces a project in which her ninth-grade students must propose a solution to reduce food waste in the cafeteria, gather data, and present recommendations to the principal. This project-based approach BEST promotes critical thinking by requiring students to:
options: Complete a worksheet independently
Apply knowledge to an authentic problem and justify their reasoning with evidence
Recall facts from the textbook
Memorize the steps of the scientific method
questions.rationale: Authentic, problem-based projects require students to apply knowledge, analyze data, and justify reasoning, which are hallmarks of critical thinking.

questions.stem: Mr. Castillo plans a lesson with a clear objective but realizes mid-lesson that students are confused by the vocabulary he is using. The MOST effective immediate adjustment to his communication is to:
options: Tell students the vocabulary will make sense eventually
Skip the rest of the lesson
Rephrase concepts using familiar language and provide concrete examples
Continue with the same vocabulary so students get used to it
questions.rationale: Responsive teachers monitor comprehension and adjust their language in the moment, using accessible wording and examples to restore understanding.

questions.stem: Ms. Okonkwo allows students to choose from several formats—an essay, a podcast, or a poster—to demonstrate their understanding of a unit. This use of varied assessment formats BEST supports:
options: Giving diverse learners multiple valid ways to demonstrate mastery
Eliminating the need for clear criteria
Making the unit easier for everyone
Reducing the rigor of the content
questions.rationale: Offering varied, equally rigorous assessment formats lets students demonstrate learning through their strengths while still measuring the same objectives.

questions.stem: Ms. Farrell integrates a graphing technology into her algebra class and notices that some students rely on it to get answers without understanding the underlying concepts. The BEST instructional response is to:
options: Allow students to use the tool with no expectations
Design tasks that require students to interpret, predict, and justify results, using the tool to deepen rather than replace understanding
Ban the technology entirely for the rest of the year
Replace all conceptual instruction with technology practice
questions.rationale: Technology should enhance, not substitute for, conceptual understanding. Restructuring tasks to require interpretation and justification ensures the tool deepens learning.

questions.stem: In a tenth-grade English class, Ms. Delacroix wants to scaffold critical thinking for a diverse group that includes struggling readers and advanced students. Which approach BEST balances support and challenge for all learners during a text analysis discussion?
options: Assigning the same single open-ended essay with no scaffolds
Using tiered questions and graphic organizers that move from comprehension toward analysis and evaluation
Grouping all advanced students together and ignoring the others
Asking only literal questions so everyone can answer
questions.rationale: Tiered questioning and scaffolds let every student enter at an appropriate level and progress toward higher-order thinking, balancing support with challenge.

questions.stem: Mr. Bianchi analyzes his class's performance data and finds that English learners scored much lower on a unit test than their classmates, even though classroom discussions suggested they understood the content. The MOST likely explanation and appropriate response is that:
options: The assessment may have contained language barriers; he should review it for linguistic accessibility and consider accommodations
He should lower expectations for these students permanently
The students did not study, so he should assign more homework
English learners simply cannot master this content
questions.rationale: A gap between demonstrated understanding and test performance for English learners often signals that the assessment measured language rather than content; reviewing for linguistic load and providing accommodations addresses validity.

questions.stem: Ms. Engstrom wants to build a classroom culture where students engage in respectful academic discourse and challenge ideas without attacking peers. Which approach is MOST effective for establishing this communication norm?
options: Explicitly teaching, modeling, and providing sentence stems for academic conversations, then reinforcing them consistently
Allowing only the teacher to evaluate ideas
Telling students once at the start of the year to be respectful
Avoiding controversial topics so disagreements never arise
questions.rationale: Productive academic discourse must be explicitly taught, modeled, scaffolded with tools like sentence stems, and consistently reinforced for the norm to take hold.

questions.stem: A middle school team is selecting a digital tool to support inquiry in science. To evaluate whether the technology genuinely enhances learning rather than merely digitizing existing tasks, the team should PRIMARILY ask whether the tool:
options: Can be used without any teacher planning
Is the cheapest option available
Looks similar to tools students use for entertainment
Enables learning experiences—such as modeling, data analysis, or collaboration—that would be difficult or impossible without it
questions.rationale: Technology adds the most value when it enables tasks otherwise difficult or impossible, transforming rather than merely substituting for traditional methods.

questions.stem: Ms. Holcomb wants to develop her students' capacity to assess their own learning. Which practice would MOST effectively build students' self-assessment skills over time?
options: Grading every assignment herself and returning only scores
Teaching students to use rubrics and reflection prompts to evaluate their own work and set goals
Comparing each student's score to the class average publicly
Telling students their grades but not why they earned them
questions.rationale: Self-assessment is cultivated by teaching students to apply rubrics, reflect on their work, and set goals, fostering ownership and metacognition.

questions.stem: Mr. Vasquez plans a unit and wants every lesson to consistently push students toward higher-order thinking while still ensuring foundational understanding. Which planning practice BEST achieves this balance across the unit?
options: Sequencing lessons so foundational knowledge is built early and progressively integrated into analysis, evaluation, and creation tasks
Avoiding higher-order tasks until students have memorized all content
Using only open-ended creative tasks from day one regardless of readiness
Front-loading all lower-order tasks and saving thinking for a single end-of-unit project
questions.rationale: A coherent unit deliberately builds foundational knowledge and then progressively integrates it into higher-order analysis, evaluation, and creation, balancing rigor with readiness throughout.

questions.stem: Ms. Alvarez, a 4th-grade teacher, wants to begin a science lesson on ecosystems in a way that activates students' prior knowledge and makes them curious. Which opening question is most effective for this purpose?
options: "What living and nonliving things do you think depend on each other in the pond behind our school, and why?"
"Will you be quiet so we can start the lesson on time?"
"Please copy the definition of 'ecosystem' from the board into your notebooks."
"How many of you have ever seen a pond before today?"
questions.rationale: An effective lesson opener taps prior knowledge and provokes thinking. The pond question asks students to predict and justify relationships, engaging higher-order thinking while connecting to a familiar context.

questions.stem: A 7th-grade English teacher wants students to move beyond summarizing a short story to evaluating the author's choices. According to Bloom's taxonomy, which task best targets the highest cognitive level?
options: Judge whether the author's ending was justified by the characters' development, citing evidence
Explain the meaning of three vocabulary words from the text
List the main events of the story in order
Identify the protagonist and antagonist
questions.rationale: Judging the appropriateness of the ending and defending it with evidence is an Evaluate-level task, the higher end of Bloom's revised taxonomy, requiring students to form and justify a judgment.

questions.stem: A kindergarten teacher notices that only a few outgoing children answer her questions during circle time. Which strategy most equitably increases participation from all students?
options: Reward the children who answer most often with stickers
Use a 'turn-and-talk' so every child responds to a partner before sharing whole-group
Skip the quiet children to keep the lesson moving
Ask harder questions so quiet students must concentrate
questions.rationale: Turn-and-talk gives every student a low-risk opportunity to respond, increasing engagement and accountability for all learners, not just the eager few.

questions.stem: A 10th-grade chemistry teacher designs a unit so that early questions ask students to recall properties of elements, middle questions ask them to apply periodic trends, and final questions ask them to design an experiment to test an unknown substance. What instructional principle is the teacher applying?
options: Differentiating only by student interest
Replacing assessment with discussion
Reducing rigor over time to avoid frustration
Sequencing questions to progress from lower- to higher-order thinking (Bloom's)
questions.rationale: The teacher deliberately moves from Remember/Apply toward Create-level tasks, scaffolding cognitive demand so students build the foundation needed for higher-order work.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of an open-ended (divergent) question rather than a closed (convergent) one?
options: How many sides does a hexagon have?
What is the capital of Texas?
Is water composed of hydrogen and oxygen?
In what ways might a city reduce traffic congestion, and what are the trade-offs?
questions.rationale: Open-ended questions invite multiple valid responses and reasoning, whereas closed questions have a single correct answer.

questions.stem: Mr. Castillo wants students to engage in productive academic discourse during a math discussion rather than directing every comment to him. Which teacher move best promotes student-to-student dialogue?
options: Call on students in alphabetical order regardless of the discussion
Repeat each student's answer and immediately evaluate it as right or wrong
Answer student questions before they finish asking them
Ask, "Do you agree or disagree with Jordan's strategy, and why? Build on what was just said."
questions.rationale: Inviting students to agree, disagree, and build on peers' ideas creates accountable talk and shifts the cognitive work to students, fostering a community of discourse.

questions.stem: Ms. Patel returns a 6th-grade essay with the comment, "Good job!" written at the top. A mentor suggests her feedback could be more effective. What characteristic of high-quality feedback is most clearly missing?
options: It should be specific and actionable, telling the student what was done well and what to improve
It should be delivered only in writing
It should include a letter grade
It should always be positive
questions.rationale: Effective feedback is specific, descriptive, and actionable—it identifies strengths and concrete next steps rather than offering only vague praise.

questions.stem: A 9th-grade student submits a draft of a lab report with strong data but a weak conclusion. Which feedback comment is most likely to improve the student's learning?
options: "This is not your best work."
"Your conclusion needs work."
"Your conclusion restates the data but doesn't explain whether it supports your hypothesis. Revise it to state your claim and connect it to two specific data points."
"C+. See me."
questions.rationale: Effective feedback is specific and forward-looking, pinpointing the gap (no connection to the hypothesis) and giving a concrete revision strategy the student can act on.

questions.stem: Mr. Owusu wants the feedback he gives during a writing unit to develop students' ability to monitor and improve their own work over time. Which approach best supports this goal?
options: Provide feedback tied to a rubric and ask students to self-assess against the same rubric before revising
Correct every error himself so students see the right version
Tell students their work is fine to maintain motivation
Give only summative scores at the end of the unit
questions.rationale: Feedback linked to clear criteria, combined with student self-assessment against those criteria, builds metacognition and self-regulation, fostering independent learners.

questions.stem: During a math unit, Ms. Lin notices a student becomes anxious and disengaged whenever feedback focuses on what was wrong. To keep feedback effective while supporting the student's motivation, which strategy best reflects research on feedback?
options: Praise the student's intelligence frequently to build confidence
Stop giving the student any corrective feedback to protect self-esteem
Frame feedback around effort and specific strategies (process), and present errors as information for the next attempt
Compare the student's score to classmates' scores to spur improvement
questions.rationale: Process- and strategy-focused feedback paired with a growth mindset—treating errors as useful information—sustains motivation while still guiding improvement, unlike ability praise or social comparison.

questions.stem: Which scenario best illustrates timely feedback that supports learning?
options: A teacher posts final semester grades online with no comments
During practice, a teacher circulates and corrects students' bowing technique while they play their instruments
A teacher returns graded tests four weeks after the exam, after the next unit has begun
A teacher tells students at the end of the year which assignments they failed
questions.rationale: Timely feedback is given close to the performance so students can immediately apply it, as when a teacher corrects technique during practice.

questions.stem: Mr. Reyes gives extensive written feedback on final drafts that students never revise. A colleague suggests his feedback would have more impact if repositioned. Which change best maximizes the instructional value of his feedback?
options: Replace all written feedback with a numeric score
Give feedback only to students who request it
Provide detailed, specific feedback on drafts and build in time for students to revise based on it before final submission
Provide the same detailed feedback only on the final, non-revised draft
questions.rationale: Feedback has the greatest impact when students can act on it; giving it on drafts and providing revision time closes the learning loop, whereas feedback on un-revised final work is rarely used.

questions.stem: Ms. Flores wants to integrate technology into a 3rd-grade lesson. Using the SAMR model, which use of a word-processing tool represents 'Substitution'?
options: Students type their stories instead of writing them by hand, with no change to the task
Students publish their stories to an authentic online audience and gather feedback
Students collaboratively write and comment on a shared document in real time
Students use multimedia to create an interactive digital story impossible on paper
questions.rationale: In SAMR, Substitution means technology replaces a traditional tool with no functional change—typing instead of handwriting the same story.

questions.stem: A high school geography teacher has students use video conferencing to interview students in another country, then co-create a multimedia presentation comparing local environments—a task that would be impossible without the technology. Which SAMR level does this represent?
options: Modification
Augmentation
Substitution
Redefinition
questions.rationale: Redefinition is the highest SAMR level: technology enables a new task previously inconceivable. A cross-country collaborative interview and co-created multimedia product fits this level.

questions.stem: Before adopting a new educational app for her 8th-grade math class, Ms. Khan evaluates it. Which consideration should most strongly guide her decision to integrate it?
options: Whether the app is the newest one available
Whether other teachers have posted about it on social media
Whether the app meaningfully advances the lesson's learning objectives and supports student thinking
Whether the app has bright colors and animations students will enjoy
questions.rationale: Technology integration should be driven by instructional goals; the central question is whether the tool advances learning objectives and supports student thinking, not novelty or appearance.

questions.stem: A district provides every student a tablet. A first-year teacher uses them daily but mostly to display digital worksheets that mirror the old paper ones. A mentor encourages 'transformative' use. Which lesson redesign best moves the technology toward the higher levels of SAMR?
options: Project the worksheets on the board instead of distributing them
Increase the number of digital worksheets completed each day
Have students design and conduct a digital survey, analyze the live data, and present data-driven recommendations to a community partner
Add a timer to the worksheets to increase pace
questions.rationale: Moving toward Modification/Redefinition means redesigning tasks so technology enables new kinds of learning—collecting and analyzing real data and acting on it—rather than digitizing existing worksheets.

questions.stem: Mr. Davis plans to have students use the internet for a research project. To promote responsible and ethical technology use, what should he most importantly teach alongside the research skills?
options: How to type faster on a keyboard
How to download as many files as possible
How to evaluate source credibility and properly cite information to avoid plagiarism
How to change the device's wallpaper
questions.rationale: Digital citizenship—evaluating credibility and citing sources to avoid plagiarism—is essential when students conduct online research, supporting ethical and effective technology use.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to use a collaborative online platform but is concerned about safety, privacy, and equity because some students lack reliable home internet. Which response best balances effective technology integration with these concerns?
options: Allow students to use any social media platform they prefer
Use a school-approved, privacy-compliant platform, build in class time for collaboration, and provide alternatives for students without home access
Cancel the technology component entirely to avoid any risk
Require all collaborative work to be completed at home using personal accounts
questions.rationale: Responsible integration uses vetted, privacy-compliant tools, addresses the digital divide by providing in-class time and alternatives, and protects student data—balancing benefits with safety and equity.

questions.stem: Ms. Obi is teaching a lesson and notices through questioning that most students are confused about a key step. What does responsive, data-driven teaching call for her to do?
options: Tell students they will understand it later and move on
Adjust instruction in the moment—slow down, provide a clearer example or model, and recheck understanding
Continue with the planned lesson exactly as written
Assign the confusing material as homework instead
questions.rationale: Responsive teaching means using real-time evidence of student understanding to adjust instruction immediately—reteaching or modeling and then rechecking—rather than rigidly following the plan.

questions.stem: A 6th-grade team analyzes common-assessment data and finds that across all classes, students missed items requiring them to interpret graphs, while items requiring computation were answered well. Which conclusion and action are best supported by the data?
options: A skill gap in graph interpretation exists across classes; plan targeted instruction on reading and interpreting graphs
The assessment was too hard and should be discarded
Only one teacher's class needs reteaching
Students simply did not study; assign more computation practice
questions.rationale: Disaggregating by item/skill reveals a specific, shared weakness—graph interpretation—pointing to targeted instruction on that skill rather than broad assumptions or discarding the data.

questions.stem: Mr. Lee wants his assessments to accurately measure whether students achieved the lesson's stated learning objective about analyzing primary sources. Which assessment design principle is most important here?
options: The assessment should be as long as possible
The assessment should align with the objective, requiring students to actually analyze primary sources
The assessment should be identical to last year's test
The assessment should use only multiple-choice items for easy grading
questions.rationale: Validity through alignment is key: the assessment must measure what was taught and stated in the objective. If the objective is analysis of primary sources, the task must require that analysis.

questions.stem: Ms. Romero uses only end-of-unit tests to gauge learning and is frustrated that she discovers misconceptions too late to help. Which change best addresses the root problem?
options: Grade the end-of-unit tests more leniently
Stop testing altogether
Make the end-of-unit tests longer and more difficult
Embed frequent formative checks throughout the unit and use the results to adjust instruction before the summative test
questions.rationale: The problem is timing: relying only on summative data prevents timely intervention. Frequent formative assessment surfaces misconceptions early, allowing adjustment before it is too late.

questions.stem: A bilingual student understands science content but scores low on a written test full of complex English sentences. To get a more valid measure of the student's science knowledge, what should the teacher do?
options: Conclude the student has not learned the science content
Reduce unnecessary language complexity and allow the student to demonstrate understanding through multiple means (e.g., diagrams, oral explanation)
Lower expectations for the student's science learning permanently
Give the student the same test again unchanged
questions.rationale: When language demands obscure content knowledge, the assessment lacks validity for that student. Reducing irrelevant language load and offering alternative ways to show understanding yields a fairer, more valid measure.

questions.stem: At a data meeting, Mr. Tran's class shows strong average scores, but disaggregating the data reveals a subgroup of English learners performing well below peers on the same standards. Which response best reflects equitable, data-informed practice?
options: Rely on the strong class average and make no changes
Use the disaggregated data to design targeted, linguistically responsive supports for the English learners on those standards
Assume the gap will close on its own with more time
Exclude the English learners' scores so the average looks consistent
questions.rationale: Equitable data use requires looking beyond averages to disaggregated results, then designing targeted, responsive supports for the underserved subgroup so all students master the standards.

questions.stem: During a conference, a parent becomes upset and says, "You clearly don't like my son—he always gets in trouble in your class." Which response by the teacher best maintains a productive partnership?
options: "I can see you're concerned. Let's look together at what's happening and plan how we can support him."
"That's not true; I treat all my students exactly the same way."
"If he followed the rules like the other students, this wouldn't be an issue."
"We should probably end here and reschedule when you've calmed down."
questions.rationale: Acknowledging the parent's feelings and shifting to collaborative problem-solving preserves the relationship and focuses on the student's needs.

questions.stem: Ms. Castillo notices that families of her English learners rarely attend school events, even though she sends home flyers in English. Which strategy is most likely to increase their engagement?
options: Require attendance at one event as part of the students' participation grades
Conclude that these families are not interested in their children's education
Personally call or text families in their home language and offer flexible event times and childcare
Continue sending the same flyers, since the information is already available
questions.rationale: Personalized, language-accessible outreach combined with reducing practical barriers respects families' circumstances and boosts engagement.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to communicate a student's recent decline in reading performance to the family in a way that prompts collaboration rather than defensiveness. Which message is most effective?
options: "I'm not sure what's wrong with Diego's reading, but you should probably get him tested."
"Diego's reading scores have dropped over the past month; I'd love to share what I'm seeing and hear your thoughts on how we can help him together."
"Diego has fallen behind and isn't trying hard enough during reading time."
"Diego needs to read more at home or he will fail this grading period."
questions.rationale: The best message presents objective information, avoids blame, and explicitly invites the family into shared problem-solving.

questions.stem: Mr. Reyes maintains a classroom communication log documenting his contacts with families. What is the primary professional purpose of keeping such a log?
options: To meet a minimum quota of parent contacts required for evaluation
To create an accurate record of outreach and follow-up that supports continuity and accountability
To prove to administrators that certain parents are uncooperative
To collect personal information families share so it can be discussed in the teachers' lounge
questions.rationale: A communication log documents outreach and responses, helping teachers follow up consistently and demonstrate professional accountability.

questions.stem: Ms. Nguyen, a first-year teacher, is paired with a veteran mentor. Which action best reflects her professional responsibility to grow from this mentoring relationship?
options: Wait for the mentor to identify all her weaknesses before making any changes
Accept only the feedback that confirms what she already does
Avoid sharing struggles so the mentor reports that she is performing well
Reflect on feedback, ask questions, and apply suggested strategies in her instruction
questions.rationale: Professional growth requires active reflection, openness to feedback, and willingness to apply new strategies.

questions.stem: Mr. Okafor receives a formal evaluation in which his appraiser notes that students are frequently off-task during transitions. Which response best demonstrates professional responsibility?
options: Seek additional resources or coaching on transition routines and revise his classroom procedures
Tell colleagues the appraiser is biased against new teachers
Dismiss the feedback because the appraiser only observed for part of a lesson
File a grievance arguing that transitions are not part of his job
questions.rationale: Using evaluation feedback to seek support and improve practice reflects a professional commitment to growth.

questions.stem: Ms. Patterson wants to engage in self-directed professional growth aligned with her campus improvement goal of increasing student writing proficiency. Which plan best reflects reflective, goal-driven professional development?
options: Attend whatever conference sessions have the shortest wait lists, regardless of topic
Ask a colleague to share her lesson plans so Ms. Patterson can submit them as her own development
Repeat the same writing units she has always taught and wait for the next mandated training
Set a specific writing-instruction goal, gather student writing data, pursue targeted learning, and measure impact on student work
questions.rationale: Reflective professional growth is goal-oriented, data-informed, and evaluated by its effect on student learning.

questions.stem: A grade-level team is planning an interdisciplinary unit. One teacher dominates discussions and dismisses others' ideas. As a team member committed to professional collaboration, what is the most appropriate action?
options: Let the dominant teacher make all decisions to keep meetings short
Complain to the principal that the colleague should be removed from the team
Respectfully use a structured process, such as a turn-taking protocol, to ensure all voices contribute
Stop attending the planning meetings to avoid the conflict
questions.rationale: Using a structured, respectful process invites balanced participation and models constructive collaboration.

questions.stem: Under Texas law, a teacher who has reasonable cause to believe that a child has been abused or neglected must do which of the following?
options: Inform only the campus principal and consider the duty fulfilled
Wait to gather proof before telling anyone
Discuss the situation with the suspected family first to confirm it
Report the suspicion to the appropriate authorities, generally within 48 hours
questions.rationale: Texas mandatory reporting law requires educators to report suspected abuse or neglect to authorities, generally within 48 hours; proof is not required, only reasonable cause.

questions.stem: FERPA protects the privacy of student education records. Which of the following would generally be a violation of FERPA?
options: Releasing records to a parent who has formally requested to review them
Posting a class ranking by student name and grade on the hallway bulletin board
Sharing a student's records with another teacher who has a legitimate educational interest
A teacher discussing a student's grades with that student's eligible parent
questions.rationale: FERPA prohibits disclosing personally identifiable information from education records without consent; publicly posting names with grades discloses protected information.

questions.stem: A student confides to Ms. Holloway that her stepfather has been hitting her at home. The student begs the teacher not to tell anyone. What is Ms. Holloway's correct course of action?
options: Report the suspected abuse to the proper authorities as required by law, even though the student asked her not to
Tell the student to report it herself to the school counselor
Promise to watch the situation and report only if she sees visible injuries
Honor the student's wishes and keep the disclosure confidential
questions.rationale: Mandatory reporting overrides a student's request for confidentiality; the teacher must report suspected abuse to authorities.

questions.stem: A teacher suspects that a struggling student may have a learning disability that has not been identified. Which action best aligns with IDEA and appropriate professional procedures?
options: Tell the parents their child clearly has a disability and should be medicated
Quietly place the student in a separate special education class without any formal process
Follow the campus referral process, documenting interventions and requesting an evaluation through the appropriate team
Lower the student's workload permanently and avoid involving anyone else
questions.rationale: IDEA requires a formal, team-based referral and evaluation process with documented interventions; teachers initiate this through proper channels rather than acting unilaterally.

questions.stem: An ARD (Admission, Review, and Dismissal) committee meeting is scheduled for a student receiving special education services. Which statement best reflects the role of the student's parents in this process?
options: Parents are required members of the ARD committee and equal participants in decision-making
Parents are notified of decisions after the committee has finalized the IEP
Parents may observe the meeting but cannot influence placement decisions
Parents may attend only if the school administrator grants permission
questions.rationale: Under IDEA, parents are required members of the ARD/IEP team and full participants in decisions about their child's services and placement.

questions.stem: During an informal hallway conversation, a parent of one of Ms. Alvarez's students asks her how a different student in the same class is performing academically. Which response best reflects the teacher's professional and legal obligations?
options: Politely decline to discuss the other student and explain that student records are confidential
Share only the other student's letter grades since names are not mentioned in report cards
Provide a general summary as long as the parent promises not to repeat it
Answer fully because both children are friends and play together after school
questions.rationale: Under FERPA and the Texas Educators' Code of Ethics, a teacher must protect the confidentiality of every student's records and may not disclose one student's information to another student's parent.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher wants to grow professionally during the school year. Which action best demonstrates a commitment to ongoing professional development?
options: Seeking out a mentor and regularly reflecting on feedback to refine instruction
Limiting collaboration so that personal teaching style remains unchanged
Repeating the same lesson plans each year to maintain consistency
Avoiding feedback from administrators to prevent criticism of new methods
questions.rationale: Competency 011 emphasizes that effective educators engage in continuous self-reflection, seek mentorship, and use feedback to improve their practice.

questions.stem: A counselor leaves a printed list of students' confidential disability and counseling information on a shared workroom table. A teacher walks in and sees it. What should the teacher do to uphold confidentiality?
options: Share the relevant entries with each affected student's other teachers
Secure the document, return it to the counselor, and note that it was left exposed
Photograph the list for reference in case any of those students are in class
Leave it where it is since the counselor is responsible for the document
questions.rationale: All educators share responsibility for protecting confidential student information; the teacher should secure the exposed document and alert the counselor rather than copy or further distribute it.

questions.stem: A teacher disagrees with a new district reading curriculum but is required to implement it. Which response best reflects professional responsibility?
options: Tell students the new curriculum is poor and not worth their effort
Implement the curriculum with fidelity while voicing concerns through appropriate channels
Quietly continue using the old curriculum and ignore the directive
Refuse to teach reading until the district reverses the decision
questions.rationale: Professional responsibility includes following lawful directives and policies while advocating for change through appropriate, constructive channels rather than undermining them.

questions.stem: A teacher suspects that a student's bruises are the result of abuse but is told by a colleague that 'the family is going through a lot, so let's not get involved.' What is the teacher's correct course of action?
options: Confront the family directly to ask whether abuse occurred
Defer to the colleague's judgment and take no action
Report the suspicion personally to the proper authorities despite the colleague's advice
Document the bruises and revisit the situation in a few weeks
questions.rationale: The duty to report suspected abuse is individual and cannot be waived by a colleague's opinion; the teacher must report directly to the proper authorities within the legal timeframe.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to involve families more meaningfully in their children's education in a culturally diverse community. Which approach best reflects professional collaboration with families?
options: Offer multiple communication methods and times, and provide translation when needed
Communicate with families only when a student is in disciplinary trouble
Schedule all conferences during the workday and require in-person attendance only
Send all notices in English and assume families will arrange their own translation
questions.rationale: Effective family collaboration requires flexible, accessible communication that accounts for families' languages, schedules, and circumstances.

questions.stem: A teacher posts a photo on a public social media page from a class field trip. The photo clearly shows several identifiable students, and the caption names one student and references his special education services. Which aspect of this post is the most serious professional violation?
options: Using social media to share a positive classroom moment
Disclosing a specific student's special education status to the public
Failing to tag the school district's official account in the post
Posting a field trip photo that includes students in the background
