questions.stem: Mr. Lefevre projects his voice clearly, varies his tone, and pauses for emphasis while reading aloud to his first-grade class. These verbal communication choices are MOST likely to
options: maintain student attention and convey meaning effectively
discourage students from listening
confuse students with inconsistent delivery
make the read-aloud take much longer than necessary
questions.rationale: Vocal variety, clear projection, and purposeful pauses help hold attention and emphasize meaning, supporting comprehension during a read-aloud.

questions.stem: After students complete a research project, Ms. Adeyemi asks them to write a brief reflection on which research strategies worked well, which did not, and what they would do differently next time. This activity primarily develops
options: speed of task completion
metacognitive and self-regulatory skills
spelling accuracy
handwriting fluency
questions.rationale: Reflecting on what strategies worked and planning improvements engages metacognition and self-regulation, helping students monitor and adjust their own learning.

questions.stem: During a whole-class discussion, Mr. Okonkwo notices that two students give conflicting interpretations of a poem. Which teacher move would BEST leverage this disagreement to promote critical thinking?
options: Telling the class which interpretation is correct so they can move on
Inviting each student to explain the textual basis for their view and asking the class to weigh both
Asking the students to drop the topic to avoid conflict
Choosing the interpretation that matches the answer key
questions.rationale: Productive disagreement is a rich opportunity for critical thinking when the teacher has students articulate their evidence and asks the class to evaluate competing claims.

questions.stem: Ms. Hollingsworth wants her ninth-grade students to apply the math concept of proportional reasoning beyond the textbook. Which task BEST encourages transfer to a real-world context?
options: Reciting the cross-multiplication procedure
Solving twenty proportion problems identical to the examples
Calculating how much paint is needed to cover a wall of given dimensions using a coverage ratio
Copying the definition of a proportion
questions.rationale: Applying proportional reasoning to a practical situation like estimating paint needed demonstrates transfer of the concept to a new, authentic context.

questions.stem: Ms. Underwood asks a question, then waits several seconds after a student finishes answering before responding or calling on someone else. This second pause, often called 'wait time II,' primarily allows
options: the teacher to plan the next unit
the teacher to grade homework quietly
students to add to, refine, or build on the response
the class to transition to a new subject
questions.rationale: Wait time II, the pause after a student response, gives students room to elaborate, reconsider, or build on what was said, leading to richer discussion.

questions.stem: Mr. Castellano wants students to lead more of the discussion in his tenth-grade literature class. Which structure would BEST shift intellectual ownership to students while keeping the dialogue productive?
options: Having the teacher ask every question and call on students one by one
Allowing only the highest-achieving students to speak
Limiting students to repeating the teacher's interpretations
Using student-generated questions and a discussion protocol where peers respond to each other
questions.rationale: Using student-generated questions within a structured protocol that has peers respond to one another transfers ownership of the discussion to students while maintaining focus and productivity.

questions.stem: A fourth-grade teacher poses a rich problem with no obvious single solution and asks groups to develop and defend multiple possible approaches. A student asks, 'Which way is the right way?' Which teacher response BEST supports the goals of inquiry-based learning?
options: 'Wait until I show you the correct method.'
'There may be several reasonable approaches; explain why your method makes sense.'
'The right way is the one in the textbook—use that.'
'Just pick any answer; it doesn't really matter.'
questions.rationale: Inquiry-based learning values multiple valid approaches and student reasoning; encouraging the student to justify the chosen method preserves the open, thinking-centered nature of the task.

questions.stem: Ms. Delacroix kneels to a child's eye level and speaks in a calm, even voice when a kindergartner is upset. These nonverbal and verbal choices PRIMARILY help to
options: assert the teacher's authority over the child
draw the class's attention to the child's behavior
create a sense of safety and connection that supports the child
speed up the lesson
questions.rationale: Getting to a child's eye level and using a calm voice conveys warmth and safety, helping the child feel supported and ready to communicate.

questions.stem: Mr. Vasquez frequently asks his eighth-grade students, 'How did you arrive at that answer?' and 'What strategy did you use?' even when answers are correct. The MAIN benefit of these questions is to
options: make students aware of and able to explain their reasoning processes
fill time during the lesson
catch students who are guessing
reward only students who answer quickly
questions.rationale: Asking students to explain how they reached an answer surfaces and reinforces metacognitive reasoning, making thinking processes visible and transferable.

questions.stem: Ms. Lindgren wants to assess whether her students can think critically rather than just recall facts about the water cycle. Which assessment prompt is BEST aligned with this goal?
options: Define the term 'evaporation.'
Explain how a long regional drought might disrupt the water cycle and justify your reasoning.
Label the stages of the water cycle on the diagram.
List the four main steps of the water cycle.
questions.rationale: A prompt requiring students to reason about how a drought disrupts the cycle and justify their thinking targets analysis and evaluation, not mere recall.

questions.stem: Mr. Ferraro launches a problem-based unit in which seventh-graders design a budget-friendly healthy lunch menu meeting nutritional guidelines. To maximize the unit's effectiveness for developing problem-solving, Mr. Ferraro should ensure the problem is
options: authentic, open-ended, and connected to students' lives and prior knowledge
so narrow that only one correct menu is possible
unrelated to any real constraints or guidelines
fully solved by the teacher before students begin
questions.rationale: Effective problem-based learning hinges on problems that are authentic, open-ended, and meaningfully connected to students' experiences, allowing genuine inquiry and multiple solution paths.

questions.stem: While a student is explaining her solution at the board, Mr. Whitman turns toward her, makes eye contact, and refrains from interrupting. When she pauses, he says nothing for a moment to let her continue. These behaviors collectively demonstrate
options: impatience with the student's pace
effective active-listening skills that encourage full student expression
a lack of classroom management
disinterest in the student's explanation
questions.rationale: Orienting toward the speaker, maintaining eye contact, withholding interruptions, and allowing pauses are hallmarks of active listening that encourage the student to express ideas fully.

questions.stem: Ms. Romano sets a norm that during discussions, students should build on, question, or politely challenge classmates' ideas. The PRIMARY goal of this norm is to
options: foster productive academic dialogue and collaborative reasoning
ensure only the teacher's ideas are discussed
make discussions shorter
minimize the amount students talk
questions.rationale: Norms that have students build on, question, and respectfully challenge peers cultivate productive, collaborative academic discourse and shared reasoning.

questions.stem: A teacher poses the question, 'Is the capital of France Paris?' Realizing it elicits only a yes-or-no answer, she revises it to, 'Why might a country choose a particular city to serve as its capital?' The revised question is more effective because it
options: invites open-ended reasoning and multiple supported responses
can be answered without any thought
reduces the cognitive demand on students
has a single correct answer that is easy to grade
questions.rationale: Converting a closed yes-or-no question into an open-ended 'why' question invites reasoning, multiple perspectives, and supported responses, raising the cognitive demand productively.

questions.stem: In a chemistry class, students learn to balance equations in one context and later independently apply that skill to predict products in unfamiliar reactions during a lab. A teacher who wants to deliberately promote this kind of far transfer should MOST emphasize
options: drilling the same equation type repeatedly until automatic
discouraging students from connecting new tasks to prior learning
testing students only on the exact problems practiced in class
helping students identify the underlying principles and when to apply them across varied contexts
questions.rationale: Far transfer is fostered when instruction makes underlying principles explicit and helps students recognize the conditions under which those principles apply across varied, novel contexts.

questions.stem: Mr. Salgado uses a 'wait, watch, and respond' approach: he scans the room, notices puzzled facial expressions during his explanation, and adjusts by giving an additional example. This best illustrates how teachers can use
options: a single explanation regardless of student response
verbal directions that ignore student cues
strict adherence to a fixed lesson script
students' nonverbal feedback to monitor and adjust instruction
questions.rationale: Reading students' nonverbal cues, such as puzzled expressions, and adjusting instruction accordingly is an effective use of feedback to monitor and improve comprehension in real time.

questions.stem: During a sixth-grade discussion, several students give vague responses. Ms. Ekwueme follows up with, 'Can you give a specific example?' and 'What makes you think that?' These follow-up questions are BEST categorized as
options: probing questions that push for clarity and depth
closed recall questions
off-topic questions
rhetorical questions requiring no answer
questions.rationale: Asking for specifics and reasons are probing questions that prompt students to clarify, justify, and deepen their initial responses.

questions.stem: Ms. Park models her own thinking aloud while solving a problem, saying things like, 'First I need to figure out what the question is asking, so let me restate it.' This think-aloud strategy primarily helps students by
options: making the teacher's reasoning process visible so students can adopt similar strategies
keeping students passive during instruction
emphasizing speed over understanding
showing that only the teacher can solve such problems
questions.rationale: Think-alouds make expert reasoning and metacognitive strategies explicit, providing a model students can internalize and apply to their own problem-solving.

questions.stem: Mr. Aguilar wants his fifth-graders to connect a new unit on fractions to what they already know about division and sharing. Activating this prior knowledge before introducing new content primarily supports
options: memorization of unrelated facts
faster grading of assignments
reducing the need for any new instruction
meaningful learning and the transfer of existing understanding to new concepts
questions.rationale: Connecting new content to relevant prior knowledge fosters meaningful learning and enables students to transfer existing understanding to make sense of new concepts.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews her questioning patterns and finds that 90 percent of her questions are at the recall level. To better balance her questioning and develop students' thinking, she should MOST appropriately
options: intentionally plan a mix that includes more analysis, evaluation, and synthesis questions
ask only questions with a single correct answer
eliminate all recall questions from her lessons
ask fewer questions overall
questions.rationale: While some recall questions are useful, deliberately planning a balanced range that adds higher-order questions, such as analysis, evaluation, and synthesis, better develops students' thinking.

questions.stem: Mr. Castle observes that his enthusiastic verbal praise often overlaps with and cuts off students who are still speaking. To communicate more effectively and encourage complete responses, his BEST adjustment would be to
options: praise students more loudly so they hear him
interrupt students earlier to save time
wait until a student fully finishes before responding and use brief affirming nonverbal cues meanwhile
stop giving any feedback to students
questions.rationale: Allowing students to finish before responding, while using subtle affirming nonverbal cues during their turn, communicates respect and encourages complete, uninterrupted responses.

questions.stem: In a problem-based unit, Ms. Trujillo's role shifts during group investigations. Which description BEST captures the teacher's role in supporting inquiry and problem-based learning?
options: Acting as a facilitator who poses guiding questions, monitors progress, and provides scaffolding as needed
Leaving students entirely on their own with no support
Delivering all answers through lecture so students do not struggle
Requiring every group to reach the identical predetermined conclusion
questions.rationale: In inquiry and problem-based learning, the teacher serves as a facilitator who guides with questions, monitors group progress, and scaffolds, rather than simply delivering answers.

questions.stem: Mr. Liang wants students to experience how a concept learned in social studies, such as supply and demand, applies in their everyday lives. Which assignment BEST supports transfer of this concept?
options: Asking students to explain how supply and demand affect the price of a popular item they want to buy
Memorizing a list of economic terms
Reading the chapter silently without an application task
Copying the textbook definition of supply and demand
questions.rationale: Having students apply supply and demand to explain real price changes for a product they care about demonstrates transfer of the concept to an authentic, personal context.

questions.stem: A teacher wants a class discussion to engage all students in critical thinking rather than allowing a few to dominate. Which combination of strategies would BEST achieve this goal?
options: Letting the discussion proceed without any structure or norms
Calling only on volunteers and accepting the first correct answer
Using think-pair-share, wait time, and open-ended questions that require justification
Asking exclusively recall questions answered chorally
questions.rationale: Combining think-pair-share to give every student a chance to rehearse ideas, wait time for processing, and open-ended questions requiring justification distributes participation and deepens critical thinking across the class.

questions.stem: A fifth-grade teacher replaces a paper vocabulary worksheet with an identical worksheet completed in a word-processing document that students type into and print. According to the SAMR model, this use of technology is best described as which level?
options: Redefinition
Modification
Augmentation
Substitution
questions.rationale: In the SAMR model, Substitution occurs when technology acts as a direct tool substitute with no functional change to the task. Replacing a paper worksheet with a typed version of the same worksheet adds no new function, so it is Substitution.

questions.stem: A high school science teacher plans a unit using a digital simulation that lets students manipulate variables in a virtual ecosystem, collaborate in real time on a shared data dashboard, and publish findings to an authentic online audience. Which framework best captures the teacher's need to blend content knowledge, pedagogy, and technology when designing this unit?
options: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
Bloom's Taxonomy
Gardner's Multiple Intelligences
TPACK
questions.rationale: TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge) describes the intersection of technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge teachers must integrate to design effective technology-enhanced instruction, exactly what this unit requires.

questions.stem: During a lesson, several students need to quickly look up unfamiliar terms while reading a complex text. Which technology tool is MOST appropriate for this specific instructional purpose?
options: A presentation slideshow projected at the front of the room
A video-conferencing application
A spreadsheet for organizing data
An embedded digital glossary or dictionary tool within the reading platform
questions.rationale: Appropriate tool selection means matching the tool to the instructional need. An embedded digital glossary or dictionary lets students access definitions on demand at the point of need, directly supporting comprehension of the complex text.

questions.stem: A teacher redesigns a traditional book report so that students now co-author a multimedia documentary with peers in another country via video calls and a shared editing platform—a task that would be impossible without technology. On the SAMR model, this represents which level?
options: Modification
Redefinition
Substitution
Augmentation
questions.rationale: Redefinition is the highest SAMR level, where technology enables the creation of new tasks previously inconceivable. Collaborating internationally to co-author a multimedia documentary is a task impossible without technology, defining Redefinition.

questions.stem: A teacher reminds students never to share personal information such as home addresses or passwords when participating in online class discussions. This guidance most directly promotes which aspect of digital citizenship?
options: Online safety and privacy protection
Cloud storage management
Coding proficiency
Multimedia design
questions.rationale: Protecting personal information online is a core dimension of digital citizenship focused on student safety and privacy, helping learners behave responsibly and securely in digital environments.

questions.stem: A teacher is choosing among several technology tools for a project. Tool A automates grading of multiple-choice quizzes; Tool B lets students build interactive timelines with embedded primary sources; Tool C displays the teacher's lecture notes; Tool D generates random student name selectors. The learning goal is for students to analyze cause-and-effect relationships in historical events and demonstrate their reasoning. Which tool best aligns technology selection with the learning goal?
options: Tool D
Tool C
Tool B
Tool A
questions.rationale: Effective technology selection aligns the tool with the cognitive demand of the learning goal. Analyzing cause-and-effect and demonstrating reasoning requires students to construct and connect ideas; an interactive timeline with embedded sources supports analysis and demonstration of reasoning far better than grading, lecture display, or name-selection tools.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a classroom polling app that lets every student submit an answer to a conceptual question simultaneously and instantly displays the distribution of responses. The PRIMARY instructional benefit of this technology is that it allows the teacher to:
options: Eliminate the need for summative assessment
Obtain immediate, whole-class formative data to guide the next instructional move
Reduce the amount of grading at the end of the unit
Assign permanent ability-group labels to students
questions.rationale: Real-time polling provides immediate formative data from all students at once, enabling the teacher to gauge understanding and adjust instruction on the spot—its chief instructional value.

questions.stem: A district adopts a new digital learning platform. A teacher notices that some students lack reliable internet access at home, which could widen achievement gaps if assignments require nightly online work. Which response best reflects equitable, responsible technology integration?
options: Require all work to be completed online at home to build digital skills
Lower expectations only for students without home internet
Exempt the affected students from the technology-based curriculum entirely
Provide flexible options such as in-school access time, downloadable offline materials, or alternative formats
questions.rationale: Equitable technology integration addresses the digital divide by ensuring all students can access learning. Providing flexible options—school access time, offline materials, or alternatives—maintains high expectations while removing access barriers.

questions.stem: Before assigning a research project, a teacher explicitly teaches students how to cite digital sources and paraphrase rather than copy text directly. This instruction is MOST important for promoting:
options: Higher screen brightness for readability
Greater file storage capacity
Faster typing speeds
Academic integrity and ethical use of information
questions.rationale: Teaching proper citation and paraphrasing fosters academic integrity and the ethical use of others' work—central responsibilities of digital citizenship and intellectual property respect.

questions.stem: A teacher selects a text-to-speech tool so that a student with a reading disability can access grade-level science content. This use of technology primarily functions as a(n):
options: Reward for good behavior
Classroom management timer
Assistive technology that supports access to the curriculum
Method of reducing curriculum rigor
questions.rationale: Text-to-speech that enables a student with a disability to access grade-level content is assistive technology, which removes barriers and supports equitable access to the same rigorous curriculum.

questions.stem: A teacher integrates a collaborative document so that groups can draft, comment on, and revise a shared argument essay in real time, with each member's contributions visible. Beyond producing the essay, this technology choice MOST directly supports which 21st-century learning skill?
options: Rote memorization
Penmanship
Standardized test-taking speed
Collaboration and peer feedback
questions.rationale: A shared, real-time collaborative document with visible contributions and commenting fosters collaboration and peer feedback, key 21st-century skills, by making the joint construction and critique of work seamless.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to move from simply receiving information to creating original products that demonstrate deep understanding, using technology to enable tasks not previously possible. To plan this progression intentionally, the teacher is BEST served by using the SAMR model to:
options: Rank students by how quickly they finish technology tasks
Schedule device charging times during the day
Evaluate whether technology use merely substitutes for analog tasks or transforms learning toward higher-order creation
Determine which brand of device to purchase
questions.rationale: The SAMR model helps teachers reflect on whether technology is enhancing (Substitution/Augmentation) or transforming (Modification/Redefinition) learning, guiding intentional movement toward higher-order, transformative tasks like original creation.

questions.stem: A teacher establishes clear norms for respectful online communication, including how to disagree constructively in discussion boards and avoid harmful language. These norms most directly cultivate students' development as:
options: Responsible and ethical digital community members
Independent hardware technicians
Rapid test finishers
Efficient typists
questions.rationale: Norms for respectful online interaction and constructive disagreement build students' capacity to act as responsible, ethical participants in digital communities—a central goal of digital citizenship.

questions.stem: A teacher chooses a graphing application so students can instantly visualize how changing the slope alters a line, allowing rapid exploration of many examples. Compared with hand-graphing each example, this represents which SAMR level because it adds a functional improvement to the same basic task?
options: Augmentation
Modification
Substitution
Redefinition
questions.rationale: Augmentation is technology acting as a direct substitute with functional improvement. The graphing app performs the same task (graphing lines) but adds the functional benefit of instant, repeated visualization—an improvement without redesigning the task.

questions.stem: A teacher reflects that a flashy new app keeps students entertained but does not advance the lesson's objective about analyzing primary-source bias. The teacher's reflection illustrates the principle that technology integration should be:
options: Selected based on which app is most popular among students
Avoided whenever possible to save instructional time
Guided by alignment with clear learning objectives, with the tool serving the content and pedagogy
Driven primarily by how engaging or novel the tool is
questions.rationale: Sound technology integration is purposeful: the tool must serve the learning objective, content, and pedagogy rather than being chosen for novelty or engagement alone. The teacher correctly prioritizes objective alignment over entertainment value.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a project in which students use a data-collection app to gather local water-quality measurements, analyze the data in a shared spreadsheet, and present recommendations to the city council via a published report. Considering both TPACK and SAMR, the strongest justification for this technology integration is that it:
options: Integrates content, pedagogy, and technology to enable an authentic, transformative task with real-world impact
Uses the newest available devices in the school
Keeps students busy during independent work time
Replaces a textbook chapter with an online version of the same chapter
questions.rationale: The project exemplifies strong TPACK (content, pedagogy, technology integration) and high-level SAMR (Redefinition—an authentic task impossible without technology). The best justification is that it meaningfully integrates all three knowledge domains to enable transformative, real-world learning.

questions.stem: A teacher wants young students to understand that information posted online can be permanent and seen by many people, even after deletion. Teaching this concept of a 'digital footprint' best prepares students to:
options: Increase their internet download speeds
Make thoughtful, responsible decisions about what they share online
Memorize software keyboard shortcuts
Repair damaged devices independently
questions.rationale: Understanding the permanence and reach of one's digital footprint equips students to make responsible, thoughtful choices about online sharing—an essential element of digital citizenship.

questions.stem: After scoring an exit ticket, a teacher notices that 70 percent of students misidentified the same step in solving two-step equations. The MOST appropriate instructional response the next day is to:
options: Assign the same exit ticket again without any instruction
Reteach the misunderstood step using a different approach before advancing
Move on to the next unit as planned to stay on pace
Give the whole class a lower grade for the misunderstanding
questions.rationale: Data-driven instruction means using assessment results to adjust teaching. When most students share a specific misconception, the teacher should reteach that step—ideally with a new approach—before moving forward, rather than advancing or penalizing students.

questions.stem: While students work in groups, a teacher circulates, listens to conversations, asks probing questions, and jots notes on a clipboard about who is struggling. This practice is an example of:
options: Ongoing monitoring of student understanding during instruction
Parent-teacher conferencing
Standardized test administration
Summative grading
questions.rationale: Circulating, listening, questioning, and recording observations is ongoing formative monitoring of student understanding that allows the teacher to identify needs and adjust support in real time.

questions.stem: A teacher gives the same brief quiz before a unit (pre-assessment) and after several lessons (post-assessment). Comparing results, the teacher finds that students who already mastered two objectives on the pre-assessment showed little growth, while others made large gains. The BEST use of this data is to:
options: Use the pre-assessment data to differentiate—providing enrichment for those who showed early mastery and targeted instruction for others
Discard the pre-assessment because some students already knew the content
Assign identical homework to all students to ensure fairness
Conclude the lessons were ineffective for everyone and reteach the whole unit
questions.rationale: Pre- and post-assessment comparison reveals differing student needs. The data should drive differentiation: students who pre-mastered objectives need enrichment, while others need continued targeted instruction. Treating all students identically wastes the diagnostic value of the data.

questions.stem: A teacher plans frequent, low-stakes checks for understanding throughout a lesson rather than waiting until a unit test. The primary advantage of this approach is that it:
options: Allows the teacher to catch and address misunderstandings early, before they compound
Eliminates the need for any summative assessment
Guarantees every student earns a high grade
Reduces the teacher's planning workload
questions.rationale: Frequent formative checks let teachers identify misunderstandings early and adjust instruction promptly, preventing small gaps from growing—its key benefit over waiting for a single end-of-unit test.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to give feedback that develops a growth mindset and helps students improve. Which feedback statement is MOST consistent with this goal?
options: 'You're just naturally gifted at math.'
'Good job!' written at the top of the paper
'This is wrong. See me after class.'
'Your effort on revising the argument really strengthened it; next, try adding a counterargument.'
questions.rationale: Growth-mindset, improvement-oriented feedback recognizes effort and process and points to a concrete next step. The statement praising revision effort and suggesting a counterargument does exactly this, unlike vague praise or ability-focused comments.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews a class data report showing that students consistently struggle with inference questions but excel at literal-recall questions. The MOST appropriate instructional adjustment is to:
options: Assign more literal-recall practice because students do well on it
Stop assessing reading comprehension altogether
Provide targeted instruction and modeling on inference strategies
Lower the difficulty of all future reading passages
questions.rationale: Data-driven instruction targets identified weaknesses. Since students struggle specifically with inference, the teacher should provide focused instruction and modeling on inference strategies rather than reinforcing an already-mastered skill or lowering expectations.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a single multiple-choice exit ticket to decide whether the whole class has mastered a complex writing skill. A colleague suggests this may be insufficient. The colleague's concern is BEST justified by the principle that:
options: Only summative tests can measure writing skills
Multiple-choice questions are always invalid
Exit tickets should never be used in writing instruction
A single assessment format may not fully capture a complex skill; multiple measures provide a more accurate picture of understanding
questions.rationale: Sound assessment practice uses multiple measures and formats, especially for complex skills, because a single item or format may not validly capture the full skill. The colleague rightly notes that a lone multiple-choice item may inadequately assess complex writing.

questions.stem: During a lesson, a teacher notices through quick whiteboard responses that most students are confidently mastering the planned task far faster than expected. The MOST responsive instructional adjustment is to:
options: Increase the challenge by introducing a more complex application or extension task
Continue with the planned pace and additional practice on the mastered skill
End the lesson early since students understand it
Give a surprise summative test immediately
questions.rationale: Adjusting instruction based on real-time evidence means responding to students who have mastered material by raising the challenge. Introducing a more complex application keeps learning rigorous and avoids wasting time on already-mastered content.

questions.stem: A teacher provides students with a rubric before they begin a project so they understand the criteria for success. Sharing the rubric in advance MOST directly helps students by:
options: Guaranteeing all students earn the same score
Replacing the need for any feedback
Reducing the teacher's grading time only
Clarifying expectations so students can self-monitor and aim for quality
questions.rationale: Providing a rubric in advance makes success criteria transparent, enabling students to understand expectations, self-monitor their work, and target quality—supporting both learning and self-assessment.

questions.stem: A teacher implements a brief 'cold-call with wait time' routine, posing a question, pausing, then calling on a non-volunteer. The instructional value of this check for understanding is that it:
options: Gives all students reason to think and provides the teacher a sample of understanding beyond eager volunteers
Replaces the need for written assessment
Ensures only confident volunteers participate
Speeds the lesson by skipping struggling students
questions.rationale: Cold-calling with wait time holds all students accountable to think and lets the teacher gather a more representative read on understanding than relying solely on volunteers, who may not reflect the whole class.

questions.stem: A teacher analyzes formative data and forms three flexible groups: one needing reteaching of foundational concepts, one ready for guided practice, and one ready for enrichment. A week later, new assessment data shows the groups' needs have shifted. The BEST practice is to:
options: Eliminate grouping and teach only whole class
Regroup students based on the new data so grouping remains responsive to current needs
Assign permanent group labels based on the first assessment
Keep the original groups fixed for the rest of the unit to maintain stability
questions.rationale: Flexible grouping should be data-driven and dynamic. As new assessment evidence reveals shifting needs, the teacher should regroup accordingly, ensuring instruction continually matches each student's current level rather than fixing groups permanently.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students time to revise their work after receiving feedback, then resubmit it. Building in this revision opportunity reflects the understanding that feedback is most effective when:
options: Students have the opportunity to act on it and improve their work
It focuses solely on assigning a numerical grade
It is given only at the end of the grading period
It is the final word and requires no further action
questions.rationale: Feedback drives learning only when students can act on it. Providing time to revise and resubmit closes the feedback loop, allowing students to apply guidance and improve—making the feedback meaningful rather than terminal.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that whole-class reteaching of a concept did not help a small group of students who still struggle, while the rest of the class has mastered it. The MOST appropriate next step is to:
options: Move on because most students have mastered the concept
Assign the struggling students the same independent worksheet as everyone else
Provide small-group or individualized targeted intervention for the students still struggling
Reteach the entire class again using the same method
questions.rationale: When a subset of students still struggles after whole-class reteaching, the responsive step is targeted small-group or individual intervention tailored to their needs, rather than repeating ineffective whole-class instruction or abandoning the students.

questions.stem: A teacher wants formative assessment data to genuinely improve learning rather than merely document it. Which practice most fully embodies the formative assessment cycle?
options: Recording exit-ticket scores in the gradebook without changing instruction
Eliciting evidence of learning, interpreting it, and adjusting upcoming instruction and feedback in response
Administering a single end-of-unit test and reporting the results
Using formative data only to rank students against one another
questions.rationale: The formative assessment cycle involves eliciting evidence of learning, interpreting it, and then adjusting instruction and feedback in response. Merely recording scores, giving a single summative test, or ranking students omits the essential 'act on the data' step that improves learning.

questions.stem: A teacher embeds a 'turn-and-talk' followed by a quick poll after introducing a new concept. The teacher then decides, based on the poll, whether to provide more examples or move to guided practice. This sequence best illustrates:
options: Assigning summative grades during direct instruction
Avoiding student interaction to save time
Using a check for understanding to make a real-time instructional decision
Postponing all assessment until the unit test
questions.rationale: The turn-and-talk and poll function as a check for understanding, and the teacher uses the resulting evidence to decide the next instructional move in the moment—an example of formative assessment driving real-time instructional decisions.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a student feedback by first noting a strength, then identifying one specific area to improve with a suggestion, and inviting the student to ask questions. This balanced, specific approach is most likely to:
options: Replace the need for any further instruction
Discourage the student from trying again
Focus the student only on the grade received
Help the student feel supported and understand concrete steps for improvement
questions.rationale: Feedback that is balanced, specific, and dialogic—naming a strength, a concrete improvement step, and inviting questions—helps students feel supported while giving them clear direction for growth.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews unit assessment data disaggregated by skill and notices that English learners scored well on computation but low on word problems, while the gap did not appear in computation-only items. The MOST instructionally sound interpretation and response is to:
options: Assume the data is unreliable and disregard it
Remove all word problems from future assessments
Conclude the English learners cannot do mathematics and lower their math placement
Recognize the gap may reflect language demands of word problems and provide language scaffolds while maintaining grade-level math content
questions.rationale: Disaggregated data showing strong computation but weak word-problem performance for English learners suggests the barrier is the language demand, not mathematical ability. The sound response is to scaffold language access while keeping rigorous grade-level math content.

questions.stem: A teacher realizes mid-lesson, from students' puzzled responses, that an explanation was confusing. The teacher pauses, re-explains the concept using a concrete analogy and a visual model, then checks again. This responsiveness best demonstrates the teacher's ability to:
options: Ignore student confusion to maintain pacing
Defer all clarification until the next unit
Adhere rigidly to the lesson plan regardless of student response
Adjust instruction in real time based on evidence of student understanding
questions.rationale: Recognizing confusion from student responses and immediately re-explaining with a new analogy and visual, then rechecking, exemplifies adjusting instruction in real time based on formative evidence of understanding.

questions.stem: A teacher tracks each student's progress toward a learning objective on a simple data chart updated after each formative check. The primary purpose of maintaining this chart is to:
options: Replace the report card
Monitor individual progress over time and inform decisions about support or enrichment
Publicly rank students from highest to lowest
Reduce the number of lessons taught
questions.rationale: Tracking individual progress on formative data over time helps the teacher monitor growth and make informed decisions about who needs additional support or enrichment—the central purpose of progress monitoring.

questions.stem: Two teachers give the same formative assessment. One uses the results only to enter scores; the other analyzes error patterns, identifies common misconceptions, plans targeted reteaching, and adjusts upcoming lessons. The key difference illustrating effective data-driven instruction is that the second teacher:
options: Assigns harder grades than the first teacher
Avoids giving any feedback to students
Closes the loop by using assessment evidence to diagnose needs and modify instruction
Spends less time on assessment
questions.rationale: Effective data-driven instruction goes beyond recording scores to analyzing patterns, diagnosing misconceptions, and adjusting instruction. The second teacher 'closes the loop' by using evidence to change teaching, which is what makes the practice instructionally powerful.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a lesson with planned 'pause points' where students respond on individual whiteboards before the teacher decides whether to proceed. The MOST important reason to build these checkpoints into the lesson plan in advance is to:
options: Ensure the teacher gathers evidence of understanding at key moments and can adjust instruction before misunderstandings accumulate
Fill extra time if the lesson runs short
Give students a break from listening
Guarantee the lesson finishes exactly on schedule
questions.rationale: Intentionally planned checkpoints ensure the teacher collects evidence of understanding at critical junctures and can adjust before gaps grow. Building them in advance makes monitoring deliberate rather than incidental, strengthening responsive instruction.

questions.stem: Ms. Alvarez wants to keep families regularly informed about classroom learning goals and upcoming projects in her third-grade class. Which approach would BEST support consistent, two-way communication throughout the year?
options: Establishing a weekly newsletter paired with a class messaging app that invites family questions and replies
Sending a single detailed packet home at the start of the school year describing all planned units
Posting grades to the online portal as the primary means of keeping families updated
Waiting until the scheduled fall and spring conferences to share information about classroom activities
questions.rationale: Effective family communication is ongoing and reciprocal. A regular newsletter combined with a messaging tool that invites replies provides frequent updates while creating an open channel for families to ask questions and respond, supporting genuine two-way communication.

questions.stem: Before a fall parent-teacher conference about a student's reading progress, a teacher is deciding how to open the meeting. Which opening would BEST set a collaborative, family-centered tone?
options: Presenting a printed chart of test scores and asking the family to read it silently
Starting with a specific strength the student has shown and inviting the family to share their observations from home
Reviewing the classroom rules and consequences the student is expected to follow
Beginning by listing the skills the student has not yet mastered so parents understand the concerns immediately
questions.rationale: Opening a conference by naming a genuine strength and inviting the family's perspective communicates respect, builds rapport, and frames the meeting as a shared partnership rather than a one-way report of deficits.

questions.stem: A teacher serves several families who primarily speak Vietnamese and have limited English proficiency. The school sends most communication home in English only. Which action by the teacher would MOST effectively promote equitable family engagement?
options: Relying on the students to translate all important messages and conference content for their parents
Encouraging these families to enroll in English classes so they can read school communications
Arranging for key communications to be translated and securing a qualified interpreter for conferences
Sending the same English materials but highlighting the most important sentences in bold
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive, equitable engagement requires removing language barriers. Providing translated materials and qualified interpreters ensures families can fully access information and participate meaningfully in their child's education.

questions.stem: During a conference, a father expresses frustration, saying he feels his son is being unfairly singled out for behavior issues. Which response by the teacher BEST demonstrates effective communication and partnership?
options: Explaining that classroom management decisions are the teacher's professional responsibility, not the parent's
Acknowledging the father's concern, asking for his perspective, and working together to identify supports for the student
Defending the documentation by reading each recorded incident aloud to prove the concerns are justified
Suggesting the conversation be paused until an administrator can join to mediate the disagreement
questions.rationale: Validating the parent's emotion, eliciting his perspective, and collaboratively planning supports de-escalates tension and reframes the situation as a shared problem-solving effort focused on the student's success.

questions.stem: A teacher in a diverse middle school wants families from various cultural backgrounds to feel that their knowledge and traditions are valued in the classroom. Which strategy reflects the MOST culturally responsive approach to family engagement?
options: Hosting one annual multicultural food night where families bring dishes representing their heritage
Inviting families throughout the year to share expertise, stories, and perspectives that connect to current units of study
Decorating the classroom with flags and posters representing the cultures present in the class
Asking each family to complete a survey describing their cultural background at the start of the year
questions.rationale: Authentic culturally responsive engagement treats families as ongoing knowledge resources, weaving their expertise and perspectives into instruction throughout the year rather than relegating culture to a single event or surface-level display.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher notices that families in a low-income, working-class community rarely attend daytime school events, and a colleague concludes these families 'just don't care about education.' Which interpretation and response by the teacher reflects the MOST professional and culturally responsive thinking?
options: Sending letters reminding all families that attendance at school events is an expectation of being a good parent
Concluding that engagement is not possible with this community and shifting all communication to the online portal
Agreeing that attendance reflects family priorities and focusing engagement efforts only on families who already attend
Recognizing that work schedules and access barriers may prevent attendance, and offering flexible times and alternative ways to engage
questions.rationale: Low attendance often reflects structural barriers such as inflexible work hours, transportation, or childcare rather than lack of caring. A culturally responsive teacher examines barriers and offers flexible, varied engagement opportunities that meet families where they are.

questions.stem: A teacher needs to inform a parent that her daughter has been struggling academically and emotionally over the past two weeks. Which method of initial communication is MOST appropriate for this situation?
options: A message posted on the class social media page encouraging families to check in with their children
A group email sent to all parents reminding them to monitor their children's well-being
A note sent home in the student's backpack briefly stating the concern
A personal phone call or scheduled meeting to discuss the concerns and listen to the family's perspective
questions.rationale: Sensitive concerns about a student's academic and emotional well-being warrant a personal, private, and interactive communication such as a phone call or meeting, which allows for dialogue, empathy, and collaborative planning.

questions.stem: A teacher wants families to play an active role in supporting learning at home. Which practice would MOST effectively empower families as partners in their child's academic growth?
options: Asking families to sign a contract committing to two hours of supervised homework each evening
Assigning lengthy worksheets each night so parents can see the curriculum being covered
Sharing specific, manageable strategies families can use during everyday routines to reinforce skills
Requesting that parents quiz their children nightly using flashcards the teacher provides
questions.rationale: Empowering families means offering accessible, realistic strategies that fit into daily life, enabling all families—regardless of resources or schedules—to meaningfully support learning and feel like genuine partners.

questions.stem: When documenting communication with families about a student's persistent attendance problems, which practice should the teacher follow to maintain professionalism and protect everyone involved?
options: Keeping documentation only when the family initiates contact, since the teacher's notes are personal
Avoiding written records to prevent the information from being used against the school later
Recording the date, content, and outcome of each contact using objective, factual language
Writing detailed notes that include the teacher's opinions about the family's parenting choices
questions.rationale: Professional documentation of family contact should be factual, objective, and complete—including dates, content, and outcomes—so that records accurately support the student, inform decisions, and reflect ethical practice.

questions.stem: A teacher is planning a back-to-school night and wants to ensure that families who may feel intimidated by formal school settings, including those who had negative school experiences themselves, feel welcomed and able to participate. Which combination of strategies BEST addresses this goal?
options: Holding a formal presentation in the auditorium followed by a question period at the microphone
Focusing the evening on a detailed review of grading policies and academic expectations
Creating an informal, welcoming environment with small-group conversations, translated materials, and personal greetings at the door
Requiring families to RSVP and submit written questions in advance so the evening stays on schedule
questions.rationale: Families with prior negative school experiences are more likely to engage when the environment is warm, informal, and inclusive. Personal greetings, small-group dialogue, and language access reduce intimidation and foster genuine participation.

questions.stem: A parent emails the teacher expressing concern that a recent group project grade seems unfair. The teacher is busy but wants to respond appropriately. Which response best reflects effective professional communication?
options: Forwarding the email to the principal and asking the principal to handle the parent's concern
Waiting several days to respond so the parent has time to calm down before the conversation
Sending a brief reply stating that the grade is final and was applied the same way for all students
Replying within a reasonable time, thanking the parent, clarifying how the grade was determined, and offering to discuss further
questions.rationale: Timely, respectful, and transparent communication maintains trust. Acknowledging the parent, explaining the grading process clearly, and offering further discussion demonstrates openness and a collaborative orientation.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to celebrate students' progress and strengthen relationships with families. Which form of family communication would best build positive rapport over time?
options: Posting a public ranking of top-performing students for families to view
Contacting families only when problems arise so that calls home carry clear weight
Sending a standardized congratulations certificate to every family at the end of the year
Periodically reaching out with positive notes or calls recognizing a student's growth or effort
questions.rationale: Proactive positive communication—personal notes or calls recognizing growth and effort—builds trust and goodwill, making families more receptive partners and balancing the perception that contact only means trouble.

questions.stem: A new teacher joins a grade-level professional learning community (PLC) that meets weekly. Which behavior would best demonstrate the teacher's effective participation in the PLC?
options: Listening quietly and implementing whatever the most experienced teacher recommends
Volunteering to take notes each week so others can focus on the discussion
Sharing student data, contributing ideas, and collaboratively analyzing instructional practices with colleagues
Using the meeting time to plan personal lessons while others discuss shared issues
questions.rationale: Effective PLC participation is active and collaborative: members share data, contribute ideas, and jointly analyze practice to improve student learning. This reflects the collective inquiry at the heart of professional learning communities.

questions.stem: A general education teacher co-teaches an inclusion class with a special education teacher. To make their collaboration most effective for students with disabilities, the two teachers should primarily focus on which practice?
options: Dividing the class so the special education teacher works only with students who have IEPs
Jointly planning lessons and sharing instructional responsibility so both teachers support all students
Having the special education teacher serve mainly as a classroom aide during the general teacher's lessons
Alternating full control of the class week by week to give each teacher autonomy
questions.rationale: Effective co-teaching relies on shared planning and shared instructional responsibility, with both educators supporting all learners. This integrated model leverages both teachers' expertise and avoids segregating students by disability status.

questions.stem: A teacher supervises a paraprofessional assigned to support a small group of students who need additional reading practice. Which action by the teacher reflects the most appropriate working relationship with the paraprofessional?
options: Assigning the paraprofessional clerical tasks so the teacher can work with the reading group personally
Clearly communicating instructional goals, modeling expected strategies, and providing ongoing guidance and feedback
Limiting the paraprofessional's role to monitoring behavior while the teacher handles all instruction
Allowing the paraprofessional to design and lead the reading intervention independently
questions.rationale: The teacher retains responsibility for instructional direction. Communicating goals, modeling strategies, and offering ongoing feedback enables the paraprofessional to support students effectively within a clearly defined, supervised role.

questions.stem: After teaching a unit, a teacher writes in a journal about which strategies worked, which students struggled, and what to change next time. This practice is BEST described as an example of which professional behavior?
options: Curriculum mapping for the academic year
Summative assessment of student mastery
Standardized data reporting for accountability
Reflective practice that informs instructional improvement
questions.rationale: Systematically thinking back on what worked, what did not, and what to adjust is reflective practice. This habit drives continuous improvement of instruction and is a core element of professional growth.

questions.stem: A teacher attends a district workshop on a new differentiation strategy. To make the professional development most likely to improve student outcomes, what should the teacher do next?
options: Wait until the next school year to introduce the strategy so the current routine is not disrupted
Implement the strategy in the classroom, monitor its effects on learning, and refine it based on results
File the workshop materials for reference in case the strategy is ever needed
Share a summary of the workshop with colleagues without trying the strategy personally
questions.rationale: Professional development has the greatest impact when teachers apply new learning, monitor its effect on students, and adjust based on evidence. This cycle of implementation and reflection turns training into improved practice.

questions.stem: A second-year teacher is assigned a veteran teacher as a mentor. Which approach would allow the new teacher to benefit MOST from the mentoring relationship?
options: Regularly seeking feedback, observing the mentor, and openly discussing instructional challenges and goals
Asking the mentor to provide complete lesson plans so the new teacher can avoid mistakes
Limiting interactions to required meetings to avoid taking up the mentor's valuable time
Demonstrating competence by handling all challenges independently and reporting only successes
questions.rationale: A mentoring relationship is most valuable when the new teacher actively engages—seeking feedback, observing effective practice, and candidly discussing challenges. This openness accelerates professional growth and reflective improvement.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that students who are English learners consistently underperform on her end-of-unit assessments despite participating well in class. Reflecting on this pattern, which course of action best demonstrates professional reflection leading to improvement?
options: Concluding that the assessments accurately reflect the students' current abilities and continuing as planned
Lowering the passing threshold for English learners so their scores appear more comparable
Examining whether the assessment format may be creating language barriers and consulting an ESL specialist to adjust her approach
Reducing the rigor of instruction for English learners to match their assessment performance
questions.rationale: Genuine reflective practice probes possible causes—here, whether the assessment itself poses language barriers—and seeks expert collaboration to address them. Consulting an ESL specialist to adjust assessment supports improvement without lowering expectations.

questions.stem: A student in a teacher's class shows signs of a possible learning disability that the teacher is not equipped to diagnose. Which action reflects the most appropriate use of professional collaboration and school resources?
options: Modifying the student's grades so the difficulties are less noticeable on the report card
Independently researching disabilities online and informing the parents of a likely diagnosis
Waiting to see whether the difficulties resolve on their own over the next several months
Referring the concern through the school's established support process and collaborating with specialists to evaluate the student's needs
questions.rationale: Teachers are not qualified to diagnose disabilities. The appropriate step is to use the school's referral and support structures and collaborate with specialists who can properly evaluate the student and determine needed supports.

questions.stem: Two teachers on a team disagree about how to pace an upcoming shared unit, and the tension is beginning to affect their collaboration. Which approach would best resolve the conflict while preserving a productive professional relationship?
options: Asking the principal to decide the pacing so neither teacher has to concede
Deferring to whichever teacher has more years of experience to settle the matter quickly
Discussing their differing rationales, focusing on shared student-learning goals, and seeking a data-informed compromise
Each teacher proceeding with her own pacing independently to avoid further disagreement
questions.rationale: Professional conflict is best resolved through respectful dialogue centered on shared goals and evidence. By discussing rationales and using student-learning data to find common ground, the teachers preserve collaboration and serve students well.

questions.stem: A teacher sets a personal goal to strengthen her use of technology for instruction. Which action best reflects ongoing, self-directed professional development toward this goal?
options: Waiting for the district to mandate technology training before taking any action
Purchasing new classroom devices and assuming improved instruction will follow
Asking a colleague to handle all technology-based activities in her classroom
Identifying relevant courses or resources, applying new tools in lessons, and evaluating their impact on student learning
questions.rationale: Self-directed professional growth involves proactively seeking learning opportunities, applying new skills, and assessing their effect on students. This goal-driven, reflective cycle characterizes a teacher committed to continuous improvement.

questions.stem: A counselor shares with a teacher that a student is experiencing significant stress at home that may be affecting the student's behavior and focus. How should the teacher handle this collaborative information most professionally?
options: Using the information to provide appropriate support and accommodations while maintaining the student's confidentiality
Sharing the information with the class so peers can be more understanding of the student
Documenting the details in a public classroom log for substitute teachers to reference
Discussing the situation with other parents who ask why the student has been acting differently
questions.rationale: Collaborating with specialists like counselors helps teachers support students, but the information must be handled confidentially. The teacher should use it to inform supports while protecting the student's and family's privacy.

questions.stem: A teacher is invited to join a school committee that reviews schoolwide literacy data and recommends instructional improvements. Participating in this committee BEST reflects which aspect of professional practice?
options: Contributing to the broader school community and engaging in collaborative, data-informed decision making
Gaining authority over colleagues' instructional decisions across the school
Fulfilling minimum contractual obligations required of all staff
Reducing classroom workload by spending time in meetings instead of teaching
questions.rationale: Serving on a schoolwide committee that analyzes data and shapes instruction reflects a teacher's role as a contributing member of the professional community, engaging in collaborative leadership and data-informed improvement beyond the individual classroom.

questions.stem: A teacher receives constructive feedback from an instructional coach indicating that her questioning techniques rarely require students to reason beyond recall. Which response best demonstrates a professional, growth-oriented disposition?
options: Explaining to the coach that recall questions are appropriate because they keep all students engaged
Reflecting on the feedback, studying higher-order questioning strategies, and intentionally practicing them with the coach's support
Concluding that the coach does not understand the unique needs of her particular students
Continuing her current questioning approach since her students generally perform adequately on tests
questions.rationale: A growth-oriented professional treats constructive feedback as an opportunity to improve. Reflecting, studying higher-order questioning, and deliberately practicing with coaching support exemplifies openness to feedback and commitment to continuous development.

questions.stem: During a parent-teacher conference, a parent asks Ms. Alvarez how her son's reading scores compare to the specific scores of other named students in the class. What is the most appropriate response under FERPA?
options: Share the comparison because parents have a right to know their child's standing
Email the full class score list so the parent can review it at home
Provide the names but not the exact scores of the other students
Decline to disclose other students' individual records and discuss only the parent's own child
questions.rationale: FERPA protects the educational records of each student. A teacher may discuss only the parent's own child's records and must not disclose other students' personally identifiable information to a third party.

questions.stem: A first-year Texas teacher notices unexplained bruising and hears a student describe being hit at home. Under Texas law, what must the teacher do?
options: Discuss concerns directly with the parents before reporting
Wait to gather more evidence before deciding whether to report
Report the suspected abuse to the appropriate authorities, typically within 48 hours
Refer the matter only to the campus counselor and take no further action
questions.rationale: Texas law makes educators mandatory reporters who must personally report suspected child abuse or neglect to the appropriate authorities, generally within 48 hours of first suspecting it. The duty cannot be delegated.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to photocopy a short poem from a current magazine to use as a one-time supplemental example in a single lesson. Under the fair use guidelines for education, this use is most likely:
options: Prohibited unless the teacher copies the entire magazine
Permissible only if the teacher sells the copies to students
Prohibited, because any copying of copyrighted material is illegal
Permissible, as a brief, spontaneous use for a nonprofit educational purpose
questions.rationale: Fair use factors favor brief, spontaneous copying of a small portion of a work for a nonprofit educational purpose that does not harm the market for the original. A single short poem used once in one class generally qualifies.

questions.stem: Which of the following best reflects appropriate professional boundaries between a teacher and students?
options: Keeping communication professional and routed through approved school channels
Communicating with students privately through personal social-media accounts
Giving select students access to the teacher's home for tutoring after hours
Sharing personal financial difficulties with students to build rapport
questions.rationale: Maintaining professional boundaries means keeping interactions appropriate and conducting communication through approved, transparent school channels rather than private or personal venues.

questions.stem: A teacher suspects a colleague has been falsifying student attendance records to improve the campus's reported numbers. Under the Texas Educators' Code of Ethics, what is the teacher's most appropriate action?
options: Ignore the situation because it involves another teacher's records
Report the suspected falsification to the appropriate administrator or authority
Confront the colleague and agree to keep the matter private
Alter his own records to match so the data appears consistent
questions.rationale: The Code of Ethics requires honesty in official records and prohibits falsifying data. An educator aware of such misconduct has an ethical obligation to report it through proper channels rather than ignore or participate in it.

questions.stem: During an ARD meeting, the parents disagree with the proposed placement for their child and want to challenge the decision. Which procedural safeguard under IDEA is most directly available to them?
options: Filing a request for a due process hearing
Requiring the teacher to redesign the curriculum unilaterally
Removing the child from the district immediately
Voting to override the rest of the committee
questions.rationale: IDEA's procedural safeguards give parents the right to resolve disputes through mechanisms including mediation and a due process hearing, ensuring disagreements over identification, evaluation, or placement can be formally challenged.

questions.stem: A third-grade teacher notices a student who repeatedly struggles with accurate and fluent word recognition, poor spelling, and decoding despite adequate instruction and intelligence. These characteristics are most consistent with which condition that triggers specific evaluation procedures in Texas?
options: An emotional disturbance
A hearing impairment
Dyslexia
A speech articulation disorder
questions.rationale: Dyslexia is characterized by difficulties with accurate and fluent word recognition and by poor spelling and decoding abilities, typically unexpected in relation to other cognitive abilities. Texas law requires districts to screen for and address dyslexia.

questions.stem: A teacher posts a complaint on a public social-media page naming a specific student and describing the student's misbehavior in detail. This action most clearly violates which professional obligation?
options: The school's dress code policy
The duty to maintain student confidentiality and the Code of Ethics
Copyright law
The requirement to attend faculty meetings
questions.rationale: Publicly identifying a student and sharing details about their behavior breaches confidentiality and violates the Texas Educators' Code of Ethics standards on protecting students and maintaining professional conduct.

questions.stem: A teacher accepts an expensive personal gift from a parent shortly before final grades are assigned and the parent hints it would be nice if the child earned an A. The most significant ethical concern is:
options: The parent failed to follow the school's volunteer policy
The gift creates a conflict of interest and risk of improper influence on grading
The teacher should have requested a more valuable gift
The teacher exceeded the classroom supply budget
questions.rationale: Accepting a valuable gift tied to an expectation about grades creates a conflict of interest and compromises the integrity and fairness of evaluation, which the Code of Ethics prohibits.

questions.stem: A general-education teacher receives a copy of a student's IEP. Which practice best aligns with legal and professional responsibilities?
options: Ignoring the accommodations because they were not designed by this teacher
Discussing the student's diagnosis with other parents to gather advice
Leaving the IEP on a shared desk so substitutes can read it
Implementing the required accommodations and keeping the document confidential
questions.rationale: Teachers are legally obligated to implement the accommodations and modifications in a student's IEP and to safeguard the confidentiality of that protected record.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to show a full-length commercially purchased movie purely as a Friday reward unrelated to the curriculum. Regarding copyright and fair use, this is best described as:
options: Permitted only if the movie is over ten years old
Clearly permitted because the school owns a copy of the movie
Likely outside the face-to-face teaching exemption because it is not for instructional purposes
Always permitted as long as students are not charged admission
questions.rationale: The face-to-face teaching exemption allows display of lawfully obtained works for instruction, but showing a film purely for entertainment unrelated to teaching falls outside that exemption and may require a public performance license.

questions.stem: A teacher is asked to administer a state assessment but realizes the testing accommodations listed in a student's IEP were not provided. The most appropriate response is to:
options: Exempt the student from the assessment without consulting anyone
Notify the appropriate testing coordinator/administrator so required accommodations are provided
Proceed without the accommodations to keep testing on schedule
Provide additional accommodations of the teacher's own choosing not in the IEP
questions.rationale: IEP-required testing accommodations are legally mandated. The teacher should alert the testing coordinator or administrator to ensure the documented accommodations are properly provided rather than ignore them or invent unauthorized ones.

questions.stem: Which scenario best illustrates a teacher upholding the Code of Ethics standard regarding professional and ethical conduct toward the profession?
options: Sharing exam answer keys with friends seeking the same certification
Misrepresenting their certification status to obtain a coaching stipend
Accurately representing their qualifications and refraining from falsifying professional credentials
Claiming credit for a colleague's lesson plans in a portfolio review
questions.rationale: The Code of Ethics requires educators to be truthful about their qualifications and credentials and to avoid misrepresentation or falsification in professional matters.

questions.stem: A student with a disability commits a serious behavioral infraction, and the school proposes a long-term suspension that would constitute a change of placement. Before the removal, what does IDEA require the ARD/IEP team to conduct?
options: A vote by the general-education faculty
A manifestation determination review to decide whether the behavior was caused by the disability
An immediate expulsion hearing with no further review
A standardized achievement retest of the student
questions.rationale: When a disciplinary removal constitutes a change of placement, IDEA requires a manifestation determination review to decide whether the conduct was caused by, or had a direct and substantial relationship to, the student's disability or resulted from failure to implement the IEP.

questions.stem: A parent requests a comprehensive special-education evaluation, but the campus team prefers to continue informal interventions and delays consenting to evaluate. Which legal principle most directly addresses the district's obligation in this situation?
options: The fair use doctrine governing instructional materials
The face-to-face teaching exemption
The child-find duty to identify, locate, and evaluate students who may need special education
The directory-information provision of FERPA
questions.rationale: IDEA's child-find mandate obligates districts to identify, locate, and evaluate all children suspected of having a disability and needing special education; a district cannot use ongoing interventions to indefinitely delay a requested evaluation.

questions.stem: A teacher believes a student would benefit from a more restrictive, self-contained placement primarily because the student's frequent questions slow the pace of the general-education class. Why is this reasoning legally problematic under IDEA?
options: Self-contained placements are illegal under all circumstances
Only the principal may determine any student's placement
Placement decisions must be driven by the student's needs and LRE, not by classroom convenience
Teachers may never recommend changes to a student's placement
questions.rationale: Under LRE, removal to a more restrictive setting is justified only when the student's needs cannot be met in the general setting with supplementary aids and services, not because the student's presence is inconvenient for pacing.

questions.stem: A district wants to publish students' names, photographs, and grade levels in a graduation program. Under FERPA, what is the appropriate way to handle this disclosure?
options: Obtain a court order before listing any student's name
Disclose only the names of students with the highest grades
Publish freely because graduation programs are exempt from FERPA
Treat the items as directory information that may be disclosed only after proper notice and an opportunity for parents to opt out
questions.rationale: Names, photographs, and grade levels can be designated as directory information, which may be disclosed without consent only if the school has given parents annual notice and a reasonable chance to opt out of such disclosures.

questions.stem: A teacher develops a strong friendship with a student's family, begins spending significant unsupervised personal time alone with the student outside school, and gives the student gifts not provided to others. The most accurate professional analysis is that the teacher is:
options: Fulfilling a required mentoring duty under Texas law
Engaging in grooming-type boundary violations that the Code of Ethics is designed to prevent
Acting appropriately as long as the parents are aware
Demonstrating exemplary commitment that should be encouraged
questions.rationale: A pattern of unsupervised one-on-one contact, special treatment, and gifts to a single student reflects boundary violations associated with grooming behaviors that the Code of Ethics and professional standards explicitly prohibit to protect students.

questions.stem: Ms. Alvarez, a third-grade teacher, notices that her students can hold only a few new vocabulary words in mind at once before they begin to forget the earliest ones. Which component of the information-processing model is most directly responsible for this limitation?
options: Working memory
Retrieval cue system
Long-term memory
Sensory register
questions.rationale: Working memory has a limited capacity and duration, which is why only a small amount of information can be actively held and manipulated at one time before it decays without rehearsal.

questions.stem: A middle school science teacher wants to reduce extraneous cognitive load during a lesson on the water cycle. Which instructional choice would BEST accomplish this goal?
options: Placing labels directly on the diagram rather than in a separate legend
Adding background music and decorative clip art to the slides
Reading aloud text that is already displayed word-for-word on the screen
Presenting all steps of the cycle on a single dense slide at once
questions.rationale: Integrating labels directly into the diagram applies the spatial-contiguity principle, reducing the extraneous load of searching back and forth between a legend and the image.

questions.stem: Two teachers disagree about a presentation. Mr. Chen says, 'Show the animation and read the narration text on screen at the same time so students get it twice.'
