Ms. Okafor says, 'Show the animation with spoken narration only, and remove the on-screen text.' According to dual-coding and multimedia learning theory, whose approach is more defensible and why?
options: Mr. Chen, because repeating information in two visual forms strengthens memory
Ms. Okafor, because identical on-screen text and narration cause a redundancy effect that overloads the visual channel
Ms. Okafor, because spoken words are always remembered better than images
Mr. Chen, because more text always increases the depth of processing
questions.rationale: Dual coding works best when information is split across the visual and auditory channels. Presenting identical text and narration forces both into competition within the visual channel (reading) plus auditory, producing a redundancy effect that overloads working memory.

questions.stem: In a fourth-grade classroom, Mr. Davis activates students' prior knowledge of farm animals before reading a story set on a ranch. From the perspective of schema theory, what is the primary benefit of this practice?
options: It replaces the need for any new learning during the lesson
It guarantees that all students will reach the same interpretation
It eliminates the need for students to use working memory
It provides an existing mental framework into which new story details can be organized
questions.rationale: Schema theory holds that activating relevant prior knowledge gives learners an organized framework to connect and integrate incoming information, improving comprehension and retention.

questions.stem: A high school history teacher gives a brief quiz at the start of each class covering material from previous weeks, with no grade penalty. Which cognitive principle BEST explains why this practice strengthens long-term retention?
options: The serial-position primacy effect
The retrieval-practice (testing) effect
The mere-exposure effect
Operant extinction
questions.rationale: Actively retrieving information from long-term memory strengthens the memory trace and improves later recall more than simply re-reading. This is the retrieval-practice or testing effect.

questions.stem: Ms. Romero teaches her chemistry students to remember the activity series of metals by grouping the elements into three meaningful clusters and giving each cluster a memorable name. This strategy primarily helps students overcome the limits of working memory through which process?
options: Maintenance rehearsal
Stimulus generalization
Sensory adaptation
Chunking
questions.rationale: Chunking groups individual items into larger meaningful units, allowing more total information to be held within the limited capacity of working memory.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher designs a unit in which students investigate a local pond, form their own hypotheses, gather data, and revise their explanations through discussion. This approach is MOST consistent with which theoretical orientation to learning?
options: Operant conditioning
Behaviorism
Constructivism
Maturationism
questions.rationale: Constructivism emphasizes learners actively building knowledge through inquiry, hypothesis testing, and social discussion, which matches the described pond investigation.

questions.stem: All of the following are characteristic of a behaviorist approach to classroom management EXCEPT:
options: Providing immediate, consistent consequences for actions
Using a token economy to reinforce desired behaviors
Shaping behavior through successive approximations of a goal
Helping students reflect on and reconstruct their own understanding of fairness
questions.rationale: Behaviorism focuses on observable behavior and external reinforcement. Helping students reflect on and reconstruct their own understanding is a constructivist, internally focused practice.

questions.stem: A teacher observes that students solve practice problems easily when the worked examples are visible but struggle on a test without them. From a cognitive-load perspective, what is the most likely explanation, and what is the BEST next step?
options: Students have not yet built schemas in long-term memory; the teacher should gradually fade the worked examples
Students have too much intrinsic load; the teacher should remove the topic from the curriculum
Students' sensory registers are overloaded; the teacher should dim the lights
Students lack motivation; the teacher should add competitive rewards
questions.rationale: Reliance on visible examples indicates that automated schemas have not yet formed in long-term memory. Gradually fading worked examples (the guidance-fading effect) builds independent schema use while managing germane load.

questions.stem: Mr. Lee wants new information to move from working memory into long-term memory in a durable, retrievable form. Which student activity would BEST promote this transfer?
options: Listening passively while the teacher lectures
Copying definitions verbatim several times
Connecting new concepts to personal experiences and explaining them in their own words
Highlighting large portions of the textbook
questions.rationale: Elaborative encoding, in which learners connect new material to prior knowledge and restate it in their own words, produces deeper processing and more durable, retrievable long-term memories.

questions.stem: According to Erikson's psychosocial theory, the central conflict that most elementary-age students (roughly ages 6–11) work through is:
options: Trust vs. mistrust
Industry vs. inferiority
Identity vs. role confusion
Initiative vs. guilt
questions.rationale: Erikson identified industry vs. inferiority as the stage of middle childhood, when children develop a sense of competence through school tasks and comparison with peers.

questions.stem: A high school student frequently disrupts class and shows little interest in academics. The counselor learns the student is often hungry and uncertain where they will sleep. Using Maslow's hierarchy of needs, what is the teacher's most appropriate FIRST consideration?
options: Assigning extra homework to increase engagement
Immediately raising academic expectations to build self-esteem
Publicly praising the student to boost motivation
Connecting the student with resources that address food and shelter security
questions.rationale: Maslow's hierarchy holds that basic physiological and safety needs must be reasonably met before higher needs like esteem and self-actualization can be effectively pursued. Addressing food and shelter comes first.

questions.stem: After a difficult math test, Ms. Patel tells a struggling student, 'You haven't mastered this yet, but your strategy is improving and effort like that pays off.' This feedback is MOST aligned with which concept?
options: Extrinsic token reinforcement
Fixed mindset reinforcement
Growth mindset cultivation
Learned helplessness
questions.rationale: Praising effort, strategy, and the word 'yet' frames ability as improvable through effort and process, which is the hallmark of cultivating a growth mindset.

questions.stem: Which classroom practice BEST supports the development of students' self-management, one of the core competencies in social and emotional learning (SEL)?
options: Grading homework promptly
Posting the daily schedule on the board
Teaching and modeling strategies for calming down when frustrated
Arranging desks in rows
questions.rationale: Self-management in SEL involves regulating emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. Teaching and modeling calming strategies directly builds students' capacity to manage frustration.

questions.stem: During a lecture, a teacher pauses every ten minutes to have students summarize the key idea to a partner. Which is the LEAST accurate description of how this benefits learning?
options: It allows students to retrieve and reconstruct what they heard
It provides an opportunity to rehearse and encode information
It reduces the risk of working-memory overload from continuous input
It transfers information directly into long-term memory without any effort
questions.rationale: The pause-and-summarize technique helps because it requires active rehearsal, retrieval, and reduces overload. The claim that it transfers information effortlessly is inaccurate; effortful processing is what produces durable encoding.

questions.stem: A teacher introduces a complex statistics concept by first reviewing the simpler component skills (calculating a mean, finding deviations) before combining them. From cognitive-load theory, this sequencing primarily manages which type of load, and how?
options: Intrinsic load, by reducing element interactivity until components are partly automated
Extraneous load, by adding more visual decoration
Sensory load, by limiting the number of senses used
Germane load, by removing all connections to prior knowledge
questions.rationale: Intrinsic load arises from element interactivity in the material itself. Pre-teaching component skills so they become partly automated reduces the number of interacting elements students must hold simultaneously, managing intrinsic load.

questions.stem: Two educators discuss a kindergartner who hesitates to try new activities and asks permission constantly. Mr. Flores says, 'Push them to comply quietly.' Ms. Nguyen says, 'Encourage them to make small choices and explore safely.' According to Erikson, which response better supports the child's current developmental stage and why?
options: Mr. Flores, because limiting choices builds industry
Ms. Nguyen, because encouraging exploration and choice supports initiative vs. guilt
Ms. Nguyen, because permissiveness resolves identity vs. role confusion
Mr. Flores, because compliance resolves the trust vs. mistrust crisis
questions.rationale: Children in early childhood are navigating Erikson's initiative vs. guilt stage. Supporting safe exploration and self-directed choices fosters initiative, while excessive control can foster guilt and dependence.

questions.stem: A teacher presents a labeled diagram alongside a spoken explanation rather than presenting the same information as a long paragraph of text alone. Which learning principle does this BEST illustrate?
options: Classical conditioning
The law of effect
The dual-coding principle
Negative reinforcement
questions.rationale: Dual-coding theory proposes that information processed through both visual and verbal channels is encoded and retained more effectively than information processed through a single channel.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to support students' responsible decision-making, an SEL competency, during a group conflict. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Guiding students to identify the problem, consider options, and evaluate consequences before choosing a solution
Allowing the loudest student to decide the outcome
Telling students to ignore the disagreement and move on
Immediately assigning blame and a punishment to end the conflict
questions.rationale: Responsible decision-making in SEL involves identifying problems, analyzing situations, generating options, and evaluating consequences. Guiding students through this process builds the competency.

questions.stem: Students in Ms. Bauer's class can recite the steps of long division but cannot apply the procedure to a real word problem. From an information-processing standpoint, this most likely indicates that the knowledge is:
options: Encoded in a rote, isolated form lacking meaningful connections
Permanently lost from long-term memory
Stored as well-connected, flexible schemas
Held only in the sensory register
questions.rationale: The ability to recite steps but not transfer them suggests rote, decontextualized encoding. Knowledge stored without meaningful connections to problem contexts does not transfer flexibly.

questions.stem: A teacher praises a student by saying, 'You're so smart, you got them all right!' Over time the student begins avoiding challenging tasks. Drawing on mindset research, what is the most likely cause and the BEST corrective strategy?
options: The student needs more tangible rewards; introduce prizes for correct answers
The praise fostered a fixed mindset; shift to praising effort, strategies, and persistence
The student lacks ability; reduce task difficulty permanently
The praise built intrinsic motivation; continue praising intelligence
questions.rationale: Praising intelligence can foster a fixed mindset, leading students to avoid challenges that might threaten their 'smart' label. Praising effort, strategy, and persistence promotes a growth mindset and willingness to take on challenges.

questions.stem: A teacher distributes review of a unit across several short sessions over two weeks rather than one long cram session the night before the test. This practice draws on which principle of effective learning?
options: The recency effect
The spacing (distributed practice) effect
Massed practice
Sensory gating
questions.rationale: The spacing effect shows that distributing study over time produces more durable long-term retention than massing the same study into one block.

questions.stem: A teacher begins each morning by having students identify and name how they are feeling using an emotions chart. This routine most directly develops which SEL competency?
options: Relationship skills
Self-awareness
Responsible decision-making
Social awareness
questions.rationale: Self-awareness in SEL includes the ability to recognize and accurately label one's own emotions. Naming feelings on an emotions chart directly builds this competency.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a multimedia lesson and finds that low-prior-knowledge learners benefit from detailed on-screen guidance, while high-prior-knowledge learners actually perform worse with the same guidance. This pattern is BEST explained by which concept?
options: The primacy effect
Stimulus discrimination
The expertise-reversal effect
The Hawthorne effect
questions.rationale: The expertise-reversal effect describes how instructional supports that help novices can hinder experts, because for experts the extra guidance becomes redundant and adds extraneous cognitive load.

questions.stem: Mr. Tran uses a scaffolded approach: he models a skill, then guides students through it together, then has them practice independently. This gradual release of responsibility is most directly grounded in which theoretical idea?
options: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development
Skinner's schedules of reinforcement
Pavlov's conditioned reflex
Thorndike's law of exercise
questions.rationale: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development describes tasks a learner can accomplish with guidance but not yet alone. Scaffolding and gradual release move support within this zone toward independence.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST describes the function of the sensory register in the information-processing model?
options: It retrieves stored knowledge on demand
It permanently stores all life experiences
It briefly holds incoming sensory information until attention selects some of it for further processing
It manipulates and reasons about a few items at a time
questions.rationale: The sensory register holds large amounts of raw sensory input for a very brief period; attention determines which information moves on to working memory for further processing.

questions.stem: In a project-based learning unit, a teacher serves as a facilitator who poses questions, provides resources, and lets students construct explanations through collaboration. A colleague argues the teacher should instead deliver direct instruction and have students memorize the answers. Which statement BEST captures the constructivist rationale for the original approach?
options: Knowledge is most durable when transmitted unchanged from teacher to student
Collaboration prevents any meaningful individual learning
Memorization of facts is the highest goal of instruction
Learners build understanding more deeply when they actively construct and connect ideas themselves
questions.rationale: Constructivism holds that learners actively build knowledge by connecting new ideas to existing understanding, often through inquiry and collaboration, producing deeper and more transferable learning than passive transmission.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to relate a new poem to their own lives, creating richer, more memorable associations. Which encoding strategy is she promoting?
options: Maintenance rehearsal
Elaborative rehearsal
Overlearning of isolated facts
Rote memorization
questions.rationale: Elaborative rehearsal links new information to existing knowledge and personal meaning, producing deeper processing and stronger long-term retention than simple repetition.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a capable seventh grader has stopped completing assignments, saying, 'There's no point, I always fail anyway.' Considering both attribution and motivation theory, which intervention is MOST appropriate?
options: Telling the student that some people are just not good at school
Lowering expectations so the student rarely encounters difficulty
Removing all feedback so the student does not feel discouraged
Helping the student attribute outcomes to controllable factors like effort and strategy, and structuring early successes
questions.rationale: The student shows signs of learned helplessness and maladaptive attributions (failure seen as stable and uncontrollable). Reframing outcomes as due to controllable factors and arranging early successes rebuilds a sense of efficacy and motivation.

questions.stem: Which scenario BEST illustrates a student using a schema to comprehend new information?
options: A student stares blankly at a passage with no idea what it is about
A student forgets material immediately after a test
A student who has eaten at restaurants quickly understands a story about ordering food by drawing on what they know about menus and servers
A student copies a paragraph word-for-word without reading it
questions.rationale: A schema is an organized mental framework. Using prior 'restaurant' knowledge to interpret a new story exemplifies how schemas support comprehension of related new information.

questions.stem: A teacher establishes class norms collaboratively, holds regular community circles, and teaches conflict-resolution language. These practices most directly build which two SEL competencies?
options: Decision-making and academic content knowledge
Self-awareness and self-management only
Sensory processing and memory consolidation
Social awareness and relationship skills
questions.rationale: Collaborative norms, community circles, and conflict-resolution language develop students' understanding of others' perspectives (social awareness) and their ability to communicate and cooperate (relationship skills).

questions.stem: During a complex lab procedure, a teacher provides a step-by-step checklist so students do not have to hold all instructions in mind at once. This support primarily functions to:
options: Increase the intrinsic difficulty of the content
Offload demands from limited working memory so capacity is freed for learning
Eliminate the need for long-term memory
Reduce student motivation by oversimplifying
questions.rationale: An external checklist serves as a cognitive aid that offloads procedural steps from working memory, freeing limited capacity for the conceptual aspects of the task.

questions.stem: Which teacher action BEST reflects a behaviorist principle of reinforcement?
options: Asking students to reflect on how their understanding has changed
Awarding a sticker each time a student turns in homework on time, increasing the behavior
Encouraging students to construct their own meaning from an experiment
Having students debate multiple interpretations of a text
questions.rationale: Behaviorism explains learning through consequences. Awarding a sticker to increase on-time homework is positive reinforcement, a core behaviorist principle.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a lesson that deliberately includes well-chosen practice problems requiring students to compare and contrast examples, which increases mental effort directed at building understanding. According to cognitive-load theory, this beneficial effort is best categorized as:
options: Extraneous load
Germane load
Intrinsic load
Sensory load
questions.rationale: Germane load is the productive mental effort devoted to processing information and constructing or automating schemas. Comparing and contrasting examples to build understanding is germane load.

questions.stem: Two teachers discuss adolescent identity development. Ms. Carter says high schoolers should be given opportunities to explore different roles, values, and interests. Mr. Hayes says they should simply be told who to be to avoid confusion. According to Erikson, why is Ms. Carter's view better supported?
options: Because exploration of roles and values supports healthy resolution of the identity vs. role confusion stage
Because identity is fully formed before adolescence and exploration is irrelevant
Because adolescents are in the trust vs. mistrust stage and need exploration
Because telling students who to be resolves the industry vs. inferiority crisis
questions.rationale: Adolescents are in Erikson's identity vs. role confusion stage. Opportunities to explore roles, values, and beliefs help them form a coherent personal identity rather than experience role confusion.

questions.stem: A teacher notices students consistently recall the first and last items of a vocabulary list better than the middle items. This pattern is BEST explained by:
options: Cognitive dissonance
The expertise-reversal effect
The serial-position effect (primacy and recency)
Negative transfer
questions.rationale: The serial-position effect describes superior recall of items at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of a list compared with middle items, reflecting how information is processed and stored.

questions.stem: A teacher who wants to strengthen students' empathy and ability to consider viewpoints different from their own is primarily targeting which SEL competency?
options: Self-management
Self-awareness
Social awareness
Responsible decision-making
questions.rationale: Social awareness in SEL includes empathy and the ability to take the perspective of others, including those from diverse backgrounds.

questions.stem: When introducing a new abstract concept, a teacher uses a concrete analogy to something students already understand. From a cognitive standpoint, the analogy works mainly because it:
options: Connects the new concept to an existing schema, making it easier to integrate
Removes the need for students to think about the concept
Stores the concept in the sensory register for long-term use
Increases extraneous load by adding unrelated detail
questions.rationale: A well-chosen analogy links new, abstract material to a familiar schema in long-term memory, providing a framework that makes the new concept easier to understand and remember.

questions.stem: A teacher implements an SEL program but a colleague claims that focusing on emotions wastes academic time. Which response BEST reflects the research-based rationale for integrating SEL?
options: Emotions have no measurable effect on cognition or learning
SEL is only appropriate for students with behavioral diagnoses
SEL should replace academic instruction entirely
Developing self-regulation and relationship skills supports the engagement and focus that underlie academic learning
questions.rationale: Research indicates that SEL competencies such as self-regulation and positive relationships support attention, engagement, and a productive classroom climate, which in turn enhance academic achievement rather than detracting from it.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to assess whether students have built robust, transferable schemas rather than rote knowledge. Which assessment task would provide the STRONGEST evidence of deep schema development?
options: A novel problem that requires applying the concept in an unfamiliar context
A timed test of how quickly students can recite memorized facts
A matching quiz pairing terms with textbook definitions
A fill-in-the-blank worksheet using the exact wording from notes
questions.rationale: Transfer to novel, unfamiliar contexts is the strongest evidence that knowledge is organized into flexible schemas rather than memorized in a rote, context-bound form.

questions.stem: A teacher consistently provides choices, supports student autonomy, and helps students see the relevance of tasks. According to self-determination theory, which need is the teacher LEAST directly supporting through these specific actions?
options: Sense of control over one's work
Autonomy
Relevance and ownership of learning
Competence through immediate skill feedback
questions.rationale: Self-determination theory identifies autonomy, competence, and relatedness as basic needs. Offering choice, autonomy support, and relevance directly serves autonomy. Building competence specifically requires skill-focused feedback, which is the need least directly addressed by the listed actions.

questions.stem: Ms. Quinn observes that when she gives directions verbally while a busy animated graphic plays on screen, students miss key steps. Which cognitive principle BEST explains the breakdown, and what should she do?
options: Working-memory overload from competing demands; she should simplify or sequence the visual and verbal input
The redundancy effect; she should repeat the directions louder
Long-term memory decay; she should reteach the entire unit
The recency effect; she should give directions only at the end of class
questions.rationale: Simultaneous busy visuals and verbal directions overload limited working memory and divide attention. Simplifying the visual or sequencing the inputs so they do not compete reduces load and improves comprehension.

questions.stem: Ms. Alvarez, a third-grade teacher, learns that several of her students help their families run a small bakery on weekends. She designs a measurement unit using recipes and scaling ingredient quantities. This approach BEST reflects which instructional principle?
options: Reducing rigor for struggling learners
Tracking students by ability level
Drawing on students' funds of knowledge
Maintaining strict curricular fidelity
questions.rationale: Funds of knowledge refers to the accumulated knowledge, skills, and experiences embedded in students' households and communities. Connecting a measurement unit to the family bakery taps these resources to make learning relevant and meaningful.

questions.stem: A middle school teacher wants to make content comprehensible for emergent bilingual students. Which strategy aligns MOST directly with the English Language Proficiency Standards (ELPS) for sheltered instruction?
options: Delivering instruction faster to cover more material
Pairing visuals and graphic organizers with explicit academic vocabulary
Excusing emergent bilinguals from content assessments
Requiring all responses in complete written paragraphs only
questions.rationale: Sheltered instruction and the ELPS emphasize making content comprehensible through visuals, graphic organizers, and explicit vocabulary support while maintaining grade-level content. These scaffolds give emergent bilinguals access to rigorous learning.

questions.stem: Mr. Chen notices that his gifted and talented students finish assignments quickly and appear disengaged. Which differentiation approach would BEST meet their needs?
options: Assigning additional practice problems of the same difficulty
Providing open-ended, complex tasks that require higher-order thinking
Allowing them free time once their work is complete
Having them tutor peers for the entire class period daily
questions.rationale: Gifted learners benefit from depth and complexity rather than more of the same work. Open-ended tasks requiring analysis, synthesis, and evaluation provide appropriate challenge and engagement.

questions.stem: Ms. Patel offers students three ways to demonstrate their understanding of the water cycle: a labeled diagram, a written explanation, or a recorded oral presentation. This is an example of differentiating which element of instruction?
options: Learning environment
Product
Process
Content
questions.rationale: Differentiating product means varying how students demonstrate what they have learned. Offering a diagram, written explanation, or recording lets students show mastery in different ways while addressing the same learning goal.

questions.stem: Which scenario BEST illustrates the distinction between equity and equality in the classroom?
options: Each student receives the specific supports needed to access the same learning goal
Every student receives the identical worksheet at the same time
All students are graded on the same scale regardless of effort
Students are seated alphabetically for fairness
questions.rationale: Equality means giving everyone the same thing; equity means giving each student what they need to reach the same goal. Providing tailored supports so all can access a common objective exemplifies equity.

questions.stem: A high school teacher in a low-income community plans a unit requiring students to complete extensive online research at home. Several students lack reliable internet access. Which response BEST demonstrates awareness of socioeconomic factors?
options: Replacing the research project with a textbook quiz for everyone
Assigning the same task and expecting families to find solutions
Lowering the grades of students who do not finish at home
Providing class time and school technology resources for the research
questions.rationale: Recognizing that home internet access varies by socioeconomic status, the equitable response provides in-school time and resources so all students can complete the work without penalizing those facing barriers outside their control.

questions.stem: Mr. Okafor teaches a diverse fourth-grade class. He selects literature featuring characters from his students' varied cultural backgrounds and invites students to connect texts to their own experiences. A colleague asks why he does not simply use the standard anthology. Which rationale BEST justifies his approach?
options: Culturally relevant texts guarantee higher standardized test scores
The standard anthology is required to be replaced by law
Diverse texts are easier to teach than canonical works
Students learn more effectively when they see themselves reflected and validated in curriculum
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive teaching holds that when students see their identities reflected and affirmed in the curriculum, engagement, belonging, and learning improve. This is the strongest justification, grounded in research on relevance and identity.

questions.stem: A teacher uses tiered assignments in which all students explore the same essential concept but work with materials matched to their readiness levels. This practice MOST directly differentiates which element?
options: Assessment format
Product
Behavior expectations
Content
questions.rationale: Tiered assignments that adjust the difficulty and complexity of the materials students engage with, while keeping the same essential concept, differentiate content based on readiness.

questions.stem: During a lesson, a newcomer emergent bilingual student in the beginning stage of English proficiency is hesitant to speak. Which teacher action is MOST appropriate to support this student's language development?
options: Calling on the student frequently to read aloud to the whole class
Translating every sentence of instruction into the home language
Reducing expectations and excusing the student from participation
Allowing a silent period and providing low-stakes opportunities to respond nonverbally
questions.rationale: Beginning-level emergent bilinguals often experience a silent period. Allowing this period while offering low-stakes, nonverbal ways to participate respects their development and gradually builds confidence and comprehension.

questions.stem: All of the following are appropriate strategies for differentiating instruction for academically diverse learners EXCEPT:
options: Permanently assigning students to fixed ability groups for the year
Offering choice in how students demonstrate mastery
Using flexible grouping that changes based on task and need
Providing scaffolds that are gradually removed as students gain independence
questions.rationale: Effective differentiation relies on flexible, changing groupings and supports. Permanently fixing students in static ability groups (tracking) limits opportunity and contradicts responsive, flexible instruction.

questions.stem: Ms. Reyes notices she frequently calls on boys to answer math questions and praises girls more for neatness than for reasoning. To create an equitable classroom, what should be her FIRST step?
options: Separate boys and girls into different math groups
Reflect on and monitor her own patterns of interaction and feedback
Assume the pattern is unimportant since all students are passing
Stop praising any students to avoid bias
questions.rationale: Equitable teaching begins with self-awareness. Recognizing and monitoring one's own interaction and feedback patterns is the necessary first step to interrupting unintentional bias and ensuring all students receive challenging, growth-oriented feedback.

questions.stem: A teacher co-plans with the ESL specialist to integrate language objectives alongside content objectives in a biology lesson. The BEST reason to include explicit language objectives is to:
options: Limit instruction to vocabulary memorization
Reduce the amount of biology content students must learn
Make the academic language demands of the content visible and teachable
Replace content standards with language standards
questions.rationale: Language objectives surface the academic language students need to access and express content. Making these demands explicit and teachable supports emergent bilinguals in learning rigorous content, consistent with the ELPS.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST describes culturally responsive teaching?
options: Focusing exclusively on celebrating cultural holidays
Treating all students identically regardless of background
Using students' cultural references and assets as bridges to academic learning
Lowering academic standards for students from marginalized groups
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive teaching uses students' cultural knowledge, experiences, and frames of reference as assets and bridges to rigorous academic learning, maintaining high expectations for all.

questions.stem: Mr. Daniels has a student with ADHD who struggles to stay focused during long independent reading. Which classroom-level differentiation would BEST support this student without singling him out?
options: Breaking work into shorter segments with brief movement breaks for the class
Reducing the student's grade for incomplete work
Removing the student from the activity entirely
Seating the student facing the wall away from peers
questions.rationale: Chunking tasks into shorter segments with movement breaks supports attention and self-regulation for students with ADHD while benefiting the whole class and avoiding stigma.

questions.stem: A teacher administers a pre-assessment before a unit and discovers a wide range of prior knowledge. Some students have already mastered most objectives while others lack prerequisite skills. Which use of this data BEST supports differentiated instruction?
options: Teaching the entire class at the average level indicated by the data
Giving advanced students the role of grading classmates' work
Reporting the scores to parents and proceeding with the standard plan
Forming flexible groups and planning tiered tasks based on demonstrated readiness
questions.rationale: Pre-assessment data should inform instruction. Using it to form flexible, readiness-based groups and to design tiered tasks ensures both advanced and struggling students receive appropriately challenging instruction.

questions.stem: During a sheltered instruction lesson, Ms. Flores activates students' prior knowledge by linking a new concept to a familiar experience from their communities before introducing academic vocabulary. This practice PRIMARILY supports emergent bilinguals by:
options: Eliminating the need to teach new vocabulary
Avoiding the use of any English during instruction
Lowering the cognitive demand of the entire lesson
Building meaningful connections that anchor new learning
questions.rationale: Activating prior knowledge and connecting new concepts to familiar experiences builds schema that anchors new vocabulary and content, making learning more comprehensible and durable for emergent bilinguals.

questions.stem: Which action would LEAST support an inclusive classroom for students with disabilities?
options: Collaborating with special education staff on accommodations
Assuming a student cannot succeed and lowering expectations
Providing flexible options for students to demonstrate understanding
Using Universal Design for Learning to offer multiple means of engagement
questions.rationale: Inclusion rests on high expectations and access. Assuming a student cannot succeed and lowering expectations undermines inclusion, unlike collaboration, UDL, and flexible demonstration options.

questions.stem: Ms. Nguyen wants to honor the linguistic diversity of her emergent bilingual students as an asset. Which practice BEST reflects an asset-based view of students' home languages?
options: Allowing home language only during non-instructional time
Treating the home language as an obstacle to overcome quickly
Prohibiting the use of home languages anywhere in the classroom
Encouraging students to use their home language to clarify and deepen understanding
questions.rationale: An asset-based view treats the home language as a resource for learning. Encouraging strategic use of the home language to clarify concepts supports comprehension and affirms students' linguistic identities.

questions.stem: A gifted student is also receiving special education services for a writing disability. This student is described as twice-exceptional. Which instructional approach BEST serves this learner?
options: Removing the student from advanced content until writing improves
Focusing only on remediating the writing disability
Simultaneously challenging strengths while accommodating the disability
Treating the student the same as the rest of the class
questions.rationale: Twice-exceptional students need both enrichment for their gifts and support for their disability. Effective practice nurtures strengths through challenge while providing accommodations so the disability does not block advanced learning.

questions.stem: A teacher provides sentence stems and a word bank during a class discussion so emergent bilingual students can participate in academic conversation. As students gain proficiency, the teacher gradually removes these supports. This practice is BEST described as:
options: Tracking students by language ability
Scaffolding that builds toward independence
Lowering expectations for emergent bilinguals
Eliminating academic rigor
questions.rationale: Scaffolding provides temporary supports that are gradually withdrawn as students develop competence, enabling participation in rigorous academic discourse while building independence.

questions.stem: Mr. Lopez surveys students at the start of the year about their interests, hobbies, and home experiences. How does this information BEST support differentiation?
options: It allows him to rank students by ability
It helps him connect content to students' interests and experiences
It replaces the need for ongoing assessment
It lets him assign permanent seating
questions.rationale: Knowing students' interests and experiences enables a teacher to differentiate by interest, increase relevance, and build on existing knowledge, strengthening engagement and learning.

questions.stem: In a lesson on civic participation, a teacher includes perspectives and contributions from multiple cultural and ethnic groups rather than a single dominant narrative. This practice MOST directly promotes:
options: Avoidance of all controversial topics
Reduced content coverage to save time
Multiple perspectives that validate diverse students and deepen understanding
A standardized, one-size-fits-all curriculum
questions.rationale: Incorporating multiple cultural perspectives validates diverse students, counters single-narrative bias, and deepens all students' understanding of complex social topics, a hallmark of culturally responsive, equitable curriculum.

questions.stem: A student newly identified for gifted and talented services excels in mathematics but is bored by grade-level pacing. Which option BEST provides appropriate challenge?
options: Giving the same assignments with stricter deadlines
Compacting the curriculum and offering advanced, accelerated content
Limiting the student to grade-level work to avoid gaps
Assigning the student to help slower peers indefinitely
questions.rationale: Curriculum compacting lets students skip mastered material and move into advanced, accelerated content, providing the depth and pace gifted learners need while maintaining engagement.

questions.stem: A teacher reflects that her assumptions about a student's home life, based on the student's neighborhood, may be affecting her expectations. Which concept does this reflection MOST directly address?
options: Standardized testing protocols
Classroom seating arrangements
Grade-level pacing guides
Deficit thinking and its impact on expectations
questions.rationale: Deficit thinking attributes lower potential to students based on background, lowering expectations. Recognizing how assumptions about a neighborhood shape expectations is a step toward countering deficit thinking with an asset-based stance.

questions.stem: Ms. Tran allows students to choose a learning center based on whether they prefer to work with manipulatives, read independently, or collaborate in a group. This is an example of differentiating based on:
options: Student learning preferences and interests
Grade-point averages
Standardized test scores
Student readiness only
questions.rationale: Offering choices among manipulatives, reading, and collaboration differentiates by students' learning preferences and interests, increasing engagement and ownership of learning.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the BEST first step when a teacher wants to build relationships that support culturally diverse learners?
options: Learn about students' individual cultures, experiences, and identities
Assume all students from the same background share the same needs
Avoid discussing cultural differences to prevent discomfort
Apply identical interventions to all students
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive relationships start with getting to know students as individuals, including their cultures, experiences, and identities, rather than relying on assumptions or generalizations.

questions.stem: A teacher provides an emergent bilingual student with a graphic organizer, a bilingual glossary, and access to visuals during a content assessment, consistent with the ELPS. These supports are intended to:
options: Replace the assessment with a translated version
Give the student an unfair advantage over peers
Allow the student to demonstrate content knowledge despite developing English
Reduce the content standards the student is assessed on
questions.rationale: Linguistic accommodations under the ELPS allow emergent bilinguals to show what they know about content without language barriers masking their understanding, ensuring valid measurement of content learning.

questions.stem: Mr. Abara wants to ensure his differentiation does not inadvertently create lowered expectations for some students. Which principle should guide his planning?
options: Differentiation should sort students permanently by ability
Advanced students alone deserve challenging tasks
All students should work toward the same high-level standards through varied paths
Differentiation means assigning easier work to struggling students
questions.rationale: High-quality differentiation maintains rigorous, common standards for all students while varying the paths, supports, and scaffolds to reach them, ensuring high expectations are preserved.

questions.stem: A teacher observes that a student frequently arrives hungry and tired, affecting concentration. Which response BEST reflects awareness of how socioeconomic factors influence learning?
options: Ignore the situation since it is outside school responsibility
Connect the family with school resources while maintaining high academic expectations
Publicly question the student about home conditions
Assume the student is unmotivated and lower expectations
questions.rationale: Understanding that basic-needs insecurity can affect learning, the teacher should discreetly connect the family with support services while keeping expectations high, addressing barriers without lowering academic goals.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of differentiating PROCESS rather than content or product?
options: Offering texts at varied reading levels on the same topic
Varying the activities students use to explore a concept, such as a simulation or a discussion
Adjusting the difficulty of the source materials
Letting students choose to present learning as a poster or essay
questions.rationale: Process differentiation varies the activities and sense-making strategies students use while learning. Choosing among a simulation, discussion, or other activity to explore the same concept differentiates process.

questions.stem: Ms. Carrillo notices that a culturally relevant lesson she planned relies on a holiday her students do not all celebrate, and a few feel excluded. To move beyond surface-level cultural recognition, she should:
options: Integrate students' diverse lived experiences and perspectives meaningfully throughout the curriculum
Continue using the holiday since most students celebrate it
Limit cultural content to a single multicultural week
Remove all cultural content to avoid offending anyone
questions.rationale: Deep culturally responsive teaching weaves students' authentic lived experiences and varied perspectives throughout the curriculum rather than relying on isolated holidays or single events, which risk tokenism and exclusion.

questions.stem: During collaborative group work, a teacher intentionally forms heterogeneous groups that mix readiness levels, language backgrounds, and strengths. The PRIMARY benefit of this grouping is that it:
options: Promotes peer learning and exposes students to diverse perspectives and supports
Allows higher-achieving students to do most of the work
Permanently labels students by their group role
Eliminates the need for teacher facilitation
questions.rationale: Heterogeneous grouping fosters peer learning, gives students access to diverse perspectives and natural language and content models, and builds collaborative skills, provided roles and tasks are structured so all contribute.

questions.stem: A teacher learns that a student's family has expertise in traditional weaving and invites the family to share with the class during a unit on patterns and geometry. This BEST demonstrates:
options: Treating the family as a distraction from the curriculum
Replacing the standards with cultural activities
Drawing on community funds of knowledge to enrich academic content
Lowering the rigor of the geometry unit
questions.rationale: Inviting family expertise in weaving connects community funds of knowledge to academic concepts of pattern and geometry, enriching content, validating the family's knowledge, and increasing relevance.

questions.stem: A general education teacher is unsure how to support a student with a hearing impairment included in her class. What is the MOST appropriate first action?
options: Assume the student will request help when needed
Collaborate with special education staff and review the student's IEP for needed supports
Wait until problems arise before seeking guidance
Seat the student in the back to minimize disruption
questions.rationale: The teacher should proactively collaborate with special education staff and review the IEP to understand and implement the supports and accommodations the student needs, rather than waiting for problems or relying on the student to self-advocate.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to assess whether her differentiation is effective for diverse learners. Which approach provides the MOST useful evidence?
options: Comparing her class to a neighboring teacher's class
Analyzing ongoing formative assessment data across student groups to monitor growth
Counting how many different activities she offered
Asking students whether they enjoyed the lesson
questions.rationale: The strongest evidence of effective differentiation is ongoing formative data disaggregated across student groups, which reveals whether all learners, including diverse subgroups, are progressing toward the learning goals.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST reflects an equitable grading practice for a diverse classroom?
options: Grading emergent bilinguals' content knowledge based primarily on English grammar errors
Awarding bonus points only to students who can afford extra materials
Assessing content mastery using accommodations that separate language from content demands
Lowering grading standards for students from low-income families
questions.rationale: Equitable grading measures the intended learning. For emergent bilinguals, assessing content mastery with accommodations that separate language from content ensures grades reflect content knowledge rather than developing English proficiency.

questions.stem: Mr. Salazar wants emergent bilingual students to develop academic language during a science lab. According to the ELPS, which combination of language domains should he intentionally plan to develop?
options: Only listening and speaking
Only reading and writing
Only the home language
Listening, speaking, reading, and writing in an integrated way
questions.rationale: The ELPS call for integrated development of all four language domains, listening, speaking, reading, and writing, across content areas so emergent bilinguals build comprehensive academic English alongside content learning.

questions.stem: A teacher posts and explains both a content objective and a language objective at the start of each lesson for her linguistically diverse class. The MAIN purpose of sharing these objectives is to:
options: Fill required wall space in the classroom
Make learning expectations clear and give students a purpose for the lesson
Replace the lesson plan entirely
Limit what advanced students can explore
questions.rationale: Clearly stated content and language objectives make learning targets transparent, give students a sense of purpose, and help emergent bilinguals understand both what they will learn and the language they will use.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a referral pattern in her school sends disproportionately more students of one demographic group to special education. As a reflective, equity-minded educator, her BEST initial response is to:
options: Refer more students from other groups to balance the numbers
Conclude that the affected group simply needs more services
Assume the referrals are always accurate and take no action
Examine her own and the school's referral practices for possible bias and ensure interventions precede referral
questions.rationale: Disproportionality in special education referrals can signal bias or inadequate prior intervention. An equity-minded educator examines referral practices, ensures robust interventions and supports precede referral, and reflects on potential bias rather than accepting the pattern uncritically.

questions.stem: Mr. Alvarez is beginning to plan a sixth-grade science unit on ecosystems. According to the principle of backward design, what should he do FIRST?
options: Select a textbook chapter and supplementary videos to use during instruction
Draft a weekly schedule that distributes content across the available class days
Create a set of engaging hands-on laboratory activities for each lesson
Identify the desired results by determining what students should know and be able to do by the end of the unit
questions.rationale: Backward design begins with identifying desired results (the learning goals and standards), then determining acceptable evidence of learning, and only then planning learning experiences. Establishing clear outcomes first ensures that all subsequent decisions support intended learning.

questions.stem: A measurable instructional objective written in the ABCD format includes an audience, a behavior, a condition, and a degree. Which component is represented by the phrase 'with at least 80% accuracy'?
options: Condition
Behavior
Degree
Audience
questions.rationale: In the ABCD model, the degree specifies the criterion or standard of acceptable performance. A phrase such as 'with at least 80% accuracy' defines how well the student must perform the behavior to demonstrate mastery.

questions.stem: When planning a unit, a teacher consults the Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills (TEKS) for her grade level and subject. What is the primary purpose of aligning instruction to the TEKS?
options: To guarantee that every student will earn a passing score on standardized tests
To ensure that classroom instruction addresses the state-mandated knowledge and skills students are expected to learn
To reduce the amount of planning time the teacher must devote to each lesson
To allow the teacher to select only the topics she personally finds most interesting
questions.rationale: The TEKS define the required curriculum for each grade level and subject in Texas. Aligning instruction to the TEKS ensures students receive the knowledge and skills the state expects them to master and provides a consistent statewide framework.

questions.stem: Ms. Tran is writing objectives for a high school algebra lesson. Which of the following is the MOST measurable objective?
options: Students will be able to solve systems of two linear equations using substitution with 90% accuracy
Students will become familiar with multiple methods for solving systems of equations
Students will appreciate the usefulness of systems of linear equations
Students will understand how to solve systems of linear equations
questions.rationale: A measurable objective uses an observable verb and a clear performance criterion. 'Solve... with 90% accuracy' identifies a specific behavior and a measurable degree of success, whereas 'understand,' 'appreciate,' and 'become familiar' describe internal states that cannot be directly observed or measured.

questions.stem: A fourth-grade teacher plans a writing unit. He first decides that the culminating assessment will be a persuasive letter scored with a rubric, and then he designs daily lessons to build the skills the letter requires. This planning approach BEST illustrates which principle?
options: Backward design with alignment between assessment and instruction
Differentiated instruction based on readiness
Spiral curriculum design
Inquiry-based discovery learning
questions.rationale: The teacher identified the final assessment and its criteria before designing lessons, then built instruction to develop exactly the skills that assessment requires. This is backward design, in which assessment evidence is determined before learning experiences and instruction is aligned to that evidence.

questions.stem: Mrs. Okafor is sequencing a multi-week unit on fractions for her fifth graders. Which sequencing decision BEST reflects sound instructional design?
options: Building from concrete representations of fractions to pictorial models and then to abstract procedures
Presenting all fraction concepts in a single lesson so students see the full scope at once
Teaching the most difficult operation, division of fractions, on the first day to challenge students
Introducing addition of unlike fractions before students can identify equivalent fractions
questions.rationale: Effective sequencing moves from simpler, foundational, concrete experiences toward more complex and abstract understanding (the concrete-pictorial-abstract progression). This builds prerequisite knowledge before more demanding skills, supporting comprehension and retention.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to write a SMART objective for a unit. Which feature is MOST associated with the 'R' in SMART?
options: The objective can be tracked with concrete evidence of progress
The objective is relevant and meaningful to students' broader learning goals
The objective is attainable given the time and resources available
The objective includes a clear deadline for completion
questions.rationale: In SMART objectives, the components are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. The 'R' stands for Relevant, meaning the objective is meaningful and connected to broader learning goals and student needs.

questions.stem: Mr. Bennett is selecting instructional resources for a seventh-grade geography unit. Which factor should be his PRIMARY consideration when choosing materials?
options: Whether the materials align with the unit's learning objectives and TEKS
Whether the materials are visually attractive and colorful
Whether the materials are the newest products available from publishers
Whether the materials were used successfully in a different subject area
questions.rationale: Resource selection should be driven first by alignment with learning objectives and standards. Materials must support the intended outcomes; other qualities like appeal or novelty are secondary to whether the resource helps students meet the objectives.

questions.stem: Ms. Delgado has written the objective: 'Given a primary source document, students will analyze the author's purpose and support their analysis with two pieces of textual evidence.' She wants to align her instruction to the cognitive demand of this objective. Which classroom activity is BEST aligned?
options: Students match a list of vocabulary terms to their correct definitions
Students copy the definition of 'author's purpose' from the board into their notebooks
Students recite a memorized list of common reasons authors write texts
Students read a primary source, determine why the author wrote it, and cite specific passages that justify their reasoning
questions.rationale: The objective requires analysis and the use of textual evidence, which are higher-order cognitive tasks. Instruction must engage students in actually analyzing a source and citing evidence to align with that demand. Copying, matching, and reciting target recall, a lower level of cognition than the objective requires.

questions.stem: During unit planning, a teacher reviews the relevant TEKS and notices that one student expectation requires students to 'compare and contrast' two historical events. To preserve alignment, the daily objectives and assessment items should require students to do which of the following?
options: Identify and explain the similarities and differences between the two events
Recall the dates on which each event occurred
Memorize a textbook summary of each event
List the leaders involved in each event
questions.rationale: Alignment requires that objectives and assessments match the verb and cognitive level of the standard. Because the TEKS expectation is to 'compare and contrast,' instruction and assessment must require students to identify and explain similarities and differences, not merely recall facts.

questions.stem: A second-grade team is designing a thematic unit that integrates reading, writing, and science around the topic of weather. Which is the GREATEST benefit of this kind of integrated unit planning?
options: It eliminates the need to align instruction to the TEKS for each subject
It ensures every lesson takes exactly the same amount of time
It removes the need for any formative assessment during the unit
It allows students to make connections across disciplines and apply skills in meaningful contexts
questions.rationale: Integrated, thematic units help students transfer and connect skills across content areas and apply learning in meaningful, real-world contexts. The integration still requires alignment to standards and ongoing assessment.

questions.stem: Mr. Castillo notices that his planned objective uses the verb 'know,' as in 'Students will know the causes of the American Revolution.' To make the objective measurable, which revision is MOST appropriate?
options: Students will truly know the causes of the American Revolution
Students will learn about the causes of the American Revolution in depth
Students will be exposed to the causes of the American Revolution
Students will explain three causes of the American Revolution and provide supporting evidence for each
questions.rationale: Measurable objectives replace vague verbs like 'know,' 'learn,' or 'be exposed to' with observable action verbs and clear criteria. 'Explain three causes... and provide supporting evidence' specifies an observable behavior and a degree, making student performance measurable.

questions.stem: A teacher is planning a lesson and wants to determine students' existing knowledge before introducing new content. Which planning element addresses this need?
options: Writing the closure activity for the end of the lesson
Identifying and assessing prerequisite knowledge through pre-assessment
Selecting the homework assignment for the evening
Determining the seating arrangement for group work
questions.rationale: Determining students' existing knowledge requires identifying prerequisite skills and gathering data through pre-assessment. This information allows the teacher to build new learning on what students already know and to address gaps before introducing new content.

questions.stem: Ms. Park wants her instructional objectives to address a range of cognitive levels. According to Bloom's revised taxonomy, which list places the levels in order from LOWEST to HIGHEST cognitive demand?
options: Apply, remember, create, understand, evaluate, analyze
Create, evaluate, analyze, apply, understand, remember
Understand, remember, analyze, apply, create, evaluate
Remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create
questions.rationale: Bloom's revised taxonomy orders cognitive processes from lowest to highest as remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create. Writing objectives across these levels helps teachers plan for both foundational recall and higher-order thinking.

questions.stem: A high school teacher is designing a project-based unit. To ensure the project functions as a meaningful performance task, which characteristic is MOST important?
options: The project can be completed entirely from memory without any resources
The project is graded solely on neatness and the use of color
The project asks students to apply targeted knowledge and skills to an authentic, complex problem
The project results in a product that is identical for every student
questions.rationale: A performance task requires students to apply knowledge and skills to authentic, often complex situations and to produce evidence of learning. The task's value lies in demanding genuine application aligned to the targeted objectives, not in superficial features.

questions.stem: Mr. Nguyen is planning a unit and lists these steps in random order: (1) design the summative assessment, (2) identify the TEKS and learning goals, (3) plan daily learning experiences, (4) determine criteria for acceptable evidence. Following backward design, in which order should he complete them?
questions.rationale: Backward design proceeds by first identifying the goals and standards, then determining acceptable evidence of learning (the criteria), designing the assessment that will produce that evidence, and finally planning the learning experiences. This sequence keeps instruction aligned to the desired results.

questions.stem: A teacher writes the following objective: 'Using a microscope and a prepared slide, the student will correctly identify three types of plant cells in four out of five attempts.' Which part of this objective states the CONDITION?
options: Using a microscope and a prepared slide
The student
In four out of five attempts
Will correctly identify three types of plant cells
questions.rationale: The condition describes the circumstances, tools, or materials under which the behavior is performed. 'Using a microscope and a prepared slide' specifies the conditions for the task. The behavior is the identification, and the degree is the four-out-of-five criterion.

questions.stem: Ms. Howard is choosing between two digital resources for a unit on the water cycle. Both are engaging. Which question is MOST important for her to ask to make an instructionally sound choice?
options: Which resource best helps students achieve the unit's specific learning objectives?
Which resource has more animated graphics and sound effects?
Which resource takes the least amount of class time to use?
Which resource is the most popular with teachers on social media?
questions.rationale: The central criterion for selecting any resource is whether it advances the targeted learning objectives. Engagement and other features matter only insofar as they support meeting the objectives; alignment to goals is the decisive question.

questions.stem: A district curriculum specialist reviews a teacher's unit plan and finds that the objectives emphasize higher-order thinking, but every assessment item is a multiple-choice question asking students to recall vocabulary definitions. What is the MOST significant problem with this plan?
options: The assessment is misaligned with the cognitive level of the objectives
The assessment includes too many vocabulary terms
The assessment is too short to cover the entire unit
The assessment uses a format that students dislike
questions.rationale: When objectives target higher-order thinking but assessments measure only recall, the assessment is misaligned with the cognitive demand of the objectives. This means the assessment will not provide valid evidence about whether students achieved the intended higher-order outcomes.

questions.stem: When planning a lesson, the teacher includes a brief opening activity that connects to students' prior knowledge and previews the day's learning. This opening is BEST described as which lesson component?
options: Closure
Independent practice
An anticipatory set, or hook
Summative assessment
questions.rationale: An anticipatory set, or hook, is the opening of a lesson designed to engage students, activate prior knowledge, and focus attention on the day's objective. Closure occurs at the end, independent practice follows instruction, and summative assessment measures cumulative learning.

questions.stem: A teacher plans to scaffold a complex research project across several weeks. Which approach BEST reflects effective scaffolding in instructional design?
options: Assigning the entire finished project on the first day and providing no further guidance
Eliminating teacher feedback so students learn entirely through trial and error
Breaking the project into sequenced sub-tasks with decreasing support as students gain competence
Requiring all students to complete every step at exactly the same pace regardless of need
questions.rationale: Effective scaffolding breaks complex tasks into manageable, sequenced steps and gradually withdraws support as learners become more capable. This gradual release builds competence while ensuring students can manage the cognitive demands at each stage.

questions.stem: Mr. Ellis is planning a lesson for a class that includes English learners and students with learning disabilities. As he designs the lesson, when should he plan for differentiation?
options: Never, because differentiation undermines the rigor of the objective
Only after the lesson fails and students show confusion
Only for the summative test at the end of the unit
Proactively, during the initial planning, by anticipating varied needs and building in supports
questions.rationale: Differentiation is most effective when planned proactively. Anticipating learners' varied needs during initial planning and building in supports, options, and flexible strategies allows all students to access the same rigorous objectives from the start.

questions.stem: A teacher's unit goal is for students to 'design and conduct a scientific investigation.' Which sequence of objectives BEST builds toward this goal over the unit?
options: Conduct an independent investigation; then identify variables; then state a hypothesis
Identify variables and form a hypothesis; then plan a procedure; then conduct and analyze an investigation
Analyze published research; then memorize the scientific method; then take a vocabulary quiz
Write a lab report; then design an investigation; then list lab safety rules
questions.rationale: To build toward designing and conducting an investigation, objectives should follow the logical order of the inquiry process: first identifying variables and forming a hypothesis, then planning a procedure, and finally conducting and analyzing the investigation. This sequence develops prerequisite skills before the culminating performance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LEAST appropriate consideration when a teacher selects technology resources for a lesson?
options: Whether the technology is developmentally appropriate for the students
Whether the technology is the most expensive option available
Whether the technology supports the lesson's learning objectives
Whether all students will have equitable access to the technology
questions.rationale: Sound technology selection considers alignment to objectives, equitable access, and developmental appropriateness. The cost or expense of a tool, by itself, is not a sound rationale; more expensive does not mean more effective for learning.

questions.stem: A teacher writes daily learning objectives on the board and reviews them with students at the start of each lesson. What is the PRIMARY instructional benefit of this practice?
options: It makes the learning goals clear so students understand what they are expected to achieve
It fills time at the beginning of class
It allows the teacher to avoid planning the rest of the lesson
It guarantees that all students will earn the same grade
questions.rationale: Sharing clear learning objectives helps students understand the purpose of the lesson and what they are expected to learn and do. This focus supports engagement, self-monitoring, and alignment of effort toward the intended outcomes.

questions.stem: Ms. Rivera is creating a unit calendar. She decides to allocate more instructional days to a TEKS concept that is both foundational for later learning and historically difficult for students. This decision BEST reflects which planning skill?
options: Prioritizing and pacing content based on its importance and difficulty
Randomly distributing time equally across all topics
Selecting only the topics that require the least preparation
Eliminating assessment to make room for more instruction
questions.rationale: Thoughtful pacing means allocating instructional time according to the importance, complexity, and difficulty of content. Giving more days to foundational and historically challenging concepts reflects deliberate prioritization to support mastery.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a quick exit ticket at the end of each lesson to check whether students grasped the day's objective and to adjust the next lesson. This is an example of which type of assessment?
options: Standardized assessment
Formative assessment
Norm-referenced assessment
Summative assessment
questions.rationale: Formative assessment is ongoing assessment used during instruction to monitor student learning and inform adjustments to teaching. An exit ticket used to gauge understanding and shape the next lesson is a classic formative tool.

questions.stem: A science test is intended to measure students' understanding of the rock cycle, but it is written at such a high reading level that struggling readers cannot understand the questions. This situation MOST directly threatens the test's:
options: Format
Reliability
Validity
Length
questions.rationale: Validity refers to whether an assessment measures what it is intended to measure. If reading difficulty prevents students from showing their science knowledge, the test is partly measuring reading ability instead of science understanding, which undermines its validity.

questions.stem: A teacher administers the same well-constructed quiz to a class on two occasions a few days apart and obtains very similar scores each time. This consistency of results is evidence of the quiz's:
options: Validity
Reliability
Authenticity
Bias
questions.rationale: Reliability refers to the consistency or stability of assessment results. When an assessment yields similar scores across administrations under comparable conditions, it demonstrates reliability. Validity, by contrast, concerns whether the test measures the intended construct.

questions.stem: Mrs. Sandoval reviews a word problem on her math test that asks students to calculate the cost of attending an opera and purchasing season tickets to a country club. Several students have limited experience with these contexts. Why is this item potentially problematic?
options: It is too easy and will not differentiate among students
It cannot be scored objectively because math has multiple answers
It may introduce cultural and socioeconomic bias that disadvantages students unfamiliar with these contexts
It measures reading speed rather than mathematical computation
questions.rationale: Assessment bias occurs when item content unfairly advantages or disadvantages a group for reasons unrelated to the skill being measured. Unfamiliar cultural or socioeconomic contexts can impede some students' performance on the math itself, introducing bias even though the underlying computation is the same.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to score student essays consistently and to communicate clear expectations to students in advance. Which tool BEST serves both purposes?
options: An analytic rubric with defined criteria and performance levels
A multiple-choice answer key
A simple letter grade with no comments
A norm-referenced percentile chart
questions.rationale: An analytic rubric defines criteria and describes performance levels for each, promoting consistent scoring across students and clearly communicating expectations beforehand. This supports both scoring reliability and transparency for learners.

questions.stem: Mr. Foster's learning objective states that students will 'orally present a persuasive argument using appropriate evidence and delivery.' Which assessment is BEST aligned to this objective?
options: A performance task in which students deliver a persuasive speech scored with a rubric for evidence and delivery
A multiple-choice quiz on the definition of persuasion
A matching activity pairing rhetorical terms with examples
A written summary of a persuasive speech the students read
questions.rationale: Alignment requires the assessment to elicit the exact performance described in the objective. Because the objective calls for an oral persuasive presentation with evidence and delivery, a scored speech-delivery performance task is the only option that directly measures that behavior.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a rubric for a group presentation. Which feature would MOST improve the rubric's ability to produce consistent, fair scores across different raters?
options: Providing clear, specific, and observable descriptions for each performance level
Assigning points based on the teacher's overall impression of each group
Using vague descriptors such as 'good' and 'poor' without further explanation
Keeping the criteria secret from students until after grading
questions.rationale: Clear, specific, observable descriptors for each performance level reduce subjectivity and help different raters apply the rubric consistently. Vague terms, overall impressions, and hidden criteria increase inconsistency and unfairness.

questions.stem: A teacher claims her unit test is valid because students who study hard get high scores and students who do not get low scores. This reasoning is flawed because validity is BEST established by:
options: Counting how many students passed the test
Confirming that the test measures the specific knowledge and skills described in the objectives it is intended to assess
Verifying that students enjoyed taking the test
Ensuring the test is the same length as last year's test
questions.rationale: Validity concerns whether a test actually measures the intended construct, that is, the knowledge and skills its objectives target. A correlation between studying and scores does not by itself establish that the test measures the right content. Validity evidence comes from alignment between the test and the intended objectives.

questions.stem: Mr. Diaz wants to gather evidence of his students' ability to apply scientific reasoning to a real situation, rather than simply recall facts. Which assessment format is MOST appropriate?
options: A timed test of definitions from the glossary
A performance task requiring students to investigate a problem and justify their conclusions
A fill-in-the-blank worksheet on memorized formulas
A true-false quiz on science vocabulary
questions.rationale: Performance tasks require students to apply knowledge and skills to authentic problems and to justify their thinking, making them well suited to assessing higher-order application and reasoning. Recall-oriented formats cannot capture that applied reasoning.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST describes the primary purpose of formative assessment?
options: To compare students against a national norm group
To determine which students qualify for graduation
To assign final grades at the end of a course
To monitor student learning during instruction and guide adjustments to teaching
questions.rationale: Formative assessment's primary purpose is to monitor learning while instruction is ongoing so that teachers can adjust instruction and students can improve. It is assessment for learning, distinct from summative assessment used to evaluate final achievement.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that on her unit test, several questions contain unintentional clues, such as the longest option always being correct and grammatical mismatches that rule out distractors. What is the MOST significant consequence of these flaws?
options: The test's validity is reduced because students can answer correctly without mastering the content
The test will take longer to administer
The test will automatically be more reliable
Students will find the test more enjoyable
questions.rationale: Unintentional clues let students answer items correctly using test-taking strategies rather than content knowledge. This means the items no longer measure the intended learning, reducing the test's validity as a measure of mastery.

questions.stem: To reduce potential bias in a classroom assessment, which practice should a teacher follow?
options: Ensure that item contexts and language are accessible and do not depend on knowledge unrelated to the skill being measured
