Include questions that assume all students share the same family traditions
Use idiomatic expressions and culturally specific references that only some students will recognize
Make all questions as difficult as possible for every student
questions.rationale: To minimize bias, assessment items should use accessible language and contexts that do not require background knowledge unrelated to the skill being measured. Idioms, culturally specific assumptions, and references familiar to only some students can unfairly disadvantage others.

questions.stem: Ms. Bauer notices that her assessment is reliable, producing consistent scores, but she is unsure whether it actually measures the objectives she taught. Which statement BEST captures the relationship between reliability and validity?
options: Validity and reliability are the same concept under different names
An assessment can be reliable without being valid, so consistency alone does not guarantee it measures the right thing
A valid assessment cannot be reliable
A reliable assessment is always automatically valid
questions.rationale: Reliability (consistency of results) is necessary but not sufficient for validity (measuring the intended construct). A test can yield consistent scores while consistently measuring the wrong thing, so reliability alone does not guarantee validity.

questions.stem: During the first week of school, a third-grade teacher wants students to know exactly how to line up, sharpen pencils, and turn in work. Which approach will most effectively establish a smoothly functioning classroom?
options: Waiting until problems arise and then correcting individual students as needed
Allowing students to discover the most efficient methods through trial and error over the year
Posting a long list of rules and reviewing the penalties for breaking them
Explicitly teaching, modeling, and having students practice each procedure until it becomes routine
questions.rationale: Classroom procedures become automatic routines only when they are directly taught, modeled, and rehearsed, which prevents lost instructional time and reduces disruptions.

questions.stem: A high school teacher greets each student by name at the door every morning and asks about their interests. This practice most directly contributes to which aspect of the classroom environment?
options: Efficient transitions between activities
Standardized assessment of prior knowledge
Clear academic content objectives
A positive climate built on caring, respectful relationships
questions.rationale: Personal greetings and genuine interest in students build rapport and a sense of belonging, which are foundations of a positive, supportive classroom climate.

questions.stem: Mr. Alvarez notices that while helping one small group, he continually scans the rest of the room and quietly redirects an off-task student across the room with a glance. This behavior best illustrates which of Kounin's concepts?
options: Overlapping
Withitness
Ripple effect
Satiation
questions.rationale: Withitness is the teacher's communicated awareness of everything happening in the classroom, allowing problems to be addressed before they escalate.

questions.stem: A teacher reads aloud, takes attendance, and monitors a student returning from the office all at the same time without interrupting the lesson. According to Kounin, this skill is called:
options: Group alerting
Momentum
Overlapping
Smoothness
questions.rationale: Overlapping is the ability to attend to two or more events or tasks simultaneously, which keeps instruction flowing while managing the classroom.

questions.stem: Ms. Park's lesson loses energy when she stops mid-activity to hunt for a worksheet, abandons a topic, then returns to it minutes later. Which of Kounin's principles for maintaining lesson flow is she failing to apply?
options: Withitness
Smoothness and momentum
Group focus
The ripple effect
questions.rationale: Smoothness and momentum keep lessons moving at a steady pace without abrupt interruptions (jerkiness) or slowdowns, sustaining engagement.

questions.stem: According to the work of Lee and Marlene Canter, an assertive teacher responds to misbehavior by:
options: Ignoring minor infractions to avoid power struggles
Clearly and calmly stating expectations and following through with consistent consequences
Allowing the class to vote on appropriate consequences
Negotiating each consequence individually with the student involved
questions.rationale: Canter's Assertive Discipline emphasizes teachers calmly and firmly communicating expectations and consistently applying pre-established consequences, neither hostile nor passive.

questions.stem: A student forgets to bring her homework, and the teacher has her use part of her free-choice time to complete it rather than assigning detention. This response best exemplifies:
options: A logical consequence connected to the behavior
An arbitrary punishment unrelated to the behavior
A tangible extrinsic reward
Negative reinforcement of effort
questions.rationale: A logical consequence is reasonably related to the misbehavior, helping students see the connection between actions and outcomes; completing missed work during free time fits the offense.

questions.stem: A first-grade teacher wants to reduce the chaos that occurs when students move from the carpet to their desks. Which proactive strategy is most effective?
options: Reprimanding students who move too loudly after the fact
Teaching and rehearsing a clear signal and step-by-step routine for the transition
Allowing students to move whenever they individually feel ready
Eliminating carpet activities to avoid transitions entirely
questions.rationale: Smooth transitions depend on clearly taught and practiced routines with consistent signals, which minimize lost time and disruption proactively.

questions.stem: A teacher displays student work prominently, celebrates diverse cultural backgrounds, and ensures every student is called on equitably. These actions primarily promote:
options: Faster pacing of the curriculum
A competitive ranking among students
Stricter enforcement of consequences
An equitable and inclusive classroom climate
questions.rationale: Honoring all students, valuing diversity, and ensuring equitable participation create an inclusive climate where every student feels valued and respected.

questions.stem: Two teachers disagree about engagement. Mr. Diaz says, 'I keep all students accountable by asking a question, pausing, then calling on a random student.' Ms. Cole says, 'I prefer calling on the volunteer who raises a hand first.' Whose practice better reflects Kounin's principle of group alerting and accountability?
options: Ms. Cole, because volunteers are most motivated to participate
Mr. Diaz, because the pause and random selection keep all students mentally engaged and accountable
Neither, because questioning techniques do not affect engagement
Both equally, since any questioning method ensures full participation
questions.rationale: Posing a question, pausing for think time, and then calling on a random student (group alerting) keeps every student prepared to respond, maximizing accountability and engagement.

questions.stem: A teacher tells a struggling student, 'I know this is challenging, and I believe you can master it with practice. Let's break it into steps.' This statement most directly communicates:
options: An extrinsic reward for completion
A logical consequence for poor performance
Low expectations to reduce student frustration
High expectations paired with appropriate support
questions.rationale: Expressing belief in a student's ability while providing scaffolding conveys high expectations with support, which fosters motivation and achievement.

questions.stem: Which scenario best illustrates a student who is intrinsically motivated?
options: Ava participates only when the teacher promises bonus points
Liam completes extra reading because he finds the topic fascinating and enjoys learning about it
Sofia finishes her assignment quickly to earn a sticker on the chart
Marcus studies hard mainly to avoid losing recess privileges
questions.rationale: Intrinsic motivation comes from internal satisfaction, interest, or enjoyment in the activity itself, rather than from external rewards or pressures.

questions.stem: A middle school teacher notices that students finish independent work at very different times, leading to off-task behavior. What is the best proactive solution?
options: Slowing the entire class to match the slowest student
Punishing students who finish early for being disruptive
Eliminating independent work from the lesson plan
Establishing meaningful 'anchor' or extension activities for students who finish early
questions.rationale: Providing planned extension or anchor activities ensures early finishers remain productively engaged, preventing the idle time that leads to off-task behavior.

questions.stem: All of the following are effective ways to maximize academic learning time EXCEPT:
options: Using brief, clear signals to gain attention quickly
Having materials prepared and accessible before the lesson begins
Spending extended time addressing each minor disruption individually during instruction
Establishing routines for distributing and collecting materials
questions.rationale: Stopping instruction for extended periods to handle each minor disruption reduces academic learning time; minor issues are better handled with quick, low-profile interventions.

questions.stem: A student begins to escalate, raising his voice and clenching his fists during a conflict with a peer. Which teacher response best reflects effective de-escalation?
options: Threatening an office referral if he does not stop at once
Demanding an immediate apology in front of the class
Raising her own voice to assert control immediately
Speaking calmly, lowering her voice, and giving the student space and time to cool down
questions.rationale: De-escalation relies on a calm tone, reduced volume, non-threatening body language, and giving the student time and space, which helps lower emotional arousal.

questions.stem: A teacher establishes a consistent signal, such as raising a hand and counting down from five, to gain the class's attention. The primary benefit of this practice is that it:
options: Encourages students to talk among themselves longer
Replaces the need for any classroom procedures
Provides a predictable, efficient way to refocus students and reduce lost time
Increases the number of rules students must memorize
questions.rationale: A consistent attention signal gives students a clear, predictable cue to refocus quickly, minimizing time lost to regaining attention.

questions.stem: A teacher relies heavily on prizes and points for nearly all desired behaviors. Over time she notices students ask, 'What do I get?' before doing any task and show less genuine interest. This pattern most likely illustrates:
options: The strengthening of intrinsic motivation through reinforcement
A successful use of self-determination principles
The overjustification effect, in which excessive external rewards undermine intrinsic motivation
An appropriate application of logical consequences
questions.rationale: The overjustification effect occurs when heavy reliance on extrinsic rewards reduces a person's intrinsic interest in an activity, shifting focus to the reward itself.

questions.stem: A teacher quietly walks toward a student who is whispering during a lesson and continues teaching without comment; the student stops talking. This low-key intervention is best described as:
options: Proximity control
A logical consequence
Time-out
Public reprimand
questions.rationale: Proximity control uses the teacher's physical nearness to redirect minor off-task behavior without interrupting instruction or drawing attention to the student.

questions.stem: Which classroom action best reflects a teacher's effort to build a sense of community and belonging?
options: Limiting all communication to teacher-to-student directives
Posting only individual achievement rankings on the wall
Seating students in rows facing forward with no interaction
Implementing weekly class meetings where students share concerns and solve problems together
questions.rationale: Regular class meetings give students voice, shared ownership, and collaborative problem-solving, all of which strengthen community and belonging.

questions.stem: A new teacher's well-planned lesson is repeatedly derailed because students do not know how to ask for help, get supplies, or move into groups. What is the most important first step to address the underlying problem?
options: Send frequent off-task students to the office
Systematically teach and practice the specific procedures students need for these tasks
Reduce the rigor of the lesson content
Increase the severity of consequences for off-task behavior
questions.rationale: The disruptions stem from undefined procedures; explicitly teaching and rehearsing the needed routines addresses the root cause proactively.

questions.stem: A teacher arranges desks in clusters, posts a 'we' agreement created with students, and uses inclusive language like 'our classroom.' These choices most clearly aim to:
options: Create a safe and supportive emotional environment
Reduce the number of instructional objectives
Increase test scores directly
Speed up grading procedures
questions.rationale: Collaborative agreements, inclusive language, and a thoughtful arrangement signal shared ownership and safety, fostering a supportive emotional environment.

questions.stem: Two educators discuss responding to misbehavior. Ms. Reed says, 'I prevent most problems by planning engaging lessons and clear routines.' Mr. Hall says, 'I focus on having strong punishments ready for when students act out.' Which statement reflects a more proactive management philosophy?
options: Mr. Hall's, because punishments deter all misbehavior
Ms. Reed's, because prevention through engagement and routines reduces misbehavior before it occurs
Neither, because misbehavior cannot be influenced by teacher planning
Both equally, because punishment and prevention are interchangeable
questions.rationale: Proactive management prevents problems through engaging instruction and clear routines, whereas relying on punishment is reactive and addresses misbehavior only after it occurs.

questions.stem: A student says, 'I am terrible at math; there is no point in trying.' Which teacher response best supports a growth mindset?
options: 'You may just not be a math person, and that is okay.'
'You should earn a reward each time you finish a math problem.'
'You have not mastered this yet, but with practice and the right strategies, you can improve.'
'Math is not that important; let's focus on your strengths.'
questions.rationale: A growth mindset emphasizes that ability can develop through effort and effective strategies; using 'yet' and highlighting practice reinforces this belief.

questions.stem: During a lab activity, the teacher circulates among groups, asks probing questions, and provides feedback. Beyond instruction, this circulation primarily serves to:
options: Lengthen the time needed to complete the lab
Eliminate the need for any classroom rules
Reduce the teacher's planning workload
Monitor student behavior and engagement, allowing early redirection of off-task students
questions.rationale: Circulating throughout the room keeps the teacher aware of behavior and engagement (withitness), enabling early, low-key redirection before problems grow.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to increase a reluctant reader's intrinsic motivation. Based on self-determination theory, which strategy best supports the need for autonomy?
options: Assigning the same required book to all students with strict deadlines
Publicly comparing her reading log to her classmates'
Allowing the student to choose from a curated set of texts that match her interests
Giving the student a prize for every chapter completed
questions.rationale: Offering meaningful choice within structure supports autonomy, a key driver of intrinsic motivation in self-determination theory.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a multi-step direction, but many students appear confused and begin asking neighbors what to do. What is the best immediate response?
options: Repeat the directions louder in the same words
Punish students who asked their neighbors
Let students figure it out on their own
Restate the directions clearly, model the steps, and check for understanding before students begin
questions.rationale: When directions are unclear, restating them clearly, modeling, and checking for understanding ensures all students know what to do before beginning, preventing further confusion.

questions.stem: A teacher plans the first ten minutes of class with a posted warm-up that students begin independently as soon as they arrive. The main management benefit of this routine is that it:
options: Engages students immediately and minimizes the unstructured time when problems often arise
Replaces the need for lesson objectives
Eliminates the need for instruction during the period
Guarantees higher scores on standardized tests
questions.rationale: A bell-ringer or warm-up routine engages students from the moment they enter, removing the idle, unstructured start-of-class time when off-task behavior commonly begins.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of an extrinsic motivator?
options: A student's curiosity about how volcanoes form
A student's enjoyment of painting during art class
A student earning a pizza party for the class reaching a reading goal
A student's pride in solving a difficult problem
questions.rationale: Extrinsic motivation comes from external rewards or outcomes; a pizza party for reaching a goal is a tangible external incentive.

questions.stem: A teacher gives the same long, monotonous worksheet every day, and students grow increasingly restless and inattentive. In Kounin's terms, this restlessness most likely results from:
options: Satiation caused by repetitive, unvaried tasks
Excessive overlapping
Too much group alerting
A lack of withitness
questions.rationale: Satiation occurs when students become bored and disengaged due to repetitive, monotonous tasks lacking variety, challenge, or novelty.

questions.stem: A teacher reprimands one student for blurting out, and the rest of the class immediately becomes quieter and more attentive. Kounin termed this phenomenon the:
options: Momentum effect
Satiation effect
Overlapping effect
Ripple effect
questions.rationale: The ripple effect describes how a teacher's correction of one student influences the behavior of others who observe it.

questions.stem: A teacher provides specific feedback such as, 'Your introduction clearly states your claim and previews your reasons,' rather than just 'Good job.' This kind of feedback best supports motivation by:
options: Encouraging competition among classmates
Reducing the difficulty of future assignments
Building students' sense of competence through informative, specific praise
Offering a tangible reward for the work
questions.rationale: Specific, informative feedback helps students recognize what they did well and builds their sense of competence, which supports intrinsic motivation.

questions.stem: A teacher establishes a routine for what students should do when they finish early, need to use the restroom, and turn in completed work. These routines primarily help to:
options: Limit students' independence
Reduce interruptions and keep the classroom running efficiently
Increase the amount of teacher lecturing
Make the classroom rules more complicated
questions.rationale: Clear routines for common situations reduce repeated questions and interruptions, allowing the classroom to operate smoothly and efficiently.

questions.stem: Two teachers debate consequences. Ms. Tran says, 'A student who writes on a desk should clean it; the consequence should relate to the act.' Mr. Boyd says, 'Any misbehavior should result in the same loss of recess for fairness.' Which approach better reflects the principle of logical consequences?
options: Mr. Boyd's, because identical consequences are always the fairest
Ms. Tran's, because consequences logically tied to the behavior help students learn from their actions
Neither, because consequences should never be used in classrooms
Both equally, since the type of consequence does not matter
questions.rationale: Logical consequences are meaningfully related to the misbehavior, helping students understand the impact of their actions; cleaning a desk after writing on it fits this principle.

questions.stem: A student who is normally quiet suddenly shouts in frustration during a group task. Before responding, the teacher considers possible triggers such as the task's difficulty or a peer conflict. This reflective approach is important because it helps the teacher:
options: Assign the harshest possible consequence quickly
Ignore the student's emotions to maintain order
Publicly identify who is to blame
Respond to the underlying cause rather than only the surface behavior
questions.rationale: Considering the function or cause of behavior allows the teacher to address the real issue, leading to more effective and supportive responses than reacting to the surface behavior alone.

questions.stem: A teacher arranges the classroom so that all students can clearly see the board, traffic paths are unobstructed, and high-traffic areas are kept clear. This physical arrangement primarily supports:
options: Increased homework volume
Higher textbook costs
Fewer learning objectives
Effective classroom management and reduced disruptions
questions.rationale: A well-planned physical arrangement improves visibility, movement, and access, which supports smooth management and minimizes disruptions.

questions.stem: A teacher establishes that all students have the right to learn and no one has the right to interfere with that learning. This guiding principle most directly supports a classroom that is:
options: Focused only on the highest achievers
Loosely structured with few expectations
Competitive and individualistic
Safe and conducive to learning for all students
questions.rationale: Affirming everyone's right to learn without interference establishes a safe, respectful environment where all students can engage in learning.

questions.stem: During independent work, a student crumples his paper and puts his head down. The teacher quietly kneels beside him and says, 'I see this is frustrating. Let's look at the first step together.' This response is most effective because it:
options: Publicly corrects the student to deter others
Addresses the likely cause of the behavior with private, supportive redirection
Removes the student from the activity immediately
Ignores the behavior to avoid reinforcing it
questions.rationale: A private, empathetic response that acknowledges frustration and offers support addresses the underlying cause (task difficulty) while preserving the student's dignity and re-engaging him.

questions.stem: Which teacher action best demonstrates communicating high expectations equitably to all students?
options: Calling on stronger students for hard questions and weaker students only for easy ones
Praising only students who already perform well
Lowering standards for students who struggle to keep them comfortable
Providing all students with challenging tasks and the support needed to succeed
questions.rationale: Holding all students to high expectations while providing the support they need conveys belief in every student's capacity to succeed, which is equitable and motivating.

questions.stem: A teacher's classroom-management plan emphasizes catching students behaving well and acknowledging it, rather than focusing mainly on misbehavior. This emphasis is most consistent with which principle of effective management?
options: Relying solely on public criticism to shape behavior
Reinforcing positive behavior to encourage its recurrence
Eliminating all consequences from the classroom
Reactive discipline that waits for problems
questions.rationale: Acknowledging and reinforcing positive behavior increases the likelihood it will recur and helps create a positive, proactive classroom climate.

questions.stem: A teacher gradually shifts from offering frequent stickers for reading toward conversations about interesting books, student choice, and sharing reactions in literature circles. The teacher's long-term goal is best understood as:
options: Reducing the amount of reading students do
Fostering intrinsic motivation so students read for personal interest and meaning
Standardizing all students' reading preferences
Increasing dependence on external rewards
questions.rationale: Moving from extrinsic rewards toward choice, meaningful discussion, and interest cultivates intrinsic motivation, helping students read for genuine personal value rather than rewards.

questions.stem: During a class discussion, Mr. Chen asks a question and then silently counts to five before calling on anyone. This deliberate pause is BEST described as which questioning technique?
options: Probing
Redirecting
Cueing
Wait time
questions.rationale: Pausing several seconds after posing a question to give students time to think before responding is the technique known as wait time.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher, Ms. Patel, notices that the same four students answer nearly every question in her ninth-grade history class. Which strategy would MOST effectively increase participation from the rest of the class?
options: Allowing students to call out answers without raising hands
Using random selection tools such as name cards to call on students
Praising the four frequent participants to model engagement
Lowering the difficulty of the questions she asks
questions.rationale: Random selection methods distribute opportunities to respond equitably and signal that any student may be called on, increasing overall accountability and participation.

questions.stem: After a student gives a partially correct answer, Mr. Okafor responds, "That's a start. What evidence from the text makes you think that?" This response BEST illustrates the teacher's use of which technique?
options: Accountable talk stems
Wait time II
Choral response
Probing
questions.rationale: Asking a follow-up question that pushes the student to justify or extend an initial answer is the technique of probing.

questions.stem: Ms. Reyes wants to model active listening during a class meeting. Which of the following behaviors BEST demonstrates active listening to her students?
options: Nodding while preparing the next slide on her laptop
Glancing at her lesson plans while a student talks
Interrupting to correct grammar in the student's statement
Paraphrasing what a student said before responding
questions.rationale: Paraphrasing a speaker's message before responding shows the listener has attended to and understood the message, a hallmark of active listening.

questions.stem: During a student-led literature circle, Mr. Davis circulates but says very little. A group stalls when two students disagree about a character's motive. Which teacher move BEST supports the student-led nature of the discussion?
options: Ending the disagreement by moving the group to the next question
Asking, "What in the text could help you settle this?" and stepping back
Assigning each student a turn to speak in a fixed order
Telling the group the correct interpretation so they can move on
questions.rationale: Prompting the group to return to the text and then stepping back keeps ownership of the discussion with students while providing a productive strategy for resolving disagreement.

questions.stem: Ms. Nguyen records herself teaching and notices she averages less than one second between asking a question and calling on a student. Research on wait time suggests that extending this pause to three to five seconds is MOST likely to produce which outcome?
options: Longer and more elaborate student responses
Fewer students volunteering to answer
More frequent off-task behavior during the pause
Shorter, one-word student responses
questions.rationale: Increasing wait time to three to five seconds is associated with longer, more thoughtful student responses, greater participation, and higher-level thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher posts the sentence stems "I agree with ___ because ___" and "I'd like to add to what ___ said" for students to use in discussion. The PRIMARY purpose of these stems is to
options: Limit the number of students who can speak at one time
Help students respond to and build on one another's ideas
Reduce the amount of time the teacher must spend talking
Ensure every student uses identical wording when speaking
questions.rationale: Accountable talk stems are designed to help students connect to and extend their peers' contributions, fostering a coherent, collaborative discussion.

questions.stem: Mr. Torres asks his second graders, "What do you think will happen next in the story, and why?" This question is BEST classified as
options: A rhetorical question
A closed (lower-order) question
An open-ended (higher-order) question
A procedural question
questions.rationale: A question that invites prediction and reasoning with multiple possible responses is an open-ended, higher-order question.

questions.stem: Ms. Bell gives directions, then says, "Turn to your partner and tell them the first thing you will do." Pairs share, and she listens in. This routine MOST directly serves which purpose?
options: Building students' vocabulary for the task
Giving students a brain break before working
Allowing the teacher to take attendance
Checking for comprehension of the directions
questions.rationale: Having partners restate the first step lets the teacher monitor whether students understood the directions before they begin, a comprehension check.

questions.stem: In a tenth-grade seminar, Mr. Lin wants students to engage in accountable talk. He notices students give opinions but rarely reference one another or the text. Which sustained instructional approach is MOST likely to develop accountable talk over time?
options: Grading students individually on the number of times they speak
Reducing class discussions in favor of written responses
Explicitly teaching, modeling, and practicing discussion norms and talk moves
Calling on students in alphabetical order each session
questions.rationale: Accountable talk develops when teachers explicitly teach, model, and give repeated practice with discussion norms and talk moves so students learn to connect to peers and to evidence.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the BEST example of a teacher using clear verbal communication when assigning a task?
options: "In your groups, complete problems one through four on page 52 within fifteen minutes."
"Do the thing we talked about with your groups, you know how."
"Get started on the work and figure it out as you go."
"Work on math for a while and let me know if you have questions."
questions.rationale: Clear directions specify exactly what to do, where, with whom, and how long, removing ambiguity for students.

questions.stem: A student answers, "I don't know," when Mr. Hassan asks a question. Which teacher response BEST keeps the student engaged while still supporting accountability for thinking?
options: Immediately moving on to another student
Answering the question himself to save time
Saying, "That's fine, you don't have to answer"
Offering a cue and returning to the student shortly: "Think about the title; I'll come back to you"
questions.rationale: Providing a cue and signaling that the teacher will return communicates the expectation that all students think and respond, while scaffolding the student toward an answer.

questions.stem: Ms. Flores wants to ensure her questioning reaches a range of cognitive levels during a unit on ecosystems. Which sequence of questions BEST reflects a progression from lower-order to higher-order thinking?
options: Evaluate, compare, describe, list
List, describe, compare, evaluate
Evaluate, analyze, define, list
Compare, list, evaluate, define
questions.rationale: A progression from recalling (list) and explaining (describe) to analyzing (compare) and judging (evaluate) moves from lower-order to higher-order thinking.

questions.stem: Mr. Abara wants whole-class discussions in which students respond to each other rather than always routing comments through him. Over several weeks, his contributions become brief redirections like "Who can respond to Maya's point?" This shift BEST reflects the teacher's intentional effort to
options: Reduce the rigor of classroom dialogue
Limit the topics students are allowed to discuss
Position himself as the sole authority on content
Foster a discourse community where students build on peers' ideas
questions.rationale: Redirecting comments back to students and prompting them to respond to peers cultivates a discourse community in which students interact with one another's ideas rather than only with the teacher.

questions.stem: A teacher stands at the front of the room, makes eye contact, and uses an open posture and calm gestures while explaining a concept. These behaviors are examples of
options: Accountable talk
Wait time
Probing questions
Nonverbal communication
questions.rationale: Eye contact, posture, and gestures are nonverbal cues that convey meaning and support communication alongside spoken words.

questions.stem: Ms. Carter notices a student in the back row frowning and crossing her arms during a lesson. Reading this nonverbal cue, which teacher response is MOST appropriate?
options: Ignoring it because nonverbal cues are unreliable
Checking in privately to see if the student is confused or needs support
Publicly asking the student why she is upset in front of the class
Assuming the student is misbehaving and issuing a warning
questions.rationale: Interpreting nonverbal cues as possible signs of confusion or distress and following up privately respects the student and addresses a potential learning or emotional need.

questions.stem: During a whole-class discussion, three students speak at once and the conversation becomes chaotic. Which proactive strategy would BEST prevent this in future discussions?
options: Eliminating whole-class discussions entirely
Speaking louder than the students to regain control
Establishing and teaching clear discussion protocols at the start of the year
Calling only on students who never interrupt
questions.rationale: Teaching clear protocols and norms for discussion ahead of time gives students a shared structure for taking turns and listening, preventing chaos.

questions.stem: Mr. Solis poses a complex question, waits, calls on Dana, and after Dana finishes, he pauses again for several seconds before responding or calling on anyone else. The second pause, after Dana's answer, is BEST identified as
options: Wait time II
Cueing
Wait time I
Redirecting
questions.rationale: The pause after a student responds, before the teacher reacts or another student speaks, is wait time II, which allows for elaboration and gives others time to consider the answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following teacher questions would MOST effectively check whether students comprehend a set of directions, rather than simply whether they heard them?
options: "What is the first step you will take, and what should it look like when you finish?"
"Does anyone have any questions before we start?"
"Did you all hear what I said?"
"Are you ready to begin?"
questions.rationale: Asking students to state the first step and the expected outcome requires them to demonstrate comprehension of the directions, not merely confirm they were heard.

questions.stem: Ms. Okeke asks, "What's the capital of Texas?" then quickly asks, "And why might its location have mattered historically?" The second question differs from the first PRIMARILY because it
options: Is a procedural management question
Requires recall of a single fact
Demands higher-order reasoning and analysis
Cannot be answered by students
questions.rationale: The first question asks for factual recall; the second asks students to analyze and reason about cause and significance, which is higher-order thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher consistently rephrases student answers as "So what you're saying is..." and then waits for the student to confirm or revise. This practice MOST directly supports
options: Reducing the number of questions asked
Confirming understanding and validating student contributions
Discouraging students from speaking at length
Speeding up the pace of the lesson
questions.rationale: Restating a student's answer and inviting confirmation checks the teacher's understanding while signaling that the student's contribution was valued and heard.

questions.stem: Mr. Vance wants a Socratic seminar in which he intervenes minimally. To prepare students for this student-led format, which preparation step is MOST essential?
options: Telling students that only volunteers will be expected to speak
Teaching students how to ask open-ended questions and respond to peers with evidence
Giving students the discussion questions only at the moment the seminar begins
Assigning students to memorize the teacher's preferred answers
questions.rationale: For a successful student-led seminar, students must be equipped to generate open-ended questions and respond to one another using evidence, so this preparation is essential.

questions.stem: Which scenario BEST demonstrates a teacher facilitating, rather than dominating, a whole-class discussion?
options: The teacher answers each question right after asking it.
The teacher reads a lecture from notes for the full period.
The teacher asks a question, then invites several students to respond and react to one another before commenting.
The teacher calls on one student, corrects the answer, and moves to the next topic.
questions.rationale: Facilitation involves posing questions and guiding student-to-student interaction rather than supplying answers or controlling all exchanges.

questions.stem: During discussion, Mr. Ibarra hears a student make a vague claim. He responds, "Can you say more about that?" This move is BEST described as
options: Giving corrective feedback
Probing for elaboration
Providing a cue
Redirecting the question to another student
questions.rationale: Asking the student to expand on a vague statement is probing, which pushes the student to elaborate and clarify their thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher analyzes a discussion transcript and finds that after most student answers she immediately says "Good" and asks the next question. A mentor suggests this pattern may LIMIT learning because it
options: Provides too much wait time II
Cuts off opportunities for students to elaborate or for peers to respond
Encourages excessive student-to-student talk
Makes questions too open-ended
questions.rationale: Immediately evaluating and moving on eliminates wait time II and forecloses chances for the student to extend the answer or for peers to build on it, narrowing the discourse.

questions.stem: Ms. Yamamoto notices English learners in her class rarely participate in fast-paced oral discussions. Which adjustment would BEST support their participation while maintaining rigorous content?
options: Calling on them first so they cannot avoid speaking
Excusing them from discussions until their English improves
Providing extended wait time, sentence stems, and a chance to rehearse with a partner first
Simplifying the content so questions require only yes or no answers
questions.rationale: Extended wait time, sentence stems, and partner rehearsal give English learners processing and language support to participate meaningfully without lowering the cognitive demand of the content.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to listen actively to peers during presentations rather than just waiting for their own turn. Which strategy would BEST promote active listening?
options: Grading only the presenters and not the audience
Having students record one question or connection for each peer's presentation
Allowing students to study their own notes during others' presentations
Telling students simply to "pay attention"
questions.rationale: Requiring students to capture a question or connection for each presentation gives them an authentic listening task that keeps them attending to and processing peers' content.

questions.stem: Mr. Quint asks a higher-order question and a student gives a thoughtful but incomplete answer. Mr. Quint wants to deepen thinking without giving the answer away. Which response BEST accomplishes this?
options: "You're overthinking this; the answer is simpler."
"Interesting. What would happen if we changed one of the conditions you mentioned?"
"That's correct, let's move on."
"Not quite. Who else can try?"
questions.rationale: A probing follow-up that introduces a new variable extends the student's reasoning and deepens thinking while leaving the discovery to the student.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the BEST example of a teacher checking for understanding during a lesson rather than at the end?
options: Collecting homework the next morning
Reviewing the gradebook at the end of the term
Giving a unit test at the end of the week
Pausing mid-lesson to have students summarize the key idea on a whiteboard
questions.rationale: A mid-lesson summary on whiteboards provides immediate, formative information about understanding while there is still time to adjust instruction.

questions.stem: Ms. Delgado wants students to take greater ownership of a discussion. She introduces a "discussion captain" role that rotates among students to pose questions and call on classmates. The PRIMARY benefit of this structure is that it
options: Frees the teacher from monitoring the discussion at all
Guarantees that all answers will be correct
Distributes leadership and fosters student responsibility for the conversation
Eliminates the need for discussion norms
questions.rationale: Rotating a student leadership role distributes responsibility for guiding the conversation, building student ownership and discourse skills.

questions.stem: A teacher asks a question, and a student responds with an answer that contains a misconception. Which response BEST balances respect for the student with the need to address the error?
options: Repeating the original question louder until the right answer emerges
Ignoring the misconception to avoid embarrassment
Telling the student the answer is wrong and moving on quickly
Asking a follow-up question that leads the student to examine the reasoning behind the answer
questions.rationale: A guiding follow-up that invites the student to reexamine their reasoning addresses the misconception while preserving the student's dignity and engagement.

questions.stem: Mr. Eze gives detailed directions, asks "Any questions?", hears none, and lets students begin, but several students immediately raise their hands confused. Which conclusion is MOST warranted about his check for comprehension?
options: The students were not paying attention and are at fault
He should have given the directions only in writing
Asking "Any questions?" is an unreliable check because silence does not confirm understanding
The directions were too easy for the students
questions.rationale: Silence in response to "Any questions?" does not verify understanding; students may not know what they don't know, so a more active comprehension check is needed.

questions.stem: A teacher lowers her voice and slows her speech to signal that an important point is coming. This use of tone, pace, and volume to convey meaning is an aspect of
options: Paralinguistic (vocal) communication
Wait time II
Written communication
Probing
questions.rationale: Tone, pace, pitch, and volume are paralinguistic features of spoken communication that carry meaning beyond the words themselves.

questions.stem: In a fourth-grade class, Ms. Romero uses a "think-pair-share" before whole-class discussion. Which BEST explains how this routine improves the quality of the whole-class discussion that follows?
options: It eliminates the need for the teacher to ask questions
It replaces the need for accountable talk norms
It ensures only the strongest students share their answers
It gives all students time to formulate and rehearse ideas before speaking publicly
questions.rationale: Think-pair-share lets every student think and rehearse with a partner, so more students enter the whole-class discussion with developed, confident contributions.

questions.stem: Mr. Adeyemi wants to LEAST interrupt students' developing reasoning during a discussion. Which teacher behavior should he AVOID?
options: Inviting other students to build on a peer's idea
Asking a student to explain their thinking further
Finishing students' sentences when they hesitate
Pausing after a student finishes before responding
questions.rationale: Finishing students' sentences interrupts and takes over their reasoning; the other options support student thinking and should be retained.

questions.stem: A teacher's questions during discussion are nearly all answered correctly within one second, with brief responses. A coach reviewing the lesson would MOST likely recommend that the teacher
options: Stop asking questions and lecture instead
Ask more open-ended questions and increase wait time to elicit deeper thinking
Call on students faster to keep the pace high
Continue, since quick correct answers indicate ideal questioning
questions.rationale: Rapid, brief, uniformly correct answers suggest low-level recall questions; asking more open-ended questions and increasing wait time would elicit deeper, more elaborated thinking.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST describes the purpose of "accountable talk" in a classroom discussion?
options: To hold students responsible for reasoning, using evidence, and responding to others' ideas
To grade students on how loudly they speak
To ensure students stay quiet and listen to the teacher
To limit discussion to one correct answer per question
questions.rationale: Accountable talk holds students accountable to the learning community, to accurate knowledge, and to rigorous reasoning, including using evidence and engaging with peers' ideas.

questions.stem: Ms. Brooks asks, "Why do you think the author chose to end the story this way?" and waits. A student answers, and she asks, "Does anyone see it differently?" Her overall approach BEST reflects an effort to
options: Encourage multiple perspectives and sustained dialogue among students
Reduce the cognitive demand of the discussion
Confirm there is one acceptable interpretation
Quickly arrive at the right answer and move on
questions.rationale: Posing an open interpretive question, waiting, and inviting differing views encourages multiple perspectives and keeps the dialogue going among students.

questions.stem: A teacher gives directions for a complex group project and wants to be confident that each group understands before beginning. Which approach provides the STRONGEST evidence that all groups comprehend the directions?
options: Asking the whole class, "Are we all clear?"
Reading the directions aloud a second time
Having each group write and submit a brief plan of their first three steps for a quick teacher review
Telling groups to ask for help if they get stuck
questions.rationale: Requiring each group to produce and submit a brief plan of their first steps gives the teacher concrete, group-by-group evidence of comprehension before work begins.

questions.stem: Ms. Alvarado wants her third-grade students to do more than recall facts about the water cycle. She designs a lesson asking them to predict what would happen to a local lake during an extended drought and justify their reasoning. Which level of thinking is she primarily targeting?
options: Remembering, because students name the stages of the water cycle
Higher-order thinking, because students must analyze conditions and evaluate outcomes
Applying, because students copy a diagram from the textbook
Understanding, because students restate the definition of evaporation
questions.rationale: Predicting outcomes under new conditions and justifying reasoning requires analysis and evaluation, which are higher-order thinking skills on Bloom's taxonomy.

questions.stem: Mr. Beckett begins a unit by posing the question, 'Why do some communities recover quickly from natural disasters while others struggle for years?' Students then gather data, form hypotheses, and investigate. This approach is best described as:
options: Direct instruction
Drill and practice
Rote memorization
Inquiry-based learning
questions.rationale: Starting with a driving question that students investigate through data gathering and hypothesis testing defines inquiry-based learning.

questions.stem: During a problem-based learning project, Ms. Cho's seventh graders work to design an affordable filter for a contaminated creek. Several groups become frustrated when their first prototypes fail. What is the MOST appropriate teacher response to support learning?
options: Reassign the frustrated students to easier tasks
End the project early to avoid student discouragement
Provide the correct design so groups can finish on time
Acknowledge the difficulty and prompt groups to analyze why the prototype failed and revise
questions.rationale: Productive struggle is valuable; the teacher should validate the difficulty while scaffolding reflection and revision rather than removing the challenge.

questions.stem: Mr. Dunn uses Socratic questioning during a discussion of a short story. A student claims the main character is selfish. Which follow-up question BEST deepens the student's critical thinking?
options: Can you say that a little louder for the class?
Does everyone agree with that?
Is that your final answer?
What evidence from the text supports that interpretation, and could the character's actions be read another way?
questions.rationale: A strong Socratic prompt asks students to ground claims in evidence and consider alternative interpretations, pushing analysis and evaluation.

questions.stem: Which of the following classroom tasks best promotes the 'create' level of higher-order thinking?
options: Students match vocabulary terms to definitions
Students label parts of a plant cell on a worksheet
Students recite the steps of photosynthesis from memory
Students design an original experiment to test how light affects plant growth
questions.rationale: Designing an original experiment requires synthesizing knowledge into a new product, the hallmark of the 'create' level.

questions.stem: Ms. Fernandez wants students to transfer a math concept learned in class to situations outside school. Which assignment BEST promotes transfer?
options: Calculate the better deal between two phone plans using percentage discounts and explain the choice
Memorize the formula for percentage change
Copy the teacher's worked example into a notebook
Complete 30 identical practice problems on percentages
questions.rationale: Transfer is supported when students apply a concept to a novel, authentic context and explain their reasoning, as in comparing real phone plans.

questions.stem: Ms. Hale notices that when she asks a question, the same three students always answer within two seconds while others stay silent. To engage more students in higher-order thinking, her BEST first step is to:
options: Increase wait time after questions and use a structured turn-and-talk before calling on anyone
Replace open questions with yes/no questions for faster pacing
Lower the difficulty of every question so more students respond
Call only on students who raise their hands quickly
questions.rationale: Extending wait time and adding a brief partner talk gives all students processing time, broadening participation in deeper thinking.

questions.stem: In a problem-based unit, eighth graders investigate whether their school cafeteria menu meets nutritional guidelines and propose changes. Which feature of this task most strongly fosters critical thinking?
options: Students follow a fixed worksheet with one correct answer
The teacher provides all data and the final recommendation
Students complete the task individually without discussion
The problem is authentic, open-ended, and requires students to evaluate evidence and justify recommendations
questions.rationale: Authentic, open-ended problems requiring evaluation of evidence and justification are central to fostering critical thinking in PBL.

questions.stem: Mr. Ibrahim wants to encourage creativity in a writing assignment. Which prompt BEST supports creative and divergent thinking?
options: Imagine an alternate ending to the story and explain how it would change the theme
Define the term 'protagonist'
Summarize the plot of the assigned chapter in five sentences
List the vocabulary words from the chapter
questions.rationale: Generating an alternate ending and reasoning about its effect on theme invites divergent, creative thinking.

questions.stem: Ms. Jacobs gives her students a checklist of thinking prompts—'What is my goal? What strategy will I try? Is it working? What will I change?'—to use during independent work. This scaffold primarily supports:
options: Group consensus building
Self-regulated, metacognitive learning
Spelling accuracy
Test-taking speed
questions.rationale: Prompts that guide goal-setting, strategy selection, monitoring, and adjustment build self-regulated, metacognitive learning.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher believes that to keep students from getting frustrated, she should break every task into small steps and provide immediate answers whenever students hesitate. From a critical-thinking standpoint, the LEAST defensible aspect of this belief is that it:
options: Offers timely feedback
Reduces classroom confusion during instructions
Provides clear structure for new content
Eliminates productive struggle that students need to develop persistence and deeper understanding
questions.rationale: Always supplying answers removes productive struggle, which is essential for developing persistence, problem-solving, and durable understanding.

questions.stem: Mr. Klein wants his history students to evaluate the reliability of two conflicting primary sources about the same event. Which task aligns BEST with this goal?
options: Students copy quotations from each source
Students compare the authors' perspectives, purposes, and evidence, then judge which source is more credible
Students memorize the dates in each source
Students rewrite each source in their own words
questions.rationale: Comparing perspective, purpose, and evidence to judge credibility is the evaluation work that source-reliability analysis requires.

questions.stem: Which question is a higher-order (analyze/evaluate) question rather than a lower-order (recall) question?
options: Who was the main person involved?
What is the definition of the term?
What year did the event take place?
How would the outcome have differed if a key decision had been made differently, and why?
questions.rationale: Asking how a different decision would change the outcome and why requires analysis and evaluation, not simple recall.

questions.stem: Ms. Lin notices students can solve textbook fraction problems but cannot apply fractions when measuring ingredients in a class cooking activity. This gap most directly signals a need to strengthen students':
options: Ability to transfer learning to real-world contexts
Reading fluency
Handwriting
Memorization of multiplication facts
questions.rationale: Success on isolated problems but failure in authentic application indicates weak transfer of learning to real contexts.

questions.stem: During an inquiry lesson, Mr. Morales wants students to generate their own questions about a set of unusual photographs before investigating. The BEST way to launch this is to:
options: Tell students exactly which question to investigate
Give students the answers and ask them to confirm them
Have students copy a list of teacher-written questions
Display the photographs and invite students to record everything they notice and wonder
questions.rationale: A notice-and-wonder routine prompts students to generate authentic questions, the foundation of student-driven inquiry.

questions.stem: Ms. Nguyen's students complete a rich problem and arrive at the correct answer quickly. To extend their thinking toward higher-order goals, her MOST effective next move is to:
options: Praise the speed and end the task
Reteach the same procedure to the whole class
Move immediately to the next worksheet
Ask students to find a second method, explain why the answer makes sense, or pose a related problem
questions.rationale: Prompting for alternate methods, justification, or problem extension pushes students from getting an answer to analyzing and creating—higher-order work.

questions.stem: A teacher posts a 'productive struggle is part of learning' norm and praises students for persisting through difficulty rather than only for correct answers. This practice primarily aims to:
options: Foster a mindset that challenge and effort lead to growth
Eliminate the need for feedback
Ensure all students finish at the same time
Discourage students from asking questions
questions.rationale: Valuing persistence through difficulty cultivates a growth-oriented mindset in which effort and challenge drive learning.

questions.stem: Mr. Ortiz wants to use real-world application to motivate a unit on linear equations. Which lesson opening BEST achieves this?
options: Present the slope-intercept formula and have students copy it
Ask students to model how much money they would save over time under two different savings plans
Have students memorize key vocabulary before any context is introduced
List the steps for solving an equation on the board
questions.rationale: Anchoring the concept in a relevant, real savings scenario gives students an authentic reason to learn linear equations.

questions.stem: In a Socratic seminar, Ms. Patel's role is best described as that of a:
options: Facilitator who poses probing questions and encourages students to respond to one another
Observer who remains silent the entire time and gives no structure
Grader who interrupts to correct each student
Lecturer who delivers the correct interpretation
questions.rationale: In a Socratic seminar the teacher facilitates—posing probing questions and guiding student-to-student dialogue rather than delivering answers.

questions.stem: A school adopts problem-based learning, but Mr. Quill worries students will miss essential content while solving open problems. The BEST way to address this concern is to:
options: Assess only the final product and ignore the content learned along the way
Abandon PBL and return to lecture for all content
Let students choose any topic regardless of the curriculum
Design problems intentionally around the required standards and embed targeted mini-lessons as needs arise
questions.rationale: Effective PBL aligns problems to standards and weaves in just-in-time mini-lessons, ensuring content coverage within the inquiry.

questions.stem: Ms. Reyes asks students, 'How do you know that?' and 'What would change your mind?' throughout a discussion. These questions primarily encourage students to:
options: Recall memorized definitions
Finish the discussion as quickly as possible
Copy answers from a partner
Examine and defend the reasoning and evidence behind their claims
questions.rationale: Asking how students know and what would change their minds prompts them to surface and evaluate the reasoning and evidence behind their claims.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the clearest example of an authentic, real-world task?
options: Filling in a worksheet of isolated grammar exercises
Matching terms to definitions on a quiz
Writing a persuasive letter to the city council proposing a new bike lane
Reciting a list of prepositions
questions.rationale: Writing a persuasive letter to a real audience for a real purpose is an authentic task connected to the world beyond the classroom.

questions.stem: Mr. Salazar plans a lesson and wants to be sure his discussion questions span a range of cognitive levels. The MOST useful planning tool for this purpose is:
options: Bloom's taxonomy used to draft questions at multiple levels
A seating chart
An attendance roster
A behavior log
questions.rationale: Bloom's taxonomy helps teachers intentionally write questions ranging from recall to higher-order analysis, evaluation, and creation.

questions.stem: Ms. Tran wants students to develop independent problem-solving rather than always relying on her. When a student says 'I'm stuck,' her BEST habitual response is to:
options: Give the answer to keep the lesson moving
Tell the student to wait until everyone else is finished
Ask, 'What have you already tried, and what do you notice?' to prompt the student's own thinking
Immediately show the student the next step
questions.rationale: Prompting students to articulate what they have tried and noticed builds independent problem-solving and keeps the cognitive work with the student.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a unit in which students research a local environmental issue, interview a stakeholder, and present a proposed solution to a community panel. This design BEST exemplifies:
options: Isolated skill drills
Project-based learning with authentic audience and real-world relevance
Pure lecture-based instruction
Timed multiple-choice testing
questions.rationale: An extended investigation culminating in a solution presented to an authentic audience is the hallmark of project-based learning.

questions.stem: Which teacher action best supports students in becoming aware of their own thinking processes?
options: Forbidding students from discussing their reasoning
Asking students to explain how they arrived at an answer and where they got confused
Grading only the final product
Providing answer keys before students attempt problems
questions.rationale: Having students explain their reasoning and identify points of confusion makes their thinking visible, building metacognitive awareness.

questions.stem: Mr. Underwood gives a complex, multi-step problem that most students cannot solve immediately. To maintain productive struggle without causing unproductive frustration, he should:
options: Remove the problem and assign easier worksheets
Provide the full solution at the first sign of difficulty
Offer just-in-time hints and questions that keep students working within reach of success
Tell students the problem is too hard for their grade level
questions.rationale: Calibrated, just-in-time scaffolding keeps the challenge within students' reach, sustaining productive struggle while preventing frustration.

questions.stem: Ms. Vega wants her assessment to require higher-order thinking rather than recall. Which assessment item EXCEPT one would meet her goal? Choose the item that does NOT require higher-order thinking.
options: List the four stages of the process in order
Design an investigation to answer a student-generated question
Critique two proposed solutions to a community problem and recommend one with justification
Analyze a data set and draw a supported conclusion
questions.rationale: Listing stages in order is recall, while critiquing, designing, and analyzing all require higher-order thinking; the listing item is the exception.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a 'think-aloud' to model how she works through a difficult reading passage, narrating her predictions, questions, and self-corrections. This strategy primarily helps students learn to:
options: Memorize the passage word for word
Read silently at all times
Monitor and regulate their own comprehension as they read
Skip difficult passages
questions.rationale: A think-aloud makes invisible comprehension strategies visible, helping students learn to monitor and regulate their own understanding.

questions.stem: Ms. Xiong notices that her higher-order questions often receive one-word answers. To elicit more elaborated reasoning, the BEST revision is to:
options: Reduce the number of questions she asks
Add more yes/no questions
Follow initial answers with prompts like 'Tell me more—what makes you say that?'
Answer the questions herself to save time
questions.rationale: Probing follow-ups such as 'What makes you say that?' push students to expand and justify their reasoning rather than stop at a brief answer.

questions.stem: Mr. Young plans an inquiry lesson but realizes some students lack the background knowledge to investigate productively. The MOST appropriate way to honor inquiry while addressing this gap is to:
options: Cancel the inquiry and lecture on all the content first
Let students investigate with no support and hope they figure it out
Give students the conclusions so they do not need background knowledge
Provide a brief, targeted experience or resource that builds needed background, then release students to investigate
questions.rationale: Brief, targeted background-building before releasing students preserves the inquiry while ensuring they can investigate productively.

questions.stem: A teacher closes each lesson by asking students to write one thing they understand well and one question they still have. This routine BEST supports:
options: Faster grading of homework
Memorization of vocabulary
Behavior management only
Metacognitive reflection and identification of learning gaps
questions.rationale: Reflecting on what is understood and what remains unclear is metacognition that also surfaces learning gaps for both student and teacher.

questions.stem: Ms. Zamora wants students to apply a science concept to an unfamiliar situation on an assessment. Which item BEST measures transfer rather than recall?
options: Given data about a new object not discussed in class, predict whether it will float and explain why
State the definition of density
List three properties of matter
Reproduce the class diagram of the experiment
questions.rationale: Predicting behavior of a novel object using a learned principle measures transfer, whereas the other items measure recall.

questions.stem: Which of the following is LEAST likely to promote critical thinking in a lesson?
options: Having students solve an open-ended problem
Encouraging students to justify their answers with evidence
Asking students to evaluate competing claims
Requiring students to copy notes verbatim without discussion
questions.rationale: Copying notes verbatim without discussion is a passive recall task and is least likely to engage critical thinking among the options.

questions.stem: Mr. Abara wants students to see connections between math and other subjects to deepen understanding and transfer. The BEST approach is to:
options: Teach math facts in isolation with no context
Keep each subject entirely separate to avoid confusion
Limit math to textbook word problems only
Design an interdisciplinary task, such as using statistics to analyze a social studies data set
questions.rationale: Interdisciplinary tasks help students connect and transfer skills across domains, deepening understanding.

questions.stem: In a problem-based unit, one group reaches a solution by reasoning carefully but makes a computational error, while another reaches the correct answer by guessing. To best promote critical thinking, the teacher's feedback should:
options: Reward only the group with the correct final answer
Emphasize and value the quality of reasoning in both groups while helping each refine accuracy
Ignore the reasoning and focus solely on the numbers
Tell the guessing group their luck proves their method is sound
questions.rationale: Valuing the reasoning process—while still attending to accuracy—signals that sound thinking matters more than a lucky answer, promoting critical thinking.

questions.stem: Ms. Briggs wants to increase the cognitive demand of a lesson where students currently just identify examples of figurative language. The BEST revision is to have students:
options: Highlight every metaphor in the passage
Copy each example into a chart
Analyze how the author's figurative language shapes the tone and create an original passage using a similar technique
Count the number of similes in the text
questions.rationale: Analyzing the effect of figurative language and creating an original passage raises the task from identification to analysis and creation.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a rubric and asks them to assess their own draft before submitting it, noting strengths and areas to improve. This practice primarily builds:
options: Group decision-making
Faster reading rates
Spelling memorization
Self-assessment and metacognitive monitoring
questions.rationale: Using a rubric to judge one's own work and identify improvements develops self-assessment and metacognitive monitoring.

questions.stem: Mr. Castillo's principal asks him to justify why he spends class time on open-ended investigations instead of more practice worksheets. His STRONGEST research-based justification is that open-ended investigations:
options: Require less planning than direct instruction
Are easier to grade than worksheets
Engage students in higher-order thinking and promote deeper, more transferable understanding
Guarantee that all students will earn the same grade
questions.rationale: The defensible rationale is that open-ended investigations engage higher-order thinking and build understanding that transfers, which worksheets seldom achieve.

questions.stem: Ms. Alvarez, a fourth-grade teacher, wants her students to use tablets to record short video reflections on a science experiment instead of writing the reflections by hand. Using the SAMR model, at which level is this technology use best classified?
options: Modification, because the task is significantly redesigned through video recording capabilities
Substitution, because the tablet simply replaces paper with no functional change
Redefinition, because the task could not be conceived without the technology
Augmentation, because the tablet replaces paper with some functional improvement such as easy revision
questions.rationale: Recording spoken video reflections is a significant task redesign that is not possible with paper alone, placing it at the Modification level of SAMR, where technology allows for significant task redesign.

questions.stem: The TPACK framework describes the knowledge teachers need to integrate technology effectively. The intersection of all three core knowledge domains in TPACK refers to understanding how to:
options: Operate hardware and software independently of any subject matter
Teach content using effective strategies and appropriate technology together in a given context
Manage classroom behavior during computer lab sessions
Select the least expensive devices for a school district
questions.rationale: TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge) is the integrated understanding of how content, pedagogy, and technology interact, so teachers can teach specific content with appropriate strategies and tools.

questions.stem: Mr. Cho teaches seventh-grade U.S. history and wants to integrate technology in a way that reaches the Redefinition level of SAMR. Which activity best accomplishes this?
options: Having students take an online multiple-choice quiz that is automatically graded
Having students collaborate in real time with peers in another state to co-create a multimedia documentary on shared historical events
Having students type their essay responses and use a built-in grammar checker
Having students read the textbook chapter on a digital screen instead of in print
questions.rationale: Redefinition involves tasks that were previously inconceivable without technology. Real-time collaboration across states to co-create a multimedia product is a new task made possible only by technology.

questions.stem: A high school biology teacher, Ms. Okafor, has a student who is blind. To ensure the student can access an interactive online lab simulation, which step should the teacher take FIRST?
options: Verify that the simulation is compatible with screen-reader software and provides text alternatives for visual content
Print all simulation screens in large color photographs
Assume the student will use a peer to describe everything on the screen
Excuse the student from the lab activity and assign a written summary instead
questions.rationale: Ensuring accessibility means confirming the digital tool works with assistive technology such as a screen reader and provides text alternatives, so the student has equitable access to the same learning.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of teaching responsible digital citizenship to elementary students?
options: Encouraging students to post personal home addresses on a class website
Instructing students to share their passwords with classmates to make group logins easier
Teaching students to evaluate whether an online source is credible before using its information
Allowing students to copy and paste online text into reports without citation
questions.rationale: Digital citizenship includes evaluating source credibility and using information responsibly and ethically; teaching students to assess credibility supports these goals.

questions.stem: Mr. Daniels wants third graders to practice multiplication facts and receive immediate corrective feedback while he works with a small group. Which technology use is MOST appropriate for this purpose?
options: A whole-class lecture streamed on the projector
A printed worksheet photographed and emailed to families
A documentary video about the history of mathematics
An adaptive math-fact practice app that adjusts difficulty and gives instant feedback
questions.rationale: Appropriate tool selection matches the tool to the instructional goal. An adaptive practice app provides individualized, immediate feedback while freeing the teacher to work with a small group.

questions.stem: Each of the following is an appropriate way to support a student with a learning disability through assistive technology EXCEPT:
options: Allowing word-prediction software to help the student compose written work
Providing text-to-speech software so the student can listen to grade-level reading passages
Offering speech-to-text software so the student can dictate written responses
Removing all grade-level content and replacing it with picture-only activities
questions.rationale: Assistive technology provides access to grade-level content; it does not lower expectations. Replacing all content with picture-only activities removes access to grade-level learning.

questions.stem: Ms. Pereira designs a unit in which sixth graders use a shared digital document to collect data, then create individual infographics, and finally publish their work to an authentic audience through a class blog with comment moderation. Which statement BEST describes the strength of her technology integration?
options: The technology focuses only on entertainment value rather than learning outcomes
The technology transforms tasks and connects students to authentic audiences while embedding digital citizenship practices
The technology is limited to substitution because students could do all of this on paper
The technology is used mainly for classroom management and saving paper
questions.rationale: Strong integration goes beyond substitution: collaboration, publishing to an authentic audience, and moderated commenting transform tasks and embed responsible digital citizenship while serving learning goals.

questions.stem: A teacher discovers that two students used a generative writing tool to produce an essay and submitted it as their own original work. The MOST appropriate response that supports digital citizenship is to:
options: Use the situation to teach about academic integrity and the ethical, transparent use of digital tools, then have students revise authentically
Permanently ban all students from using any digital device
Give the whole class a zero to discourage future misuse
Ignore the situation because the technology is widely available
questions.rationale: Responsible digital citizenship includes teaching ethical use and academic integrity. Addressing the specific behavior and guiding authentic revision is constructive and instructive.

questions.stem: Mr. Nguyen wants students to demonstrate their understanding of the water cycle using technology at the Augmentation level of SAMR. Which task fits this level?
options: Students draw the water cycle on paper and turn it in
Students create a labeled digital diagram using a drawing app with features that let them easily edit, add audio labels, and link definitions
Students read an online article about the water cycle that mirrors the textbook
Students collaborate with scientists worldwide to design an original simulation
questions.rationale: Augmentation is a direct tool substitute with functional improvement. A digital diagram with easy editing, audio labels, and linked definitions enhances the familiar diagram task without redesigning it.

questions.stem: A middle school teacher notices that her digital learning activity excludes students who lack reliable home internet. Applying principles of equitable technology integration, which approach is LEAST appropriate?
options: Coordinating with the school to provide device checkout and hotspot lending
Assigning all technology-dependent homework that requires home broadband and counting it heavily toward grades
Designing assignments that can be completed at school or with downloadable offline access
Providing alternative non-digital options that meet the same learning objectives
questions.rationale: Equitable integration ensures all students can access learning regardless of home resources. Heavily weighting broadband-dependent homework penalizes students for circumstances beyond their control.

questions.stem: Which scenario best illustrates a teacher using technology to support student self-directed learning?
options: Students watch a video together with no interaction or follow-up
The teacher uses a projector to deliver the same lecture to all students
Students use an online learning platform with a menu of resources and checkpoints to set goals, monitor their progress, and choose practice based on their needs
The teacher collects all devices and reads aloud from the screen
questions.rationale: Self-directed learning is supported when technology lets students set goals, monitor progress, and make choices. A platform with goal setting, progress monitoring, and choice fosters learner agency.

questions.stem: A teacher is helping students understand online privacy. Which guideline BEST reflects responsible digital citizenship?
options: Use the same simple password for every account so it is easy to remember
Accept all friend or follow requests to build a large network quickly
Think carefully before sharing personal information online and adjust privacy settings appropriately
Click on any link received to see what it contains
questions.rationale: Digital citizenship emphasizes protecting personal information and managing privacy settings. Thinking before sharing and adjusting settings reflects responsible online behavior.
