questions.stem: A ninth-grade biology teacher, Mr. Okafor, designs a unit in which students first manipulate physical models of cells, then create diagrams, and finally write abstract explanations of cellular transport using only text. A colleague asks why he sequences the unit this way. Which rationale best reflects an understanding of cognitive development in adolescents?
options: Adolescents cannot understand abstract concepts, so the written explanations should be removed entirely
Concrete experiences build the conceptual foundation that supports later abstract reasoning, even as adolescents develop formal operational thought
The sequence is arbitrary because by ninth grade all students reason identically about abstract content
Physical models are only appropriate for elementary students, so the sequence reverses best practice
questions.rationale: Although adolescents are developing formal operational reasoning, abstract understanding is strengthened when grounded in concrete and representational experiences. Sequencing from concrete to abstract supports the transition and accommodates variation in students' developmental readiness.

questions.stem: In a kindergarten class, Ms. Park observes that several children insist a tall, narrow glass holds more water than a short, wide glass even after watching the same amount poured between them. According to Piaget's framework, which instructional response best supports these learners?
options: Skip all volume activities until the children reach third grade
Tell the children they are wrong and have them memorize that the amounts are equal
Give a written quiz on conservation to identify which students need remediation
Provide repeated hands-on pouring and measuring experiences over time, recognizing conservation develops with maturation and experience
questions.rationale: The children are exhibiting a typical preoperational lack of conservation. Rather than correcting them verbally or testing them, the teacher should provide rich, repeated concrete experiences that support the natural development of conservation through interaction and maturation.

questions.stem: Seventh-grade teacher Ms. Reyes notices that her students are intensely concerned with fairness, peer opinion, and whether class rules apply equally to everyone. She wants to design a classroom management approach that leverages this developmental characteristic rather than fighting it. Which approach best aligns with the social-emotional development of early adolescents?
options: Impose all rules unilaterally and refuse to explain the reasoning behind them
Eliminate all rules and allow students to self-govern without structure
Use individualized secret consequences so students cannot compare how rules are applied
Collaboratively develop a class constitution with students, emphasizing consistent and transparent application of agreed-upon norms
questions.rationale: Early adolescents have a heightened sense of fairness and a strong orientation toward peers. Involving them in creating norms and applying them transparently respects their developmental need for justice and belonging while maintaining structure.

questions.stem: A first-grade teacher plans a science lesson and wants to account for the typical attention span and physical development of six-year-olds. Which lesson design choice is most developmentally appropriate?
options: A two-hour independent reading block with no movement or interaction
A timed written essay with no breaks to maximize focus
Several short, varied segments that alternate between brief instruction and active, hands-on exploration
A single 50-minute lecture with students seated and listening throughout
questions.rationale: Young children have shorter attention spans and a developmental need for movement and concrete activity. Breaking the lesson into short, varied, active segments matches their physical and cognitive development.

questions.stem: Mr. Castillo, an eleventh-grade English teacher, observes that several students are deeply preoccupied with questions about identity, future career paths, and 'who they really are.' He wants to connect his literature unit to this developmental phase. Which instructional decision most authentically does so?
options: Select texts featuring protagonists navigating identity and choices, and invite students to analyze characters' decisions in relation to their own emerging values
Assign only plot-summary worksheets to keep the content concrete and impersonal
Forbid any personal connection to the texts to maintain academic objectivity
Replace literature with rote vocabulary drills unrelated to identity themes
questions.rationale: Late adolescents are actively engaged in identity formation. Choosing texts about identity and allowing students to relate characters' choices to their own values leverages this developmental stage to deepen engagement and analysis.

questions.stem: A high school chemistry teacher, Mr. Bowman, has a student, Layla, who is an emergent bilingual at an intermediate English proficiency level. Layla understands chemistry concepts but struggles to express her reasoning in written lab reports. Which instructional support best maintains rigor while addressing her language needs?
options: Provide a sentence-stem scaffold and a content word bank so Layla can articulate her scientific reasoning in writing
Exempt Layla from all written lab reports so she avoids the language demand entirely
Lower the conceptual difficulty of Layla's chemistry tasks until her English improves
Grade Layla's reports solely on grammar to motivate language improvement
questions.rationale: Sentence stems and content word banks scaffold language production without reducing the cognitive demand of the chemistry content. This supports emergent bilinguals in demonstrating their understanding while continuing to develop academic English.

questions.stem: Ms. Tran teaches a sixth-grade class that includes Marcus, who has an IEP specifying extended time and a scribe for extended written responses, and Priya, identified as gifted who finishes assignments rapidly and shows boredom. Ms. Tran wants to differentiate appropriately for both within the same writing lesson. Which plan best meets both students' needs without lowering expectations?
options: Provide Marcus his IEP accommodations on the grade-level prompt, and offer Priya an extension that deepens analysis at greater complexity
Give Marcus a shorter, simpler prompt and let Priya act as Marcus's tutor for the period
Allow Priya free time when finished early and reduce the rigor of Marcus's content
Give all students the identical task and timing, ignoring the IEP and the gifted profile
questions.rationale: Effective differentiation provides legally required accommodations to maintain access to grade-level content for Marcus while extending depth and complexity for Priya. Both keep high expectations; neither involves reducing rigor or misusing a student as a substitute teacher.

questions.stem: During a small-group math task, second-grade teacher Ms. Holloway notices that one group's only English learner remains silent while peers dominate the discussion. To promote equitable participation grounded in the student's strengths, which strategy is most effective?
options: Remove the English learner from the group to work alone
Allow the dominant students to continue, assuming the English learner is learning by listening
Tell the English learner to simply speak up more often
Assign each group member a specific role and provide the English learner a role with built-in visual and manipulative supports to contribute meaningfully
questions.rationale: Structured group roles with embedded supports ensure the English learner has a defined, accessible way to contribute, promoting equitable participation and using visual and manipulative scaffolds aligned to the learner's needs.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to ensure that classroom materials and examples reflect the diversity of her students and the broader world. Which action best supports this goal?
options: Use only examples and images featuring a single cultural group
Display materials only in the teacher's home language regardless of student backgrounds
Select texts, images, and examples that represent a range of cultures, family structures, and backgrounds
Avoid any references to culture to keep the curriculum neutral
questions.rationale: Including diverse, representative materials helps all students see themselves reflected and exposes them to varied perspectives, supporting inclusion and engagement.

questions.stem: Mr. Adeyemi reviews his classroom data and finds that boys are called on far more often than girls during whole-class math discussions, and that this pattern correlates with declining math confidence reported by girls in a survey. Which response best demonstrates a commitment to equity in his practice?
options: Call only on girls for the remainder of the year to compensate
Conclude that girls are simply less interested in math and continue current practices
Implement an equitable participation system, such as randomized response tools, and monitor the data to ensure balanced engagement over time
Stop conducting class discussions entirely to avoid any participation disparity
questions.rationale: Recognizing an inequitable participation pattern, the teacher should adopt a structured, data-monitored strategy to ensure all students are engaged equitably, then track results. This addresses the disparity systematically rather than through avoidance or overcorrection.

questions.stem: Ms. Delgado is planning a three-week eighth-grade unit on persuasive writing. The TEKS objective requires students to compose an argument with a clear claim, relevant evidence, and acknowledgment of counterclaims. She wants her summative assessment, daily lessons, and formative checks to be tightly aligned. Which planning sequence best ensures alignment?
options: Plan the formative quizzes first and infer the objectives from the quiz questions
Choose a published worksheet packet and let it determine the unit's objectives
Design engaging daily activities first, then create a test at the end based on whatever was covered
Identify the objective and design the summative assessment of argument writing first, then plan lessons and formative checks that build the specific skills the assessment requires
questions.rationale: Backward design begins with the objective, defines how mastery will be measured through the summative assessment, then builds aligned lessons and formative checks. This ensures every component targets the intended learning outcome.

questions.stem: A seventh-grade science teacher writes the following objective: 'Students will understand photosynthesis.' A mentor advises that the objective is difficult to assess. Which revision best makes the objective measurable and instructionally useful?
options: Students will be exposed to photosynthesis content during the unit
Students will model the inputs and outputs of photosynthesis and explain how energy is transformed during the process
Students will know about photosynthesis by the end of the week
Students will appreciate the importance of photosynthesis in nature
questions.rationale: Measurable objectives use observable verbs that specify what students will do to demonstrate learning. 'Model' and 'explain' produce assessable evidence, unlike vague verbs such as understand, know, appreciate, or be exposed to.

questions.stem: Mr. Castaneda's tenth-grade geometry objective asks students to 'construct a logical proof justifying triangle congruence using appropriate theorems.' He is selecting a summative task. Which assessment best aligns with the cognitive level of this objective?
options: A multiple-choice test asking students to recall the names of congruence theorems
A matching activity pairing theorem names with their definitions
A task requiring students to write an original proof of triangle congruence and justify each step with theorems
A fill-in-the-blank worksheet on vocabulary terms related to triangles
questions.rationale: The objective targets a high-level skill: constructing and justifying a proof. Only a task that requires students to actually produce and justify a proof aligns with that cognitive demand; recall and matching tasks assess lower-level knowledge.

questions.stem: Ms. Whitfield notices that her third graders consistently master each day's lesson in isolation but struggle to connect ideas across the unit on ecosystems. To strengthen coherence, which planning adjustment is most effective?
options: Increase the number of unrelated worksheets per lesson
Use an anchoring essential question and recurring connections that thread individual lessons into a cohesive conceptual arc
Teach each lesson as a fully separate topic with no references to prior lessons
Test each lesson immediately and never revisit earlier content
questions.rationale: An essential question and intentional cross-lesson connections help students integrate discrete lessons into a coherent understanding of the larger concept, addressing the fragmentation Ms. Whitfield observed.

questions.stem: When planning a unit, a teacher wants to make sure the lessons build on what students already know. Which step best supports this goal?
options: Cover content in the textbook order regardless of student readiness
Begin teaching new material without considering students' prior knowledge
Assess students' existing knowledge and skills before planning, then connect new content to that foundation
Assume all students start with identical background knowledge
questions.rationale: Effective planning begins by identifying students' prior knowledge so that new learning can be connected to and built upon what students already understand.

questions.stem: Ms. Okonkwo's eleventh-grade history unit objective requires students to 'evaluate competing historical interpretations of an event using primary source evidence.' She drafts three potential summative tasks. To best align the assessment with the objective's analytical demand, which task should she choose?
options: A timeline-ordering activity placing events in chronological sequence
A coloring map activity labeling the regions where the event occurred
An essay in which students weigh two conflicting historian interpretations and defend a position using cited primary sources
A quiz asking students to define key vocabulary terms from the unit
questions.rationale: The objective requires evaluation of competing interpretations using evidence, a high-level analytical task. An argumentative essay weighing interpretations and citing primary sources matches that demand, while sequencing, defining, and labeling tasks assess lower-level skills.

questions.stem: After administering a formative quiz on fractions, Ms. Bautista analyzes the results: 80 percent of students answered conceptual items correctly but a specific subgroup consistently missed items requiring conversion of improper fractions to mixed numbers. Which instructional decision best uses this data?
options: Record the scores in the gradebook and make no instructional changes
Form a targeted small group for the identified students to reteach improper-to-mixed conversion while others extend their learning
Reteach the entire fractions unit to the whole class from the beginning
Move on to the next unit because most of the class passed the quiz
questions.rationale: Formative data should drive responsive, targeted instruction. The data pinpoints a specific skill gap in a subgroup, so a focused reteach for that group while others extend is the most efficient, differentiated use of the information.

questions.stem: Mr. Sandoval reviews a class set of student lab reports and notices that nearly every student wrote an accurate procedure but failed to connect their data to the underlying scientific principle in the conclusion. Before reteaching, he wants to determine the root cause. Which next step best informs his instructional response?
options: Examine the pattern more closely and ask targeted questions to determine whether students lack the conceptual link or the writing skill to express it
Conclude the lab was too difficult and remove conclusions from future reports
Assume all students are simply careless and assign the reports to be redone for homework
Lower everyone's grade and move on to the next experiment
questions.rationale: A widespread, consistent error suggests an instructional gap rather than individual carelessness. Diagnosing whether the issue is conceptual understanding or written expression allows the teacher to target reteaching precisely rather than guessing.

questions.stem: Ms. Iverson wants to use formative assessment to adjust instruction in real time during a sixth-grade lesson on ratios. Which technique best provides immediate, actionable evidence of understanding for all students before she proceeds?
options: Ask 'Does everyone understand?' and continue when no one objects
Call on one volunteer and assume the answer represents the whole class
Wait until the end-of-unit test to gauge understanding
Have every student solve a quick ratio problem on individual whiteboards and display answers simultaneously for the teacher to scan
questions.rationale: All-student response techniques such as individual whiteboards give the teacher simultaneous evidence from every learner, enabling immediate instructional adjustment. Yes/no questions and single volunteers do not reveal class-wide understanding.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a short ungraded check at the start of a lesson to find out what students already know about the topic. What is the primary purpose of this assessment?
options: To assign final grades for the unit
To fulfill a paperwork requirement only
To gather diagnostic information that guides how the lesson should be taught
To rank students against one another publicly
questions.rationale: A pre-lesson ungraded check is a diagnostic or formative assessment used to reveal students' existing knowledge so instruction can be adjusted to meet their needs.

questions.stem: Ms. Pruitt examines results from a unit test and a separate performance task on the same objective. On the multiple-choice test most students scored well, but on the performance task many struggled to apply the concept. What is the most valid conclusion she can draw?
options: The multiple-choice test alone fully measures mastery, so no further action is needed
Students simply did not try on the performance task
Students may have surface-level recall but have not yet developed the deeper application the objective requires, so instruction should target transfer
The performance task was unfair and should be discarded
questions.rationale: Using multiple measures reveals that strong recall does not guarantee application. The discrepancy indicates students need instruction that builds transfer and application, demonstrating the value of varied assessment formats for valid conclusions.

questions.stem: Mr. Beauchamp is designing a rubric for an eighth-grade research presentation. He wants the rubric to support learning, not just sort students. Which rubric feature best serves this purpose?
options: Clearly described performance levels for each criterion that students can use to understand expectations and guide improvement
A pass/fail mark given only after the presentation with no advance sharing
A single overall score with no description of what each level means
Criteria written in technical jargon students cannot interpret
questions.rationale: A rubric supports learning when it includes clear, descriptive performance levels for each criterion, shared in advance, so students understand expectations and can use it to improve their work.

questions.stem: Ms. Fontaine notices that her students perform well on assessments immediately after a unit but score poorly on cumulative reviews weeks later. To improve long-term retention as measured by her assessments, which instructional adjustment is most supported by learning research?
options: Eliminate cumulative reviews so the retention problem is no longer visible
Allow students to keep notes open during all assessments to mask retention gaps
Test students only once, immediately after each unit, and never revisit content
Incorporate spaced, cumulative retrieval practice so students repeatedly recall earlier content over time
questions.rationale: Spaced practice and retrieval practice strengthen long-term retention. Revisiting earlier content through distributed, cumulative recall opportunities directly addresses the drop in delayed performance the data revealed.

questions.stem: Mr. Yamamoto teaches a class that includes a student, Tomas, who has a documented learning disability in reading and a 504-related need for content presented through multiple modalities. When planning a social studies lesson on the Texas Revolution, which approach best applies principles of Universal Design for Learning to benefit Tomas and the whole class?
options: Offer the content through multiple means, such as audio, visuals, and text, and allow varied ways for students to demonstrate understanding
Require all students to take notes by hand at the same fixed pace
Give Tomas an entirely different, simpler topic from his classmates
Present all content exclusively through a dense textbook reading
questions.rationale: Universal Design for Learning provides multiple means of representation, engagement, and expression. Offering content in varied modalities and accepting varied demonstrations of learning supports Tomas while benefiting all learners, without segregating him.

questions.stem: Ms. Escobar teaches third grade and wants to support students' growing capacity for self-regulation, which is still developing at this age. A student becomes frustrated and gives up quickly when a task is challenging. Which response best supports the development of self-regulation?
options: Remove all challenging tasks so the student never feels frustrated
Immediately complete the task for the student to relieve the frustration
Tell the student to simply try harder and stop being frustrated
Teach and model concrete coping strategies, such as taking a breath and breaking the task into smaller steps, then scaffold the student's use of them
questions.rationale: Self-regulation develops with explicit instruction and scaffolding. Teaching and modeling coping strategies and supporting their use helps the child build the skills to manage frustration, appropriate to this developmental stage.

questions.stem: Ms. Abernathy is designing a project-based unit for tenth-grade environmental science with the objective that students 'design and justify a solution to a local water-quality problem using evidence.' She must sequence learning experiences so students can succeed at the culminating project. Which sequence best aligns instruction to the objective?
options: Assign the final project on day one with no preparatory instruction and grade the results
Spend the entire unit lecturing and reserve no time for students to design a solution
Have students memorize water-quality vocabulary as the sole preparation for the project
Build prerequisite knowledge and skills, water-quality concepts, data analysis, and argumentation, then scaffold toward the independent solution-design project
questions.rationale: Aligning instruction to a complex performance objective requires sequencing that builds the prerequisite knowledge and skills, then gradually scaffolds students toward independent application in the culminating project. This ensures students are prepared to meet the objective.

questions.stem: During independent reading time in a 4th-grade class, two students at the back begin a loud argument over a shared dictionary. Most of the class stops reading to watch. Which action should the teacher take FIRST?
options: Move calmly toward the two students while giving a brief, neutral redirection that lowers the volume and signals the rest of the class to return to reading
Send both students to the office to file a referral so the rest of the class can resume reading
Stop the lesson and lead a whole-class discussion about how to share classroom materials respectfully
Assign the two students a written reflection about their behavior to complete during recess
questions.rationale: The teacher's first priority is to de-escalate and restore the learning environment with the least disruption. Proximity plus a calm, neutral redirection interrupts the conflict and cues the class to refocus without amplifying attention on the misbehavior. Larger consequences or instruction can follow once the situation is stable.

questions.stem: A high school teacher notices that the same five students dominate every class discussion while quieter students rarely speak. The teacher wants to increase equitable participation without embarrassing reluctant students. Which approach BEST accomplishes this goal?
options: Institute a 'think-write-pair-share' routine and use randomized response strategies that give all students processing time before sharing
Tell the five dominant students they may no longer answer questions for the rest of the unit
Call on quiet students by name without warning so they learn to stay prepared
Award participation points only to students who volunteer, motivating the quiet students to speak up
questions.rationale: Equitable engagement is built through structures that give every student think time and a low-risk way to share. Think-write-pair-share plus randomized response distributes participation, lowers anxiety, and ensures all students rehearse ideas before speaking—without singling out or penalizing anyone.

questions.stem: A teacher is planning seating and traffic patterns for a new science lab where students rotate among stations. The teacher's main goal is to minimize off-task behavior and maximize safety. Which arrangement decision reflects the strongest proactive management?
options: Group the most capable students together at each station so they can finish quickly and help others
Design clear, unobstructed pathways between stations and position the teacher's circulation route so all students remain in view at all times
Place all stations along one wall so students stay in a single line and the teacher can watch from the front
Seat students alphabetically so the teacher can quickly take attendance during transitions
questions.rationale: Proactive management designs the physical environment to support supervision and smooth movement. Clear pathways prevent crowding and accidents, and a circulation route that maintains full visibility allows the teacher to monitor, intervene early, and keep students safe and on task.

questions.stem: Three weeks into the school year, a middle school teacher realizes that transitions between activities consistently waste 8-10 minutes and trigger most of the day's behavior problems. The teacher wants a lasting fix. Which step should the teacher take NEXT?
options: Assign detention to the last three students to be ready after each transition
Explicitly teach, model, and practice a specific transition routine with a timed signal until students can perform it fluently
Reduce the number of activities each period so fewer transitions are needed
Add the rule 'transition quickly' to the posted classroom rules and remind students daily
questions.rationale: Transitions are a learned routine. The most durable solution is to explicitly teach and have students rehearse a concrete procedure with a clear signal until it becomes automatic. Practicing the routine builds the habit that prevents the disruption, rather than just naming an expectation or punishing the slowest students.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher wants students to internalize classroom expectations from day one. Which practice is the MOST effective way to establish workable rules and procedures?
options: Collaboratively develop a small set of positively stated expectations with students, then teach and practice the procedures that support them
Post a long list of detailed rules covering every possible situation and read them aloud
Adopt the exact rules from a veteran teacher's classroom without modification
Wait until the first serious misbehavior occurs, then create rules in response
questions.rationale: Effective expectations are few, positively stated, and developed with student input to build ownership, then reinforced by explicitly taught procedures. This combination promotes buy-in and gives students the concrete behaviors needed to meet the expectations.

questions.stem: A student who has had several recent conflicts arrives at class visibly agitated, slams a backpack down, and mutters that 'this day is already ruined.' The bell has just rung. Which teacher response is MOST appropriate?
options: Announce to the class that disruptions will not be tolerated today
Ignore the behavior entirely and proceed as though nothing happened
Quietly approach, acknowledge the student's frustration in a calm private tone, and offer a brief moment to settle before joining the activity
Immediately confront the student about the backpack in front of the class to establish authority
questions.rationale: De-escalation begins with calm acknowledgment and giving the student a face-saving way to regroup. A quiet, private check-in respects the student's dignity, reduces the chance of a power struggle, and supports a return to learning, addressing the emotional state driving the behavior.

questions.stem: A teacher relies heavily on stickers and a class store to motivate work completion. Over the semester, students increasingly ask 'What do we get?' before starting any task and produce minimal work when no reward is attached. The teacher wants to shift toward durable motivation. Which approach is BEST?
options: Eliminate all reinforcement immediately and rely solely on grades
Increase the value of the rewards so students stay motivated to complete work
Gradually reduce tangible rewards while increasing tasks that offer meaningful choice, relevance, and visible progress toward students' own goals
Add public rankings of who has earned the most rewards to spur competition
questions.rationale: Over-reliance on extrinsic rewards can crowd out intrinsic motivation. The durable fix is to fade tangible rewards while designing tasks that satisfy students' needs for autonomy (choice), relevance, and competence (visible progress)—the drivers of intrinsic motivation.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a quiet hand signal to gain attention. One day, after the signal, most students quiet down but a small group keeps talking. Which response is the LEAST effective for maintaining the established procedure?
options: Calmly restate the expectation and give the group a few seconds to comply
Loudly shout over the talking group to begin the lesson immediately so no time is lost
Wait briefly in silence while using proximity, then thank the class once everyone is attentive
Make brief eye contact with the talking students while continuing to hold the signal
questions.rationale: The question asks for the LEAST effective response. Shouting over students abandons the calm attention procedure, models the loud behavior the teacher is trying to reduce, and rewards talking by allowing it to continue. The other options reinforce the established quiet signal.

questions.stem: Two students have a building conflict that erupts into shouting. One student steps toward the other with clenched fists. The class falls silent. Which sequence of teacher actions reflects sound de-escalation and safety priorities?
options: Step between the students physically and demand they both apologize immediately
Order the angrier student to leave the room while continuing to teach the others
Calmly direct the rest of the class to a known safety routine, use a low steady voice to separate the two by giving each space, and call for support if the situation does not de-escalate
Raise your voice to match theirs so they understand the seriousness of the situation
questions.rationale: Safety is the first priority. The teacher should secure the rest of the class, use a calm, low voice and spatial separation rather than physical intervention, and summon support if needed. Lowering one's own intensity and creating space reduces the chance of physical escalation while protecting everyone.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to take more responsibility for managing the classroom community. Which strategy BEST promotes student self-regulation and shared ownership rather than teacher-controlled compliance?
options: Assign the teacher's aide to monitor and report every rule violation
Post a behavior chart that publicly tracks each student's daily color status
Promise a pizza party only if zero rule violations occur all month
Establish rotating classroom jobs and regular class meetings where students help solve community problems and set goals
questions.rationale: Self-regulation and shared ownership grow when students have authentic roles and a voice in solving problems. Rotating jobs and class meetings give students responsibility and practice in collaborative problem-solving, building an internal sense of community rather than externally enforced compliance.

questions.stem: As students enter class, a teacher greets them at the door and points to a posted 'Do Now' task displayed on the board. What is the PRIMARY classroom-management benefit of this routine?
options: It replaces the need for any lesson objectives during the period
It guarantees that all students will earn high marks on the bell-ringer
It allows the teacher to grade homework while students wait
It minimizes unstructured downtime at the start of class, reducing opportunities for off-task behavior and signaling an immediate purposeful start
questions.rationale: A bell-ringer routine engages students productively the moment they arrive, eliminating the unstructured time when off-task behavior typically emerges. It sets a purposeful tone and supports smooth, proactive management at a high-risk transition point.

questions.stem: A teacher consistently uses a fixed wait time, calm tone, and predictable consequences. One student, however, escalates dramatically whenever redirected, apparently to draw an audience. The teacher has documented the pattern. Which response is MOST likely to reduce the escalations over time?
options: Deliver the redirection more sternly so the student understands the teacher is serious
Privately conference with the student to identify triggers, teach a discreet self-regulation cue, and minimize the public audience during redirections
Place the student's name on the board each time an escalation occurs
Stop redirecting the student to avoid triggering the escalation
questions.rationale: When attention-seeking maintains the behavior, the effective strategy removes the audience while teaching the student a replacement self-regulation skill. A private conference to identify triggers and establish a discreet cue addresses the function of the behavior rather than feeding it with public attention.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a group project and anticipates that some groups will finish early while others struggle. To keep all students productively engaged and prevent management problems, which proactive structure is MOST important to prepare in advance?
options: Clear anchor or extension activities for early finishers and built-in checkpoints with support for groups that fall behind
A rule that no one may move on until every group finishes
A single deadline with no flexibility so all groups feel equal pressure
A promise of extra credit for whichever group finishes first
questions.rationale: Proactive management plans for varied pacing. Meaningful extension activities keep early finishers engaged, while checkpoints with support keep struggling groups on track—both prevent the idle or frustrated time that produces off-task behavior. This anticipates problems before they arise.

questions.stem: During a lesson, a teacher notices a student quietly doodling instead of working but otherwise not disturbing anyone. The teacher wants to redirect without interrupting the flow of instruction for the rest of the class. Which intervention BEST fits the principle of least-intrusive redirection?
options: Take the student's notebook away for the rest of the period
Stop the lesson and ask the student why they are not working
Continue teaching while moving toward the student and placing a hand gently near their materials as a nonverbal cue
Announce to the whole class that everyone should be working, not drawing
questions.rationale: The least-intrusive intervention redirects the individual without halting instruction or drawing class attention. Proximity and a subtle nonverbal cue refocus the student while the lesson continues, preserving the learning flow for everyone—the appropriate low-level response to minor off-task behavior.

questions.stem: A teacher's class has a small group of students whose home language is not English and who appear hesitant during fast-paced oral question-and-answer sessions. The teacher wants to maintain rigor while ensuring these students engage equitably. Which adjustment BEST balances both goals?
options: Translate every question into the students' home language before asking it aloud
Lower the difficulty of questions directed to these students so they can answer easily
Increase wait time, allow brief partner rehearsal before responding, and provide sentence frames that support academic language without reducing cognitive demand
Excuse these students from oral participation and give them written work instead
questions.rationale: Equitable engagement maintains high expectations while removing barriers. Extended wait time, partner rehearsal, and sentence frames scaffold language and confidence so multilingual learners can access rigorous content and participate fully—supporting access without lowering the intellectual demand.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to find a new unit personally meaningful so they invest effort. Which planning move is MOST likely to increase students' intrinsic motivation at the start of the unit?
options: Open with a compelling problem or question connected to students' lives and invite them to generate questions they want to investigate
Tell students the unit will be difficult so they take it seriously
Begin by announcing the test date and the percentage of the grade the unit is worth
List all the standards the unit covers and have students copy them
questions.rationale: Intrinsic motivation rises when learning connects to students' interests and gives them a sense of agency. A compelling, relevant problem plus the chance to pose their own questions taps curiosity and relevance, two strong drivers of engagement, far more than emphasizing grades or difficulty.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a capable student has stopped trying on challenging tasks, saying 'I'm just not a math person.' The teacher wants to rebuild the student's motivation and persistence. Which combination of strategies is MOST aligned with research on motivation and a growth mindset?
options: Reduce the difficulty of all the student's tasks so they experience constant success
Praise the student's intelligence whenever they get an answer right to boost confidence
Compare the student's work publicly to higher-performing peers to inspire improvement
Provide specific feedback on effort and strategy, set attainable challenge goals, and help the student attribute success to controllable factors like persistence and approach
questions.rationale: Growth-oriented motivation comes from attributing outcomes to controllable factors. Feedback on effort and strategy, appropriately challenging goals, and helping the student credit success to persistence and approach build self-efficacy and the belief that ability can grow—countering the fixed 'not a math person' belief.

questions.stem: A teacher designs choice into a project: students may demonstrate their understanding through an essay, a model, a presentation, or a podcast. From a motivation standpoint, what is the PRIMARY benefit of offering these options?
options: It guarantees the project will be easier for all students
It supports students' need for autonomy and allows them to engage through strengths and interests, increasing investment in the task
It ensures every student produces the identical product
It reduces the teacher's grading workload
questions.rationale: Offering meaningful choice satisfies the psychological need for autonomy, a core driver of intrinsic motivation, and lets students leverage their strengths and interests, which raises engagement and ownership of learning. Difficulty and grading workload are not the central motivational rationale.

questions.stem: A teacher returns assignments with the comment 'Good job!' on most papers and notices little change in student effort over time. Which feedback practice would MOST improve student motivation and learning?
options: Stop giving any feedback so students rely on themselves
Replace 'Good job!' with a letter grade only
Write longer general comments praising the student's overall attitude
Provide specific, descriptive feedback that names what the student did well and offers a clear next step for improvement
questions.rationale: Effective feedback is specific and actionable: it identifies what was done well and gives a concrete next step. This guides improvement and supports a sense of competence and progress, which sustains motivation far better than vague praise or a bare grade.

questions.stem: A teacher sets up a class economy where students earn points for grades and behavior to 'buy' privileges. After several months, the teacher observes that students avoid challenging optional enrichment tasks because those tasks 'aren't worth points.' What does this pattern MOST clearly illustrate, and what is the BEST instructional response?
options: Students are lazy; the teacher should add more point-earning rules
The students need stricter consequences for skipping enrichment
The point system is working perfectly and should be expanded to all tasks
An over-reliance on extrinsic rewards can suppress intrinsic interest; the teacher should connect enrichment tasks to students' curiosity and goals while fading point dependence
questions.rationale: This illustrates the undermining effect: when rewards are tied to everything, students disengage from activities that carry no reward, signaling that extrinsic incentives have crowded out intrinsic interest. The best response is to fade point dependence and reconnect enrichment to curiosity, relevance, and personal goals.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to persist through a difficult multi-step problem-solving unit. Which instructional design choice BEST supports sustained motivation by building students' sense of competence?
options: Sequence tasks so difficulty increases gradually, build in frequent opportunities for students to see their progress, and celebrate growth on challenging steps
Present the entire unit's hardest problems on day one to set high expectations
Grade only the final product so students focus on the end goal
Tell students that only the strongest will succeed in this unit
questions.rationale: A sense of competence sustains motivation, especially through difficulty. Gradually increasing challenge keeps tasks within reach, frequent progress checkpoints make growth visible, and recognizing growth on hard steps reinforces effort—together building the self-efficacy that fuels persistence.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to communicate high expectations to ALL students, including those who have historically struggled. Which teacher behavior is MOST consistent with conveying high expectations equitably?
options: Calling on confident students more often to keep the pace brisk
Accepting incomplete answers from struggling students to avoid discouraging them
Reserving challenging tasks for the highest-achieving group
Giving struggling students the same rigorous questions as others, paired with appropriate scaffolding and sufficient wait time to respond
questions.rationale: Equitable high expectations mean holding all students to rigorous content while providing the scaffolding and wait time that make success attainable. Lowering demands or excluding students from challenge communicates low expectations and limits growth.

questions.stem: A teacher introduces a new technology tool for collaborative writing, but several students disengage, saying the tool is 'pointless' and they'd rather write on paper. Before abandoning the tool, what should the teacher consider FIRST to address the motivation problem?
options: Replace the tool with a different unfamiliar technology immediately
Make the tool mandatory and grade students on whether they use it
Examine whether students understand the tool's purpose and value, ensure they have the skills to use it successfully, and connect its use to an authentic, relevant task
Allow only the most tech-savvy students to use the tool
questions.rationale: Motivation to use a tool depends on perceived value and a sense of competence with it. The teacher should first check that students see the purpose, have the skills to succeed, and use the tool for an authentic, relevant task—addressing the 'pointless' perception rather than coercing use or switching tools blindly.

questions.stem: A teacher displays a rubric and student exemplars before students begin a writing task. From a motivation and learning standpoint, what is the PRIMARY benefit of this practice?
options: It clarifies expectations and success criteria, helping students set goals and self-monitor, which increases their sense of control and engagement
It allows the teacher to finish grading faster
It eliminates the need for any teacher feedback during the task
It guarantees that all students will earn the highest score
questions.rationale: Clear success criteria and exemplars help students understand the target, set goals, and self-assess their progress. This sense of clarity and control supports engagement and self-regulated learning, the central motivational benefit, rather than speeding grading or replacing feedback.

questions.stem: A teacher observes that students put real effort into a service-learning project that helps a local food bank but disengage from a similar textbook exercise on the same concepts. Which motivational principle BEST explains the difference, and how should the teacher apply it going forward?
options: Students simply prefer being out of the classroom; the teacher should plan more field trips
The textbook exercise was too easy; the teacher should make all assignments harder
Authentic, purposeful tasks with real-world relevance increase motivation; the teacher should design more learning experiences with genuine purpose and audience
Students were motivated by avoiding the textbook; the teacher should remove textbooks entirely
questions.rationale: Tasks perceived as authentic and purposeful, with real-world relevance and an audience, are more motivating than decontextualized exercises. The teacher should apply this by designing learning experiences that have genuine purpose and connect to students' lives and communities.

questions.stem: A teacher gives frequent timed competitions with public leaderboards to motivate a math class. A few high-achievers thrive, but many students grow anxious and some stop participating. The teacher's goal is broad engagement and persistence. Which redesign BEST serves that goal for the whole class?
options: Keep the leaderboard but add a small prize for last place to include everyone
Remove all forms of feedback so students feel no pressure
Shift toward goal structures that emphasize personal improvement and mastery, give private progress feedback, and use collaborative challenges so all students experience success
Increase the frequency of the leaderboard competitions to build a competitive culture
questions.rationale: Public, competitive, performance-oriented structures motivate a few but increase anxiety and disengagement for many. A mastery and personal-improvement orientation with private feedback and collaborative challenges lets all students experience competence and progress, broadening engagement and persistence across the class.

questions.stem: During a class discussion, a fifth-grade teacher poses a question and immediately calls on the first student who raises a hand, who gives a one-word answer. The teacher repeats this pattern for several questions, and participation steadily narrows to the same four students. Which adjustment would MOST effectively broaden meaningful participation?
options: Reduce the number of questions asked so the discussion moves more quickly and stays focused
Call on students in alphabetical order so that every student is required to answer at least once
Reward the four active students with extra points to model the desired behavior for the rest of the class
Increase wait time after each question and ask students to discuss their thinking with a partner before any individual responds
questions.rationale: Extending wait time and inserting a partner-talk step gives all students time to formulate and rehearse responses, distributing cognitive engagement and participation beyond the few quick responders. This is a research-supported communication strategy for equitable discussion.

questions.stem: A high school science teacher wants students to move beyond restating textbook definitions toward evaluating competing claims. After students read two articles offering opposing conclusions about a local water-quality issue, which task would BEST promote critical thinking?
options: Have students annotate each article to identify and highlight the main idea of every paragraph
Ask students to summarize both articles accurately in a single paragraph each
Have students construct an evidence-based argument for which claim is better supported and defend it against a counterargument
Ask students to list the vocabulary terms in both articles and define each one
questions.rationale: Constructing and defending an evidence-based argument while addressing a counterargument requires analysis, evaluation, and synthesis—higher-order thinking that moves students beyond comprehension toward reasoned judgment about competing claims.

questions.stem: A middle school teacher notices that several English learners rarely contribute orally, though their written work shows strong understanding. The teacher wants to increase their verbal participation without singling them out. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Pair these students together so they feel comfortable speaking with someone at a similar language level
Build in structured small-group routines with sentence frames so students rehearse academic language before whole-class sharing
Allow these students to respond in writing only, since their writing demonstrates understanding
Call on these students more frequently so they get accustomed to speaking in front of peers
questions.rationale: Structured small-group talk with sentence frames provides scaffolded, low-anxiety opportunities to rehearse academic language, building the confidence and linguistic resources needed before whole-class participation. This supports oral language development for English learners.

questions.stem: A teacher launches a problem-based unit asking students to design a cost-effective garden for the school courtyard within a fixed budget. Midway, several groups stall because they cannot decide how to begin. Which teacher response BEST sustains students' problem-solving while preserving their ownership?
options: Pose guiding questions that prompt groups to define constraints, list what they know, and identify what they still need to find out
Reassign the stalled students to the groups that are making the most progress
Distribute a step-by-step worksheet that breaks the project into required tasks in order
Provide each stalled group with a completed sample design they can adapt to the courtyard
questions.rationale: Guiding questions that help students define constraints and identify knowns and unknowns scaffold the problem-solving process without removing the cognitive work, preserving student ownership while modeling how to approach an open-ended problem.

questions.stem: A teacher gives oral directions for a multi-step lab, but many students begin asking what to do next almost immediately. Which strategy would MOST improve students' ability to follow the directions?
options: Repeat the same oral directions more loudly and slowly
Provide the directions both orally and in writing, with numbered steps posted for reference
Ask the students who understood to explain the directions to those who did not
Give the directions one step at a time and wait for all students to finish before continuing
questions.rationale: Presenting directions in multiple modalities—spoken plus posted, numbered written steps—supports diverse learners and gives students a reference they can consult, reducing the need to ask what comes next. This reflects effective communication of expectations.

questions.stem: After a unit on persuasive writing, a teacher wants students to apply their learning in a new context rather than repeat practiced examples. Which assignment BEST promotes transfer and higher-order application?
options: Ask students to copy three persuasive sentences from the textbook and label the techniques
Have students write a persuasive letter to a real audience proposing a solution to a problem they care about
Ask students to identify the persuasive techniques used in the teacher's model essay
Have students rewrite the persuasive essay they completed during the unit to fix grammatical errors
questions.rationale: Writing for a real audience about a self-selected problem requires students to transfer persuasive techniques to a novel, authentic context and make strategic rhetorical choices—application and synthesis rather than recall or revision of practiced work.

questions.stem: During a Socratic seminar, a teacher observes that two confident students dominate while others defer to them, and the conversation circles without deepening. Which facilitation move would MOST effectively redistribute participation AND deepen the discourse?
options: End the seminar and assign the discussion question as individual written work
Introduce a talking token system in which each student must use a token to speak and may not speak again until others have contributed
Step in to summarize the dominant students' points so the rest of the class can follow
Direct a probing question to a quieter student and ask the group to build on or challenge that response with textual evidence
questions.rationale: Inviting a quieter student with a probing question and then requiring the group to build on or challenge it with evidence both redistributes the floor and raises the cognitive demand, deepening discourse rather than merely managing turn-taking.

questions.stem: A teacher consistently asks questions like "What year did the event happen?" and "Who was the leader?" A mentor suggests increasing cognitive demand. Which revised question best moves students toward analysis?
options: How did the differing goals of the two groups contribute to the outcome, and what evidence supports your reasoning?
What is the definition of the key term introduced in today's reading?
What were the three main events in the order they occurred?
Can anyone tell me the name of the document we read about?
questions.rationale: Asking how differing goals contributed to an outcome and requiring evidence prompts students to analyze causal relationships and justify claims—analytical, higher-order thinking—rather than recalling facts, names, or definitions.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to give one another useful feedback during peer review, but early attempts produce only vague comments like "good job" or "I liked it." Which approach would MOST improve the quality of students' communication during peer review?
options: Reduce peer review and have the teacher provide all feedback to ensure quality
Tell students that vague comments are unacceptable and will lower their participation grade
Model specific feedback using a sample paper and provide a structured protocol with criteria and sentence stems
Have students grade each other's papers with a numerical score instead of comments
questions.rationale: Modeling specific feedback and supplying a protocol with criteria and stems teaches students what useful feedback looks like and gives them the language to produce it, directly improving the quality and specificity of peer communication.

questions.stem: A teacher poses an open question, a student gives a partially correct answer, and the teacher wants to extend the student's reasoning without simply confirming or correcting. Which teacher response BEST promotes deeper thinking?
options: "Not quite. Does anyone else have the correct answer?"
"Interesting. What in the text led you to that conclusion, and how might it change if we considered the next paragraph?"
"That's partly right—let me give you the complete answer so we can move on."
"Good try. The answer is actually the opposite of what you said."
questions.rationale: Asking the student to ground the claim in the text and then consider how new evidence might shift it presses for justification and re-evaluation, extending reasoning and modeling reflective thinking rather than supplying the answer.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher tends to speak quickly and use complex academic vocabulary that confuses many students. Which adjustment would MOST improve communication with the class?
options: Speak the same way but provide a glossary at the end of the semester
Monitor students' nonverbal cues, adjust pacing, and define new terms in accessible language as they arise
Continue using advanced vocabulary so students are exposed to challenging language
Ask students to look up any unfamiliar words on their own after class
questions.rationale: Reading nonverbal cues, adjusting pace, and defining terms in the moment makes communication responsive and comprehensible, ensuring students can access content as it is taught. Effective teachers monitor and adjust their communication to learners' needs.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to develop metacognitive awareness while solving multi-step math problems. Which routine would BEST foster this?
options: Have students memorize the steps of the standard algorithm
Provide the answer key so students can check their work immediately
Require students to explain their problem-solving strategy aloud or in writing and reflect on why they chose it
Have students complete twenty similar problems for speed and accuracy
questions.rationale: Explaining and reflecting on the chosen strategy makes students aware of their own thinking processes—the essence of metacognition—and helps them monitor, evaluate, and adjust their approaches to problem solving.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a whole-class discussion on a controversial historical decision and wants every student engaged in reasoning, not just listening. Which structure would MOST effectively ensure broad, accountable participation?
options: Use a structured discussion protocol in which students prepare positions in advance, talk in rotating small groups, and report shared conclusions
Call on volunteers and let the discussion flow naturally based on who wishes to speak
Lead a lecture summarizing the major viewpoints, then ask if there are questions
Assign a written essay on the topic instead of discussing it
questions.rationale: A protocol requiring advance preparation, rotating small-group talk, and reporting holds every student accountable for reasoning and contributing, ensuring broad engagement rather than reliance on volunteers or passive listening.

questions.stem: A teacher gives feedback on student writing but finds students rarely act on it. Reviewing the feedback, the teacher sees comments such as "awkward," "unclear," and "expand." Which change would MOST likely lead students to use the feedback?
options: Write longer comments explaining everything that is wrong with each paragraph
Provide specific, actionable feedback tied to criteria, and build in time for students to revise based on it
Reduce the amount of feedback so students are not overwhelmed
Assign a grade only, since detailed comments are not being used anyway
questions.rationale: Specific, actionable feedback connected to criteria tells students exactly what to do, and dedicated revision time ensures they apply it. Feedback is most effective for communication and learning when it is clear, actionable, and acted upon.

questions.stem: In a project requiring students to propose a solution to traffic congestion near the school, a group proposes the first idea they think of and stops. The teacher wants to push them toward more rigorous problem solving. Which prompt would BEST advance their thinking?
options: "Let me tell you the solution the city actually used so you can use that one."
"That's a fine idea—write it up and you're done."
"Why don't you just go with the most obvious solution to save time?"
"What other possible solutions could address the problem, and how does each compare against your criteria for success?"
questions.rationale: Prompting students to generate alternatives and compare them against defined criteria pushes them to consider multiple solutions and evaluate trade-offs—key features of rigorous problem solving that move beyond settling for the first idea.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to communicate lesson objectives so students understand the purpose of each activity. Which practice is MOST effective?
options: Keep objectives in the lesson plan so they do not distract students during activities
State and post objectives in student-friendly language and refer to them throughout the lesson
Read the standard's exact wording aloud once at the start of class
Reveal the objective only at the end of the lesson as a summary
questions.rationale: Stating and posting objectives in accessible language and revisiting them helps students understand the purpose of their work, monitor their progress, and connect activities to learning goals—clear communication of expectations.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to engage in productive academic discourse where they challenge ideas respectfully and build on each other's reasoning. Early discussions consist mostly of students taking turns sharing unrelated opinions. Which strategy would MOST improve the quality of discourse?
options: Assign each student a single point to share so everyone contributes equally
Have students write their opinions instead of speaking to avoid conflict
Teach and have students practice accountable-talk stems such as "I agree because..." and "I see it differently because..."
Allow students to speak only when called on to maintain order
questions.rationale: Accountable-talk stems give students the language to respond directly to one another's ideas—agreeing with reasons, respectfully disagreeing, and building on contributions—transforming parallel sharing into connected, reasoned discourse.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a question-and-answer review before a test. Most questions are answered chorally and quickly, and the teacher feels confident students are ready. On the test, results are poor. What is the MOST likely communication-related flaw in the review, and the best fix?
options: Choral, rapid responses masked individual understanding; the teacher should use techniques that surface each student's thinking, such as written responses or randomized cold calls
The students did not study; the teacher should assign more homework
The review was too long; the teacher should shorten it to keep attention
The questions were too hard; the teacher should use easier review questions next time
questions.rationale: Choral, fast-paced responses let a few confident voices carry the group and conceal individual gaps. Techniques that require every student to commit a response—written answers, response cards, or randomized calling—surface real understanding so the teacher can adjust before the test.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to recognize that a problem can have multiple valid approaches. After students solve a math problem, which teacher move BEST promotes flexible, creative thinking?
options: Mark only answers that used the method taught in class as fully correct
Invite several students to share different strategies, then have the class compare the approaches' efficiency and reasoning
Show students the one correct method and have them practice it repeatedly
Move on quickly once one student gives the right answer
questions.rationale: Sharing multiple strategies and having the class compare them validates diverse reasoning, helps students see problems from several angles, and builds flexible, creative problem solving rather than reliance on a single procedure.

questions.stem: During small-group work, a teacher circulates and notices one group is silent and unsure how to proceed, while another is off task and loud. The teacher wants a communication approach that re-engages both groups appropriately. Which is BEST?
options: Address the whole class loudly, telling everyone to get back on task
Ask the silent group a focusing question to clarify their next step, and privately redirect the off-task group to their goal
Wait for both groups to resolve their issues on their own
Reassign all students to new groups to break up the dynamics
questions.rationale: Differentiated, targeted communication—prompting the stuck group with a focusing question and quietly redirecting the off-task group—matches each group's actual need, re-engaging both without disrupting the rest of the class.

questions.stem: A teacher assigns an inquiry task and provides so much structure—step-by-step instructions, predetermined data, and a required conclusion—that students simply follow directions. A coach notes this undermines the inquiry goal. Which redesign BEST restores genuine inquiry while keeping appropriate support?
options: Provide the conclusion in advance so students know what they are working toward
Pose a driving question, let students design part of the investigation and analyze their own data, while providing scaffolds such as a planning template and check-ins
Add more detailed step-by-step instructions to reduce student confusion
Remove all structure and let students figure out everything on their own
questions.rationale: Genuine inquiry requires students to grapple with a question, make investigative decisions, and reason from their own data. A driving question with student-designed components, supported by a planning template and check-ins, preserves the intellectual work while offering appropriate scaffolding.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to demonstrate active listening during peer presentations. Which strategy MOST directly supports this?
options: Give listeners a focused task, such as noting one strength and one question for each presenter
Let students leave the room until it is their turn to present
Allow students to work on other assignments while classmates present
Have the teacher take all the notes and share them later
questions.rationale: Assigning listeners a specific task—identifying a strength and forming a question—gives them an active purpose, keeping them engaged and accountable during peer presentations and reinforcing active-listening skills.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to connect new content to prior knowledge and real-world contexts to deepen understanding. Which questioning approach BEST supports this goal?
options: "What is the textbook definition of this concept?"
"Can you repeat the rule I just stated?"
"Where have you seen something like this in your own life, and how does it relate to what we learned earlier this year?"
"What page in the book covers this topic?"
questions.rationale: Asking students to connect a concept to personal experience and to earlier learning activates prior knowledge and builds meaningful, transferable understanding through relevant connections—deeper than recall of definitions or facts.

questions.stem: A teacher introduces hand signals (thumbs up/sideways/down) for students to indicate understanding during instruction. Most students show thumbs up, but later work reveals widespread misunderstanding. Which interpretation and adjustment is MOST sound?
options: Self-reported signals can reflect overconfidence or social pressure; the teacher should pair or replace them with checks that require demonstrating understanding, such as a quick problem or explanation
The signals worked; the later work must reflect a different problem
Students were dishonest and should be told to use the signals correctly
The teacher should use the signals more often to build the habit
questions.rationale: Self-report signals are vulnerable to overconfidence and conformity (students mirror peers). Checks that require students to demonstrate understanding—solving a problem or explaining their thinking—provide more valid evidence the teacher can act on.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to analyze the reasoning behind their answers rather than focus only on correctness. After a debate, which reflection prompt BEST develops critical self-examination?
options: Did you enjoy the debate activity?
Which team won the debate?
Which of your arguments was strongest and weakest, and what evidence would have made your weaker point more convincing?
How many points did each side score?
questions.rationale: Asking students to evaluate the strength of their own arguments and identify how to strengthen weaker ones requires critical self-examination and reasoning about evidence quality—reflective, higher-order thinking beyond outcomes or enjoyment.

questions.stem: A teacher communicates with families about a project but finds many families are not engaged, partly because some are more comfortable in languages other than English and some lack internet access. Which approach would MOST improve communication and partnership?
options: Wait for families to contact the teacher if they have questions
Communicate only with families who attend school events
Send all communication by email in English, since that is the school's standard
Provide information in families' home languages and through multiple channels, such as printed notes, phone calls, and translated messages
questions.rationale: Offering information in home languages and through varied channels removes language and access barriers, ensuring all families can receive and respond to communication—an equitable approach that strengthens family partnership.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to develop the ability to ask their own meaningful questions rather than only answering the teacher's. Which sustained practice would BEST cultivate student questioning?
options: Allow questions only at the end of class to avoid interrupting instruction
Praise students who answer the teacher's questions correctly and quickly
Use a routine in which students generate, categorize, and prioritize their own questions about a topic, then investigate the ones they select
Provide a list of pre-written questions for students to answer about each unit
questions.rationale: A structured routine in which students produce, sort, prioritize, and pursue their own questions builds the disposition and skill of inquiry, shifting students from passive responders to active questioners who drive their own learning.

questions.stem: A teacher wants nonverbal communication to support a positive, focused classroom environment. Which use of nonverbal communication is MOST effective?
options: Facing the board while explaining so students can see the notes
Avoiding eye contact so students do not feel pressured
Using purposeful movement, eye contact, and proximity to engage students and signal expectations
Standing behind the desk for the entire lesson to maintain authority
questions.rationale: Purposeful movement, eye contact, and proximity convey attentiveness, sustain engagement, and signal expectations without interrupting instruction—effective nonverbal communication that supports a focused, connected classroom.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to scaffold higher-order thinking for a struggling student without lowering the cognitive demand of the task. Which approach BEST achieves this?
options: Provide a graphic organizer and guiding questions that support the student in completing the same analytical task
Replace the analysis task with a simpler recall worksheet for that student
Have the student copy a model analysis the teacher has written
Excuse the student from the analytical portion of the assignment
questions.rationale: A graphic organizer and guiding questions scaffold the process while keeping the analytical task intact, allowing the struggling student to access higher-order thinking with support rather than reducing the cognitive demand.

questions.stem: A teacher's questions during discussion are clear, but responses stay shallow because the teacher follows each answer with another new question, never pausing on a single idea. A coach suggests using follow-up moves. Which sequence of moves would MOST deepen a single line of reasoning?
options: After a response, immediately ask a different student a new, unrelated question
After a response, pause, ask the student to elaborate, then invite a peer to agree, disagree, or extend with evidence
After a response, ask the class to applaud good answers before continuing
After a response, restate the correct answer and move to the next topic
questions.rationale: Pausing, asking for elaboration, and then inviting peers to agree, disagree, or extend with evidence keeps the class focused on developing one idea collaboratively, deepening reasoning rather than scattering attention across disconnected questions.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to apply learning to solve an authentic, open-ended challenge connected to their community. Which task design BEST supports higher-order application and problem solving?
options: A multiple-choice quiz on the key concepts from the unit
A reading comprehension assignment on a related article
A worksheet asking students to match terms with definitions
A challenge in which students investigate a real community need, propose and justify a solution, and present it to an authentic audience
questions.rationale: Investigating a real need, proposing and justifying a solution, and presenting to an authentic audience requires students to apply, analyze, evaluate, and create in a meaningful context—rich, higher-order problem solving with real-world relevance.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to evaluate the validity of arguments they encounter and detect flawed reasoning. Which sustained instructional approach would MOST effectively develop this critical-thinking skill?
options: Provide students with conclusions and ask them to accept them as expert-supported
Have students memorize a list of logical fallacy names and definitions for a quiz
Regularly analyze real arguments to identify claims, evidence, assumptions, and reasoning flaws, then construct improved versions
Have students summarize editorials without evaluating the reasoning
questions.rationale: Repeatedly analyzing authentic arguments for claims, evidence, assumptions, and flaws—then improving them—builds the transferable analytical skill of evaluating reasoning, far more than memorizing fallacy terms or passively accepting or summarizing arguments.

questions.stem: A seventh-grade science teacher has students use a digital probe and graphing app to collect temperature data during a chemical reaction, then annotate and share their real-time graphs to compare reaction rates across groups. Previously, students copied a static data table from the textbook and answered fixed questions. Using the SAMR model, this change is best classified as which level, and why?
options: Augmentation, because the app adds graphing features but the task is essentially unchanged
Redefinition, because students are now using a device instead of paper for the same activity
Modification, because the task is significantly redesigned through live data collection and cross-group comparison that were not previously feasible
Substitution, because the app simply replaces the paper data table with a digital one
questions.rationale: Modification occurs when technology allows for significant task redesign. Collecting live data with probes and comparing real-time graphs across groups transforms the original copy-and-answer task into something functionally different, though students are still analyzing reaction-rate data rather than creating an entirely new, previously inconceivable product.

questions.stem: A high school history teacher wants to integrate technology meaningfully into a unit on local civil-rights history. She is skilled with the content and with general teaching strategies but has not previously used digital tools for primary-source analysis. Drawing on the TPACK framework, which planning step most directly strengthens the weakest component of her professional knowledge for this unit?
options: Reviewing general classroom-management routines for group work
Researching how a specific archival database's search and annotation tools can support students' source-analysis reasoning in this content area
Selecting a more engaging novel about the civil-rights era for independent reading
Rereading the unit's content standards to ensure historical accuracy of her lectures
questions.rationale: TPACK identifies the intersection of technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge. The teacher already has strong content (CK) and pedagogical (PK) knowledge; her gap is technological knowledge and how it intersects with content and pedagogy (TPACK/TPK/TCK). Studying how a specific database's tools support source-analysis reasoning develops exactly that integrated knowledge.

questions.stem: During a one-to-one device lesson, a teacher notices that most students are using a collaborative document mainly to retype notes she has already posted. She wants the technology to do more than digitize existing work. Which redesign would most clearly move the activity up the SAMR ladder toward transformation?
options: Have students print their notes and store them in a binder for review
Have students copy the notes into a different note-taking app instead
Have students change the document font and add colored headings to make their notes attractive
Have students co-author a shared document that synthesizes multiple sources, embeds their own data, and is published for an authentic audience to use
questions.rationale: Transformation (Modification/Redefinition) in SAMR involves significant redesign or new tasks made possible by technology. Co-authoring a synthesized, source-rich, publicly published product creates a task that could not exist without the technology, moving well beyond the substitution-level note retyping.

questions.stem: A teacher is selecting a new digital tool for a project. Which question should guide her decision FIRST to ensure the technology serves learning rather than driving it?
options: Which tool is the newest release this school year?
What specific learning objective do students need to reach, and how would a tool help them reach it better?
