Which tool do most other teachers in the building happen to be using?
Which tool has the most features and visual appeal?
questions.rationale: Effective technology integration is purpose-driven: the learning objective comes first, and the tool is chosen because it advances that objective. Starting with features, novelty, or popularity risks letting the tool drive instruction.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a unit in which students use video-conferencing to interview marine biologists in three countries, then collaboratively build a multimedia conservation proposal that is presented to a local city council. A colleague argues this is merely 'Substitution' because students could have written a research paper instead. What is the strongest reason the colleague is mistaken according to SAMR?
options: The technology enables an authentic, globally connected, audience-driven task that was not previously possible, which is characteristic of Redefinition
The activity takes longer than a research paper, so it must be Modification
Any use of video automatically counts as Augmentation regardless of the task
The activity uses more devices, and more devices always indicates a higher SAMR level
questions.rationale: Redefinition involves new tasks that were previously inconceivable without technology. Connecting students with global experts and producing an authentic proposal for real decision-makers creates a task impossible to replicate with a traditional paper, distinguishing it sharply from Substitution.

questions.stem: A teacher with a student who has a visual impairment is choosing a digital reading platform. To make the most accessible and equitable choice, which feature set should she prioritize when evaluating platforms?
options: A platform compatible with screen readers, offering adjustable text size, high-contrast modes, and keyboard navigation
The platform that requires students to use a mouse for all interactions
The platform that is cheapest, regardless of accessibility features
The platform with the brightest colors and most animations to keep attention
questions.rationale: Accessibility and Universal Design for Learning require tools that provide multiple means of representation and access. Screen-reader compatibility, adjustable text, high-contrast modes, and keyboard navigation directly serve a student with a visual impairment and benefit many other learners.

questions.stem: A teacher designs an online research task and wants to apply Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles. To provide multiple means of engagement AND representation while keeping rigor high, which approach is most consistent with UDL?
options: Require every student to read the same dense text and answer the same worksheet in silence
Allow students to skip the assignment if the format does not suit them
Offer the same content through text, captioned video, and audio, and let students choose to demonstrate understanding through a written report, a recorded explanation, or an infographic
Lower the learning objective for students who struggle and keep it high only for advanced students
questions.rationale: UDL provides multiple means of representation (varied input formats) and multiple means of action/expression (varied output options) while holding the learning goal constant. Offering content in several formats and allowing varied products meets all learners without reducing rigor.

questions.stem: A teacher introduces an AI-powered writing assistant that gives students instant grammar suggestions. After two weeks, she notices many students accept every suggestion without reading it and can no longer explain their own revisions. What instructional adjustment best preserves the tool's benefit while addressing the learning problem?
options: Ban the tool entirely and return to handwritten drafts only
Require students to annotate which suggestions they accepted or rejected and justify each decision in a brief revision log
Let students keep using the tool exactly as before, since their final drafts have fewer errors
Increase the number of AI suggestions students must accept per draft
questions.rationale: The goal is for students to think about their writing, not outsource the thinking. Requiring students to evaluate and justify each suggestion restores metacognition and ownership while still using the tool's feedback, balancing technological support with genuine learning.

questions.stem: A district provides a learning platform that logs each student's time-on-task, attempts, and accuracy. A teacher wants to use this technology to personalize instruction responsibly. Which use of the data is most appropriate and consistent with effective, ethical practice?
options: Ignore the data because instructional decisions should rely only on teacher intuition
Use the data privately to identify students who are repeatedly missing a particular concept and form small targeted reteaching groups
Share each student's full usage log with the whole class to encourage transparency
Publicly rank students on a classroom screen by their accuracy scores to motivate competition
questions.rationale: Platform analytics are most valuable when used privately and formatively to identify learning gaps and group students for targeted support. Public ranking or sharing individual data violates privacy and can harm motivation; ignoring data wastes a useful resource.

questions.stem: A teacher in a school where some students lack reliable home internet plans a project requiring nightly online collaboration in a shared document. Recognizing the equity concern, which redesign best preserves the learning goals while addressing the digital divide?
options: Require affected students to stay after school every night to use the computer lab
Replace the entire project with an individual worksheet so no technology is needed
Build dedicated in-school collaboration time and allow offline-capable tools that sync when a connection is available, so all students can contribute equitably
Proceed as planned and lower grades for students who cannot complete the nightly online work
questions.rationale: Equity in technology integration requires anticipating access gaps. Providing in-school time and offline-capable, syncing tools lets all students reach the same collaborative learning goals without penalizing those who lack home access, addressing the digital divide proactively.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to use technology to develop higher-order thinking rather than simply consume content. Which technology-supported task best targets analysis, evaluation, and creation?
options: Students play a timed drill game to memorize vocabulary definitions
Students watch an instructional video and take an auto-graded recall quiz
Students use simulation software to test competing hypotheses, evaluate the outcomes, and design an improved experiment to share
Students reread a digital textbook chapter and highlight key terms
questions.rationale: Higher-order thinking involves analyzing, evaluating, and creating. Using simulations to test hypotheses, judge results, and design improved experiments engages all three, whereas the other tasks remain at lower levels (remembering/understanding).

questions.stem: A teacher integrating a new classroom-response (clicker/polling) system wants it to inform instruction in real time. Which use of the system best leverages it as a formative-assessment tool rather than mere novelty?
options: Using polls only at the end of the unit to assign final grades
Posing a conceptual question mid-lesson, viewing the response distribution, and adjusting the next explanation based on common misconceptions revealed
Letting students poll on what snack to bring to a class party
Collecting poll responses but never reviewing them so the lesson stays on schedule
questions.rationale: Formative assessment provides real-time evidence that guides immediate instructional adjustment. Posing a conceptual question, reading the distribution, and reteaching to the revealed misconceptions uses the polling system to its formative potential.

questions.stem: A teacher reflects that her flashy multimedia presentations earn praise but recent exam data shows little gain in conceptual understanding. Applying a critical view of technology integration, which conclusion should most guide her next planning cycle?
options: She should abandon all technology and lecture without any media
She should add more animations and sound effects to increase engagement further
Engagement with media does not guarantee learning; she should align each technology choice to a measurable objective and check whether it advances conceptual understanding
She should switch to a more expensive presentation program to improve results
questions.rationale: Effective integration distinguishes engagement from learning. The data signal that media presence alone is not improving understanding, so she should tie each tool to a measurable objective and evaluate its actual impact on conceptual learning.

questions.stem: An English teacher wants ninth graders to collaborate on a digital literary analysis. To ensure the technology supports collaboration AND individual accountability, which design choice is most effective?
options: Assign one shared grade for the whole group with no record of individual contributions
Use a shared document with version history and assign each student a distinct analytical role, then assess both the joint product and each student's tracked contribution
Have one student type while the others watch, to avoid editing conflicts
Let students divide the document so each works alone and never reads the others' sections
questions.rationale: Productive technology-supported collaboration combines a genuine shared task with individual accountability. Using version history and distinct roles lets the teacher assess the joint product and each student's documented contribution, ensuring all participate meaningfully.

questions.stem: A teacher posts students' project videos to a public class website. To protect students and act ethically, which step is most important before publishing?
options: Schedule the posts to publish at exactly midnight
Obtain proper parental/guardian consent and follow district privacy policies regarding student images and identifying information
Choose the highest video resolution available
Add upbeat background music to each video
questions.rationale: Publishing student work and images publicly requires informed parental/guardian consent and adherence to district and legal privacy policies. Protecting student privacy is an ethical and legal obligation that precedes technical considerations.

questions.stem: Midway through a unit, a teacher gives a short ungraded check and finds that about 70 percent of students hold the same misconception about how to set up a proportion. Which instructional decision best reflects effective use of formative-assessment data?
options: Wait for the unit test to see whether the misconception persists
Record the results, return graded papers, and continue to the next planned topic
Pause and reteach the proportion setup to the whole class using a different representation, then recheck before moving on
Assign extra homework on the same problems and move on without explanation
questions.rationale: Formative data should drive immediate instructional adjustment. When a misconception is widespread, reteaching with a fresh representation and rechecking for understanding addresses the gap before it compounds, which is the purpose of monitoring during instruction.

questions.stem: A teacher returns essays with the comment 'Good work, 82' at the top. She notices students glance at the number and discard the essays without revising. To make her feedback more likely to improve learning, which change is most effective?
options: Provide specific, actionable comments tied to the rubric criteria, delay the grade, and require students to use the feedback to revise before scoring
Add a longer general praise comment such as 'Excellent effort overall'
Stop returning essays so students cannot compare grades
Replace the number with a letter grade so students take it more seriously
questions.rationale: Effective feedback is specific, actionable, tied to criteria, and used by students. Research indicates that pairing a grade with comments often makes students ignore the comments; delaying the grade and requiring revision based on rubric-aligned feedback focuses students on improvement.

questions.stem: After a unit test, a teacher disaggregates item-level results and finds that students mastered computation items but most missed multi-step word problems requiring them to identify the relevant operation. Which reteaching plan most precisely targets the diagnosed gap?
options: Design lessons focused on interpreting problem situations and selecting operations, using think-alouds and worked examples for word problems
Move on to the next unit because computation, the foundational skill, was mastered
Reteach the entire unit from the beginning to all students
Provide additional timed computation drills since practice is always beneficial
questions.rationale: Effective use of assessment data means targeting the specific diagnosed weakness. The data show computation is mastered but problem interpretation is not, so reteaching should focus on understanding problem situations and choosing operations rather than reteaching mastered or unrelated skills.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to distinguish between formative and summative purposes when planning assessments for a six-week grading period. Which pairing correctly matches the purpose to its appropriate use?
options: Use a unit final exam formatively to adjust the same day's lesson
Use frequent exit tickets and quick checks formatively to guide ongoing instruction, and use the end-of-unit exam summatively to evaluate overall mastery
Use exit tickets summatively as the primary basis for report-card grades
Use both exit tickets and the unit exam only to rank students against one another
questions.rationale: Formative assessments (exit tickets, quick checks) inform ongoing instruction; summative assessments (unit exams) evaluate cumulative mastery. Matching each tool to its purpose ensures assessment supports both learning during the unit and judgment of achievement at the end.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a project rubric but finds that two colleagues scoring the same student work assign very different scores. To improve the reliability of the assessment, which step is most appropriate?
options: Average the two colleagues' differing scores and use that as the final grade going forward
Add more point levels to the rubric so scores can be finer-grained
Revise the rubric to use clear, observable, criterion-specific descriptors and calibrate scoring with anchor papers before grading
Switch to grading only on overall impression to save time
questions.rationale: Reliability (consistent scoring across raters) improves when rubric descriptors are specific and observable and when scorers calibrate using anchor papers. Vague criteria cause divergent judgments; clear descriptors plus calibration align raters' interpretations.

questions.stem: A teacher claims her quiz is a valid measure of students' ability to analyze primary historical documents, but the quiz consists entirely of multiple-choice items asking students to recall dates and names. What is the most accurate evaluation of this assessment?
options: It lacks validity for the stated purpose because the items measure factual recall, not the analytical skill the teacher intends to assess
It is valid because multiple-choice items are objective and easy to score
It is valid as long as the items are reliable and consistently scored
It is valid because it covers content from the unit
questions.rationale: Validity concerns whether an assessment measures what it claims to measure. Recall-of-facts items cannot measure document-analysis skill, so the quiz is not valid for its stated purpose even if it is reliable or content-related.

questions.stem: Near the end of a lesson, a teacher asks each student to write on a sticky note one thing they learned and one question they still have. What is the primary instructional purpose of this routine?
options: To fill the last few minutes of class with a calming activity
To create a summative record for the report card
To gather quick formative evidence of understanding and lingering confusion that can inform the next lesson
To assign homework points for participation
questions.rationale: An exit ticket is a formative-assessment routine that gives the teacher rapid evidence of what students learned and where confusion remains, directly informing planning for the next lesson.

questions.stem: A teacher analyzes a multiple-choice item that nearly every student answered incorrectly, with most choosing the same wrong option. Before concluding students did not learn the content, which interpretation should she investigate first?
options: Conclude the whole class is low-achieving and reteach everything
Raise the difficulty of future items so this does not happen again
Examine whether the item itself was flawed, ambiguous, or miskeyed, or whether the common wrong answer reveals a specific shared misconception to target
Discard the data because one item cannot be informative
questions.rationale: Sound use of assessment data includes item analysis. A near-universal wrong answer concentrated on one option may indicate a flawed or miskeyed item or a specific shared misconception. Investigating the item and the distractor pattern leads to an accurate, targeted response.

questions.stem: A teacher wants her grading to communicate what students actually know and can do relative to the standards. She currently averages all scores, so a student who struggled early but mastered the standards by unit's end still receives a low grade. Which grading change best aligns the grade with demonstrated learning?
options: Give bonus points for participation to raise the struggling student's average
Drop the lowest score at random to inflate the grade
Continue averaging because every score should count equally regardless of when earned
Weight or emphasize later, more comprehensive evidence of mastery so the grade reflects students' demonstrated proficiency on the standards
questions.rationale: Grades should reflect what students know and can do relative to standards. Emphasizing later, more comprehensive evidence of mastery (rather than averaging early formative struggles) produces a grade that more accurately represents demonstrated proficiency.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews aggregated formative data and finds that one small group of students has mastered the objective, a large middle group is nearly there with one persistent error, and a few students lack key prerequisites. Which response best uses these data to differentiate the next class period?
options: Focus only on the few students lacking prerequisites and have everyone else wait
Move the whole class forward at the pace of the most advanced group
Provide extension for the mastery group, targeted correction of the specific error for the middle group, and prerequisite reteaching for the few who need it
Reteach the lesson identically to the entire class to be fair
questions.rationale: Data-informed differentiation matches instruction to each group's needs. Extension for those who mastered it, targeted correction for the near-mastery group's specific error, and prerequisite reteaching for those who need it keeps all students appropriately challenged and supported.

questions.stem: After reteaching a concept to a small group, a teacher wants to verify whether the reteaching closed the gap before advancing the group. Which action provides the most valid evidence that the reteaching was effective?
options: Assume the reteaching worked because she explained it more slowly the second time
Wait until the next graded unit test weeks later to see whether scores improved
Ask the group, 'Does everyone understand now?' and proceed when they nod
Administer a brief check using new items that require students to apply the retaught concept, and analyze whether the original error has been resolved
questions.rationale: Verifying that reteaching worked requires fresh evidence of application. A short check with new items targeting the concept lets the teacher judge whether the specific error is resolved, providing valid, timely confirmation before advancing.

questions.stem: A noncustodial parent, who retains legal parental rights per a court order on file, requests to see his daughter's report card and attendance records. The custodial parent has verbally told the teacher she does not want her ex-husband to receive any information. How should the teacher respond?
options: Honor the custodial parent's verbal request and deny the noncustodial parent access
Provide the records to the noncustodial parent, since FERPA grants both parents access unless a court order specifically removes those rights
Require the noncustodial parent to obtain written permission from the custodial parent before releasing anything
Refuse both parents until the school's attorney reviews the divorce decree
questions.rationale: Under FERPA, both parents have equal access to a student's education records unless a court order, state statute, or legally binding document specifically revokes that right. A custodial parent's preference does not override the noncustodial parent's legal access.

questions.stem: During a Saturday youth soccer game where a teacher volunteers as a coach, a 7-year-old player who is not a student at the teacher's school tells the teacher that her stepfather 'hits her with a belt until she bleeds.' The teacher is not acting in any school capacity at the time. What is the teacher's legal obligation in Texas?
options: Report the suspected abuse to DFPS or law enforcement within 48 hours, as Texas law makes the duty personal and non-delegable
Refer the child to her own school counselor since the abuse falls outside the teacher's jurisdiction
No obligation, because the disclosure did not occur during the teacher's professional school duties
Inform the soccer league director and let the league decide whether to report
questions.rationale: In Texas, the duty to report suspected child abuse is a personal, non-delegable obligation that applies to any person regardless of whether they are 'on the clock.' Professionals such as teachers must report within 48 hours of having cause to believe abuse occurred.

questions.stem: A teacher suspects a student is being neglected based on chronic hunger and unwashed clothing but is not certain abuse is occurring. The campus principal tells the teacher, 'Let me handle it; don't file a report.' What should the teacher do?
options: Defer to the principal's instruction, since the principal is the teacher's supervisor and assumes responsibility
Make a personal report to DFPS, because the duty to report cannot be satisfied by notifying a supervisor and reasonable suspicion is the threshold, not certainty
Wait to gather definitive proof of neglect before reporting to avoid a false accusation
Document the concern in a private file and report only if the conditions worsen
questions.rationale: Texas law requires a person with cause to believe a child has been or may be abused or neglected to make a report personally. The standard is reasonable suspicion, not proof. A supervisor cannot relieve an individual of this duty, and a principal's instruction not to report does not override the legal obligation.

questions.stem: A teacher posts on a personal social media account, set to 'friends only,' a humorous photo of a stack of graded essays with one visible student name and a comment joking about the student's poor spelling. A parent learns of the post. Which statement best evaluates the teacher's conduct under the Educators' Code of Ethics?
options: The conduct is acceptable because the account was private and visible only to friends
The conduct is a minor lapse that requires no corrective action since the student was not directly harmed
The conduct is acceptable because no grade or test score was disclosed
The conduct violates the Code by failing to protect the student from disparagement and exposing confidential student information
questions.rationale: The Educators' Code of Ethics requires educators not to reveal confidential information about students and not to intentionally expose a student to disparagement or embarrassment. Posting an identifiable student's work and mocking it breaches confidentiality and professional standards regardless of privacy settings.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a high-achieving student from a recently immigrated family rarely completes homework and her parents never attend conferences. The teacher learns the parents work two jobs and have limited English proficiency. Which approach best reflects culturally responsive family engagement?
options: Reduce the student's homework load so the family does not feel pressured
Refer the matter to an administrator to formally address the lack of parental involvement
Send a sternly worded letter home explaining the consequences of missed homework
Offer flexible communication options such as translated messages, phone calls in the family's home language, and evening or virtual meeting times
questions.rationale: Effective, culturally responsive engagement removes barriers to participation. Providing translated materials, communication in the home language, and flexible scheduling respects the family's circumstances and invites collaboration rather than assigning blame.

questions.stem: A parent emails a teacher asking for the names and contact information of other students in her child's class so she can organize a carpool. The class roster, including addresses, is part of the school's records. Under FERPA, what is the most appropriate response?
options: Forward the roster after redacting the names of students receiving special education services
Share only the names but withhold all contact information
Explain that student names and addresses are protected and direct the parent to the school's policy on directory information opt-outs before any release
Provide the requested roster information because carpooling benefits the students
questions.rationale: Other students' personally identifiable information is protected under FERPA. Some information may be released as 'directory information' only if the district has designated it as such and families have been given the chance to opt out. A teacher should not release it unilaterally and should refer the parent to school policy.

questions.stem: At an ARD/IEP committee meeting, a parent disagrees with the proposed placement, and the committee cannot reach consensus by the end of the meeting. The proposed services would begin the next school day. What is the legally appropriate next step for the committee?
options: Offer the parent the right to recess the meeting for up to a specified period to allow time to reach mutual agreement, while keeping the current IEP in effect
Postpone the meeting indefinitely until the parent agrees to the placement
Implement the proposed placement immediately since the school staff hold a majority
Defer all decisions to the special education director, who can override parental objection
questions.rationale: In Texas, when an ARD committee cannot reach consensus, the parent is entitled to a recess (typically up to 10 school days) to allow additional time to reach mutual agreement. During the recess the student's existing IEP remains in effect. This protects the parent's procedural rights.

questions.stem: A student with a documented peanut allergy has a Section 504 plan requiring an epinephrine auto-injector be kept accessible. A substitute teacher is covering the class during a field trip and was not informed of the plan. Which action by the regular classroom teacher best fulfills the legal duty to implement the 504 plan?
options: Provide the substitute, before the trip, with written information about the student's accommodation and the location and use of the auto-injector
Tell the student to remind the substitute about the allergy if a problem arises
Assume the substitute will check the student's file if needed
Leave a note in the classroom for the substitute to read upon arrival
questions.rationale: A 504 plan must be implemented consistently across all settings and by all staff responsible for the student. The teacher has an affirmative duty to ensure that anyone supervising the student, including a substitute on a field trip, is informed in advance of the accommodation and emergency procedures.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher accepts an offer to tutor one of her current students privately for pay during the summer, at the family's request. The family also offers to pay her to tutor the student during the upcoming school year in the same subject she teaches. Which response best reflects ethical professional judgment?
options: Accept both offers, since tutoring outside class hours is unrelated to her teaching role
Decline private paid tutoring of her own current-year students in her own subject, as it creates a conflict of interest, but consider tutoring students she does not grade
Accept only the school-year offer because continuity benefits the student
Accept both but disclose the arrangement to the principal afterward
questions.rationale: Accepting payment to tutor a student the teacher currently grades in the same subject creates a conflict of interest and may compromise impartial evaluation and create the appearance of favoritism. Ethical practice avoids financial relationships that could bias grading. Tutoring students she does not evaluate avoids this conflict.

questions.stem: A teacher discovers that a colleague has been routinely changing failing test scores to passing grades for athletes to keep them eligible. The colleague asks the teacher to 'keep it between us.' What is the most ethically appropriate course of action?
options: Report the falsification of academic records to the appropriate administrator, as the Code of Ethics requires honesty in academic records and prohibits complicity in fraud
Confront the colleague privately and require them to stop, but take no further action
Honor the request to maintain collegial trust and stay out of another teacher's gradebook
Anonymously warn the affected students' parents about the inflated grades
questions.rationale: The Educators' Code of Ethics prohibits falsifying records and requires educators to comply with standards of professional conduct, which include not knowingly participating in or concealing academic fraud. Grade falsification is serious misconduct that must be reported through proper channels.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old student tells her teacher she is being abused at home but begs the teacher not to report it because she fears retaliation. The teacher believes the student and is concerned reporting could escalate the danger. What must the teacher do?
options: Report the suspected abuse to DFPS or law enforcement, because confidentiality cannot override the mandatory duty to report, and convey the student's safety concerns to authorities
Promise confidentiality but quietly notify the school counselor only
Respect the student's autonomy as a near-adult and keep the disclosure confidential
Wait until the student turns 18 so she can report it herself
questions.rationale: Teachers are mandatory reporters and cannot promise confidentiality that would prevent reporting suspected abuse, regardless of the student's age (under 18) or wishes. The teacher should report and can communicate the student's fear of retaliation to investigators to inform their safety planning.

questions.stem: A general education teacher and a special education co-teacher disagree about how to modify an assignment for a student with a learning disability. The general education teacher wants to keep grade-level rigor; the special education teacher wants significant modifications. What is the most professional way to resolve the disagreement?
options: The general education teacher's view should prevail because it is her classroom and her content
Review the student's IEP together to ensure modifications align with the documented goals and accommodations, and collaborate within that framework
Let the student choose which version of the assignment to complete
Alternate approaches each week to give both teachers an equal say
questions.rationale: In co-teaching, decisions about modifications for a student with a disability must be grounded in the student's IEP, which is a legally binding document. Both teachers should collaborate within the framework of the IEP's goals and accommodations rather than asserting personal preference.

questions.stem: A teacher and an 18-year-old senior in her class develop a friendly rapport. After the student graduates in May, the student, now 18, asks the teacher to meet for coffee 'as friends.' The teacher is still employed at the school the student attended. Which consideration best guides an ethical response?
options: Graduation fully ends all professional obligations, so the meeting is purely personal
Because the student is now a legal adult and graduated, any social relationship is automatically appropriate
The teacher may meet privately as long as no romantic intent exists

The teacher should maintain professional boundaries and avoid social relationships that could compromise professional judgment or create the appearance of impropriety, recognizing recent students remain a sensitive category
questions.rationale: The Educators' Code of Ethics emphasizes maintaining appropriate professional relationships and avoiding the appearance of impropriety. Recent graduates remain a sensitive category, and an educator still employed at the school should exercise caution to protect professional integrity and avoid relationships that could compromise judgment or perception.

questions.stem: A researcher from a local university asks a teacher to share students' standardized test scores and demographic data for a study, offering to keep the data 'anonymous' by removing names. The teacher believes the study could benefit education. What is the appropriate action under FERPA?
options: Obtain verbal permission from the parents and then share the data
Decline to release the data personally and direct the request to the district, which must determine whether a FERPA-compliant studies exception or written consent applies
Share only the test scores but not the demographic data
Share the data since names will be removed, making it anonymous and exempt
questions.rationale: Removing names does not automatically anonymize data, as combinations of demographic and score data can be personally identifiable. Releasing education records to third parties such as researchers must comply with FERPA, typically requiring written parental consent or a qualifying studies exception administered at the district level, not by an individual teacher.

questions.stem: A teacher leaves a stack of graded quizzes face-up on a table by the classroom door so students can pick them up as they leave. Each quiz shows the student's name and score. What is the primary concern with this practice?
options: It wastes instructional time as students stop at the door
It prevents the teacher from confirming each student received their quiz
It risks quizzes being lost on the way out
It improperly exposes individual students' grades to other students, violating confidentiality of education records
questions.rationale: Allowing students to see one another's names and scores discloses confidential grade information, which violates the privacy protections afforded to education records. Grades should be returned in a manner that prevents disclosure to other students.

questions.stem: During a parent-teacher conference, a parent becomes visibly angry and raises his voice, accusing the teacher of 'picking on' his son. Which initial teacher response best supports a productive, collaborative outcome?
options: Calmly end the conference and reschedule once the parent has calmed down
Acknowledge the parent's concern, listen actively to understand the specific issue, and refocus the conversation on shared goals for the student's success
Ask another staff member to join immediately to serve as a witness
Defend the teaching decisions firmly to establish authority
questions.rationale: De-escalating an emotional parent begins with active listening and validating their concern, which builds trust and shifts the conversation toward collaborative problem solving focused on the student. Acknowledgment does not mean agreement but signals respect and openness.

questions.stem: A teacher is offered free season tickets to a professional sports team by the parent of a struggling student, with the parent commenting, 'I'm sure you'll keep an eye on my son's grades.' How should the teacher respond under the Code of Ethics?
options: Decline the gift, since accepting a significant gift that could appear to influence professional judgment violates ethical standards
Accept the tickets and report the gift to the principal for transparency
Accept the tickets only if the student's grade is already passing
Accept the tickets but assure the parent grades are based on merit
questions.rationale: The Code of Ethics prohibits educators from accepting gifts or favors that could reasonably be construed as influencing professional decisions. A valuable gift tied to a parent's expectation of grade leniency creates an unacceptable conflict and must be declined.

questions.stem: A student transfers into a teacher's class mid-year. The previous district sends the student's complete records, which include a confidential note from a former counselor describing a past mental health hospitalization. A coach asks the teacher to share 'anything in the file that explains his behavior.' What is the appropriate response?
options: Explain that access to confidential records is limited to those with a legitimate educational interest and that sensitive mental health information should not be shared casually
Share the counselor's note since the coach works with the student and has a need to know
Share the note only if the coach agrees to keep it confidential
Give the coach a verbal summary but not the actual document
questions.rationale: FERPA limits access to education records to school officials with a legitimate educational interest, determined by the district. Sensitive mental health information is not to be shared casually. A teacher should not unilaterally disclose such records and should ensure access follows district policy and the need-to-know standard.

questions.stem: A teacher observes a kindergartner come to school with the same bruise pattern on the back of both arms three days in a row. The child flinches when an adult raises a hand nearby. The teacher is unsure whether the marks are from abuse or rough play. What is the threshold for reporting in Texas?
options: The teacher must report when there is cause to believe the child may have been abused, since reasonable suspicion, not certainty, triggers the duty
The teacher should report only after consulting the school nurse to confirm the injuries
The teacher must have proof of abuse before reporting to avoid harming the family
The teacher should report only if the child explicitly states a parent caused the injuries
questions.rationale: Texas law requires a report when a person has cause to believe a child's physical or mental health has been adversely affected by abuse or neglect. The standard is reasonable suspicion. The teacher need not confirm the cause, obtain a confession, or have a nurse verify before reporting.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to strengthen partnerships with families at the start of the year. Which strategy best establishes a foundation of two-way communication?
options: Schedule a single back-to-school night and consider the relationship established
Send home a syllabus listing classroom rules and consequences
Make positive introductory contact with each family early, inviting them to share insights about their child and their preferred ways to communicate
Post all assignments online so families can monitor progress
questions.rationale: Two-way communication is built by reaching out proactively, sharing positive information, and inviting families to contribute their knowledge of their child and their communication preferences. This signals partnership rather than one-directional information flow.

questions.stem: An ARD committee is meeting to consider disciplinary removal of a student with an IEP who has accumulated 9 days of out-of-school suspension this year, and the principal now proposes a 5-day suspension for a new incident. What procedural protection is triggered by this proposal?
options: The student must be expelled and referred to an alternative campus automatically
The parent must waive procedural rights before any further suspension
A manifestation determination review must be conducted, because the additional removal would exceed 10 cumulative days and may constitute a change of placement
No protection is triggered because each suspension is under 10 consecutive days
questions.rationale: Under IDEA, removals exceeding 10 cumulative school days in a year may constitute a change of placement, triggering a manifestation determination review to decide whether the behavior was caused by or directly related to the student's disability. The committee cannot simply add the suspension without this review.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a popular AI grammar app to draft personalized progress comments. To use it, she pastes students' full names and detailed behavioral notes into the third-party tool. A colleague questions whether this is appropriate. What is the primary ethical and legal concern?
options: The tool may make the comments sound less professional
Entering identifiable student information into an unvetted third-party tool may improperly disclose confidential education records
The teacher should write comments without technological assistance
The tool may produce comments that are too generic to be useful
questions.rationale: Pasting personally identifiable student information and behavioral records into an external tool that the district has not approved can disclose confidential education records to a third party, potentially violating FERPA and student privacy obligations. The concern is data privacy, not the quality of the writing.

questions.stem: A teacher refers a student for evaluation for special education services. The parent, who comes from a community where disability carries stigma, refuses to consent to the evaluation. What is the most appropriate next step for the teacher and school?
options: Proceed with the evaluation anyway because the school suspects a disability

Respect that initial evaluation requires informed parental consent, while continuing to provide research-based interventions and to communicate respectfully about the purpose and benefits of evaluation
Document the refusal and provide no further support or intervention
Report the parent to authorities for educational neglect
questions.rationale: An initial special education evaluation requires informed parental consent. If a parent refuses, the school generally cannot proceed but should continue offering general-education interventions and engage the family with culturally sensitive communication about the evaluation's purpose, addressing concerns and building trust.

questions.stem: A teacher is finalizing semester grades and realizes that a student who failed by two points is the daughter of the school board president, who has publicly praised the teacher. The teacher feels subtle pressure to round the grade up. The student's actual performance does not warrant it. What does ethical conduct require?
options: Consult the board president privately about how to handle the grade
Round the grade up to maintain a positive relationship with an influential family
Assign the grade the student earned, since accurate evaluation must not be influenced by a family's status or political pressure
Lower a different student's borderline grade to make the curve appear consistent
questions.rationale: The Code of Ethics requires honesty and fairness in evaluating students. Grades must reflect actual achievement and cannot be altered due to a student's family connections or political influence. Succumbing to such pressure is unethical and compromises the integrity of assessment.

questions.stem: A teacher's 16-year-old student confides that she is pregnant and asks the teacher to keep it secret from her parents. The disclosure does not indicate abuse or danger. How should the teacher respond consistent with professional and legal responsibilities?
options: Respond supportively, avoid breaching confidentiality where no abuse or safety risk exists, and connect the student with the school counselor and appropriate support resources
Tell the student she must inform her parents within 24 hours or the teacher will
Document the disclosure and take no further action
Immediately call the student's parents to inform them
questions.rationale: Absent indicators of abuse or imminent danger, there is no mandatory-reporting trigger, and the teacher should respond with support rather than disclosing to parents. The appropriate professional step is to connect the student with the counselor and support resources who can help her navigate her options safely.

questions.stem: A new teacher is assigned a veteran mentor who frequently makes dismissive comments about students from low-income families, suggesting they 'won't amount to much.' The new teacher disagrees but fears damaging the mentoring relationship. What is the most professionally and ethically sound response?
options: Ignore the comments since the mentor outranks the new teacher
Request a different mentor immediately without addressing the issue
Adopt the mentor's view to maintain a harmonious relationship
Maintain high expectations for all students in her own practice and, where appropriate, respectfully challenge deficit thinking rather than internalizing it
questions.rationale: Professional ethics require maintaining high expectations for all students and not discriminating based on socioeconomic status. A teacher should resist deficit thinking, uphold equitable beliefs in her own practice, and constructively challenge biased attitudes rather than absorbing them.

questions.stem: A student turns 18 during the school year. His parents call the teacher demanding to know why his grades dropped and insisting on a meeting. The student has explicitly asked that his parents not be given information about his academic records. How should the teacher handle the parents' request under FERPA?
options: Refuse all communication with the parents entirely
Provide the grades because the parents still claim the student as a dependent

Recognize that FERPA rights have transferred to the now-adult student and that records cannot be disclosed to parents without the student's consent, unless a recognized exception such as dependent status is established by the district
Share the grades since parents have an inherent right to their child's school information
questions.rationale: When a student turns 18 (or attends a postsecondary institution), FERPA rights transfer to the student. Parents generally need the student's consent to access records, though an exception exists if the student is a dependent for tax purposes, which the district, not the teacher, must verify. Absent that, the teacher should not disclose against the student's wishes.

questions.stem: A teacher texts students directly from her personal cell phone to remind them about assignments, sometimes late at night, and occasionally exchanges casual personal messages. The district has an approved communication platform. Why is the personal texting practice problematic?
options: Students may not have unlimited texting plans
Text messages are an ineffective way to communicate about assignments
It blurs professional boundaries and bypasses district-approved, monitored communication channels, raising boundary and accountability concerns
Personal phones have poor battery life for constant messaging
questions.rationale: Using personal devices for unmonitored, informal communication with students blurs professional boundaries and circumvents district channels designed for transparency and accountability. The concern is maintaining appropriate boundaries and using sanctioned, documented communication methods.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to involve parents who have historically felt unwelcome at school in decisions about a new reading initiative. Which approach most authentically positions families as partners rather than passive recipients?
options: Provide parents with a brochure explaining the research behind the program
Form a planning group that includes parent representatives whose input shapes the design and implementation of the initiative
Invite parents to a meeting where the finalized initiative is presented for their information
Send a survey after the initiative launches to gauge satisfaction
questions.rationale: Authentic partnership involves families in shared decision-making before decisions are finalized, giving their input genuine influence over the design and implementation. Including parent representatives in the planning group treats families as co-creators rather than an audience.

questions.stem: A teacher overhears two students in the hallway discussing that one of them brought a knife to school 'just in case' someone bothers him. The student who allegedly has the weapon is not in the teacher's class. What is the teacher's most appropriate immediate action?
options: Mention it to the student's own teacher and let that teacher decide what to do
Wait to see whether the student actually displays the weapon before involving administration
Speak privately with the student to ask him to take the knife home
Immediately notify administration and follow the school's safety protocol, since a potential weapon on campus is a serious safety threat regardless of whose class the student is in
questions.rationale: Student and campus safety is a paramount professional responsibility. A credible report of a weapon on campus must be reported to administration immediately so the school's safety protocols can be activated. The teacher should not delay, investigate alone, or hand off the responsibility.

questions.stem: A teacher is asked by a colleague to 'cover' for her by signing an attendance verification form stating the colleague attended a required professional development session she actually skipped. What should the teacher do?
options: Sign but add a note that she was not present to witness attendance
Decline to sign, because verifying false information is dishonest and violates the Code of Ethics
Sign only if the colleague promises to attend the next session
Sign the form to support a fellow teacher
questions.rationale: Falsifying or verifying false official records violates the Code of Ethics' requirements for honesty and integrity. The teacher must decline to certify information she knows to be untrue, regardless of collegial pressure.

questions.stem: A student with diabetes has an IEP-related health plan permitting her to check her blood sugar and eat a snack during class as needed. A substitute teacher, unaware of the plan, publicly tells the student to put the food away and stop 'breaking the rules.' Afterward, the regular teacher learns of the incident. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Tell the student to be more discreet next time to avoid confusion
Ensure the student's plan is honored, clarify the accommodation with relevant staff and substitutes going forward, and address the embarrassment caused to the student
Add a note to the student's file noting she ate in class
Inform the student that substitutes are not required to follow her plan
questions.rationale: A documented health accommodation must be honored by all staff, including substitutes. The teacher should ensure systems are in place so substitutes are informed, reaffirm the accommodation, and address the harm to the student. Substitutes are required to implement the plan.

questions.stem: A teacher serves on a campus committee revising the student handbook. She notices the proposed dress code uses language that could disproportionately target students of a particular cultural or religious background. What is the most professionally responsible action?
options: Vote against the entire handbook to register a protest
Privately advise affected students to challenge the policy themselves
Raise the concern with the committee, advocating for inclusive language that respects cultural and religious diversity and does not discriminate
Stay silent because the dress code applies to everyone equally on its face
questions.rationale: Educators have a responsibility to promote equity and nondiscrimination and to advocate for fair policies. Raising the concern constructively within the committee and proposing inclusive language addresses potential discrimination through appropriate professional channels.

questions.stem: A teacher receives a subpoena from an attorney demanding that she personally hand over copies of a student's complete education records for use in the parents' custody dispute. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Refuse to provide anything because student records are always confidential
Notify campus administration and the district's records custodian, who will determine FERPA-compliant procedures, including any required parental notification, before any release
Provide only the records the teacher personally created
Comply immediately and provide the records to avoid contempt of court
questions.rationale: FERPA permits disclosure pursuant to a lawfully issued subpoena, but the process must be handled through the district, which typically must make a reasonable effort to notify parents before releasing records. An individual teacher should not respond unilaterally; she should refer the subpoena to administration and the records custodian.

questions.stem: A teacher posts on a public social media page criticizing a named student's parent by calling them 'impossible to work with' after a difficult conference. A community member screenshots the post. Which best describes the ethical problem?
options: The teacher should have made the post private rather than public
The teacher should not use social media during the school year
The teacher disparaged a parent publicly and identified a family, violating professional conduct standards regarding respectful interaction and confidentiality
The post might lead to fewer parents volunteering
questions.rationale: The Code of Ethics requires educators to interact with parents in a professional manner and not to misuse their position. Publicly disparaging an identifiable parent breaches professional conduct and confidentiality expectations, regardless of privacy settings.

questions.stem: At an ARD meeting, the committee proposes removing a related service (speech therapy) that the data show the student no longer needs. The parent insists the service continue 'just to be safe.' How should the committee proceed in a legally sound and student-centered way?
options: Continue the service indefinitely to satisfy the parent regardless of need

Review the evaluation data with the parent, ensure decisions are individualized and based on the student's documented needs, and seek consensus while honoring the parent's procedural rights if disagreement persists
Remove the service immediately by staff vote since the data support it
Tell the parent the decision is final and not subject to discussion
questions.rationale: ARD decisions must be individualized, data-based, and reached through a consensus process that includes the parent. The committee should review the data collaboratively, base the decision on the student's documented needs, and respect the parent's procedural rights (such as a recess or dispute resolution) if disagreement continues.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to communicate a student's ongoing behavioral struggles to the family without damaging the relationship. Which approach is most constructive?
options: Open with genuine positives about the student, describe specific behaviors objectively, and invite the family to collaborate on solutions
Lead with a list of every infraction the student has committed
Communicate only through formal disciplinary referrals
Wait until the behavior becomes severe before contacting the family
questions.rationale: Constructive family communication builds on a foundation of trust by acknowledging the student's strengths, describing concerns specifically and objectively rather than judgmentally, and framing the conversation as a collaborative effort to support the student.

questions.stem: A teacher already made a good-faith report to DFPS about suspected abuse of a student. Two weeks later, the parent, having learned a report was filed, threatens to sue the teacher for defamation. The teacher worries she made the wrong call because the investigation is ongoing. What protection applies, and what should the teacher understand?
options: A person who reports suspected abuse in good faith is immune from civil and criminal liability, and an unsubstantiated finding does not equal a bad-faith report
The teacher should retract the report to avoid the lawsuit
The teacher should have consulted the parent before reporting to avoid this conflict
The teacher is personally liable if the investigation finds the report unsubstantiated
questions.rationale: Texas law grants immunity from civil and criminal liability to those who report suspected abuse in good faith. An investigation that does not substantiate the report does not mean the report was made in bad faith. Retracting or consulting the parent beforehand would be improper and contrary to the duty to report.

questions.stem: A teacher learns that a standardized test she is administering contains an error in the answer key that benefits students. She is told by a colleague to 'just go with it' so the scores look better for the campus. What does professional integrity require?
options: Report the suspected error through proper channels so the assessment results are accurate and valid, consistent with standards for honest assessment practices
Ignore it because a single test error is unlikely to matter
Go along with it since higher scores help the whole campus
Quietly correct the key herself and rescore the tests
questions.rationale: Educators must adhere to standards for administering assessments accurately and honestly. Knowingly allowing an error that inflates scores compromises the validity of the results and violates professional integrity. The proper response is to report the suspected error through appropriate channels.

questions.stem: A parent volunteer who helps in the classroom asks to look through the teacher's gradebook to 'see how the other kids are doing compared to mine.' How should the teacher respond?
options: Politely decline, explaining that other students' grades are confidential and cannot be shared with anyone other than authorized parties
Show the parent only the top and bottom scores without names
Allow the parent to view the gradebook but ask her not to discuss it
Allow it since the parent is a trusted volunteer who helps regularly
questions.rationale: Other students' grades are confidential education records that cannot be disclosed to a parent volunteer, who has no legitimate educational interest in another child's records. The teacher must protect the confidentiality of all students' information regardless of the volunteer's helpfulness.

questions.stem: Ms. Alvarez teaches a third-grade class and notices that several students who could decode fluently in second grade are now struggling to comprehend longer chapter texts. Drawing on knowledge of human development, which interpretation best explains this shift and points to the most appropriate instructional response?
options: The students have regressed cognitively, so Ms. Alvarez should reteach phonics from the beginning of the year
As texts demand more abstract reasoning and working-memory coordination, decoding alone is insufficient; she should explicitly teach comprehension strategies
The students need glasses, so she should refer all of them for vision screening before any instruction
The students are simply unmotivated, so she should introduce a token reward system for finishing books
questions.rationale: As reading shifts from 'learning to read' to 'reading to learn,' texts require coordinating decoding with abstract reasoning and working memory. The developmentally appropriate response is to explicitly teach comprehension strategies rather than assume regression, low motivation, or a sensory deficit.

questions.stem: A kindergarten teacher plans a lesson and wants the activity to match her students' typical level of cognitive development. Which choice best reflects developmentally appropriate practice for most five-year-olds?
options: Asking students to write a two-paragraph persuasive essay independently
Providing concrete manipulatives and hands-on sorting activities to explore categories
Lecturing for 40 minutes on the life cycle of plants
Requiring students to take detailed notes from a textbook chapter
questions.rationale: Most five-year-olds learn best through concrete, hands-on experiences. Manipulatives and sorting align with their developmental stage, whereas abstract writing, extended lecture, and textbook note-taking exceed typical kindergarten capacities.

questions.stem: Mr. Trinh, a seventh-grade science teacher, observes that one student dominates group work, dismisses peers' ideas, and shows little awareness of how his comments affect others. Considering social and emotional development at this age, which response would most effectively support the student's growth while maintaining group productivity?
options: Assigning the student a defined rotating role (e.g., 'recorder') and debriefing afterward on how each member contributed
Publicly correcting the student each time he interrupts so peers see the consequence
Ignoring the behavior because adolescent self-centeredness will resolve naturally with age
Permanently removing the student from all group work to protect classmates
questions.rationale: Early adolescents are developing perspective-taking and social awareness. Structuring interdependent roles plus reflective debriefing scaffolds these skills, fostering empathy and accountability rather than isolating or shaming the student or doing nothing.

questions.stem: During a high school geometry unit, Ms. Okafor notices that some students can manipulate formulas procedurally but cannot explain why the Pythagorean theorem works. To advance students from procedural to conceptual understanding in a developmentally supportive way, she should first:
options: Require students to memorize the proof verbatim for a quiz
Have students physically construct squares on the sides of right triangles and compare areas
Move on, since procedural fluency is sufficient for the state exam
Increase the number of timed practice problems to build automaticity
questions.rationale: Connecting abstract relationships to a concrete, visual model bridges procedural and conceptual understanding. Constructing and comparing areas lets students reason about why the theorem holds, supporting the transition to formal abstract reasoning.

questions.stem: A fourth-grade teacher, Mr. Bello, has a student who melts down whenever an activity changes unexpectedly but thrives with predictable routines. Understanding individual differences in self-regulation, the teacher's most appropriate first step is to:
options: Tell the student to 'just calm down' whenever transitions occur
Remove all transitions from the day to prevent any meltdowns
Send the student to the office each time a meltdown begins
Provide advance warning and a visual schedule so the student can anticipate transitions
questions.rationale: Supporting self-regulation begins with proactive, individualized scaffolds. Advance warnings and visual schedules help the student anticipate and prepare for change, reducing dysregulation—more effective than vague commands, avoidance, or punitive removal.

questions.stem: Ms. Delgado teaches a multi-age 1st-2nd grade class. One activity asks students to predict whether objects will sink or float, test them, and revise their thinking. A first grader insists a heavy object must sink even after seeing it float. Which developmental concept best explains the student's reasoning, and what should the teacher do?
options: The student's prior schema overrides contradictory evidence; the teacher should provide repeated, varied experiences to prompt accommodation
The student lacks intelligence; the teacher should provide easier objects
The concept is too advanced for any first grader; the teacher should drop the lesson
The student is being defiant; the teacher should require an apology
questions.rationale: The student is assimilating evidence into an existing schema ('heavy = sinks'). Repeated, varied disconfirming experiences encourage accommodation—restructuring the schema. This reflects constructivist development and the teacher's role in promoting cognitive conflict.

questions.stem: A middle school teacher wants to support students' growing need for peer acceptance and identity formation during a unit. Which strategy best aligns with adolescents' social-emotional development?
options: Incorporating structured peer discussion and choice in how students demonstrate learning
Grading students publicly from highest to lowest to motivate effort
Assigning permanent seats with no interaction allowed
Eliminating all collaborative activities to keep students focused
questions.rationale: Adolescents value peer interaction and autonomy. Structured peer discussion and choice respect their developmental needs for belonging and identity, whereas isolating, silencing, or publicly ranking students undermines these needs.

questions.stem: Mr. Castillo teaches ninth-grade English and has a student whose written ideas are sophisticated but whose handwriting and spelling lag well behind peers. Recognizing that development across domains can be uneven, the teacher's best response is to:
options: Refuse to accept any work until handwriting improves
Conclude the student cannot really think well and place him in a lower track
Lower expectations for the depth of the student's ideas to match the mechanics
Allow the student to use a word processor with spell-check while continuing targeted support for mechanics
questions.rationale: Development is uneven across domains; strong reasoning can coexist with delayed fine-motor or spelling skills. Providing assistive tools lets the student express advanced thinking while targeted instruction addresses mechanics—rather than capping potential or withholding work.

questions.stem: Ms. Pham notices that her sixth-grade class includes recent immigrants, students reading two grade levels above peers, and students with IEPs. To address this diversity in a single novel-study unit, which approach best reflects differentiated, learner-centered instruction?
options: Teach to the middle and offer the same worksheet to everyone
Group students permanently by ability and give the advanced group all enrichment
Require every student to complete identical timed reading quizzes daily
Provide tiered texts and assignments, flexible grouping, and varied response options around shared essential questions
questions.rationale: Differentiation maintains common essential questions while varying content (tiered texts), process (flexible grouping), and product (varied responses). This meets diverse readiness and needs better than one-size-fits-all instruction, rigid tracking, or uniform timed quizzes.

questions.stem: A second-grade teacher, Mr. Ramirez, has an emergent bilingual student whose home language is Spanish and who is in early stages of English acquisition. During a math word-problem lesson, the student understands the math but struggles with the English text. Which strategy best supports both content learning and language development?
options: Give the student only single-digit computation with no words
Excuse the student from word problems until English improves
Pair visuals, manipulatives, and sentence frames with the problems, and permit the student to first reason in Spanish
Translate every problem fully into Spanish so the student never uses English
questions.rationale: Effective practice for emergent bilinguals scaffolds content with comprehensible input (visuals, manipulatives, sentence frames) and leverages the home language as a resource, allowing access to grade-level math while developing English—not excluding, fully replacing, or watering down the content.

questions.stem: A first-year teacher learns that one of her fifth graders has a documented learning disability in reading and an IEP. Which is the teacher's most appropriate action?
options: Read and implement the IEP accommodations and collaborate with the special education team
Hold the student to a lower standard in every subject area
Assume the general curriculum is inappropriate and remove the student from class activities
Wait to see if the student struggles before reading the IEP
questions.rationale: Teachers are legally and professionally obligated to implement IEP accommodations and collaborate with the special education team from the outset. Lowering all standards, waiting passively, or excluding the student misapplies the IEP's purpose.

questions.stem: In an eighth-grade class, Ms. Nguyen has a gifted student who finishes work quickly and then disrupts others out of boredom, alongside a student who needs extended time. Which plan best meets both learners' needs without singling either out negatively?
options: Slow the whole class down to the pace of the student who needs more time
Build in tiered extension tasks and flexible pacing so each student works at an appropriately challenging level
Let the gifted student grade other students' papers while waiting
Give the gifted student more of the same worksheets to stay busy
questions.rationale: Differentiation by readiness and pacing—offering genuine extension (not more of the same) and flexible time—challenges the gifted learner and supports the student needing more time, without holding the class back or assigning the gifted student a teaching role.

questions.stem: Mr. Quintero teaches third grade and wants to ensure his classroom library and lesson examples reflect the diversity of his students and the broader world. The primary instructional benefit of doing so is that it:
options: Guarantees higher standardized test scores automatically
Helps all students see themselves represented and develop understanding of others, increasing engagement and belonging
Eliminates the need to teach the required curriculum
Reduces the amount of planning the teacher must do
questions.rationale: Representation in materials provides both 'mirrors' (seeing oneself) and 'windows' (understanding others), fostering belonging, engagement, and empathy. It is not a guaranteed score booster, a planning shortcut, or a curriculum replacement.

questions.stem: A teacher notices a student who is frequently tired, hungry, and unable to concentrate. Recognizing how out-of-school factors affect learning, the teacher's most appropriate response is to:
options: Publicly ask the student why he is always tired
Lower the student's grades for poor participation
Ignore it, since out-of-school factors are not the teacher's concern
Connect the family with school counseling and support resources while adjusting support in class
questions.rationale: Basic needs strongly influence learning. The professional response is to connect the family to appropriate resources and provide compassionate classroom support, rather than penalizing, embarrassing, or dismissing the student.

questions.stem: Ms. Ferguson has a student with ADHD who struggles to sustain attention during long independent assignments but excels in short, active bursts. Which combination of strategies best leverages this learner's profile while keeping rigor high?
options: Eliminate all challenging assignments to avoid frustration
Chunk tasks into shorter segments with movement breaks and clear checkpoints while maintaining grade-level expectations
Require the student to sit completely still for the entire period as practice
Exempt the student from all timed work permanently with no other changes
questions.rationale: Chunking work, embedding movement, and using checkpoints align instruction with the student's attentional profile while preserving rigor. Removing challenge, enforcing rigid stillness, or blanket exemptions either lower expectations or fight the student's needs.

questions.stem: Mr. Solis is planning a fourth-grade unit on ecosystems. He wants to design instruction that begins with the end in mind. Following a backward-design approach, his first step should be to:
options: Create the daily worksheets for each lesson
Choose engaging activities and videos students will enjoy
Order the textbook chapters in sequence
Identify the desired learning outcomes and the evidence that will show students met them
questions.rationale: Backward design begins with identifying desired results and acceptable evidence (assessment) before planning learning activities. Selecting activities, sequencing chapters, or making worksheets comes only after outcomes and assessments are clear.

questions.stem: A high school chemistry teacher, Mr. Adeyemi, wants his unit objectives to align tightly with both the state standards (TEKS) and his end-of-unit assessment. Which planning practice best ensures this alignment?
options: Deriving objectives from the TEKS and designing assessment items that directly measure those same objectives
Selecting assessment items only by how easy they are to grade
Using last year's test regardless of this year's objectives
Writing the test after teaching, based on whatever was covered
questions.rationale: Alignment requires objectives drawn from standards and assessments designed to measure those very objectives. Writing tests after the fact, reusing mismatched assessments, or choosing items for grading convenience breaks the standards-objective-assessment chain.

questions.stem: While planning a lesson, Ms. Carter wants to activate students' prior knowledge before introducing new material on fractions. Which opening activity best accomplishes this?
options: Beginning immediately with the formal definition of a fraction
Reading the lesson objective aloud and moving on
Distributing the end-of-unit test to preview vocabulary
Asking students to share real-life situations where they have split things into equal parts
questions.rationale: Activating prior knowledge means eliciting what students already know and connecting it to new content. Asking for real-life examples of splitting into equal parts surfaces relevant experience, unlike jumping to definitions, previewing a test, or merely reading an objective.

questions.stem: Mr. Lindqvist plans a project-based learning unit for seventh-grade geography. He worries students may stay engaged but not master key content. To balance engagement with rigorous learning, his plan should most importantly:
options: Anchor the project to specific learning objectives and embed formative checkpoints that assess content mastery
Grade only the final product's visual appeal
Remove all structure so creativity is unconstrained
Let students choose any topic with no required learning targets
questions.rationale: Effective PBL ties projects to clear objectives and uses formative checkpoints to monitor content mastery, ensuring engagement serves learning. Open-ended topics with no targets, grading on appearance, or removing structure all risk activity without learning.

questions.stem: Ms. Obi is sequencing a unit on persuasive writing for ninth grade. She wants the sequence to scaffold complexity appropriately. Which ordering of learning experiences best reflects sound instructional sequencing?
options: Teach only grammar rules, then assign the essay with no element instruction
Have students write a full persuasive essay first, then study its elements
Analyze model arguments, practice individual elements (claim, evidence, counterargument), then compose a full essay
Begin with a timed final draft, then teach revision
questions.rationale: Sound sequencing moves from analyzing models, to practicing component skills, to integrating them in a full performance—building complexity gradually. Starting with the full essay, a timed final draft, or grammar alone fails to scaffold the component skills first.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews her lesson plan and realizes she has not planned what to do if students finish the main task early or if some need more practice. Adding which element would most directly address this?
options: A stricter late-work policy
Planned extension activities and reteaching or support options for varied pacing
More decorative items for the bulletin board
A longer lecture introduction
questions.rationale: Anticipating varied pacing means planning extensions for early finishers and reteaching/support for those who need it. A longer lecture, a late-work policy, or decorations do not address differing rates of progress within the lesson.

questions.stem: Mr. Whitfield is designing a fifth-grade science lesson and wants students to engage in higher-order thinking, not just recall. According to a cognitive taxonomy of learning, which objective targets the highest level?
options: Students will define the term 'photosynthesis'
Students will design and justify a model of a sustainable habitat using ecological principles
Students will list the planets in order from the sun
Students will label the parts of a plant cell
questions.rationale: Designing and justifying a model engages creating and evaluating—the highest levels of cognitive taxonomies. Listing, defining, and labeling target lower-order remembering and understanding.

questions.stem: Mr. Iverson wants his eleventh-grade students to monitor and direct their own learning during a research project. Which set of practices most directly fosters metacognition and self-regulated learning?
options: Grading only the final paper with no interim feedback
Telling students exactly what to do at each step so they never get stuck
Having students set goals, self-assess against rubrics, and reflect on which strategies worked
Forbidding students from choosing their own research questions
questions.rationale: Metacognition is cultivated when students set goals, monitor progress via self-assessment, and reflect on strategy effectiveness. Spoon-feeding steps, grading only the end product, or removing choice all reduce opportunities for self-regulation.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to make abstract science content more accessible by helping students connect it to what they already know. Which strategy best supports this goal?
options: Reading the textbook aloud word for word
Listing vocabulary terms on the board to copy
Using analogies and real-world examples that link new concepts to familiar experiences
