Requiring silent reading with no discussion
questions.rationale: Analogies and real-world examples build bridges from new, abstract content to students' existing knowledge, aiding comprehension. Reading aloud verbatim, silent reading without discussion, or copying vocabulary do not actively connect to prior understanding.

questions.stem: Ms. Yamamoto teaches a lesson and uses a gradual-release approach. After modeling a skill and guiding practice, she observes that most students are accurate but a few still struggle. The most appropriate next step is to:
options: Pull the small group needing help for additional guided practice while others begin independent work
Immediately move the whole class to independent practice
Assign the struggling students extra homework with no further instruction
Reteach the entire lesson to everyone from the start
questions.rationale: In the gradual-release model, students move to independent practice when ready. Differentiating by pulling a small group for more guided practice while others advance respects varied readiness—better than rushing everyone, reteaching to all, or assigning unsupported homework.

questions.stem: Mr. Castellano notices that his eighth graders can recall facts about the water cycle but cannot apply the concept to explain a local flooding event. To promote transfer of learning, he should design tasks that:
options: Require students to memorize the water cycle diagram more thoroughly
Have students recopy their notes neatly
Ask students to apply water-cycle principles to novel, real-world problems and explain their reasoning
Give more multiple-choice quizzes on water-cycle vocabulary
questions.rationale: Transfer is promoted by applying learned principles to new contexts with explanation of reasoning. More memorization, vocabulary quizzes, or recopying notes reinforce recall but do not build the application and reasoning that transfer requires.

questions.stem: During cooperative group work in a tenth-grade class, Ms. Pruitt finds that one or two students do all the work while others coast. To ensure all members learn and contribute, the most effective structural change is to:
options: Grade only the group's final product
Assign interdependent roles and use individual accountability measures alongside the group product
Let groups self-organize with no defined roles or accountability
Eliminate group work and have everyone work alone
questions.rationale: Effective cooperative learning requires positive interdependence and individual accountability—defined roles plus individual checks ensure everyone contributes and learns. No structure, group-only grading, or abandoning collaboration each fail to ensure shared participation.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to think more critically during a reading lesson rather than simply locating facts. Which type of question best promotes critical thinking?
options: 'What is the main character's name?'
'How might the story change if it were set in a different time period, and why?'
'On what page does the conflict begin?'
'What color is the house described in paragraph two?'
questions.rationale: Open-ended, analytical questions requiring reasoning ('how might... and why') promote critical thinking, while questions asking for names, page numbers, or specific details require only literal recall.

questions.stem: Mr. Donovan uses technology in his fourth-grade lesson by having students play a fast-paced math game on tablets. He realizes the game keeps students busy but is not advancing the lesson's objective on multi-step problem solving. To use technology more effectively, he should:
options: Let students choose any app they like during math time
Add more game time so students stay entertained
Select or design a digital tool that directly requires the targeted multi-step problem-solving and reasoning
Remove all technology since it is distracting
questions.rationale: Technology should serve the learning objective. Choosing a tool that directly demands the targeted multi-step reasoning aligns the tech with the goal, unlike adding entertainment time, abandoning technology entirely, or allowing unaligned free choice.

questions.stem: Mr. Halloran is planning a cross-disciplinary unit linking a ninth-grade history topic (industrialization) with persuasive writing in English. To ensure the integrated unit develops both content knowledge and developmentally appropriate skills, his planning should most importantly:
options: Focus only on the history content and treat writing as decoration
Keep the two subjects' goals entirely separate to avoid confusion
Identify shared and discipline-specific objectives and design tasks where historical analysis informs and strengthens the persuasive writing
Assign a single grade for creativity regardless of either subject's standards
questions.rationale: Effective interdisciplinary planning clarifies both shared and discipline-specific objectives and designs tasks where the disciplines reinforce one another—here, historical analysis fueling evidence-based persuasion. Keeping goals separate, neglecting writing, or grading only creativity undermines true integration and standards alignment.

questions.stem: A second-grade teacher notices that several students who are strong oral storytellers struggle to write complete sentences. Knowing that children develop different skills at different rates, which instructional response best reflects an understanding of typical developmental variation at this age?
options: Build on the students' oral strengths by having them dictate stories before writing them, gradually increasing the writing demand
Delay all writing instruction for these students until their handwriting improves
Place the students in a remedial group separated from peers during all language arts time
Require the students to copy paragraphs repeatedly until their sentences improve
questions.rationale: Recognizing that oral language often develops ahead of written expression in young children, the teacher leverages an existing strength (oral storytelling) as a bridge to the emerging skill (writing), scaffolding rather than penalizing or isolating the learners.

questions.stem: A middle school science teacher observes that a 12-year-old student who previously participated eagerly now appears self-conscious, frequently checks how peers react before answering, and resists tasks that might expose mistakes publicly. Which understanding of early-adolescent development should most guide the teacher's response?
options: Social concerns are irrelevant to cognitive learning and should be ignored during science instruction
The behavior indicates a learning disability that requires immediate referral for special education testing
The student is being deliberately defiant and should lose participation points
Heightened sensitivity to peer evaluation is typical in early adolescence and instruction should provide lower-risk ways to demonstrate learning
questions.rationale: Early adolescents become acutely aware of peer judgment as part of normal social-emotional development; effective teachers reduce public risk (e.g., think-pair-share, written responses, anonymous polling) so students can engage without fear of embarrassment.

questions.stem: A high school English teacher wants to design a unit that respects adolescents' growing capacity for abstract reasoning and identity exploration. Which task best aligns with the cognitive and social-emotional developmental level of 16-year-olds?
options: Analyzing how a novel's protagonist navigates competing values and connecting that conflict to ethical dilemmas in students' own lives
Coloring illustrations that depict scenes from the assigned reading
Memorizing and reciting definitions of literary terms for a quiz
Copying the plot summary from the back cover into their notebooks
questions.rationale: Mid-adolescents can engage in abstract, hypothetical, and ethical reasoning and are actively forming identity; tasks asking them to analyze value conflicts and relate them to their own lives match both cognitive and social-emotional development.

questions.stem: A fourth-grade teacher notices that a student grasps new math concepts quickly but becomes frustrated and gives up when a problem requires several steps. Which response best supports the student's developmental needs?
options: Explicitly teach a strategy for breaking multi-step problems into manageable parts and praise persistence
Provide only single-step problems so the student never feels frustrated
Tell the student that capable learners do not get frustrated
Move the student to a lower grade-level group
questions.rationale: Developing self-regulation and persistence is part of childhood social-emotional growth; teaching a concrete problem-decomposition strategy plus reinforcing effort builds both skill and resilience without lowering rigor.

questions.stem: A seventh-grade teacher has students from several cultural and linguistic backgrounds, including recent immigrants from three countries. To create an inclusive classroom that values diversity, which approach is most effective?
options: Lower academic expectations for students whose first language is not English
Ask the recent immigrants to present their cultures while excusing other students from the activity
Treat all students identically and avoid any reference to their backgrounds to be fair
Incorporate students' cultural knowledge and experiences as assets within academic content and classroom discussion
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive teaching positions students' backgrounds as assets and integrates them into rigorous content for all, fostering belonging without lowering expectations or singling students out.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that classroom examples in the adopted curriculum consistently reflect one cultural perspective, and a few students seem disengaged because they see little of themselves in the material. Which instructional decision best demonstrates culturally responsive pedagogy while maintaining alignment to standards?
options: Supplement standards-aligned content with diverse texts, examples, and perspectives so all students see themselves and learn about others
Ignore the issue because the curriculum is district-approved and must be followed exactly
Replace the curriculum entirely with materials about only the disengaged students' cultures
Address culture only during designated heritage months and not in daily lessons
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive teachers augment required content with varied perspectives and examples that remain standards-aligned, ensuring representation and broadening understanding without abandoning the curriculum or relegating diversity to isolated occasions.

questions.stem: During a class discussion, a student makes a comment that reflects a stereotype about a group of people. The teacher wants to maintain a respectful, inclusive environment. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Publicly reprimand the student and send them to the office
Calmly invite reflection by asking questions that prompt the class to examine the assumption and consider multiple perspectives
Ignore the comment to avoid embarrassing the student in front of peers
End the discussion immediately and change the subject
questions.rationale: Teachers foster inclusion by treating such moments as teachable opportunities, guiding respectful examination of assumptions and perspectives rather than ignoring, shaming, or avoiding them.

questions.stem: A third-grade teacher wants families from diverse backgrounds to feel welcome and engaged. Which strategy best supports equitable family engagement?
options: Require all parents to attend a single daytime conference or forfeit involvement
Send all communication home in English only and assume families will translate it
Offer communication in families' home languages and provide multiple flexible ways to participate, including evenings and virtual options
Limit family involvement to fundraising activities
questions.rationale: Equitable engagement removes language and logistical barriers, offering communication in home languages and flexible participation formats so all families can be involved meaningfully.

questions.stem: An eighth-grade social studies teacher is planning a unit and wants to ensure that students develop respect for diverse viewpoints while thinking critically. Which design best balances inclusivity with rigorous, standards-based analysis?
options: Assign each student to defend the viewpoint that matches their own background
Present only one interpretation of historical events to avoid confusing students
Allow students to choose any opinion and avoid challenging their conclusions with evidence
Have students examine multiple primary sources representing different groups' experiences and evaluate evidence to construct reasoned interpretations
questions.rationale: Inclusive, rigorous instruction has students engage multiple perspectives through evidence-based analysis, building both respect for diversity and critical reasoning aligned to standards.

questions.stem: A fifth-grade teacher wants students to understand why they are learning about persuasive writing. Which action best establishes a clear and meaningful learning goal?
options: Begin the activity without stating any purpose to save time
Share a student-friendly objective and explain how persuasive writing connects to real-world situations such as letters and advocacy
Write the standard code on the board without explanation
Tell students to simply complete pages 40-45 in the workbook
questions.rationale: Effective instruction communicates clear, student-friendly objectives and relevance, helping learners understand the purpose and value of what they are learning.

questions.stem: A high school biology teacher is planning a lesson on cellular respiration. Before deciding how to sequence instruction, which planning step is most important for ensuring the lesson is appropriately challenging?
options: Determining students' prior knowledge of related concepts and aligning the lesson objectives to that starting point
Selecting an engaging video to show at the end of class
Deciding which students will be allowed to ask questions
Choosing the brightest colors for the slide presentation
questions.rationale: Sound planning begins with knowing learners' prior knowledge and aligning objectives accordingly, so instruction is neither too easy nor too hard and builds logically from where students are.

questions.stem: A teacher is designing a multi-day unit and wants each day's lesson to build coherently toward a culminating performance assessment in which students design a solution to a community problem. Which planning approach best ensures coherence and alignment?
options: Use backward design: define the culminating outcome and assessment first, then sequence lessons and formative checks that build the needed knowledge and skills
Choose activities students will find fun and fit the content around them afterward
Plan each day independently and hope the activities connect by the end
Cover as much content as possible regardless of the final task
questions.rationale: Backward design starts with the desired results and assessment evidence, then plans aligned learning experiences and formative checks, ensuring each lesson contributes to the culminating outcome.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a lesson with a clear objective but realizes during planning that students will need to manipulate physical objects to grasp an abstract concept about volume. Which planning decision best reflects effective use of resources and materials?
options: Assign the textbook reading as the only means of learning the concept
Show a single static diagram and move on quickly
Describe the concept verbally only, since materials take time to prepare
Gather manipulatives such as unit cubes and containers so students can build and measure to develop conceptual understanding
questions.rationale: Selecting appropriate manipulatives that match the cognitive demand allows students to construct conceptual understanding of abstract ideas, reflecting thoughtful planning of resources aligned to the objective.

questions.stem: A high school chemistry teacher wants to gather evidence of student reasoning during a lab on reaction rates without interrupting the flow of the activity. Which formative assessment strategy provides the most useful real-time insight into student thinking?
options: Collecting completed worksheets at the end of the period for grading
Circulating with a focused observation checklist and asking targeted probing questions about students' predictions and reasoning as they work
Giving a multiple-choice quiz the following Monday
Grading the final lab report submitted a week later
questions.rationale: Real-time formative assessment captures thinking as it happens; structured observation with targeted probing questions during the lab reveals reasoning and allows immediate instructional adjustment, unlike delayed or summative measures.

questions.stem: A teacher is selecting an assessment to measure whether students can apply the scientific method to design an investigation. Which assessment type provides the most valid evidence of this skill?
options: A spelling quiz on science vocabulary
A true/false test about definitions of scientific terms
A matching activity pairing scientists with their discoveries
A performance task in which students design and justify their own investigation to answer a testable question
questions.rationale: Validity requires that the assessment measure the intended construct; designing an investigation is a performance skill best assessed through a performance task, not recall-based formats.

questions.stem: After a summative unit test, a teacher analyzes results and finds that nearly all students missed items addressing one specific standard, while performing well on others. Which conclusion and next step are most warranted?
options: The test was too easy overall and should be made harder
The students are simply low achievers and nothing can be done
The instruction or items for that standard may have been inadequate; the teacher should review how it was taught and reteach with adjusted methods
The standard is unimportant and can be skipped in the future
questions.rationale: A pattern of widespread failure on one standard amid otherwise strong performance points to an instructional or assessment issue with that standard; the appropriate response is to analyze and adjust teaching and reteach, using data to improve practice.

questions.stem: A first-grade teacher wants a quick check of whether students understood a brief lesson on identifying the main idea. Which formative assessment is most appropriate for this age and purpose?
options: No assessment, since the lesson was short
A timed two-page essay
Asking students to give a thumbs-up, thumbs-sideways, or thumbs-down to show confidence, followed by a one-sentence main idea on a card
A standardized end-of-year exam
questions.rationale: A quick, developmentally appropriate formative check (self-rating gesture plus a brief response) gives immediate, low-stakes insight into first graders' understanding without overwhelming them.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a pre-assessment at the start of a geometry unit. Several students already demonstrate mastery of the first three objectives. Which differentiation decision best uses this assessment data?
options: Move those students to a different grade level immediately
Require those students to complete the same introductory lessons as everyone else
Provide those students with extension tasks or more complex problems while others build foundational skills
Allow those students to do unrelated free-time activities for the rest of the unit
questions.rationale: Pre-assessment data should drive differentiation; students who have mastered foundational objectives need appropriately challenging extension or deeper tasks rather than repetition or unrelated busywork.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that an emergent bilingual student answers content questions incorrectly on a written test but explains the same concepts accurately in a one-on-one oral conversation in simplified English. Which interpretation and assessment adjustment are most appropriate?
options: The oral answers should be disregarded because only written tests are valid
The written format may be assessing language rather than content; provide accommodations such as oral response or simplified language to validly measure content knowledge
The student should be exempted from all assessment until fully fluent in English
The student does not understand the content and needs remediation in the concept
questions.rationale: When a language barrier confounds a content assessment, the result lacks validity for measuring content; appropriate accommodations (oral responses, linguistic simplification) separate language from content so the assessment measures what it intends.

questions.stem: A teacher plans to use both formative and summative assessments in a unit. Which statement best describes the appropriate role of each?
options: Formative and summative assessments serve identical purposes and are interchangeable
Formative assessments monitor learning and guide ongoing instruction, while summative assessments evaluate cumulative learning at the end of a period
Only summative assessments provide useful information about students
Formative assessments should always count heavily toward final grades
questions.rationale: Formative assessment is for learning (monitoring and adjusting instruction during the process), while summative assessment is of learning (evaluating achievement at the conclusion); understanding this distinction guides appropriate use.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to ensure a unit test is both reliable and fair for all students, including those with documented accommodations in their IEPs. Which set of actions best supports this goal?
options: Align items to taught objectives, write clear unambiguous items, and provide each student's required IEP accommodations such as extended time or read-aloud
Allow students to grade their own tests to save time
Give every student exactly the same test under identical conditions regardless of IEPs, to be 'fair'
Make the test very long so that luck plays no role
questions.rationale: Reliability and fairness come from objective-aligned, clearly written items and from providing legally required IEP accommodations so the test validly measures learning for each student; identical conditions ignore documented needs.

questions.stem: A teacher analyzes a class set of formative writing samples and groups students by the specific skill each needs next: organization, evidence use, or sentence variety. What is the primary instructional benefit of this data-driven grouping?
options: It reduces the teacher's need to give any further feedback
It allows targeted small-group instruction that addresses each group's specific learning need
It ensures all students receive identical instruction
It permanently labels students by ability for the rest of the year
questions.rationale: Using formative data to form flexible, skill-based groups lets the teacher target instruction to each group's specific need, increasing efficiency and responsiveness; such groups are flexible, not permanent labels.

questions.stem: A teacher is planning a lesson for a mixed-readiness class and wants every student appropriately challenged. Which planning strategy best differentiates while keeping all students working toward the same essential standard?
options: Design tiered tasks that vary in complexity and scaffolding but all target the same key concept, with flexible entry points
Lower the standard for the whole class so everyone can succeed easily
Teach to the middle and let faster or slower students adjust on their own
Give advanced students the grade-level task and assign struggling students unrelated easier worksheets
questions.rationale: Tiered instruction differentiates the complexity and support of tasks while keeping all students focused on the same essential learning, ensuring appropriate challenge without lowering expectations or fragmenting the goal.

questions.stem: A teacher learns that a new student has a hearing impairment and uses an interpreter. When planning upcoming lessons, which proactive decision best ensures the student can access instruction?
options: Wait until the student struggles before making any changes
Assume the interpreter will handle all of the student's learning needs
Plan ahead by positioning visuals, providing written directions, ensuring clear sightlines to the interpreter, and pacing to allow interpretation
Seat the student in the back to avoid drawing attention
questions.rationale: Proactive, universally designed planning anticipates the student's access needs (visual supports, written directions, sightlines, appropriate pacing) so the lesson is accessible from the start rather than reactively patched.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to incorporate technology into a lesson on graphing data. Which use of technology best supports the learning objective rather than serving as a mere add-on?
options: Have students use a graphing tool to enter their own collected data, generate graphs, and analyze patterns they could not easily see by hand
Let students play educational games unrelated to graphing during class
Require students to type the lesson notes instead of writing them
Show an unrelated entertaining video at the start to grab attention
questions.rationale: Technology should be selected because it advances the learning objective; using a graphing tool to manipulate real data and reveal patterns deepens analysis in ways consistent with the goal, unlike superficial or off-task uses.

questions.stem: A teacher discovers that a student's home responsibilities, including caring for younger siblings, sometimes limit time for homework. Which response best reflects an understanding of students' diverse life circumstances while maintaining high expectations?
options: Communicate with the student and family to find flexible ways to demonstrate learning, such as in-class work time, while keeping rigorous goals
Exempt the student from all independent practice indefinitely
Lower the academic standards permanently for this student
Penalize the student for late homework to teach responsibility
questions.rationale: Equitable, responsive teaching acknowledges out-of-school circumstances and adjusts how, not whether, students meet rigorous goals, preserving high expectations while removing barriers.

questions.stem: A teacher of a multi-grade class observes that two students of the same chronological age differ markedly in their readiness for abstract problem-solving, with one reasoning hypothetically and the other relying on concrete examples. Which understanding should most inform the teacher's instructional planning?
options: Cognitive development varies among individuals, so instruction should meet each student where they are and scaffold toward abstraction
Both students must be at the same developmental stage because they are the same age
The concrete-reasoning student is below average and should be retained
Abstract reasoning cannot be developed and is fixed at birth
questions.rationale: Development proceeds at individual rates; age does not dictate cognitive stage. Effective planning meets each learner at their current level and provides scaffolds (e.g., concrete models bridging to abstraction) to support growth.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to know exactly how their performance task will be evaluated before they begin working. Which practice best supports this and promotes fairness?
options: Grade based on overall impression without explicit criteria
Decide the criteria only after seeing the submissions
Share and discuss the scoring rubric with students in advance, including examples of quality work
Keep the grading criteria private to prevent students from 'gaming' the task
questions.rationale: Sharing the rubric and exemplars before students begin clarifies expectations, supports self-monitoring, and promotes fairness and consistency in evaluation.

questions.stem: A kindergarten teacher wants students to clean up the learning centers quickly when a chime sounds. On the first day, which action best establishes this cleanup routine?
options: Sound the chime and immediately give a consequence to any student still playing
Ask a few responsible students to clean up while the others continue playing
Hang a poster of cleanup rules above each center and point to it when needed
Demonstrate the cleanup steps, have the class rehearse them after the chime, and give feedback until it is smooth
questions.rationale: Young learners internalize routines through explicit modeling, rehearsal, and feedback. Teaching and practicing the cleanup procedure on day one builds the automatic response the teacher wants.

questions.stem: A teacher wants the daily class start to be productive instead of unstructured while attendance is taken. Which routine best accomplishes this?
options: Call each student's name aloud and ask them to respond before any work begins
Post a brief warm-up that students begin independently the moment they enter
Allow students free conversation time until attendance is complete
Have students wait silently with materials out until the teacher finishes roll
questions.rationale: A bell-ringer that students start immediately engages them productively while the teacher handles administrative tasks, eliminating the unstructured opening minutes where disruptions often arise.

questions.stem: While the teacher leads a small reading group, a student at an independent station raises his hand and waits, stuck on a directions question. The teacher wants to protect small-group time. Which previously taught procedure best prevents this interruption in the future?
options: Establish an 'ask three then me' peer-help routine with a posted reference for common questions
Instruct students to skip any task they do not immediately understand
Require students to sit quietly and wait for the teacher to circulate
Tell students to come to the small-group table whenever they are confused
questions.rationale: A peer-help routine paired with accessible references lets students resolve minor questions independently, preserving small-group instruction and keeping independent work moving.

questions.stem: A teacher is rearranging the room for a unit centered on lab investigations done in groups of four, with occasional whole-class demonstrations at the front. Which arrangement best supports both formats while allowing the teacher to monitor everyone?
options: Long rows facing the front so all students can see demonstrations
Desks pushed to the walls with students standing in the center
Clustered groups of four positioned with clear sightlines to the demo area and open aisles for circulation
One large U-shape with all students facing inward
questions.rationale: The physical environment should fit instructional needs. Clusters support group investigations, while preserved sightlines to the front and open aisles allow demonstrations and continuous teacher monitoring.

questions.stem: A teacher enforces a tardy rule strictly for some students but overlooks it for others. Students have started complaining that the rule is unfair, and minor arguments are increasing. Which action should the teacher prioritize to restore a productive climate?
options: Quietly excuse the students who complain the most to keep the peace
Drop the tardy rule to end the arguments
Add new, harsher penalties for tardiness to reassert authority
Apply the rule and its consequences consistently and predictably to every student
questions.rationale: Fair, consistent enforcement is foundational to effective management. Predictable application of rules to all students rebuilds trust and ends arguments rooted in perceived inequity.

questions.stem: A middle school teacher wants students to take ownership of classroom norms while keeping expectations clear and age-appropriate. Which approach best balances ownership with structure?
options: Post a long, detailed list covering every possible infraction
Guide a discussion in which students help generate ideas, then refine them into a few clear, positively stated expectations
Distribute a finished rules contract for students to sign without discussion
Let students vote on whether the class should have any rules at all
questions.rationale: Co-creating norms builds buy-in, but the teacher remains responsible for clarity and appropriateness. Guiding students to generate ideas and then refining them into a few positive expectations balances ownership with structure.

questions.stem: Midway through the year, a teacher's previously smooth materials-distribution routine has decayed: handing out papers now takes several minutes and students chat instead of preparing. Which response is most effective and LEAST disruptive to the learning climate?
options: Single out and publicly correct the slowest students each day
Stop distributing papers and project all materials instead
Briefly reteach and rehearse the existing routine, then reinforce it consistently
Replace the routine with a new, more elaborate distribution system
questions.rationale: When an established routine deteriorates, the most effective and least disruptive fix is to reteach, rehearse, and consistently reinforce the existing expectation rather than introduce complexity or harm the climate.

questions.stem: A student with a behavior intervention plan (BIP) that specifies a nonverbal cue and access to a calm-down area begins showing early signs of frustration during a lesson. Which is the teacher's best FIRST step?
options: Wait until the student fully escalates before intervening
Pause the lesson to discuss the student's behavior with the whole class
Use the agreed-upon nonverbal cue and offer access to the calm-down area
Send the student to the office to avoid disrupting others
questions.rationale: When a student has a BIP, the teacher must implement its agreed supports. Using the nonverbal cue and offering the calm-down area follows the plan and de-escalates the situation proactively while respecting the student's individualized needs.

questions.stem: A teacher wants emergency procedures such as fire drills and lockdowns to be carried out calmly and correctly by every student. Which practice best ensures this?
options: Regularly teach, practice, and review the procedures so students respond automatically under stress
Post an evacuation map and rely on students to read it during an actual emergency
Assume older students already know the procedures from previous years
Describe the procedures once at the start of the year and trust students to remember
questions.rationale: Safety procedures must be rehearsed so students act automatically and calmly under stress, when there is no time for deliberation. Regular practice and review build that automaticity.

questions.stem: After a substitute reports that a class was chaotic and unproductive, the regular teacher wants to prevent a repeat. Which proactive step is most effective?
options: Assign silent worksheet packets for all substitute days
Establish and routinely practice clear routines and leave detailed plans so the class runs smoothly with any adult
Cancel lessons whenever a substitute is needed
Warn students they will lose privileges if they misbehave for any substitute
questions.rationale: Well-established, practiced routines plus clear plans let the classroom function regardless of who leads it. Procedures students can carry out independently support continuity and minimize disruption with a substitute.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a lesson that moves from whole-group instruction to four rotating stations and back. To minimize confusion and lost time during these shifts, which preparation is most important?
options: Allow students to move to the next station whenever they individually feel ready
Combine the stations into one long activity to avoid transitions altogether
Decide on the transitions in the moment based on how the lesson feels
Plan and communicate clear transition signals, time limits, and student roles before the lesson begins
questions.rationale: Smooth transitions require advance planning. Clear signals, time limits, and defined roles communicated beforehand reduce confusion and protect instructional time when shifting between activity structures.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a whole-class point system in which the entire class loses points when any individual misbehaves. Over time students pressure and blame peers, and the climate has worsened. Which adjustment best supports a positive environment?
options: Raise the number of points the class can lose to increase the stakes
Make the highest-achieving students responsible for monitoring classmates
Remove all systems and rely only on verbal warnings
Shift toward recognizing individual responsibility and positive behavior while rebuilding peer relationships
questions.rationale: Collective punishment that pits students against one another harms climate and relationships. Emphasizing individual accountability and positive recognition supports a respectful environment and reduces peer blaming.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to build a classroom climate where students feel safe sharing ideas that might be wrong. Which teacher behavior most directly fosters this climate?
options: Respond to incorrect answers respectfully and use them as opportunities to think and learn
Praise only final correct answers and move past student reasoning
Call only on students who reliably give correct answers
Avoid whole-class questioning so no student is ever embarrassed
questions.rationale: A psychologically safe climate is built when teachers treat errors as valuable parts of learning. Responding to wrong answers with respect and using them to extend thinking encourages participation and academic risk-taking.

questions.stem: During independent work, two students near the window begin a side conversation that is growing louder while the teacher confers with another student. Which response should the teacher use FIRST to address it with the least disruption?
options: Immediately reassign the two students to separate seats
Announce to the whole class that talking is not allowed during independent work
Use proximity and brief eye contact or a pause to redirect them nonverbally
Stop the conference and walk over to reprimand the two students
questions.rationale: Low-intervention, nonverbal redirection preserves instructional flow and avoids escalating a minor issue. Using proximity, eye contact, or a brief pause addresses the behavior before stronger measures are needed.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to increase intrinsic motivation for an upcoming inquiry project. Which approach is most aligned with that goal?
options: Allow students to investigate questions connected to their own interests and real-world curiosities
Award extra credit for the most decorative project display
Warn students that uninspired work will lower their grade
Promise a homework pass to whichever group finishes first
questions.rationale: Intrinsic motivation is fostered by autonomy and relevance. Letting students pursue interest-based, real-world questions taps their natural curiosity rather than relying on rewards or threats.

questions.stem: Partway through a lesson, a teacher notices many students appear disengaged and are no longer responding to questions. Which action should the teacher take FIRST to re-engage them?
options: Introduce an interactive strategy such as think-pair-share or a quick hands-on task
Announce that the disengaged students will be quizzed tomorrow
Continue the lecture as planned and address engagement at the end
Lower the difficulty of the content for the rest of the period
questions.rationale: Active engagement strategies increase participation and attention. Introducing an interactive task such as think-pair-share gives every student a way to process and respond, re-engaging the class in meaningful learning.

questions.stem: A teacher wants feedback to help students see that effort and improved strategies, not fixed ability, lead to success. Which feedback practice best promotes this growth-oriented mindset?
options: Tell struggling students the subject simply is not their strength
Tell correct responders 'You're so smart' to reinforce confidence
Post each student's score relative to the class average
Give specific feedback on the strategies and effort used and on how to improve next time
questions.rationale: Process-oriented feedback that highlights effort, strategies, and concrete next steps fosters a growth mindset and persistence, helping students attribute success to controllable factors.

questions.stem: A teacher wants every student cognitively engaged during whole-class discussion rather than only the few who always volunteer. Which technique best promotes broad participation and accountability?
options: Use think-pair-share with equitable cold-calling and adequate wait time
Pose questions and answer them yourself to keep the pace moving
Call on the same eager volunteers who raise their hands
Let students opt out of responding whenever they prefer
questions.rationale: Total-participation techniques like think-pair-share combined with equitable questioning and wait time require every student to think and respond, holding the whole class accountable rather than a few volunteers.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a challenging project, but lower-achieving students quickly give up, calling it 'too hard.' Which instructional adjustment best sustains their motivation while preserving rigor?
options: Allow lower-achieving students to skip the project entirely
Break the task into scaffolded steps with attainable short-term goals and timely feedback
Pair lower-achieving students with peers who will do the work for them
Remove the challenging components so the project is easier for everyone
questions.rationale: Motivation is sustained when tasks are appropriately challenging yet attainable. Scaffolding the project into manageable steps with short-term goals and feedback maintains rigor while giving students experiences of success that build self-efficacy.

questions.stem: A teacher relies heavily on points and prizes to motivate work, but students now do only the minimum needed to earn rewards and show little interest in the content. Which change should the teacher prioritize to build lasting motivation?
options: Stop giving any feedback so students focus only on the reward
Increase the value and frequency of the prizes to renew interest
Make rewards available only to the top three students each week
Gradually emphasize relevance, autonomy, mastery, and meaningful feedback while phasing down reliance on rewards
questions.rationale: Over-reliance on extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation and produce minimal effort. Shifting toward relevance, autonomy, mastery, and meaningful feedback rebuilds genuine interest while reducing dependence on prizes.

questions.stem: A teacher is planning a new unit and wants it to feel relevant so students are motivated to engage. Which planning step best supports this aim?
options: Assign the most difficult readings first to set high expectations
Open the unit with a list of vocabulary terms to memorize
Begin by telling students the unit is required by state standards
Connect the unit's content to students' lives, real-world problems, and prior knowledge
questions.rationale: Relevance drives engagement and motivation. Connecting content to students' experiences, real-world applications, and prior knowledge gives them a reason to care about the material and supports meaningful learning.

questions.stem: A normally engaged student has grown withdrawn and unmotivated over the past two weeks, and the quality of her work has declined sharply. Which action should the teacher take FIRST?
options: Speak privately with the student to express concern and seek to understand what may be affecting her
Assume it is a temporary phase and take no action
Lower the student's grade to prompt renewed effort
Publicly point out the decline to encourage her to improve
questions.rationale: A sudden change in engagement may signal an underlying personal, academic, or emotional issue. The appropriate first step is a private, supportive conversation to understand the cause before deciding how to respond, demonstrating care and respect.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to develop ownership of their learning and stay motivated across a multi-week assignment. Which strategy most directly supports student self-direction?
options: Grade only the final product with no interim feedback
Complete the difficult portions for students to prevent frustration
Provide no checkpoints so students manage entirely on their own
Help students set personal goals, monitor their progress, and reflect on their learning
questions.rationale: Goal setting, progress monitoring, and reflection develop self-regulation and ownership, sustaining motivation across long-term work by giving students agency and a clear sense of progress.

questions.stem: Reviewing a lesson that fell flat, a teacher notes students were compliant but passive, and few seemed genuinely engaged. When redesigning the lesson, which change is most likely to increase authentic engagement?
options: Add more teacher talk to clarify every detail of the content
Lengthen the silent reading portion of the lesson
Incorporate active learning such as problem-solving, discussion, and hands-on application
Replace the activities with a longer multiple-choice worksheet
questions.rationale: Authentic engagement comes from active, meaningful involvement. Incorporating problem-solving, discussion, and hands-on application moves students from passive compliance to active construction of understanding.

questions.stem: A teacher wants feedback practices to enhance motivation and effort rather than discourage students. Which feedback practice is LEAST likely to support student motivation?
options: Providing specific, actionable feedback focused on the task and next steps
Acknowledging effort and improvement alongside areas to develop
Publicly comparing each student's score against classmates' ranked scores
Giving timely feedback that students can use to revise their work
questions.rationale: This is a LEAST question. Public comparative ranking emphasizes performance relative to peers, which can damage motivation, raise anxiety, and discourage lower-ranked students. The other practices support a mastery orientation and sustained effort.

questions.stem: A teacher introduces a new technology tool to boost engagement, but students quickly become distracted by unrelated features and learning declines. Which action should the teacher take NEXT to ensure the tool genuinely supports learning?
options: Set a clear purpose and expectations for the tool, structure tasks around learning goals, and monitor use
Allow unrestricted exploration so students stay interested
Abandon technology use and return to lecture only
Use the tool only as a reward at the end of class
questions.rationale: Technology supports engagement only when it is purposefully tied to learning goals with clear expectations and monitoring. Structuring its use around objectives keeps students focused on learning rather than distracting features.

questions.stem: A kindergarten teacher is explaining a hands-on counting activity to students seated on the rug. To communicate the steps most clearly to five-year-olds, which approach should the teacher use?
options: Demonstrating each step with the actual materials while narrating in short, simple phrases
Reading a written list of steps aloud at a normal adult pace
Telling students to figure out the steps on their own after a brief overview
Describing the whole activity in one long sentence before handing out materials
questions.rationale: Young children comprehend best when verbal instruction is paired with a concrete demonstration and broken into short, manageable phrases. Modeling each step with the materials makes the procedure observable and reduces working-memory demands.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to make sure a student who is hard of hearing can fully access whole-class discussions. Which communication practice is most supportive?
options: Seating the student at the back so they can observe the whole room
Asking the student to read a transcript of the discussion afterward instead of participating live
Speaking at a louder volume than usual throughout the lesson
Facing the class while speaking, repeating peers' comments clearly, and using captioned media
questions.rationale: Accessibility for a student who is hard of hearing is supported by clear visual access to the speaker's face, repetition of classmate comments, and captioned media—practices that make spoken communication available in real time.

questions.stem: A teacher posts the day's learning objective on the board as 'SWBAT analyze theme.' Several students do not understand what they are expected to do. Which revision communicates the objective most clearly to students?
options: 'Students will be able to analyze theme using higher-order thinking skills.'
'Today we will cover theme.'
'Objective: theme analysis (see standard).'
'I can explain how a story's events reveal its message and support my explanation with examples from the text.'
questions.rationale: A student-friendly objective is stated in concrete, accessible language that tells students exactly what they will be able to do and how. Rewriting in 'I can' language with a clear product communicates expectations effectively.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to understand that tone of voice can change how a spoken message is received. Which brief activity best lets students apply this idea?
options: Having students say the phrase 'Thanks a lot' three ways—sincerely, sarcastically, and flatly—then discussing the differences
Lecturing students about the importance of tone
Listing on the board several words that describe tone
Assigning students to define 'tone' in their notebooks
questions.rationale: Application is achieved when students manipulate tone themselves and analyze how meaning shifts. Saying the same phrase with different tones and discussing the effects engages students in using and reflecting on a communication variable.

questions.stem: A teacher transitions students between centers using a single verbal cue, but transitions are noisy and slow. Which communication-focused adjustment would most improve transitions?
options: Adding more centers so students have more to do
Establishing and rehearsing a clear signal paired with a posted, predictable transition routine
Allowing students to transition whenever they individually finish a task
Giving the verbal cue more forcefully and waiting for silence each time
questions.rationale: Smooth transitions depend on clear, consistent signals and routines that students understand and have practiced. Establishing and rehearsing a predictable cue and routine communicates expectations and reduces noise and lost time.

questions.stem: A teacher is preparing to explain a complex new concept—photosynthesis—to students who have no prior exposure. Which communication strategy will most effectively build understanding?
options: Beginning with the formal chemical equation and defining each variable
Listing all vocabulary terms students must memorize before the lesson
Reading the textbook definition aloud twice
Connecting the new concept to a familiar experience, such as how plants 'eat' sunlight, before introducing technical terms
questions.rationale: Effective communication of new concepts builds from the known to the unknown. Anchoring photosynthesis in a familiar analogy before introducing technical vocabulary creates a conceptual foundation that supports comprehension.

questions.stem: A teacher is composing a weekly newsletter to families about an upcoming project. To communicate effectively with a diverse family community, which practice is most appropriate?
options: Addressing the newsletter only to families who have volunteered before
Sending a lengthy message covering every administrative detail of the term
Using detailed educational terminology to convey professionalism
Writing in clear, jargon-free language, providing translated versions, and stating one specific way families can help
questions.rationale: Effective family communication is clear, accessible, and actionable. Avoiding jargon, providing translations, and offering a concrete way to help makes the message understandable and inviting for a diverse community.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a normally talkative student has become withdrawn and is avoiding eye contact during one-on-one check-ins. Which response best reflects sensitive, responsive communication?
options: Asking the student in front of peers why they have been so quiet lately
Ignoring the change since it is not affecting academic work
Requiring the student to write a paragraph explaining their behavior
Privately expressing care, giving the student space to share, and listening without pressing for an explanation
questions.rationale: Responsive communication attends to nonverbal signals and prioritizes the student's emotional safety. Expressing care privately and listening without pressure invites the student to share when ready and preserves trust.

questions.stem: A teacher gives an explanation, then asks, 'Does everyone understand?' and most students nod. Many later show they did not understand. Which communication strategy would more reliably reveal comprehension?
options: Asking the question again more slowly
Telling students to ask questions only if they are confused
Asking students to give a thumbs-up if they understood
Asking students to summarize the idea in their own words or solve a quick example
questions.rationale: A global 'Does everyone understand?' yields unreliable agreement. Asking students to restate the idea or apply it to a quick example produces evidence of actual comprehension, allowing the teacher to adjust communication.

questions.stem: During independent work time, a teacher wants to communicate availability and expectations without interrupting focused students. Which nonverbal communication system best supports this?
options: Telling students at the start that they may interrupt the teacher anytime
Calling out across the room to ask who needs help
A posted visual signal system (e.g., colored cups or a help board) that students use to indicate they need assistance
Standing at the front and waiting for hands to be raised
questions.rationale: A nonverbal signal system lets students communicate their needs and lets the teacher respond without disrupting the working environment. It clearly conveys expectations and availability while preserving focus.

questions.stem: A teacher is meeting with a parent who is upset about a grade. The parent's tone is confrontational. Which communication approach best maintains a productive, professional exchange?
options: Matching the parent's intensity to show conviction about the grade
Ending the meeting until the parent is calmer
Defending the grade immediately before the parent finishes speaking
Listening to fully understand the concern, acknowledging the parent's feelings, and then explaining the grading evidence calmly
questions.rationale: Professional communication in a tense conference begins with active listening and acknowledgment, which de-escalates emotion, before presenting objective evidence. This preserves the relationship and keeps the focus on the student.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews video of her instruction and notices she gives praise constantly ('Great!' 'Perfect!') even for minimal effort, and students seem to tune it out. Which adjustment makes her communicative feedback more effective?
options: Replacing all praise with neutral acknowledgments like 'okay'
Increasing the frequency of general praise so students hear more encouragement
Giving specific, contingent feedback that names what the student did well and why it mattered
Saving all feedback for the end of the lesson to avoid interrupting
questions.rationale: Generic, indiscriminate praise loses meaning and informational value. Specific, contingent feedback that identifies the particular behavior and its significance is more credible and helps students understand what to repeat.

questions.stem: A teacher wants her classroom communication to consistently convey high expectations to a student who has historically been low-performing, without lowering rigor or offering empty reassurance. Which pattern of teacher communication best accomplishes this?
options: Praising the student's effort regardless of the quality of the work
Allowing the student more time on every task without any feedback on quality
Holding the student to grade-level tasks while providing scaffolds and explicit, actionable feedback toward mastery
Simplifying the student's tasks so they can experience easy success
questions.rationale: High expectations are communicated by maintaining rigorous goals while providing the scaffolds and specific feedback the student needs to reach them. This conveys belief in the student's capacity to meet grade-level standards.

questions.stem: A teacher analyzes recordings of her lessons and finds that when she asks for clarification of a confusing student comment, she often rephrases it for the student rather than letting the student restate it. What is the most significant communication drawback of this habit?
options: It makes the lesson run too slowly
It signals to students that their comments are unimportant overall
It encourages students to use more academic vocabulary
It can substitute the teacher's interpretation for the student's intended meaning, reducing accurate two-way communication
questions.rationale: When a teacher rephrases rather than letting the student clarify, she may impose her own interpretation and lose the student's actual meaning. Genuine two-way communication requires letting the speaker confirm or correct their intent.

questions.stem: A teacher wants a quick, low-stakes way to prompt students to think before a lesson begins. Which bell-ringer prompt best activates higher-order thinking?
options: 'Write the date and your name at the top of your paper.'
'If you could change one rule at our school, which would it be and why?'
'List three facts you remember from yesterday.'
'Copy today's vocabulary words from the board.'
questions.rationale: A prompt that asks students to make and justify a choice engages evaluation and reasoning. Asking which rule to change and why requires forming and defending a position, unlike copying or simple recall tasks.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to consider a question from multiple viewpoints during a discussion about a community decision. Which questioning move best supports this?
options: Asking students to recall the facts of the decision
Asking students to state only their own opinion on the decision
Asking students whether the decision is right or wrong
Asking students to consider how different stakeholders, such as residents and business owners, might view the decision
questions.rationale: Considering multiple viewpoints is prompted by asking students to take the perspectives of different stakeholders. This expands thinking beyond a single position and supports analytical reasoning about competing interests.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students in pairs to check whether their reasoning makes sense before sharing with the class. Which prompt best encourages this self-checking?
options: 'Compare your final answers and erase any that don't match.'
'Explain your reasoning to your partner and ask them to point out any step that is unclear.'
'Whoever finished first should tell the other the answer.'
'Write your answer neatly so the teacher can read it.'
questions.rationale: Asking partners to explain reasoning and identify unclear steps prompts students to examine and verify their own thinking. This self-checking through explanation strengthens reasoning before public sharing.

questions.stem: A teacher poses a question and a student responds, 'I don't know.' Which teacher response best keeps the student engaged in thinking?
options: 'That's okay,' and calling on another student
Giving the student the answer and moving on
'Let's start smaller—what is one thing you do notice about the problem?'
Telling the student to think harder and asking again
questions.rationale: Breaking a question into a smaller, accessible entry point invites a stalled student back into thinking. Asking what they do notice scaffolds participation rather than letting them disengage or handing off the question.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to justify their answers with evidence during a math discussion. Which routine question best builds this habit?
options: 'How do you know that is true?'
'Did you get the same number as everyone else?'
'Is that the answer in the back of the book?'
'Can you write your answer on the board?'
questions.rationale: Routinely asking 'How do you know?' requires students to provide justification and reasoning for their claims, building the habit of supporting answers with evidence rather than asserting them.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to evaluate the strength of arguments in two persuasive essays. Which task best develops this critical-thinking skill?
options: Having students identify each essay's claims and evidence and rate how well the evidence supports each claim
Having students pick the essay with the more interesting topic
Having students count how many paragraphs each essay contains
Having students summarize what each essay is about
questions.rationale: Evaluating argument strength requires analyzing the relationship between claims and supporting evidence and judging its adequacy. Identifying and rating claim-evidence support engages this evaluative critical thinking.

questions.stem: During a guided inquiry, a teacher wants students to form and test predictions. Which sequence of teacher questions best supports scientific reasoning?
options: 'What is the definition of a hypothesis? What is a variable? What is a conclusion?'
'What do you predict will happen? What evidence would confirm or disconfirm your prediction? What did you find?'
'What page is the experiment on? What materials are listed? Who is your partner?'
'What is the right answer? Did you get it? Why not?'
questions.rationale: Scientific reasoning is supported by questions that move from predicting, to specifying confirming or disconfirming evidence, to checking results against the prediction. This sequence engages the logic of inquiry rather than recall or logistics.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use a discussion protocol that ensures students respond directly to one another rather than only to the teacher. Which protocol feature best achieves this?
options: Having the teacher call on students in alphabetical order
Allowing students to read prepared statements one at a time
Requiring each speaker to connect their comment to the previous speaker's idea before adding a new point
Letting the teacher comment after every student response
questions.rationale: Requiring each speaker to link to the prior contribution before adding new ideas structures genuine student-to-student dialogue and accountable listening, rather than a series of teacher-mediated exchanges.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a real-world data set and wants them to draw and defend a conclusion. Which instruction best targets analytical and evaluative thinking?
options: 'Read the data aloud to your partner.'
'Use the data to support a claim about the trend, and explain why your evidence is convincing.'
'Find the largest number in the data set.'
'Copy the data table into your notebook.'
questions.rationale: Drawing and defending a data-based claim requires analyzing the data for trends and evaluating the persuasiveness of one's evidence. This integrates analysis and evaluation, unlike copying or locating single values.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students who finish a task early to extend their thinking rather than simply wait. Which extension prompt best deepens thinking?
options: 'Reread your answer to make sure it is neat.'
'Help a neighbor by giving them the answers.'
'Create a new version of the problem that would be harder, and solve it.'
'Sit quietly until the rest of the class finishes.'
questions.rationale: Asking early finishers to generate and solve a harder version of the problem engages synthesis and deeper application, extending thinking rather than offering busywork or idle time.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that during a science discussion, students accept a peer's claim simply because the peer is confident. To cultivate skepticism grounded in evidence, which teacher move is most effective?
options: Affirming the confident student so the class feels the discussion is positive
Reminding students that confident classmates are usually right
Moving on quickly once a confident answer is offered
Routinely asking the class, 'What evidence would we need to be confident this claim is correct?'
questions.rationale: Cultivating evidence-based skepticism means consistently shifting the basis for belief from a speaker's confidence to the quality of evidence. Asking what evidence would justify confidence redirects evaluation toward reasoning, not authority.

questions.stem: A teacher wants a single open-ended task that integrates problem solving, evidence use, and communication of reasoning. Which task design best accomplishes all three?
options: Having students investigate a genuine school problem, propose a data-supported solution, and present their reasoning to a panel
Having students memorize and recite a problem-solving acronym
Having students watch a video of someone solving a problem and take notes
Having students complete a worksheet of word problems and turn it in
questions.rationale: An authentic investigation that requires proposing a data-supported solution and presenting the reasoning integrates problem solving, evidence use, and communication in a single performance task—engaging all three targeted skills.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews assessment data showing students perform well on questions about facts but poorly on questions requiring them to apply concepts to new situations. Which instructional change most directly addresses this gap?
options: Increasing the number of fact-based quizzes to strengthen the knowledge base
Allowing students to retake fact-based questions until mastered
Embedding regular opportunities for students to apply concepts to varied, novel problems with feedback
Providing a study guide of definitions before each test
questions.rationale: A gap in application is addressed by repeatedly engaging students in applying concepts to new, varied situations with feedback. This builds the flexible understanding that fact-focused practice alone does not produce.

questions.stem: A teacher wants discussion questions that require students to weigh competing values rather than reach a single correct answer. Which question best fits this aim?
options: 'How many parks does the community currently have?'
'Should a community prioritize building a new park or expanding the public library, and what trade-offs justify your choice?'
'What year was the public library founded?'
'Is a library a building where books are kept?'
questions.rationale: Weighing competing values requires an open question that pits legitimate priorities against each other and demands justification of trade-offs. The park-versus-library question has no single correct answer and engages evaluative reasoning.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to evaluate the reasoning in their own first drafts of an argumentative essay. Which self-assessment prompt most directly develops critical self-evaluation?
options: 'Check that you have an introduction, body, and conclusion.'
'Identify your weakest piece of evidence and explain how you could strengthen or replace it.'
'Make sure you used at least three vocabulary words.'
'Count the number of sentences in each paragraph.'
questions.rationale: Critical self-evaluation requires students to judge the quality of their own reasoning and plan improvements. Identifying the weakest evidence and proposing how to strengthen it engages evaluative metacognition about argument quality.

questions.stem: A teacher facilitates a discussion where students quickly reach consensus and stop exploring the topic. To deepen critical thinking, which move is most effective?
options: Posing a 'devil's advocate' question that challenges the consensus and asks students to defend or revise their view
Summarizing the agreement and assigning related homework
Affirming the consensus and moving to the next topic to save time
Asking students to vote again to confirm agreement
questions.rationale: Premature consensus can shut down thinking. Introducing a counter-position prompts students to test their reasoning against a challenge, deepening analysis and guarding against superficial agreement.

questions.stem: A teacher wants struggling students to access a complex problem without lowering the cognitive demand for the whole class. Which approach best balances support and challenge?
options: Solving the first part of the problem for the whole class
Replacing the complex problem with several simpler ones
Pairing each struggling student with a peer who will explain the solution
Offering optional hint cards that students may use after attempting the problem on their own
questions.rationale: Optional, self-accessed hint cards used after an initial attempt preserve productive struggle and high cognitive demand while giving support to those who need it. Students still do the core thinking themselves.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to model her own thinking process so students learn how an expert approaches an unfamiliar problem. Which instructional strategy best accomplishes this?
options: Telling students the steps to memorize for this type of problem
Assigning the problem and circulating without demonstrating her process
Thinking aloud while solving a problem, including false starts and how she decides what to try next
Showing only the clean, correct final solution on the board
questions.rationale: A think-aloud that reveals the reasoning behind each decision—including false starts—makes invisible expert thinking visible, helping students learn how to approach unfamiliar problems strategically.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to check, in the middle of a lesson, whether students can reason through a concept—not just recall it—and adjust instruction accordingly. Which formative check best reveals reasoning?
options: Collecting a show of hands on who finished the practice set
Asking students to write a brief explanation of how they would solve a new example and why their approach works
Asking students to repeat the definition of the concept
Having students give a thumbs-up if they feel confident
questions.rationale: A short written explanation of how and why a student would approach a new example exposes their reasoning, giving the teacher actionable evidence to adjust instruction—unlike confidence self-reports or recall checks.

questions.stem: A fourth-grade teacher wants students to collaboratively build a single shared document during a research project so that all group members can edit simultaneously from their own devices. Which technology tool is BEST suited to this goal?
options: A cloud-based word-processing application with real-time co-editing and comment features
A set of individual offline word-processor files that students email to one another after each work session
A printable graphic organizer that the teacher scans and posts to the class website
A slide-presentation template that each student completes alone and submits separately
questions.rationale: Real-time collaborative goals are best met by a cloud-based application that allows simultaneous co-editing and commenting, directly supporting the described workflow.

questions.stem: Before assigning students to research a science topic using websites, a sixth-grade teacher wants to help them judge whether online sources are trustworthy. Which activity BEST develops this digital-literacy skill?
options: Allowing students to copy information from the first three links they find
Having students memorize a list of approved websites for the unit
Guiding students to evaluate each site's author, sponsoring organization, and publication date using a checklist
Telling students that any site appearing on the first page of search results is reliable
questions.rationale: Teaching students to examine authorship, sponsorship, and currency builds transferable source-evaluation skills central to digital literacy.

questions.stem: A high-school teacher plans to flip a unit so that students watch short concept videos at home and use class time for problem-solving. Several students lack reliable internet access at home. Which action BEST allows the teacher to maintain the flipped design while addressing equity?
options: Provide downloadable videos on loaned devices and offer scheduled access in the library before school
Assume the students will find access on their own and proceed without changes
Drop the flipped model entirely and return to whole-class lecture for every student
Require the students without internet to complete twice the homework to make up the gap
questions.rationale: Offering offline-capable devices and scheduled on-campus access preserves the instructional model while ensuring all students can participate equitably.

questions.stem: A teacher wants technology to deepen learning rather than simply digitize a worksheet. Which classroom use of tablets represents the HIGHEST level of meaningful integration?
options: Students design and publish an interactive multimedia model that explains a concept to an authentic audience
Students read the textbook chapter as a scanned PDF on the tablet
Students answer the same fill-in-the-blank questions on screen instead of paper
Students watch the teacher project notes from the tablet to the front screen
questions.rationale: Creating and publishing an original multimedia artifact for an authentic audience represents transformative use that would be impossible without the technology, the deepest level of integration.

questions.stem: During a one-to-one device lesson, a teacher observes several students browsing unrelated sites. Which proactive strategy would BEST keep students focused on learning tasks while using the devices?
options: Establish clear, posted expectations for on-task use and circulate to monitor screens during work time
Allow free browsing because students will eventually self-regulate
Confiscate all devices for the rest of the semester
Tell students once at the beginning of the year that off-task browsing is not allowed and never revisit it
questions.rationale: Setting explicit, visible expectations combined with active monitoring proactively supports responsible, on-task technology use.

questions.stem: A teacher of English learners wants to use technology to support both content learning and language development. Which tool use BEST serves these dual goals?
options: A timed multiple-choice quiz app delivered only in academic English with no supports
A text-only discussion board with strict spelling penalties
A long unsubtitled lecture video in English that students watch once
A multimedia tool that pairs visuals and audio with text and lets students record and replay their own spoken explanations
questions.rationale: Pairing visuals, audio, and student-recorded speech provides comprehensible input and authentic output practice, supporting content and language simultaneously.

questions.stem: A teacher integrates a new adaptive math program that adjusts problem difficulty based on each student's responses. After two weeks, the teacher wants to ensure the technology is genuinely improving learning rather than just keeping students busy. Which action provides the MOST valid evidence?
options: Record how many badges or points the program awarded to each student
Count the total number of minutes students spend logged into the program
Compare student performance on independent teacher-designed tasks before and after using the program
Ask students whether they enjoyed using the program
questions.rationale: Comparing performance on independent measures the program did not generate isolates real learning gains, providing the most valid evidence of impact.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a project in which students create digital media that remixes images, music, and text from online sources. To model responsible and ethical technology use, which guideline should the teacher emphasize MOST directly?
options: Students may use any content they find because school projects are automatically exempt from all rules
Students should cite sources and use only materials they have permission to use, such as public-domain or appropriately licensed media
Students should remove all visible credits so the work looks more professional
Students may copy whole works as long as the project is never shown outside the classroom
questions.rationale: Teaching students to attribute sources and use properly licensed or public-domain materials directly models ethical, lawful technology use regarding intellectual property.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to give and receive feedback on writing drafts using technology. Which tool feature is MOST directly useful for this purpose?
options: A commenting and suggestion feature that lets peers leave targeted notes on specific passages
A read-aloud feature that plays the entire essay at high speed
An automatic spell-checker that fixes errors without student input
A font-selection menu for changing the document's appearance
questions.rationale: A commenting and suggestion feature enables targeted, location-specific peer feedback, directly supporting the revision goal.

questions.stem: A campus is adopting a new learning-management system, and a teacher wants to use it to increase family engagement with student learning. Which use of the platform BEST advances that specific goal?
options: Sending a single welcome message at the start of the year and nothing afterward
Posting only the final grades at the end of each grading period
Using the platform solely to store the teacher's personal lesson plans
Sharing regular updates, assignment expectations, and examples of student work along with a channel for two-way communication with families
questions.rationale: Ongoing transparent updates plus a two-way communication channel actively involve families in supporting learning, fulfilling the engagement goal.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use a classroom response system, such as clickers or a polling app, during a lecture-style lesson. Which instructional purpose does this tool serve MOST effectively?
options: Eliminating the need for the teacher to plan questions in advance
Permanently replacing all discussion and questioning in the classroom
Assigning long-term research grades automatically without teacher review
