options: Offering a pizza party to the class that reads the most pages each month
Giving stickers each time a student finishes a book of any kind
Allowing students to choose books that connect to their own interests and discussing what they found meaningful
Posting a public leaderboard ranking students by the number of books read
questions.rationale: Intrinsic motivation grows when learning connects to students' interests and personal meaning and when students have autonomy; choice and meaningful reflection support these conditions far better than external rewards.

questions.stem: A student frequently says, 'I'm just not good at math,' and gives up quickly on challenging problems. To promote a growth mindset, the teacher's feedback should MOST emphasize:
options: Telling the student he is smart whenever he answers a question correctly
Reassuring the student that the work is easy and that he will get it soon
Praising the student's effort, strategies, and persistence when he works through a difficult problem
Comparing the student's progress favorably to that of his classmates
questions.rationale: Growth-mindset feedback focuses on effort, strategy use, and persistence rather than on fixed ability, helping students attribute success to controllable factors and persevere through challenge.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a unit and wants to maximize student engagement and motivation throughout. According to research on motivation, which combination of features is MOST likely to sustain student engagement?
options: Tasks that emphasize competition for the highest scores to spur students to try harder
Tasks that are easy enough to guarantee success and completed individually to avoid distraction
Tasks that are highly structured, identical for all students, and graded primarily on accuracy
Tasks that are appropriately challenging, personally relevant, and offer students meaningful choices
questions.rationale: Motivation and engagement are sustained when tasks are at an optimal level of challenge, connected to students' lives and interests, and provide autonomy through meaningful choice, which together support competence, relevance, and self-determination.

questions.stem: A teacher introduces a new unit on statistics by asking students how data is used to make decisions in sports, social media, and shopping. This opening strategy is designed primarily to increase motivation by:
options: Differentiating the lesson for students at varied skill levels
Connecting the content to students' interests and demonstrating its relevance to their lives
Establishing clear behavioral expectations for the unit
Pre-assessing students' prior knowledge of statistics
questions.rationale: Linking new content to students' real-world interests establishes relevance, which is a powerful motivator because students are more engaged when they see how learning applies to their own lives.

questions.stem: A teacher tells students at the start of a lesson, 'I know this is challenging material, but I am confident that with effort each of you can master it.' This statement is MOST likely to enhance motivation by:
options: Communicating high expectations along with the teacher's belief that students can succeed
Encouraging students to compete to be the first to master the material
Lowering the difficulty of the lesson so students feel less anxious
Reminding students of the consequences of not completing the work
questions.rationale: Communicating high expectations paired with genuine confidence in students' ability to meet them strengthens students' self-efficacy and motivation to persist with challenging work.

questions.stem: A capable student consistently turns in minimal work and appears bored during lessons. The teacher suspects the assignments are not challenging enough. To re-engage this student, the teacher should FIRST:
options: Offer more complex, open-ended tasks that extend the content and allow the student to pursue an area of interest
Assign additional problems of the same type so the student stays busy
Reduce the student's workload as a reward for finishing quickly
Move the student to a seat away from peers to limit distraction
questions.rationale: An able student who is bored is likely under-challenged; providing more complex, open-ended, interest-driven work restores the optimal level of challenge and relevance that drives engagement.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to design feedback practices that promote student motivation and self-regulation rather than dependence on the teacher. Which feedback practice BEST supports this goal?
options: Marking each error and writing the correct answer so students can study the corrections
Giving a numerical score on every assignment so students can track their averages
Providing specific, descriptive feedback that helps students identify what to improve and guides them to revise their own work
Praising completed work generously to keep students feeling positive about the class
questions.rationale: Specific, descriptive feedback that guides students to evaluate and revise their own work builds self-regulation and motivation by helping them take ownership of improvement rather than depending on the teacher to supply answers.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a group of students disengages whenever activities are entirely teacher-directed. To increase these students' engagement and sense of ownership, the teacher should:
options: Increase the pace of teacher-led instruction so there is less time for students to disengage
Shorten lessons so disengagement has fewer opportunities to occur
Incorporate student choice, collaborative problem solving, and opportunities for student-led inquiry
Call on the disengaged students more frequently to keep them accountable
questions.rationale: Providing autonomy through choice, collaboration, and student-led inquiry increases ownership and engagement, addressing the disengagement that arises when learning is exclusively teacher-directed.

questions.stem: At the close of a lesson, a teacher asks students to write one thing they learned and one goal for tomorrow. This practice supports motivation primarily by:
options: Encouraging students to reflect on their learning and set personal goals, fostering self-direction
Ensuring students have completed all the day's assigned work
Keeping students quietly occupied until the bell rings
Providing the teacher with data to assign grades
questions.rationale: Reflection and goal setting promote self-directed learning and ownership, which strengthen motivation by helping students monitor their own progress and take responsibility for their growth.

questions.stem: Several students who are learning English hesitate to participate in class discussions, appearing anxious about making mistakes. To motivate their participation, the teacher's BEST approach is to:
options: Create a supportive, low-risk climate with structured supports such as think-pair-share, sentence frames, and wait time
Require each student to speak a set number of times per discussion to build confidence
Wait until these students volunteer on their own so they are not pressured
Excuse these students from discussions until their English proficiency improves
questions.rationale: A safe, supportive classroom climate combined with scaffolds such as think-pair-share, sentence frames, and adequate wait time lowers the risk of participating and gives English learners the structure and confidence to engage.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a rubric and examples of strong work before they begin a project, and encourages them to assess their own drafts against the rubric. This practice is MOST likely to enhance motivation because it:
options: Guarantees that all students will earn high scores on the project
Reduces the amount of feedback the teacher must provide later
Clarifies expectations and gives students a sense of control over reaching a clear, attainable standard
Ensures students complete the project more quickly
questions.rationale: Clear expectations and self-assessment against a known standard increase students' sense of competence and control over their success, which enhances motivation by making the goal attainable and within their influence.

questions.stem: During a fourth-grade science lesson, Mr. Alvarez notices several students looking confused after his explanation of the water cycle. Which teacher action best demonstrates effective communication by monitoring student understanding?
options: Moving on to the next topic and revisiting the water cycle on the unit test
Telling students to reread the textbook section silently at their desks
Asking students to paraphrase the process in their own words and using their responses to clarify confusion
Repeating the same explanation more slowly and at a louder volume
questions.rationale: Effective communicators continually check for understanding and adjust based on feedback. Asking students to paraphrase reveals their level of comprehension and gives the teacher specific information to target the clarification.

questions.stem: Ms. Chen wants her second graders to think more deeply during a read-aloud rather than simply recalling plot events. Which question is most likely to promote higher-order thinking?
options: What was the name of the main character's dog?
What happened first in the story?
Why do you think the character changed her decision near the end?
Where did the story take place?
questions.rationale: Higher-order questions ask students to analyze, infer, or evaluate rather than recall facts. Asking why a character changed requires students to interpret motivation and draw inferences.

questions.stem: Mr. Davis poses a question to his seventh-grade class and immediately calls on the first student to raise a hand. Which adjustment would most improve his questioning technique?
options: Asking students to call out answers without raising hands
Answering the question himself if no one responds within two seconds
Calling only on students who consistently know the answers
Increasing wait time after asking the question before calling on anyone
questions.rationale: Adequate wait time gives all students an opportunity to process the question and formulate a response, increasing participation and the quality of answers.

questions.stem: A high school history teacher wants students to engage in a productive class discussion about competing interpretations of a historical event. Which preparation step best supports a meaningful discussion?
options: Assigning the discussion topic but withholding any background materials
Telling students the correct interpretation in advance to save time
Having students memorize key dates the night before
Providing students with primary source excerpts to read and annotate beforehand
questions.rationale: Productive discussions require that students come prepared with substantive content to draw upon. Reading and annotating primary sources gives students evidence and ideas to contribute.

questions.stem: During a small-group discussion, Mr. Lee observes that one student dominates while others remain silent. Which teacher move best promotes equitable participation?
options: Ending group work and returning to whole-class lecture
Grading only the most talkative student's contributions
Allowing the dominant student to continue since the group stays on task
Introducing a structured protocol such as assigning each member a specific role
questions.rationale: Structured protocols and assigned roles distribute responsibility and ensure that all members contribute, fostering equitable participation in discussions.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to apply a newly learned mathematical concept to an unfamiliar real-world situation. Which task best promotes this kind of problem solving?
options: Watching a video of the teacher solving a sample problem
Presenting a novel scenario where students must decide which procedure to use and justify their choice
A worksheet of 20 identical practice equations
A quiz asking students to define key vocabulary terms
questions.rationale: Application-level problem solving requires students to transfer learning to new contexts and make decisions about appropriate strategies, rather than repeating rote procedures.

questions.stem: Ms. Rivera is leading a discussion when a student gives a partially correct answer. Rather than telling the student the answer is wrong, she says, 'That's part of it; what else might be happening here?' This response best illustrates which communication principle?
options: Avoiding feedback to keep the discussion moving quickly
Using closed questions to confirm a single correct response
Redirecting the question to a more capable student
Providing feedback that affirms partial understanding while prompting further thinking
questions.rationale: Effective teacher communication acknowledges what is correct in a student response and uses probing follow-ups to extend thinking rather than shutting it down with a flat correction.

questions.stem: A fifth-grade teacher plans a lesson where students compare two ecosystems, identify patterns, and predict the effects of an environmental change. According to a hierarchy of thinking skills, the prediction component primarily engages which level?
options: Applying a memorized formula to calculate population size
Evaluating and synthesizing to forecast outcomes from analyzed patterns
Understanding the definitions of ecosystem terms
Remembering factual details about each ecosystem
questions.rationale: Predicting effects of a change requires students to synthesize analyzed information and make an evidence-based forecast, engaging higher-order evaluative and creative thinking.

questions.stem: Mr. Okafor wants to scaffold a Socratic seminar for students who have never participated in one. Which approach best prepares them to engage in productive academic discourse?
options: Grading students solely on how many times they speak
Letting students discuss freely with no guidelines to encourage natural conversation
Modeling and practicing discussion norms such as building on peers' ideas and citing evidence
Requiring each student to deliver a memorized speech in turn
questions.rationale: Students new to academic discourse benefit from explicit modeling and practice of discussion norms, which give them concrete strategies for building on ideas and supporting claims with evidence.

questions.stem: A teacher consistently uses 'I' statements and a calm tone when addressing off-task behavior, saying, 'I need everyone facing forward so we can begin.' This communication approach is most likely to support which outcome?
options: Decreased teacher authority in the classroom
A respectful classroom climate that reduces confrontation
Increased student defensiveness due to perceived blame
Confusion because the expectation is unclear
questions.rationale: Using 'I' statements and a calm tone communicates expectations clearly without assigning blame, supporting a respectful climate and reducing the likelihood of power struggles.

questions.stem: During a problem-solving lesson, students get stuck on a challenging task. Ms. Thompson resists giving the answer and instead asks, 'What strategies have we used before that might help here?' Her response best promotes which goal?
options: Ensuring all students reach identical answers
Developing students' metacognition and independent problem-solving ability
Quickly resolving the task to maintain lesson pacing
Reducing the cognitive demand of the task
questions.rationale: Prompting students to recall and select their own strategies builds metacognitive awareness and self-regulated problem solving rather than fostering dependence on the teacher.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that her questioning sequence moves only from recall to recall. To deepen thinking, she decides to use a questioning sequence that begins with recall and progressively moves to analysis and evaluation. This deliberate sequencing best reflects which instructional practice?
options: Scaffolding cognitive demand through a planned progression of questions
Avoiding wait time to keep questions flowing
Limiting questions to only the highest-achieving students
Funneling students toward one predetermined answer
questions.rationale: Intentionally sequencing questions from lower to higher cognitive levels scaffolds students' thinking, building from foundational understanding toward complex analysis and evaluation.

questions.stem: A new teacher tends to dominate class talk, speaking about 90 percent of the time. A mentor suggests increasing the ratio of student talk. Which strategy most directly accomplishes this while maintaining rigor?
options: Calling on one student to summarize each lesson at the end
Lecturing more efficiently to cover content faster
Assigning more silent independent reading
Incorporating think-pair-share so students discuss ideas before whole-class sharing
questions.rationale: Think-pair-share structures increase student talk by giving every student a chance to articulate and refine ideas with a partner, raising both participation and the quality of contributions.

questions.stem: After posing a thought-provoking question, a teacher receives a confident answer from a student. She follows up with, 'What evidence supports your thinking?' The primary purpose of this follow-up is to:
options: Move quickly to the next student before discussion stalls
Reduce the difficulty of the original question
Signal to the student that the answer was incorrect
Encourage the student to justify reasoning with supporting evidence
questions.rationale: Asking for evidence prompts students to justify their reasoning, deepening the discussion and reinforcing the expectation that claims be supported.

questions.stem: During a debate activity, a teacher assigns students to argue a position opposite to their personal view. The primary critical-thinking benefit of this approach is that it:
options: Eliminates the need for evidence in the debate
Requires students to consider multiple perspectives and understand opposing arguments
Allows students to avoid forming any opinion of their own
Guarantees that students will change their original beliefs
questions.rationale: Arguing an opposing position requires students to research, understand, and articulate perspectives different from their own, building empathy and the ability to evaluate multiple viewpoints.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to assess whether students can transfer a problem-solving strategy learned in math to a science context. Which task design best measures this transfer?
options: Presenting a science problem that requires the same underlying strategy in a new context
Asking students to solve math problems identical to those practiced in class
Reviewing the strategy together as a whole class
Having students define the strategy in writing
questions.rationale: Transfer is demonstrated when students apply a learned strategy to a genuinely new context. A science problem requiring the same underlying reasoning measures whether students can generalize the strategy.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a lesson around an open-ended driving question: 'How can our school reduce food waste in the cafeteria?' This approach is most likely to promote critical thinking because it:
options: Requires students to investigate, weigh options, and propose evidence-based solutions
Has a single correct answer that students must discover
Focuses primarily on memorizing facts about nutrition
Limits student inquiry to a predetermined procedure
questions.rationale: Open-ended, authentic driving questions require students to gather information, analyze trade-offs, and generate justified solutions, all hallmarks of critical thinking and problem solving.

questions.stem: Mr. Boateng notices that during discussions his students tend to address only him rather than responding to one another. He wants to shift toward genuine student-to-student discourse. Which combination of moves would most effectively accomplish this shift?
options: Standing at the front and repeating each student's comment before responding himself
Asking each student a separate question unrelated to others' contributions
Calling on students in a fixed order and evaluating each answer immediately
Arranging seating in a circle, teaching talk moves like 'I agree/disagree because,' and stepping back to let students respond directly to peers
questions.rationale: Genuine student-to-student discourse develops when the physical setup, explicit conversational tools, and teacher restraint all support peer interaction. Re-voicing every comment and immediate teacher evaluation keep talk routed through the teacher.

questions.stem: A teacher poses a higher-order question, but most students give superficial responses. Rather than supplying the answer, the teacher should first determine whether the issue is that students lack the prerequisite knowledge or that they need prompting to extend thinking. Which initial teacher action best distinguishes between these two causes?
options: Assigning additional homework on the topic
Lowering the difficulty of all future questions permanently
Immediately reteaching the entire unit from the beginning
Asking a targeted follow-up probe and observing whether students can extend with support
questions.rationale: A targeted probe functions as a diagnostic: if students extend their thinking with a prompt, they had the knowledge but needed scaffolding; if they cannot, a knowledge gap is more likely. This informs the appropriate instructional response.

questions.stem: During a problem-based unit, a group of students proposes a solution that is creative but contains a flawed assumption. The teacher's goal is to develop students' self-evaluation skills. Which response best serves this goal?
options: Replacing the group's solution with one from another group
Praising the creativity and accepting the solution without further review
Pointing out the flawed assumption and providing the corrected solution
Asking the group to test their assumption against the data and explain what they find
questions.rationale: Prompting students to test their own assumption against evidence builds self-evaluation and metacognition, allowing them to identify and correct the flaw themselves rather than relying on the teacher.

questions.stem: A teacher is communicating complex feedback on student essays. She wants feedback that both supports continued effort and guides specific improvement. Which feedback approach best balances these aims?
options: Marking every error in red and assigning a numerical grade only
Comparing each student's essay to the highest-scoring essay in the class
Writing 'Good job' with no further comment to maintain motivation
Identifying one or two specific strengths and one prioritized, actionable next step
questions.rationale: Effective feedback communicates specific, actionable guidance while sustaining motivation. Naming strengths and a prioritized next step gives students a clear, manageable focus for improvement without overwhelming them.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to develop the disposition of intellectual humility, recognizing the limits of their own knowledge during inquiry. Which classroom routine most directly cultivates this disposition?
options: Requiring students to defend their first answer regardless of new information
Rewarding only students who answer first and correctly
Regularly asking students to identify what they still wonder about and what evidence might change their thinking
Discouraging students from revising their initial claims
questions.rationale: Intellectual humility is fostered when students routinely acknowledge uncertainty and remain open to revising views in light of evidence. Asking what they still wonder and what would change their thinking builds this disposition.

questions.stem: In a heterogeneous class, a teacher wants a single discussion question that allows all students to enter at their own level while still pushing advanced thinkers. Which question design best achieves this 'low floor, high ceiling' goal?
options: A question with a single numeric answer reached by one method
A question requiring specialized vocabulary that only advanced students know
An open question that invites multiple valid responses and supports increasingly sophisticated justification
A yes/no question with one defensible answer
questions.rationale: A low-floor, high-ceiling question is accessible to all students yet allows for deep, sophisticated responses. Open questions with multiple valid answers and room for richer justification meet both criteria.

questions.stem: A teacher receives a one-line email from a parent expressing frustration that their child 'never gets called on.' The teacher wants to respond in a way that builds partnership and gathers useful information. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Thanking the parent, acknowledging the concern, sharing how participation is structured, and inviting a conversation to learn more
Replying that all students are treated the same and no change is needed
Replying that the perception is inaccurate and listing participation data to prove it
Forwarding the email to an administrator without responding to the parent
questions.rationale: Effective home-school communication acknowledges the parent's concern, provides relevant information, and invites collaboration. This builds partnership and opens a channel to understand and address the issue.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a sequence in which students first generate as many possible solutions as they can, then evaluate and select the strongest. Which pair of thinking processes does this sequence most directly develop?
options: Passive listening followed by note-taking
Rote memorization followed by recall
Imitation followed by repetition
Divergent thinking followed by convergent thinking
questions.rationale: Generating many possibilities engages divergent thinking, while evaluating and selecting the best option engages convergent thinking. Deliberately sequencing the two develops both creative and analytical problem-solving processes.

questions.stem: After a rich discussion, a teacher wants students to consolidate their thinking and recognize how their views may have shifted. Which closing activity best promotes reflective, metacognitive consolidation?
options: Collecting a quiz on isolated facts mentioned during the discussion
Asking the class to applaud the best speakers
Having students write briefly about how their thinking changed and what evidence influenced them
Assigning the next chapter to read for homework
questions.rationale: A reflective writing prompt that asks students to articulate how and why their thinking changed promotes metacognition, helping them consolidate learning and become aware of their own reasoning processes.

questions.stem: A fourth-grade teacher wants students to collaboratively build a shared digital timeline of events from a historical unit, with each small group responsible for adding entries and images for one decade. Which technology choice best supports this learning goal?
options: A set of printed worksheets students complete and tape onto a bulletin board
A cloud-based collaborative document or web tool that multiple groups can edit simultaneously
A drill-and-practice app that quizzes students on historical dates
A single classroom desktop computer the teacher uses to display a slideshow she created
questions.rationale: The instructional goal is collaborative construction of a shared product, so the technology should allow multiple students to contribute to one digital artifact at the same time. A cloud-based collaborative tool directly enables this, aligning the tool's affordances with the learning objective.

questions.stem: Before assigning students to research a science topic using websites, a sixth-grade teacher wants to promote responsible and effective use of online sources. Which action should the teacher take first?
options: Tell students to copy and paste text directly into their reports to save time
Require that students cite only the school's print encyclopedia
Teach students criteria for evaluating the credibility and relevance of online sources
Allow students to use any site that appears at the top of search results
questions.rationale: Effective and ethical technology use requires students to critically evaluate sources. Teaching evaluation criteria first equips students to judge credibility and relevance, supporting both information literacy and responsible use.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that one student does not have reliable internet access at home, while a homework assignment requires watching an online video and posting a response. Which adjustment best reflects equitable technology integration?
options: Lower the student's grade because the work was not submitted on time
Provide the student with a downloaded copy of the video and a printed response option, or arrange in-school access
Ask the student to complete twice as much non-technology work instead
Remove all technology from the course to avoid the problem
questions.rationale: Equitable integration means ensuring all students can access learning regardless of home resources. Providing an offline copy or arranging in-school access removes the access barrier while preserving the learning goal.

questions.stem: A high school teacher wants students to receive immediate practice feedback while reviewing chemistry vocabulary before a unit test. Which technology use is most appropriate for this specific purpose?
options: A video-editing program for creating documentaries
A self-checking digital flashcard or quiz app that tells students whether each answer is correct
A spreadsheet for tracking the school's sports scores
A class blog where students post essays for the teacher to grade next week
questions.rationale: The goal is immediate feedback during vocabulary practice. A self-checking flashcard or quiz app provides instant right/wrong feedback, allowing students to monitor their own learning before the test.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a lesson in which students use a simulation program to explore how changing variables affects the motion of a virtual roller coaster. What is the primary instructional advantage of using this simulation rather than only describing the concepts?
options: It lets students manipulate variables and observe outcomes that would be impractical or unsafe to test physically
It replaces the need for the teacher to set learning objectives
It ensures students never need to discuss their findings with peers
It guarantees that students will earn higher test scores automatically
questions.rationale: Simulations let learners actively manipulate variables and immediately see consequences, supporting inquiry and conceptual understanding of relationships that are hard to demonstrate physically in a classroom.

questions.stem: During a unit on persuasive writing, a teacher has students create short digital public-service announcements using video and audio tools. Several students spend most of their time adding flashy transitions and music rather than crafting a clear persuasive argument. What is the teacher's most effective response?
options: Eliminate the video project and return to paper essays only
Grade only the visual effects so students feel rewarded for their effort
Allow the students to continue, since engagement with the tool is the main goal
Refocus students by providing a rubric that emphasizes the persuasive content and explaining how design choices should serve the message
questions.rationale: When the tool's features overshadow the learning objective, the teacher should realign attention to content. A rubric prioritizing persuasive substance, plus guidance on how design supports the message, keeps the technology in service of the learning goal.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students in a world-languages class to practice authentic conversation but the class has no native speakers. Which technology-supported approach best advances this communicative goal while addressing safety and appropriateness?
options: Show a single recorded lecture about grammar rules with no interaction
Arrange a supervised, school-approved video exchange with a partner class in another country
Require students to memorize a translation-app output and recite it
Have students chat with random strangers on an open public messaging app
questions.rationale: Authentic communicative practice is best served by real interaction with other speakers, and a supervised, school-approved exchange provides authenticity while protecting student safety and ensuring appropriateness.

questions.stem: A teacher integrates a learning-management system where students submit drafts, receive comments, and revise. A few students share their account passwords with friends to 'help each other log in.' What is the teacher's most appropriate instructional response?
options: Use the situation to teach digital citizenship, including the importance of protecting personal account credentials and academic integrity
Ignore it, since collaboration among students is always beneficial
Tell students that account security does not matter for schoolwork
Delete the affected accounts permanently as punishment
questions.rationale: Sharing credentials raises issues of digital citizenship, privacy, and academic integrity. The teacher should treat it as a teachable moment, explaining why protecting personal credentials matters in digital environments.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a project where students gather local water-quality data with sensors, enter it into a spreadsheet, and create graphs to identify trends. Which higher-order skill does this technology use most directly promote?
options: Passive viewing of teacher-prepared charts
Rote memorization of formulas
Faster handwriting
Analysis and interpretation of authentic data to draw evidence-based conclusions
questions.rationale: Collecting real data and using software to graph and examine it engages students in analyzing patterns and drawing evidence-based conclusions, which are higher-order thinking skills that the technology directly supports.

questions.stem: An elementary teacher with one classroom tablet for every five students wants to integrate technology meaningfully despite limited devices. Which approach makes the most effective instructional use of the available resources?
options: Design station rotations in which small groups use the tablets for a targeted, collaborative task while others work offline
Have one student use a tablet while the rest watch silently each day
Cancel technology use until every student can have an individual device
Use the tablets only as a reward for students who finish work early
questions.rationale: With limited devices, station rotations let small groups engage in purposeful, collaborative technology tasks while peers complete meaningful offline work, maximizing access and instructional value.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use a class discussion forum so quieter students have more opportunities to contribute. After two weeks, participation is uneven and some posts are off-topic. Which step should the teacher take to improve the forum's instructional effectiveness?
options: Require students to post as many times as possible regardless of quality
Read posts aloud anonymously to embarrass off-topic contributors
Establish clear expectations, model a strong post, and provide focused prompts tied to learning goals
Stop using the forum because some posts were off-topic
questions.rationale: Online participation improves when students understand expectations and have focused, goal-aligned prompts. Modeling quality posts and clarifying norms guides productive, on-topic contributions.

questions.stem: A teacher plans to have students publish their research findings to an authentic audience beyond the classroom using a class website. Which benefit of this technology use most directly supports student motivation and quality of work?
options: It removes the need for students to revise their work
It guarantees that no errors will appear in the final product
Writing for a real, broader audience can increase students' sense of purpose and attention to quality
It allows students to avoid citing sources
questions.rationale: Publishing to an authentic audience gives writing a real purpose, which research links to greater student investment and care in producing high-quality work.

questions.stem: A teacher discovers that a free educational app she wants to use collects students' personal information and shares it with third parties. Before adopting it, what should the teacher do?
options: Review the app's privacy practices against district policy and laws protecting student data before using it
Adopt it immediately because it is free and popular
Have students create accounts using their full home addresses to personalize the app
Assume any educational app is automatically safe for student data
questions.rationale: Protecting student privacy is a professional and legal responsibility. The teacher must evaluate the app's data practices against district policy and student-data protection laws before adopting it.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to differentiate a reading lesson using technology for a class that includes students reading below, at, and above grade level. Which use of technology best supports this differentiation?
options: Project one text and read it aloud to the whole class at a single pace
Use a digital reading platform that adjusts text complexity and provides supports such as audio narration and adjustable vocabulary
Assign every student the same passage and the same on-screen comprehension quiz
Give above-level students extra silent reading while ignoring below-level readers
questions.rationale: Adaptive reading technology can tailor text complexity and offer supports like narration and vocabulary scaffolds, meeting the varied needs of a mixed-readiness class more effectively than a one-size-fits-all approach.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a digital concept-mapping tool so students can visually organize relationships among ideas during a unit on ecosystems. A colleague asks why she did not just have students write a paragraph instead. Which response best explains the instructional value of the tool for this goal?
options: Paragraph writing should never be used in any subject
The tool replaces the need for students to understand the content
The visual mapping makes connections among concepts explicit and easier to manipulate, supporting deeper understanding of relationships
The tool is more entertaining than writing, which is the main benefit
questions.rationale: Concept-mapping software makes relationships among ideas visible and easy to rearrange, which supports students in analyzing and understanding how concepts connect, an advantage suited to the relational learning goal.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to use a search engine to investigate a current science controversy. To help students develop critical evaluation skills rather than accepting the first result, which strategy is most effective?
options: Have students copy the entire top article without reading it
Teach students to compare multiple sources, check authorship and date, and identify potential bias
Limit students to images only, ignoring written sources
Tell students that the first result is always the most accurate
questions.rationale: Critical evaluation involves cross-checking multiple sources and examining authorship, currency, and bias. Teaching these habits builds the information literacy needed to assess online information independently.

questions.stem: A teacher introduces a coding-and-robotics activity in which students program a robot to navigate a maze and must debug errors when it fails. Beyond computer skills, which thinking process does this activity most directly develop?
options: Logical problem solving and iterative testing of solutions
Avoidance of trial and error
Handwriting fluency
Memorization of historical facts
questions.rationale: Programming and debugging require students to reason logically, test hypotheses, and refine solutions iteratively, cultivating problem-solving and computational-thinking skills.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a flipped-classroom approach in which students watch a short instructional video at home and then do application activities in class. To ensure students engage with the video meaningfully, which accompanying strategy is most effective?
options: Provide no guidance and assume students will watch carefully
Forbid students from pausing or rewatching the video
Make the video three hours long to cover everything
Pair the video with focused guiding questions or a brief note-taking guide that students complete and bring to class
questions.rationale: Passive viewing rarely ensures engagement. Pairing the video with guiding questions or a note guide gives students a clear purpose and an accountable task, promoting active processing of the content.

questions.stem: A teacher has students use generative writing-assistance software to brainstorm ideas for an argumentative essay. To keep the technology supportive of, rather than a substitute for, students' own thinking and skill development, which instructional design is most appropriate?
options: Allow students to submit the software's output unchanged as their final essay
Prohibit any planning and require students to write the final draft in one sitting
Grade only on how closely the essay matches the software's suggestions
Have students use the tool to generate possible angles, then require them to evaluate, select, and develop their own arguments with cited evidence
questions.rationale: Used well, generative tools can spark ideas, but learning requires students to do the critical work themselves. Requiring students to evaluate, choose, and develop their own evidence-based arguments keeps the tool a support rather than a replacement for their thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews engagement analytics from a digital learning platform showing that most students complete interactive practice quickly but score poorly on the embedded checks for understanding. Which interpretation and response best reflect sound use of these data?
options: The data prove the platform is broken and should be abandoned at once
Students may be clicking through without deep processing; the teacher should investigate, adjust pacing or supports, and add accountability for understanding
Fast completion always indicates mastery, so no change is needed
The teacher should reward the fastest finishers regardless of their scores
questions.rationale: The pattern of quick completion with poor understanding suggests superficial engagement. Sound data use means probing the cause and adjusting instruction, supports, or accountability rather than assuming the tool failed or that speed equals mastery.

questions.stem: A school adopts a new one-to-one device program. A teacher notices that, although every student now has a laptop, her lessons mostly use the devices for digitized worksheets that mirror the old paper tasks. To move toward more transformative technology integration, what should the teacher prioritize?
options: Use the laptops only for students to read digital versions of the textbook
Keep all tasks identical to paper, since the devices are already in use
Redesign tasks so technology enables learning that was previously impossible or impractical, such as collaboration, creation, and connection to real audiences
Have students close their laptops and return entirely to paper
questions.rationale: Simply digitizing existing tasks is substitution that adds little value. Transformative integration redesigns learning so technology makes new kinds of collaboration, creation, and authentic connection possible, expanding what students can do.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use an online collaborative platform for a multi-week group project but is concerned about ensuring individual accountability within groups. Which combination of strategies best uses the technology to support both collaboration and individual accountability?
options: Use the platform's revision history and assigned individual roles, combined with brief individual reflections, to document and assess each member's contribution
Forbid any record of who contributed what to keep the process simple
Have one student do all the work and list everyone's name on it
Assign one shared grade based only on the final product, with no record of individual contributions
questions.rationale: Collaborative platforms often log contributions, which the teacher can pair with defined roles and individual reflections to ensure each student is accountable while still collaborating, balancing group process with individual assessment.

questions.stem: During independent work time, a teacher circulates and briefly checks each student's progress, asking targeted questions and noting who is struggling. This ongoing practice is an example of which type of assessment?
options: A diagnostic test given only at the end of the year
Summative assessment used to assign final grades
Standardized assessment administered annually
Formative assessment used to monitor learning and inform instruction in real time
questions.rationale: Monitoring students during learning and using that information to adjust instruction is formative assessment. It provides real-time evidence the teacher can act on immediately.

questions.stem: A teacher plans an end-of-unit assessment and wants to ensure it accurately measures what students were taught. Which step best supports the validity of the assessment?
options: Include items on topics not covered in the unit to challenge students
Make every question extremely difficult so few students pass
Use only questions the teacher finds personally interesting
Align each assessment item to the unit's stated learning objectives
questions.rationale: An assessment is valid when it measures the intended learning. Aligning items directly to the unit's objectives ensures the test reflects what was actually taught and intended to be learned.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a digital response system in which all students answer multiple-choice questions on their devices during a lesson, and the results display instantly. What is the most effective instructional use of this immediate class data?
options: Record each response as a permanent grade without discussion
Show the results to embarrass students who answered incorrectly
Use the displayed results to decide whether to move on, reteach, or clarify a common misconception in the moment
Ignore the results and continue the lesson exactly as planned
questions.rationale: Real-time response data are most useful for adjusting instruction immediately. The teacher can see the class's understanding and decide whether to proceed, reteach, or address a misconception on the spot.

questions.stem: A teacher analyzes a class set of assessment results and finds that students performed well on factual-recall items but poorly on items requiring application and analysis. Which conclusion and instructional adjustment best reflect sound assessment interpretation?
options: Students simply lack ability, so no instructional change is warranted
Instruction and practice may have emphasized recall over higher-order thinking; the teacher should incorporate more application and analysis opportunities
The assessment is invalid and the scores should be discarded
Students have mastered the unit fully, so the teacher should move on
questions.rationale: A gap between strong recall and weak application points to instruction that under-emphasized higher-order thinking. The appropriate response is to adjust teaching to include more application and analysis, using the data to guide instruction.

questions.stem: During a casual lunch in a public restaurant, a fourth-grade teacher's friend (not an educator) asks how a specific student—whose parent the friend knows socially—is doing in class. The teacher wants to be friendly but professional. Which response best reflects the Code of Ethics and confidentiality obligations?
options: Decline to discuss the student, explaining that information about students is confidential
Share only positive comments about the student, since praise cannot harm the student
Give a general impression without naming specific grades or behaviors
Answer briefly and ask the friend not to repeat what was said
questions.rationale: Educators must not reveal confidential information about students except as permitted by law. Discussing any individually identifiable student information with a non-authorized person violates confidentiality, even if the comments are positive or vague.

questions.stem: A second-year teacher receives a formal observation report noting that her questioning strategies rarely move beyond recall. She feels defensive because she worked hard on the lesson. Which response most reflects a professional disposition toward growth?
options: Request that a different administrator re-observe the same lesson type
Explain to the principal why recall questions were appropriate that day
Wait to see whether the concern appears again before changing anything
Reflect on the feedback and seek resources or a mentor to strengthen higher-order questioning
questions.rationale: Professional growth involves using feedback constructively—reflecting on it and actively seeking strategies or support to improve, rather than dismissing or deferring action.

questions.stem: A high school teacher notices unexplained bruising on a 16-year-old student and overhears the student say a parent 'lost it' last night. The student begs the teacher not to tell anyone. What is the teacher's legal obligation in Texas?
options: Honor the student's request unless the bruising worsens
Report the suspected abuse to the appropriate authorities within the required timeframe
Notify the parent to hear their side before deciding whether to report
Ask the school counselor to investigate and confirm abuse before reporting
questions.rationale: Texas law requires educators who have cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected to make a report to authorities promptly (within 48 hours). This duty is personal, non-delegable, and cannot be waived by the student's wishes.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to strengthen a productive partnership with the family of a struggling reader. Which initial approach best builds a collaborative relationship?
options: Recommend the family hire a private tutor as soon as possible
Wait until the next report card to discuss any concerns
Invite the family to share their observations and goals for their child
Send home a list of the student's deficits so parents understand the urgency
questions.rationale: Effective family collaboration begins by treating parents as partners—inviting their perspectives and goals—rather than leading with deficits or directives.

questions.stem: A student with an IEP is consistently pulled from the general education science class for the entire period to receive services in a resource room, though the IEP team has not documented that the general setting cannot meet his needs with supports. A new teacher questions this. Which principle most directly supports the teacher's concern?
options: Free Appropriate Public Education (FAPE)
Response to Intervention (RTI)
Procedural safeguards under FERPA
Least Restrictive Environment (LRE)
questions.rationale: LRE under IDEA requires that students with disabilities be educated with non-disabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate, removing them from general settings only when supplementary aids and services cannot meet their needs there.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to show a popular full-length feature film during an indoor recess as a reward, streaming it from a personal subscription account. Which consideration is most relevant before doing so?
options: Whether the principal personally enjoys the film
Whether public performance rights or fair use apply to showing the film this way
Whether the film's rating is appropriate for the grade level only
Whether students have already seen the film at home
questions.rationale: Showing a full-length entertainment film outside a direct face-to-face teaching purpose generally requires public performance rights; personal streaming subscriptions are licensed for home use, raising copyright concerns.

questions.stem: A teacher attends a summer workshop on inquiry-based math instruction. The most effective way to translate this learning into improved practice is to:
options: Implement and reflect on one new strategy, adjusting based on student results
File the workshop certificate for the personnel record
Replace the entire current curriculum immediately with the new approach
Share the handouts with colleagues and continue teaching as before
questions.rationale: Professional growth is meaningful when new learning is applied, monitored, and refined based on student outcomes—an ongoing reflective cycle rather than a one-time event.

questions.stem: At an ARD/IEP meeting, a parent grows frustrated, saying the school 'never listens.' The general education teacher wants to support productive collaboration. The most constructive immediate response is to:
options: Defend the school's prior decisions to correct the record
Suggest the meeting be rescheduled when the parent is calmer
Refer the parent to the special education director and step back
Acknowledge the parent's concern and invite them to share specific examples
questions.rationale: Productive collaboration requires validating the parent's feelings and seeking specifics so concerns can be addressed; defensiveness or deflection damages the partnership central to the ARD process.

questions.stem: A teacher leads a grade-level team that has data showing reading scores stalling. To engage colleagues in a genuinely collaborative improvement process rather than a top-down fix, the teacher should:
options: Facilitate analysis of the data so the team jointly identifies causes and strategies
Assign each teacher a different program to try and compare later
Ask the principal to mandate a single intervention for the team
Present a finished action plan for colleagues to implement
questions.rationale: Collaborative professional learning communities work best when colleagues analyze data together and co-construct solutions, building shared ownership rather than receiving an imposed plan.

questions.stem: A teacher wants families who cannot attend daytime conferences to still stay informed and involved. The most inclusive strategy is to:
options: Offer multiple flexible options such as evening calls, translated newsletters, and a class app
Send a single comprehensive letter at the start of the year
Require parents to email questions during business hours
Hold all communication during the scheduled school day only
questions.rationale: Inclusive family engagement provides varied, flexible communication channels that accommodate different schedules, languages, and access, rather than a single rigid method.

questions.stem: A teacher discovers that a colleague has been giving a few students advance copies of the state assessment items to 'practice.' The teacher is unsure what to do. The most ethically appropriate action is to:
options: Confront the colleague privately and let it go if they stop
Report the testing irregularity to the campus testing coordinator or administrator
Document it but take no action unless asked
Warn the affected students' parents directly
questions.rationale: Compromising the security and integrity of a standardized assessment is a serious testing violation that educators are ethically obligated to report through proper channels; ignoring or privately resolving it does not fulfill that duty.

questions.stem: A teacher sets a professional goal to improve classroom assessment practices. Which goal statement best reflects effective, growth-oriented professional development planning?
options: Implement and refine formative checks weekly, using student data to adjust instruction, and review progress quarterly
Become a better teacher this year
Make sure students score higher on the next test
Attend three workshops on assessment by the end of the semester
questions.rationale: Effective professional goals are specific, measurable, tied to practice and student data, and include a cycle of implementation and reflection—not vague aims or mere attendance counts.

questions.stem: A teacher posts on a public personal blog a vivid, identifiable story about 'a student in my class today' that includes the student's behavior struggles, without naming the student. Which concern is most significant?
options: Blogging is never appropriate for educators
The concern is only relevant if the post is shared widely
The post is acceptable because no name was used
The post may violate student confidentiality because the student could still be identified
questions.rationale: Even without a name, details that make a student identifiable can breach confidentiality. Educators must protect personally identifiable student information in public forums.

questions.stem: A new special education co-teacher and the general education teacher disagree about how to divide instructional responsibilities in an inclusion class. To model effective collaboration for students, they should:
options: Take turns teaching whole lessons on alternating days
Have the general education teacher lead while the co-teacher assists
Meet to clarify shared goals and define complementary roles based on student needs
Ask students which arrangement they prefer
questions.rationale: Effective co-teaching collaboration is built on shared planning that aligns roles with student needs and instructional goals, rather than rigid or default arrangements.

questions.stem: A teacher photocopies an entire chapter from a copyrighted novel for every student to use all semester instead of purchasing the book. Regarding copyright and fair use, this practice is:
options: Acceptable because it is only one chapter
Acceptable as long as the author is cited
Likely a copyright violation because it copies a substantial portion and replaces a purchase
Acceptable because it is for educational purposes
questions.rationale: Fair use is limited; copying a substantial portion of a work in a way that substitutes for purchasing it generally exceeds fair use, even for education.

questions.stem: A teacher learns that several families in the community feel disconnected from the school because past communications assumed familiarity with school systems they did not have. To build authentic engagement, the teacher's best long-term approach is to:
options: Ask families to attend an orientation on how the school works
Send more frequent reminders about existing procedures
Learn about families' backgrounds and design communication that respects and builds on their knowledge and culture
Hold one cultural celebration event each year
questions.rationale: Authentic, asset-based engagement requires understanding families' cultural backgrounds and prior knowledge, then designing communication that respects and builds on them—rather than expecting families to adapt to the school's assumptions.

questions.stem: A student tells a teacher in confidence that they are being bullied online by classmates and shows messages, but begs the teacher not to involve administration for fear of retaliation. The teacher should:
options: Follow district policy and report the bullying through appropriate channels while supporting the student
Wait to see whether the bullying continues before acting
Keep the confidence to maintain the student's trust
Tell the student to block the classmates and handle it themselves
questions.rationale: Educators have a duty to protect student safety and follow district anti-bullying policy. The teacher must report and act while supporting the student, even though the student requested confidentiality.

questions.stem: After several lessons, a teacher notices that English learners in the class participate far less in discussions than other students. The most professionally responsible next step is to:
options: Seek out professional learning on language-supportive discussion strategies and apply them
Reduce the amount of discussion to avoid putting them on the spot
Group all the English learners together for separate, easier tasks
Assume the students are shy and will engage when ready
questions.rationale: A reflective professional responds to an observed instructional gap by seeking targeted professional learning and adjusting practice—here, strategies that support language learners' participation.

questions.stem: An ARD committee is finalizing services for a student whose behavior significantly impedes their learning and that of others. Which action best aligns with IDEA requirements in this situation?
options: Place the student in a more restrictive setting to manage the behavior
Defer the issue to the general education teacher to handle
Consider positive behavioral interventions and supports, including a behavior plan, to address the behavior
Reduce the student's instructional time to limit disruptions
questions.rationale: Under IDEA, when behavior impedes learning, the IEP team must consider the use of positive behavioral interventions, supports, and strategies—often a behavior intervention plan—rather than defaulting to more restrictive placement or reduced services.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to keep parents regularly informed about classroom learning in a positive, ongoing way. Which practice best supports this?
options: Posting grades online and assuming parents will check
Saving all communication for the end-of-year conference
Sending periodic updates that highlight learning goals and student progress
Contacting parents only when a problem arises
questions.rationale: Ongoing, positive communication—sharing learning goals and progress regularly—keeps families informed and engaged, building trust rather than associating contact only with problems.

questions.stem: A teacher is asked by a coach to release a list of students' grades so the coach can determine athletic eligibility. Under FERPA, the teacher should:
options: Share only the failing students' names to protect others
Require written parental consent before sharing with the coach
Refuse, because grades can never be shared with other staff
Share the information, since the coach is a school official with a legitimate educational interest
questions.rationale: FERPA permits disclosure of education records to school officials with a legitimate educational interest. A coach determining eligibility has such an interest, so consent is not required.

questions.stem: A veteran teacher is asked to incorporate a new digital learning platform but feels confident in long-used methods and is skeptical of the change. Which response best reflects a professional commitment to growth?
options: Wait until the platform is mandatory before trying it
Pilot the platform thoughtfully, gather evidence of its impact on learning, and adjust accordingly
Adopt the platform fully and abandon previous methods immediately
Continue current methods, since they have worked for years
questions.rationale: Professional growth includes openness to innovation evaluated through evidence. Thoughtfully piloting a new tool and judging it by student impact balances reflection with willingness to change.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to give a student a ride home alone after a late club meeting because no one has picked them up. The most appropriate action regarding professional boundaries and safety is to:
options: Give the ride since it is a kind gesture
Follow district policy—typically contacting the family and administration rather than transporting the student alone
Have the student wait outside until someone arrives
Drive the student only if another student is also in the car
questions.rationale: Transporting a student alone raises boundary and liability concerns. The appropriate step is to follow district procedures—contacting the family and administration—rather than acting independently.

questions.stem: A teacher must deliver difficult news to a family about their child's significant academic struggles. To collaborate effectively, the teacher should:
options: Lead with the list of failing grades to convey seriousness
Frame the conversation around shared concern, specific evidence, and a joint plan of support
Recommend retention as the clear solution
Keep the conversation brief to avoid upsetting the family
questions.rationale: Difficult conversations are most productive when framed collaboratively—expressing shared concern, grounding it in specific evidence, and co-developing a support plan—rather than blaming or prescribing.

questions.stem: Which scenario most clearly requires a teacher to make a report of suspected child abuse or neglect in Texas?
options: A student wears the same clothes two days in a row
A student is repeatedly late to class
A young student describes injuries caused by an adult at home and the teacher has reason to believe it
A student frequently forgets homework and seems tired
questions.rationale: A teacher must report when there is cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected. A student's description of adult-caused injuries that the teacher finds credible meets that threshold; the other behaviors alone do not.

questions.stem: A teacher reads professional research suggesting a strategy that contradicts a long-held belief about effective practice. The most professional response is to:
options: Adopt the strategy uncritically because it is published
Ignore it unless a supervisor requires the change
Critically evaluate the research and consider testing the strategy with their students
Dismiss the research because experience is more reliable
questions.rationale: Reflective professionals critically evaluate new evidence and are willing to test promising strategies, balancing research with their own context rather than dismissing or blindly adopting it.

questions.stem: A teacher coordinates with a school counselor, a reading specialist, and a parent to support a struggling student. To make this team approach effective, the teacher should:
options: Wait for each specialist to act independently
Establish shared goals, clear roles, and regular communication among all parties
Let the parent decide each professional's role
Take sole responsibility so communication stays simple
questions.rationale: Effective interprofessional collaboration depends on shared goals, defined roles, and ongoing communication so that all stakeholders coordinate their efforts toward the student's needs.

questions.stem: A teacher discovers that a student left a graded essay on a desk, and another student has read it and is teasing the first student about the score. Regarding handling of student work and records, the teacher should recognize that:
options: Only official transcripts are confidential, not classroom work
Graded work left out is no longer confidential
Student grades and work are private, and the teacher should manage return procedures to protect confidentiality
Teasing is the only issue; confidentiality is not relevant
questions.rationale: Student grades and work are confidential. Teachers should use return procedures (e.g., not leaving graded work exposed) that protect students' privacy and prevent disclosure to peers.

questions.stem: A teacher joins a professional organization in their subject area. The clearest professional benefit of this membership is:
options: Automatic eligibility for promotion
A reduced teaching workload
Exemption from district evaluations
Access to current research, resources, and a network for ongoing professional learning
questions.rationale: Professional organizations support ongoing growth by providing access to current research, instructional resources, and professional networks.

questions.stem: A teacher is approached by a parent who is also a personal friend and asks the teacher to 'go easy' on grading their child's late assignments as a favor. The teacher values the friendship. The most ethical response is to:
options: Apply the same grading standards to this student as to all others, explaining the need for fairness
Ask another teacher to grade that child's work
Grant the favor quietly to preserve the friendship
Grade the child more strictly to avoid any appearance of favoritism
questions.rationale: Educators must treat all students equitably and avoid conflicts of interest. The teacher should apply consistent standards to all students, regardless of personal relationships.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a colleague consistently excludes the parents of students with disabilities from class activities, assuming they 'won't be interested.' To advocate for inclusive family engagement, the teacher should first:
options: Report the colleague to the principal for discrimination
Accept that the colleague knows their families best
Invite those parents personally and say nothing to the colleague
Privately share strategies and evidence showing that all families benefit from engagement opportunities
questions.rationale: Promoting inclusive engagement is best approached collegially first—sharing evidence and strategies that all families, including those of students with disabilities, deserve and benefit from engagement opportunities.

questions.stem: A teacher creates original classroom materials using their school's resources during contract hours and then sells them on a commercial website. Before doing so, the teacher should:
options: Review district policy and any applicable intellectual property or work-for-hire provisions
Only share them for free to avoid any issue
Assume the materials are personal property since they created them
Sell them freely because teachers own everything they make
questions.rationale: Materials created using district resources during work time may be subject to work-for-hire or district intellectual property policies. The teacher should check those policies before commercial use.

questions.stem: After analyzing a unit's results, a teacher realizes a key concept was poorly understood across all classes, suggesting the instructional approach—not the students—was the issue. The most growth-oriented response is to:
options: Conclude the concept is simply too difficult for the grade level
Reflect on the instructional design, revise the approach, and monitor whether revised strategies improve understanding
Reteach the same way more slowly next time
Attribute the results to a lack of student effort
questions.rationale: A reflective professional examines their own instructional decisions, revises the approach based on that analysis, and evaluates whether changes improve learning—rather than blaming students or repeating ineffective methods.

questions.stem: A seventh-grade science teacher wants a quick way to see, at the end of class, which students can explain the difference between mass and weight. Which tool best serves this purpose?
options: A district benchmark given three times a year
A one-minute written response in which each student explains the difference in their own words
A homework grade averaged into the six-weeks report card
A unit test scheduled for the end of the grading period
questions.rationale: An end-of-class written response gives immediate, individual evidence the teacher can use to plan tomorrow's lesson. Tests, benchmarks, and averaged grades come too late or are too broad to guide next-day instruction.

questions.stem: A student's score report states that she performed at the 82nd percentile on a nationally normed reading test. What does this mean?
options: She scored higher than about 82 percent of the students in the norm group
She met 82 percent of the grade-level standards
She answered 82 percent of the questions correctly
She is reading at an 82nd-grade level
questions.rationale: A percentile rank compares a student with the norm group. It shows relative standing, not the share of items answered correctly or the share of standards mastered.

questions.stem: Two teachers independently score the same set of student essays using one rubric and their scores often differ by two or more levels. Which quality of the assessment is most directly in question?
options: Norm-referencing, because the rubric lacks a comparison group
Content validity, because the essay topic is too narrow
Reliability, specifically consistency of scoring across raters
Practicality, because essays take too long to read
questions.rationale: Inter-rater reliability concerns whether different scorers assign similar scores to the same work. Scoring guides, anchor papers, and calibration sessions improve it.

questions.stem: Which comment gives a student the most useful feedback on a persuasive paragraph?
options: "You are one of the best writers in the class."
"Your claim is clear, but the second reason needs a specific example to support it."
"Good job!"
"This is much better than your last paper."
questions.rationale: Effective feedback is specific, tied to the goal, and tells the student what to do next. General praise and comparisons to others do not show how to improve.

questions.stem: A teacher wants grades to reflect what students know at the end of a unit rather than how quickly they learned it. Which grading practice best supports this goal?
options: Subtract points for every day an assignment is late regardless of the reason
Allow students to retake an assessment after targeted relearning and record the most recent evidence of mastery
Average all early quiz scores with the final test score so progress is weighted equally
Curve the final scores so that a fixed percentage of students earn each letter grade
questions.rationale: Grades should communicate achievement of the standards. Using the most recent, reliable evidence after relearning reports mastery, whereas averaging early attempts or applying fixed distributions mixes in other factors.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a pretest at the start of a fractions unit. Which use of the results best reflects responsive instruction?
options: Assign the pretest scores as the first grade of the unit
Tell the class which students scored lowest so they can work harder
File the results and teach the unit the same way for every student
Form flexible groups so that students who already show mastery work on extension tasks while others receive instruction on prerequisite skills
questions.rationale: A pretest is diagnostic. Its value comes from using the results to adjust content, pacing, and grouping to meet different readiness levels.

questions.stem: A reading intervention teacher charts a student's weekly oral reading fluency scores and draws an aim line toward the end-of-year goal. After six weeks, all data points fall below the aim line. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Analyze the data and adjust the intervention, such as its intensity, focus, or group size, then continue monitoring
Stop monitoring because the data are discouraging
Wait until the end of the year to see whether the student catches up
Lower the goal immediately so that the student can reach it
questions.rationale: Progress monitoring is meant to trigger timely decisions. When data stay below the aim line, the instruction should be modified rather than waiting or lowering expectations.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a checklist during independent work to note which students can correctly set up a ratio table. This is best described as which type of assessment?
options: Formative assessment through observation
Norm-referenced standardized assessment
Summative assessment through performance
Ipsative assessment for placement decisions
questions.rationale: Observation checklists capture evidence during learning and guide the next instructional step, which makes them formative. They are not standardized, and the data are not used for final judgments.

questions.stem: A middle school math teacher notices that a student who scores well on computation tasks consistently misses multi-step word problems. Which interpretation best fits this pattern?
options: The student may understand procedures but struggle to interpret the language and structure of word problems, so instruction should target problem representation
The computation scores must be inflated by copying
The student is not capable of grade-level math
The student is not trying on word problems
questions.rationale: Strong computation paired with weak word-problem performance suggests a specific gap in reading the problem and building a representation, not a general lack of ability or effort. Targeted instruction is the logical response.

questions.stem: Which question is the best example of a check for understanding during a lesson?
options: "Is this too easy for everyone?"
"Does everyone understand?"
"Are there any questions?"
"Show me with your fingers: how many sides does a hexagon have?"
questions.rationale: Asking all students to respond visibly gives the teacher evidence from the whole class. General questions typically get silence or nods from a few students and do not verify understanding.

questions.stem: A principal asks a teacher why a student's report card grade is a B when the student scored an A on every test. The teacher explains that the grade includes points for bringing supplies and for participation. Which concern does this raise?
options: The grade may no longer be a valid report of what the student has learned
The grade is norm-referenced and should be criterion-referenced
The grade is too reliable to be useful
The grade overemphasizes standardized test results
questions.rationale: When behavior and compliance are blended with achievement, the grade is harder to interpret as a measure of knowledge and skills. Separating academic and non-academic reporting improves validity.

questions.stem: A teacher returns a graded essay with a score and no comments. Students look at the score and put the paper away. Which change would best turn the grade into a learning opportunity?
options: Return the essay with a different color of pen
Post the class average so students can compare themselves with peers
Return the essay with specific comments and give class time for students to revise one section using the feedback
Make the grade final immediately so students stop asking about it
questions.rationale: Feedback improves learning when students receive it in time to act on it. Specific comments and time to apply them close the loop between assessment and learning.

questions.stem: A district wants to use a single end-of-year test to decide which students need summer support. The test covers many topics with only two items per topic. What is the main weakness of using this test to diagnose specific needs?
options: It is too long to administer in one class period
It uses selected-response items instead of essays
It was given at the end of the year instead of the beginning
Too few items per skill make it unreliable for identifying individual strengths and weaknesses
questions.rationale: Two items per skill give a very small sample, so the results cannot reliably show which specific skills a student has mastered. Broad tests suit overall decisions better than skill-level diagnosis.
