questions.stem: A teacher records a student's reading fluency by listening to the student read aloud and marking errors on a copy of the text. What is this technique called?
options: A cloze procedure
A running record
A portfolio review
A norm-referenced screener
questions.rationale: A running record captures a student's oral reading behaviors, including errors and self-corrections, to help the teacher analyze strategies and select appropriate texts.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a project in which students build a model of a watershed and explain how human activity affects it. Compared with a multiple-choice test on the same unit, what is a primary advantage of this performance assessment?
options: It tests only memorized vocabulary
It requires no criteria for evaluation
It lets students demonstrate how they apply knowledge in a realistic task
It is quicker to score objectively
questions.rationale: Performance tasks reveal application, reasoning, and communication. They require clear scoring criteria and are slower to score than selected-response items.

questions.stem: After analyzing a unit test, a teacher sees that students who scored low on one reading standard also left blank the open-response items. Which action best addresses the pattern?
options: Give the same test again without any new instruction
Remove open-response items from all future tests
Teach and model how to plan and write a response, then give structured practice with feedback
Replace the open-response items with true-false items so every student can answer
questions.rationale: Blank responses suggest students lack the strategies or confidence to compose written answers. Explicit modeling and scaffolded practice address the skill directly.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to know whether a new unit test actually measures the skills taught in the unit. Which step best provides evidence of content validity?
options: Give the test to the same students twice and compare scores
Ask two colleagues to take the test and report how long it took
Create a blueprint that maps each test item to a unit objective and check that the weight of items matches instructional emphasis
Check that the answer key has an equal number of A, B, C, and D answers
questions.rationale: Content validity depends on whether items represent the intended learning objectives in proportion to their importance. A blueprint is the standard tool for documenting that match.

questions.stem: A teacher uses an exit ticket asking, "What is one question you still have about today's topic?" Which instructional purpose does this serve best?
options: Keeping students busy during the last minutes of class
Replacing the need for a unit test
Assigning a participation grade to each student
Identifying lingering confusions so the next lesson can begin with targeted clarification
questions.rationale: Student-generated questions reveal confusions that quizzes might miss. The teacher can sort the questions and open the next class by addressing the most common ones.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that scores on a vocabulary test were high but the same students struggled to use the words in their own writing. What does this most strongly suggest?
options: The test measured recognition of definitions rather than the ability to apply the words, so assessment and instruction should address application
The test is too easy and should be eliminated
The writing assignment is not a valid assessment
The students did not study the words
questions.rationale: Success on a recognition test does not guarantee transfer to production. The gap suggests a mismatch between what was assessed and the intended outcome of using vocabulary in writing.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of an anchor paper in a scoring session?
options: To show students the best essay in the class
To determine which students will receive awards
To replace the scoring rubric
To provide a benchmark example of student work at each score level so scorers apply the rubric consistently
questions.rationale: Anchor papers illustrate each performance level and help scorers calibrate to the same standard, which improves reliability.

questions.stem: A teacher is deciding between an analytic rubric and a holistic rubric for scoring research papers. Which statement correctly describes an advantage of the analytic rubric?
options: It eliminates the need for scorer training
It provides separate scores for criteria such as organization and evidence, giving students targeted feedback
It can be used only with multiple-choice tests
It is faster to use because it yields only one overall score
questions.rationale: An analytic rubric rates each criterion separately, which clarifies strengths and weaknesses. A holistic rubric is faster but gives less detail.

questions.stem: A teacher uses the same assessment data to decide that most of the class needs a mini-lesson on citing evidence, while three students need enrichment. Which principle of responsive teaching does this reflect?
options: Teaching to the test
Using assessment evidence to adjust instruction for the whole group and for subgroups
Tracking students permanently by ability
Delaying instruction until the next grading period
questions.rationale: Responsive teaching means analyzing evidence and making timely adjustments, including whole-class reteaching and differentiated tasks for subgroups. It does not imply fixed tracks.

questions.stem: A student sets a goal of reading 20 pages per night and tracks it on a chart. How does this practice support learning?
options: It is mainly useful for classroom management
It guarantees higher test scores
It replaces teacher instruction
It promotes self-monitoring and ownership of progress
questions.rationale: Goal setting with self-tracking builds metacognition and motivation. It supports but does not replace instruction, and it does not guarantee results.

questions.stem: A teacher wants feedback on a student's draft to be most effective. When should the feedback be provided?
options: Only when the student requests it
Only on the final version
While the student can still revise the draft and before a final grade is assigned
After the grading period ends
questions.rationale: Feedback is most useful when it arrives in time for students to act on it. Waiting until grades are final removes the opportunity to improve.

questions.stem: A teacher gives the same chapter test to two sections. Section A scored an average of 85 and Section B an average of 68. Which next step reflects sound use of the data?
options: Compare the item-level results to see which standards Section B missed, then plan targeted instruction and consider differences in instruction between sections
Conclude that Section B students are less capable
Curve Section B's scores up by 17 points
Give both sections a different test next time
questions.rationale: Item-level analysis shows where the gap occurred and informs instruction. Drawing conclusions about student ability or applying a blanket curve does not address the cause.

questions.stem: A teacher writes a quiz item: "Which of the following is NOT an example of a producer? A. Grass B. Oak tree C. Rabbit D. Algae." Which revision would most improve this item?
options: Rewrite the stem positively, such as "Which organism is a consumer?"
Add "all of the above" as option E
Make option C much longer than the others
Remove the stem and keep only the options
questions.rationale: Negatively worded stems can cause students to misread the question and test reading care more than content. A positively worded stem asks directly for the target knowledge.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a graphic organizer to have students sort examples and non-examples of a concept after a lesson. What is the main instructional value of this assessment?
options: It shows whether students can distinguish the defining features of the concept
It replaces the need to teach the concept
It measures typing speed
It is useful only for early elementary grades
questions.rationale: Sorting examples and non-examples requires students to apply defining attributes, so errors reveal specific misunderstandings. The technique works at many grade levels.

questions.stem: Which term describes assessment that happens during instruction to help students learn rather than to assign a final grade?
options: Accountability assessment
Placement assessment
Summative assessment
Formative assessment
questions.rationale: Formative assessment provides information during learning that students and teachers use to improve. Summative assessments evaluate learning at the end.

questions.stem: A teacher conferences individually with each student about a draft, asking each to describe the goal of the piece and one thing to improve. How does this practice support assessment for learning?
options: It reduces the need for a rubric
It ensures all students receive the same comments
It gathers real-time evidence of student thinking and helps students set next steps
It prepares students for a standardized test
questions.rationale: Individual conferences allow the teacher to hear student reasoning and provide personalized guidance. The approach complements rubrics and produces individualized, not identical, feedback.

questions.stem: A school uses a universal screener in the fall. A student scores just below the cut score, but classroom performance has been strong. Which approach reflects sound practice?
options: Retake the screener every day until the score rises
Gather additional information, such as a short progress-monitoring probe and classroom work, before deciding on intervention
Ignore the screener because classroom work is more important
Place the student into intensive intervention immediately
questions.rationale: Screeners are brief and can produce false positives. Combining the result with other data supports accurate decisions without over- or under-identifying students.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that students who earned high grades on homework often perform poorly on tests. Which possible explanation should the teacher investigate first?
options: Whether tests should be eliminated
Whether homework should count for 100 percent of the grade
Whether homework tasks are too easy, too heavily scaffolded, or completed with outside help rather than independent practice
Whether students dislike the teacher
questions.rationale: A mismatch between homework and test performance can signal that homework is not measuring independent mastery. Examining task design and conditions helps the teacher interpret the grades.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to support students in using feedback. Which classroom practice is most effective?
options: Return papers face down and ask students not to look until after class
Ask students to list two pieces of feedback they received and describe how they will use them in the next assignment
Collect all graded papers back immediately
Tell students feedback is optional
questions.rationale: Feedback only improves learning when students process and act on it. Structured reflection after receiving feedback builds that habit.

questions.stem: A teacher plots a class's scores on a standards-based assessment and finds a bimodal distribution, with clusters of very high and very low scores. What is the most appropriate instructional implication?
options: Teach to the average score
Plan differentiated instruction because the class includes distinct groups with different readiness levels
Conclude that the test was reliable
Remove the assessment from the grade book
questions.rationale: A bimodal pattern suggests two distinct groups. Teaching to the mean would likely miss both, so the teacher should differentiate content, process, or support for each group.

questions.stem: A teacher holds up a card with a math problem and asks students to write the answer on mini whiteboards and display them at once. What is the main advantage of this strategy?
options: Students can copy more easily
It eliminates the need for further instruction
The teacher sees every student's response at the same time
It reduces the number of students who participate
questions.rationale: Simultaneous responses give evidence from all students quickly, helping the teacher adjust immediately. Properly managed, it increases participation.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a graphing task on Tuesday and a similar task on Friday after additional instruction to measure growth. Which feature makes this comparison meaningful?
options: The scoring criteria change between tasks
The tasks assess the same skill using comparable criteria
The Friday task is easier
The tasks use identical wording and numbers
questions.rationale: To measure growth, the tasks must target the same skill and be scored with comparable criteria. Identical items invite memorization, and changing criteria breaks the comparison.

questions.stem: A teacher scores a student's essay lower after reading a very strong essay from the previous student. Which scoring error does this most likely illustrate?
options: Halo effect from the student's previous grades
Central tendency in the rubric
Contrast effect, where scoring is influenced by the quality of the work just read
Construct underrepresentation
questions.rationale: A contrast effect occurs when a paper is judged relative to the preceding one instead of the criteria. Using anchor papers and scoring in varied order can reduce it.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a student with a documented accommodation of extended time the same math test as the class, with 50 percent more time. How does this affect the validity of the test?
options: It makes the test norm-referenced
It supports validity because the accommodation removes a barrier unrelated to the math skills being measured
It threatens validity because the student has an unfair advantage
It changes the objectives of the test
questions.rationale: Accommodations provide access without altering what is being measured. When the time limit is not part of the construct, extended time helps the score reflect the student's math ability.

questions.stem: A student wears a black armband to class to silently protest a policy decision, and the principal wants to ban it. Under the U.S. Supreme Court's ruling in Tinker v. Des Moines, when may a school restrict this kind of student expression?
options: When school officials can reasonably forecast that it would cause a substantial disruption of school activities or invade the rights of others
Never, because students have no free speech rights at school
Whenever the speech occurs on school grounds
Whenever an administrator disagrees with the message
questions.rationale: Tinker held that students do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. Schools may restrict expression only when it materially and substantially disrupts the educational process or intrudes on others' rights.

questions.stem: A district refuses to enroll a child because the family cannot document the child's immigration status. Which U.S. Supreme Court case, arising in Texas, addresses this practice?
options: Brown v. Board of Education, which addressed school start times
Goss v. Lopez, which addressed teacher certification
Tinker v. Des Moines, which addressed student dress codes only
Plyler v. Doe, which held that states may not deny a free public education to children based on immigration status
questions.rationale: In Plyler v. Doe (1982), the Court struck down a Texas law that withheld funds for educating undocumented children. Public schools cannot deny enrollment based on immigration status.

questions.stem: A principal suspends a student for ten days without telling the student the charges or allowing the student to respond. Which case supports the argument that the student was denied due process?
options: Garcetti v. Ceballos, which addresses student records
Lau v. Nichols, which governs dress codes
Plyler v. Doe, which regulates curriculum
Goss v. Lopez, which requires notice and an opportunity to be heard before a short suspension
questions.rationale: Goss v. Lopez (1975) held that students facing suspension have property and liberty interests in education and are entitled to at least notice and an informal hearing.

questions.stem: A teacher publicly criticizes district policy in a memo written as part of the teacher's assigned duties and is disciplined. Under Garcetti v. Ceballos, how are such statements treated?
options: As protected under the Texas Educators' Code of Ethics
As fully protected speech on a matter of public concern
As protected only if the memo is anonymous
As statements made pursuant to official duties, which are generally not protected by the First Amendment for employment purposes
questions.rationale: Garcetti held that when public employees speak as part of their official duties, they are not speaking as citizens for First Amendment purposes, so the employer may discipline them for it.

questions.stem: A school district allowed a student to lead a prayer over the loudspeaker before football games. In Santa Fe Independent School District v. Doe, a Texas case, what did the Supreme Court decide?
options: The policy was valid because attendance at games is voluntary
The policy violated the Free Speech Clause because it banned all prayer
The policy violated the Establishment Clause because it amounted to school-sponsored religious speech
The policy was valid because the student chose to lead it
questions.rationale: The Court held that student-led, student-initiated prayer at football games under district policy was still school-sponsored, so it violated the Establishment Clause. Students remain free to pray privately.

questions.stem: A teacher in a Texas public high school discovers that a student has a vape device in a backpack and the principal conducts a search based on a teacher's report. According to New Jersey v. T.L.O., what standard governs the search?
options: Reasonable suspicion that the search will turn up evidence of a violation of law or school rules, and a search reasonable in scope
A warrant supported by probable cause
No standard, because students have no privacy at school
The consent of both parents
questions.rationale: In T.L.O. (1985), the Court held that school searches need only be reasonable under the circumstances: justified at inception by reasonable grounds and reasonable in scope.

questions.stem: A teacher has a student who reports that the student feels unsafe because of repeated online harassment by a classmate that occurs outside school hours. Under Texas law (David's Law), what is true about the district's role?
options: Teachers must wait for a parent complaint before acting
Cyberbullying can fall within the district's bullying policies even when it occurs off campus if it interferes with the education of the victim or substantially disrupts school operations
Districts have no authority over any off-campus behavior
Only law enforcement may respond to cyberbullying
questions.rationale: David's Law (2017) expanded Texas bullying requirements to include cyberbullying and conduct that occurs off campus when it affects the educational environment. Districts must have reporting and response procedures.

questions.stem: A Texas teacher learns that a parent has asked to see the contents of their child's educational record. What does FERPA generally provide?
options: Parents may view any student's education records at the school
Parents lose all rights when the child enters middle school
Parents have rights only if the child receives special education services
Parents have the right to inspect and review their child's education records and request corrections to inaccurate information
questions.rationale: FERPA gives parents of students under 18 the right to inspect education records, request amendments, and consent to most disclosures. Rights transfer to the student at 18 or when attending a postsecondary institution.

questions.stem: A teacher keeps private notes in a personal notebook, shared with no one, to help remember student behavior patterns. Under FERPA, how are such notes generally treated?
options: They are protected only if written in ink
They must be posted in the main office
They are always education records that parents may inspect
They are generally not education records if they are kept in the sole possession of the maker and not shared
questions.rationale: FERPA excludes records in the sole possession of the maker that are used only as a personal memory aid and not revealed to others. If notes are shared or placed in files, they become education records.

questions.stem: In Owasso Independent School District v. Falvo, a Texas parent argued that having students grade each other's papers violated FERPA. What did the Supreme Court conclude?
options: Peer grading does not violate FERPA because papers graded by peers are not yet maintained by the school as education records
Peer grading is illegal under Texas law
Peer grading always violates FERPA
Peer grading is allowed only with parent permission slips
questions.rationale: The Court held that grades on papers graded by classmates are not education records maintained by the district until the teacher records them. Teachers may still choose other approaches for pedagogical reasons.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old high school student receiving special education services asks the teacher not to discuss her progress with her parents. Her parents ask for a progress update. Which statement is most accurate under FERPA?
options: Teachers may disclose records to any adult family member
FERPA rights always remain with parents until graduation
Parents may access records only through a court order
FERPA rights belong to the student at age 18, so the teacher needs the student's consent unless an exception applies, such as the student being claimed as a dependent for tax purposes
questions.rationale: At 18, FERPA rights transfer to the student. Schools may disclose to parents without consent if the student is a dependent for tax purposes or in specific health and safety emergencies, so the educator should follow district procedure.

questions.stem: A teacher receives a subpoena from an attorney asking for a student's records. What is the best response?
options: Hand over the records immediately
Refer the request to school administration so the district can verify the subpoena and follow FERPA notice requirements
Ignore the subpoena because teachers cannot be served
Email the records to the attorney to save time
questions.rationale: Education records may be released in response to a lawful subpoena, but districts must generally make a reasonable effort to notify parents beforehand. Routing the request to administration protects the student and the teacher.

questions.stem: A teacher suspects that a student's bruises were caused by a parent. The teacher tells the school counselor and assumes the counselor will make the report. Which statement is correct under the Texas Family Code?
options: The teacher still has an individual duty to report within 48 hours and cannot delegate it to another person
The teacher may report only to the principal
The teacher's duty ends once a counselor is informed
The teacher should wait to collect proof before reporting
questions.rationale: Texas law requires professionals to report suspected abuse or neglect directly to DFPS or law enforcement within 48 hours. The duty cannot be transferred to a supervisor or colleague.

questions.stem: A teacher in Texas knowingly fails to report suspected abuse of a student. What is a possible consequence?
options: Criminal liability for the failure to report and possible action against the teaching certificate
A written warning only, with no legal exposure
A civil fine paid by the district alone
No consequence, because reporting is voluntary
questions.rationale: Failing to report is a criminal offense under Texas law, and the educator may also face sanctions by SBEC. Good-faith reporters are immune from liability.

questions.stem: A teacher who coaches after school texts a student privately at night about topics unrelated to school and asks the student not to tell anyone. Which standard from the Texas Educators' Code of Ethics is most directly implicated?
options: The prohibition on inappropriate communication with a student, including electronic communication, that is not for a legitimate educational purpose
The requirement to attend all school board meetings
The requirement to use district textbooks
The requirement to grade work within seven days
questions.rationale: The Code prohibits educators from engaging in inappropriate communication with students, including electronic messages, and signals that secrecy is a warning sign of boundary violations.

questions.stem: A teacher is asked by a student's parent to tutor the student privately for pay, and the teacher also grades the student's work. Which concern is most relevant?
options: A conflict of interest, since the teacher would profit from tutoring a student whose grades the teacher controls
A FERPA violation, since tutoring is a disclosure
A copyright violation, since tutoring is public performance
An IDEA violation, since tutoring is a related service
questions.rationale: Educators must avoid using their position for personal gain or creating a conflict of interest. Paid tutoring of one's own student creates pressure on the student and questions about grading fairness. Districts typically restrict this practice.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a clear violation of test security?
options: Giving students actual test questions in advance of the test
Reminding students of the test start time
Reading the administration directions exactly as written
Distributing sharpened pencils
questions.rationale: Test security rules prohibit sharing secure test content or helping students obtain answers. Following directions and logistics are acceptable.

questions.stem: A district employee shows a 90-minute commercial movie to a class to fill time. Which is true about the copyright law's face-to-face teaching exemption?
options: The exemption applies only if students pay admission
Showing a lawfully obtained copy in a classroom as part of systematic instruction can be permitted, but showing it for entertainment or reward may not qualify
Any showing of any movie at school is automatically legal
Movies may never be shown in a classroom
questions.rationale: The face-to-face teaching exemption covers performances in a classroom at a nonprofit educational institution as part of teaching activities. Entertainment, filler, or rewards are not instructional uses and may require public performance rights.

questions.stem: A teacher considers copying a chapter from a consumable workbook for the whole class. Which fair use factor weighs most strongly against this use?
options: The effect on the potential market for the original work, since consumable workbooks are designed to be purchased for each student
The age of the students
The teacher's nonprofit status
The educational purpose of the lesson
questions.rationale: Fair use considers four factors. Copying consumable materials substitutes for purchases and harms the market, which weighs heavily against fair use even in educational settings.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use a short excerpt from a copyrighted article in a lesson. Which question best helps decide if the use may be fair use?
options: Whether students enjoy it
Whether the teacher found it online
Whether the article was published recently
How much of the work is used, how it is used, and how it affects the market for the original
questions.rationale: Fair use analysis examines purpose and character of use, nature of the work, amount used, and effect on the market. Popularity or source of access is not part of the test.

questions.stem: A student with dyslexia receives services under Section 504. A teacher refuses to allow the student to use an accommodation listed in the plan because it "seems unfair." What should the teacher understand?
options: Accommodations in a 504 plan are legally required and must be provided, and concerns should be raised through the 504 team
Teachers may choose which accommodations to follow
Accommodations expire at the end of each semester
Accommodations apply only on state tests
questions.rationale: Section 504 plans are legal documents requiring implementation. Teachers who believe an accommodation is not working should share data with the committee instead of ignoring it.

questions.stem: After a student's evaluation is completed, in Texas the ARD committee must meet within a certain period to decide eligibility and develop an IEP. Which timeframe is correct?
options: Within 6 months
Within 1 year
Within 30 calendar days of the completion of the written evaluation report
Only when the parent requests a meeting
questions.rationale: Texas rules require the ARD committee to meet within 30 calendar days after the full individual evaluation is completed. Timelines protect students from delays in services.

questions.stem: A parent disagrees with a school's evaluation of their child for special education. What right do they have under IDEA?
options: To require the school to hire a new teacher
To request an independent educational evaluation at public expense under certain conditions
To change the state curriculum
To end all evaluations permanently
questions.rationale: IDEA procedural safeguards allow parents who disagree with a district's evaluation to request an IEE, which the district must pay for or defend its own evaluation in due process.

questions.stem: A student with an IEP is suspended for more than ten school days in a school year because of repeated behavior. Which action is required under IDEA?
options: Placement in a more restrictive environment without a meeting
Automatic expulsion
A manifestation determination review to decide whether the behavior was caused by or had a direct and substantial relationship to the disability, or resulted from failure to implement the IEP
Removal of the IEP
questions.rationale: When a change of placement due to discipline is considered, the district must hold an MDR within ten school days. The outcome determines whether discipline can proceed as for other students and whether further actions are needed.

questions.stem: A teacher does not like a student's family and gives the student lower marks on subjective assignments. Which part of the Educators' Code of Ethics does this behavior most directly violate?
options: The duty to treat all students fairly and not to deny a student access to equal educational opportunities because of personal bias
The duty to coach extracurricular activities
The duty to publish research
The duty to attend professional development
questions.rationale: The Code requires educators to treat students fairly, without discrimination or bias, and to evaluate work based on criteria.

questions.stem: A Texas teacher is asked by a principal to change a student's failing grade to a passing grade without any additional evidence of mastery so the student can participate in sports. Which action is most consistent with the Code of Ethics?
options: Change the grade but make a note in the margin
Change the grade because administrators outrank teachers
Give the student bonus points for athletic achievements
Decline to falsify the grade and explain the grading policy and options for earning credit
questions.rationale: Educators must not falsify records or misrepresent facts. Grades must reflect student performance, and a teacher may raise concerns through proper channels.

questions.stem: A teacher posts a photograph of a student's graded paper with the student's name visible on a public social media account to celebrate improvement. What is the most significant issue?
options: The post may use too many hashtags
The post may disclose personally identifiable information from an education record without consent
The post was made during school hours
The post lacks a copyright notice
questions.rationale: Student work and grades with identifying information are education records. Sharing them publicly without written consent risks violating FERPA and the Educators' Code of Ethics.

questions.stem: A school nurse and a teacher notice a student with signs of possible neglect, such as repeated hunger and dirty clothing. What is the appropriate response?
options: Ask the student to bring a note from home
Each professional who has reasonable cause to believe a child is neglected must make a report to DFPS or law enforcement
Wait for the situation to worsen
Discuss it with the student's classmates to confirm
questions.rationale: Neglect is a form of child maltreatment under Texas law. Professionals must report reasonable suspicions and should not investigate on their own.

questions.stem: A teacher is told by a student in confidence that the student has been thinking about self-harm. What should the teacher do?
options: Wait a week to see if the feelings pass
Follow district procedures immediately by notifying the counselor or administrator, even though the student asked for secrecy
Promise to keep the secret
Share the information with the class to offer support
questions.rationale: Safety concerns override confidentiality. Teachers cannot promise secrecy when a student is at risk, and should follow the campus protocol, which includes notifying trained staff and family as required.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a field trip and sends permission forms. A student without a signed form asks to go anyway because the student's friends are going. What should the teacher do?
options: Skip permission forms for all students
Allow the student to go because the bus has seats
Take the student's word that a parent agreed
Follow district policy and not allow the student to go without proper authorization, while working with the family to resolve the form
questions.rationale: Field trips require parental authorization, supervision, and safety planning. Teachers must follow district policy to meet duty of care and limit liability.

questions.stem: A teacher leaves a class of third-graders unsupervised for 15 minutes to make copies. A student is injured during that time. Which legal concept is most directly relevant?
options: Plagiarism
Defamation
Copyright infringement
Negligence, which can arise when an educator fails to exercise the reasonable care expected for supervising students
questions.rationale: Teachers owe students a duty of reasonable supervision. Leaving young children unattended may breach that duty and, if foreseeable harm results, can support a negligence claim.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to share a student's special education status with a colleague who does not teach the student and has no role in the student's services. What does confidentiality require?
options: The teacher may share it in the break room
The teacher may share it if the colleague asks nicely
The teacher may share it if they are friends
The teacher should not share the information because the colleague has no legitimate educational interest
questions.rationale: Student information may be shared with school officials only when they have a legitimate educational interest. Casual sharing breaches confidentiality and the Code.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to measure how well students can explain the causes of the American Revolution in their own words. Which item format best fits this goal?
options: A multiple-choice item with four short options
A matching item with dates and events
A true-false item
A short essay prompt scored with a rubric
questions.rationale: Constructed-response formats such as essays let students organize and explain ideas. Selected-response formats mainly sample recognition of facts and are less suited to explanation.

questions.stem: A student's raw score on a standardized test is 38. A teacher wants to compare how this score ranks relative to the other students who took the test. Which derived score is most useful?
options: The number of items on the test
A rubric level
The student's attendance rate
Percentile rank
questions.rationale: Derived scores such as percentile rank convert raw scores to show relative standing within a norm group. Raw scores alone do not show how a student compares to others.

questions.stem: A teacher administers the same reading comprehension test to students on Monday and again two weeks later without instruction on the passages, and the scores are very similar. This best illustrates which quality?
options: Predictive validity
Test-retest reliability
Face validity
Construct bias
questions.rationale: Consistent results over time with the same test indicate test-retest reliability. Validity is a separate question about whether the test measures what it claims.

questions.stem: A student's reported scale score is 1520 with a standard error of measurement of 40. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The student answered 40 questions incorrectly
The student's score is certain to be 1560 next time
The student's true score is likely within a range around 1520, so small differences from another score should not be over-interpreted
The student's score is exactly 1520
questions.rationale: The standard error of measurement shows the expected variation in scores due to measurement error. Educators should treat scores as bands, not exact points, especially when comparing nearly equal results.

questions.stem: A teacher administers the TELPAS-style language proficiency assessment to identify the English language development level of a newly enrolled student. How should the teacher use the results?
options: To assign the student a final course grade
To decide whether the student has a disability
To determine the student's grade-level placement permanently
To plan language supports and scaffolds appropriate to the student's proficiency level in listening, speaking, reading, and writing
questions.rationale: Language proficiency assessments describe a student's current English development so teachers can plan targeted supports. They do not diagnose disabilities or determine final grades.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to assess whether students can apply the scientific method by planning their own experiment. Which assessment is the most authentic?
options: Students memorize the steps and recite them
Students design and conduct a simple experiment and report their findings
Students complete a vocabulary matching quiz
Students copy the steps from the textbook
questions.rationale: Authentic assessments ask students to perform tasks like real-world practice. Designing and conducting an experiment demonstrates the application of the method.

questions.stem: A teacher writes a multiple-choice item and wants the distractors to be effective. Which characteristic is most important?
options: Distractors should be plausible and reflect common student errors or misconceptions
Distractors should be obviously silly so students can eliminate them
Distractors should be much longer than the correct answer
Distractors should always include the phrase "all of the above"
questions.rationale: Good distractors attract students who hold common misconceptions, so incorrect responses give diagnostic information. Implausible options reduce the item's effectiveness.

questions.stem: In a classroom with a wide range of readiness levels, a teacher wants to assess understanding of a novel in a way that allows students to show what they know through different formats. Which approach is best?
options: Offer a menu of assessment options aligned to the same learning objective and scored with the same criteria
Let each student choose what to be assessed on, regardless of objectives
Give every student the same multiple-choice test
Allow students to skip assessments they find difficult
questions.rationale: Flexible assessment formats support access while keeping the target constant. All options should measure the same standards and use shared criteria for fairness.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a summative assessment?
options: To evaluate student learning at the end of an instructional period against a standard
To place students in seats
To plan the daily warm-up
To provide hints during a lesson
questions.rationale: Summative assessments such as final exams and end-of-unit projects measure what students have learned after instruction, and they are often used for grades.

questions.stem: A teacher sets up a gradebook with categories: tests 50 percent, projects 30 percent, homework 10 percent, and participation 10 percent. A student has excellent tests but missing homework. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The weighting means homework affects the grade but tests have the largest influence, so the grade will still largely reflect test achievement
Homework will determine most of the grade
The grade will ignore tests
Participation counts more than projects
questions.rationale: Weighted categories determine how much each type of work contributes. With tests at 50 percent, strong test performance has the greatest influence on the final grade.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a pre-test and post-test to evaluate a new instructional unit. Students' average score rises from 42 percent to 78 percent. Which factor limits the conclusion that the unit alone caused the gain?
options: The absence of a comparison group, because other factors such as maturation or outside learning could contribute
The use of percentages instead of raw scores
The fact that scores increased
The use of a pre-test
questions.rationale: Without a control or comparison group, it is difficult to attribute growth solely to the intervention. A pre- and post-test design shows growth but not causation.

questions.stem: A teacher realizes a social studies test contains a reading passage far above the grade level, and English learners score lower. What is the most likely issue?
options: The test relies too heavily on selected-response items
The test is too reliable
The test is norm-referenced
The test may be measuring reading ability in addition to social studies knowledge, reducing validity for those students
questions.rationale: When the language demand exceeds the skill being measured, scores reflect reading ability as well as content knowledge. Reducing unnecessary language complexity supports valid inferences.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to design an assessment that measures students' ability to evaluate sources. Which item stem best targets that skill?
options: "List the names of the two sources below."
"Copy the first sentence of each source."
"Evaluate the credibility of the two sources below and justify which one is more reliable for the research question."
"Define the word credibility."
questions.rationale: Evaluation requires judgment supported by criteria. Items that ask students to judge and justify target higher cognitive levels than items that ask for recall.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a norm-referenced test to decide which students have mastered a specific unit's objectives. Why is this problematic?
options: Norm-referenced tests do not give numerical results
Norm-referenced tests are always unfair
Norm-referenced tests compare students to each other, so they do not show whether a student has met a defined standard
Norm-referenced tests cannot be scored
questions.rationale: Mastery decisions require criterion-referenced information tied to specified objectives. Norm-referenced results indicate relative ranking, which can mask whether the objectives were achieved.

questions.stem: A student's final grade report states: "Meets expectations on 4 of 5 standards; developing in standard 3." Which type of reporting is this?
options: Percentage-only reporting
Standards-based reporting
Curve-based reporting
Rank-order reporting
questions.rationale: Standards-based reports describe performance on specific learning goals, giving families clearer information than a single average.

questions.stem: A teacher computes a mean score of 72 and a median of 85 on a quiz. What does this difference most likely indicate?
options: The test is perfectly reliable
A few very high scores are pulling the mean up
A few very low scores are pulling the mean down, creating a negatively skewed distribution
All scores are the same
questions.rationale: When the mean is lower than the median, the distribution is typically negatively skewed by low outliers. The median better represents the typical student in this case.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to confirm that a rubric is fair before using it. Which step is most helpful?
options: Keep the rubric secret from students
Make the criteria more vague
Score several sample papers with a colleague using the rubric and discuss differences to refine the criteria
Use the rubric immediately and change it later
questions.rationale: Piloting a rubric with samples and discussing scoring differences improves clarity and consistency. Vague criteria and secrecy reduce fairness.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a short quiz after each lesson and records only whether students completed it, not the score, to encourage risk taking. What type of assessment use is this?
options: Norm-referenced placement
Low-stakes formative practice
Summative certification
High-stakes accountability
questions.rationale: Low-stakes quizzes provide practice and feedback without heavy grade consequences, encouraging students to learn from errors.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that students perform much better when problems are presented orally than on paper. Which hypothesis should the teacher test first?
options: Reading or written-language demands are interfering with demonstration of math understanding
The students have no math knowledge
The written version contains easier problems than the oral version
Oral questions are always easier
questions.rationale: A performance difference by format suggests that the medium may add barriers. The teacher can adjust the presentation while keeping the math demand constant.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to demonstrate mastery of a skill on at least two separate occasions before recording a proficiency grade. What is the primary rationale?
options: It removes the need for criteria
It makes grading harder on purpose
It guarantees students will reach mastery
A single performance may not be representative, so multiple data points improve confidence in the inference
questions.rationale: Multiple measures help ensure a score is not due to chance or an unusual day, which supports reliable decisions.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a cumulative final exam with 100 items. After scoring, the teacher computes the correlation between each item and the total test score and finds several items with very low or negative correlations. What should the teacher conclude?
options: The students did not read the items
The test is reliable
Those items are the best items on the test
Those items may not be measuring the same construct as the rest of the test or may be flawed, so they should be reviewed or revised
questions.rationale: Low or negative item-total correlations signal that high scorers do not perform better on the item, which suggests ambiguity, mis-keying, or a different construct.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to monitor students' reading growth every two weeks with a brief one-minute passage. This approach is most similar to
options: Curriculum-based measurement
A norm-referenced entrance exam
A diagnostic placement test
A summative portfolio
questions.rationale: Curriculum-based measurement uses brief, frequent, standardized probes to track progress over time and inform instructional decisions.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a rubric with four performance levels: Beginning, Developing, Proficient, and Advanced. What is the benefit of having defined levels?
options: The teacher no longer needs to read student work
Every student will receive Advanced
Students can see what each level of quality looks like and what to do to improve
Students will not need feedback
questions.rationale: Defined levels describe quality at each stage and clarify expectations, supporting self-assessment and feedback.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to collect evidence of student thinking during problem solving. Which technique best provides it?
options: Counting how many problems students complete
Checking only the final answers
Timing how quickly students finish
Asking students to think aloud or explain their reasoning as they solve the problem
questions.rationale: Explanations and think-alouds reveal reasoning and misconceptions that final answers alone might hide.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a performance task and finds that two students with identical final products received different scores because one student's work was scored first in the pile and the other last. Which strategy would best reduce this problem?
options: Score only the first half of the papers
Remove the rubric
Score each criterion across all papers in a randomized order and recheck a sample for consistency
Ask students to rank their own work
questions.rationale: Scoring order effects and rater drift reduce reliability. Randomizing order, scoring one criterion at a time, and rechecking samples promote consistency.

questions.stem: A principal reviews campus assessment data and sees that students perform lower in writing than in other areas for three years. Which action best reflects data-driven decision making?
options: Blame the students
Eliminate writing from the curriculum
Wait for a new set of data
Examine writing samples and item data, identify specific weaknesses, and implement and monitor targeted instructional changes
questions.rationale: Data-driven decisions require analyzing evidence to find specific needs, taking action, and checking whether the action works.

questions.stem: A teacher wants every student to receive useful information from a quiz within minutes. Which option accomplishes this best?
options: Wait until the next unit to return them
Use a digital quiz tool that provides immediate item-level results to the teacher and feedback to students
Grade the quizzes by hand over the weekend
Return only the class average
questions.rationale: Digital quizzes with instant results shorten the feedback loop so teachers can adjust instruction right away and students can see mistakes immediately.

questions.stem: Why might a teacher give students a rubric and examples of work at different quality levels before an assignment?
options: To avoid grading
To show what quality looks like so students can aim for the criteria
To make students copy the examples
To limit creativity
questions.rationale: Models and clear criteria help students understand expectations. Teachers should emphasize qualities rather than expect imitation.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to communicate high expectations to all students. Which verbal behavior best reflects this?
options: Rescuing struggling students by answering for them
Asking probing follow-up questions of all students, including those who are less confident, and expecting them to elaborate
Calling on higher achievers to answer difficult questions
Accepting one-word answers from some students
questions.rationale: Consistent follow-up and elaboration requests communicate that every student is capable. Rescuing and unequal questioning signal low expectations.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a verbal response to a student's incorrect answer: "Not quite. Tell me how you got that, and let's see where it changed." Which communication principle does this reflect?
options: Treating errors as information and prompting the student to reveal reasoning
Praising effort regardless of correctness
Ignoring the incorrect answer
Moving on to protect the student's feelings
questions.rationale: Responding to errors with inquiry helps uncover misconceptions and keeps the student engaged. It respects the student while focusing on thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that an English learner at the beginning proficiency level understands more than she can say. Which technique best supports her participation?
options: Require full-sentence oral answers immediately
Translate every lesson into her home language
Provide sentence frames, visuals, and opportunities to respond with gestures or partner talk before speaking to the whole class
Avoid asking her questions
questions.rationale: Language supports let students engage with content while building English. Allowing nonverbal and partner responses reduces anxiety and sustains participation.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to communicate with a student about missing work in a way that preserves the student's dignity. Which approach is best?
options: Speak privately, describe the specific concern, and ask what support the student needs to complete the work
Announce the missing work to the class
Assign a zero without comment
Send a note home without talking to the student
questions.rationale: Private, respectful conversations focused on problem-solving maintain trust and motivation. Public shaming and silent penalties harm relationships.

questions.stem: A teacher uses the word "summarize" in a direction, but students produce long retellings. What would most improve communication?
options: Eliminate summarizing tasks
Assume students were not listening
Use the same word and expect students to figure it out
Define the term, model a summary of a short text, and provide criteria such as length and key ideas
questions.rationale: Academic vocabulary needs explicit instruction and modeling. Examples and criteria make expectations visible.

questions.stem: A teacher begins a unit by telling students what they will learn, why it matters, and how they will show understanding. What is the main communication benefit?
options: The students will no longer need feedback
The lesson will take less time
Students understand the purpose and expectations, which supports engagement and self-monitoring
The teacher can avoid planning
questions.rationale: Sharing objectives and relevance gives students a clear picture of the goals. It supports motivation and helps them judge their own progress.

questions.stem: Which nonverbal behavior best communicates that a teacher values what a student is saying?
options: Crossing arms and looking away
Making eye contact, nodding, and facing the student
Checking the clock
Walking to the back of the room
questions.rationale: Positive body language such as eye contact and an open posture shows attention and respect. Negative cues can discourage students.

questions.stem: A teacher writes on a student's essay: "Your claim is vague. Rewrite it to state exactly what you will argue." How could the teacher make this written communication more effective?
options: Add more corrections in red ink
Use only abbreviations the student must decode
Pair the comment with a model of a strong claim and a brief note about what the student did well
Remove all written comments
questions.rationale: Effective feedback is specific, balanced, and supported by models. Examples show what the target looks like and acknowledgment of strengths maintains motivation.

questions.stem: A teacher communicates with families by sending weekly newsletters only in English, though many families speak Spanish. Which change would best improve communication?
options: Ask students to translate the newsletters at home
Stop sending newsletters
Send them in English and post a copy on the school website
Provide newsletters in families' home languages and use interpreters when needed
questions.rationale: Communicating in the language families understand ensures access and shows respect. Relying on students to translate is not reliable or appropriate.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a lesson and writes an objective that begins, "Students will be able to compare two characters using evidence from the text." Why is this a strong objective?
options: It states what students will feel during the lesson
It lists the activities the teacher will do
It names the textbook chapter only
It states an observable skill and the context in which it will be demonstrated
questions.rationale: Strong objectives focus on student performance using measurable verbs and conditions. They guide instruction and assessment.

questions.stem: A teacher begins planning a unit by deciding how students will demonstrate mastery before choosing activities. Which model does this reflect?
options: Spiral curriculum
Discovery learning
Backward design
Direct instruction only
questions.rationale: Backward design starts with desired results, determines acceptable evidence, and then plans learning experiences to reach those results.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews the TEKS for the grade above and the grade below the one she teaches. What is the main purpose of this vertical alignment review?
options: To understand prerequisite skills and how the current learning prepares students for future expectations
To avoid teaching difficult content
To reduce the number of assessments
To skip the current grade level
questions.rationale: Vertical alignment shows how skills progress across grades, helping teachers address gaps and build toward later learning.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a 5E lesson on photosynthesis. In which phase do students first investigate a phenomenon with minimal explanation from the teacher to build shared experiences?
options: Evaluate
Explore
Explain
Elaborate
questions.rationale: In the 5E model (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate), the Explore phase lets students investigate and gather observations before formal explanation.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use gradual release of responsibility in teaching a writing strategy. Which sequence is correct?
options: Have students practice in pairs, then explain the strategy
Model the strategy, practice together with guidance, then have students apply it independently
Present the strategy once and move on
Assign independent work, then model the strategy
questions.rationale: Gradual release moves from teacher modeling (I do) to guided practice (we do) to independent practice (you do), ensuring support is withdrawn as skill increases.

questions.stem: At the start of a lesson, a teacher displays a short video clip related to the topic and asks students what they notice. What is the primary purpose of this activity?
options: To replace direct instruction
To assign a final grade
To capture interest and activate prior knowledge
To review last year's content
questions.rationale: Anticipatory sets build interest and connect new learning to prior knowledge. They prepare students for the lesson but do not replace instruction.

questions.stem: A teacher's lesson includes a long lecture followed by a quiz. Many students struggle to recall the content. Which modification best reflects principles of learning?
options: Ask students to take more notes silently
Remove the quiz
Break the lecture into shorter segments with opportunities for students to process the information through discussion or practice
Make the lecture longer
questions.rationale: Chunking and active processing support memory by reducing cognitive load and allowing students to rehearse and organize new information.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a unit in which students revisit fractions in September, in December, and again in March, each time at greater depth. Which curriculum principle does this reflect?
options: Curriculum narrowing
Pacing guide compression
Spiral review
Tracking
questions.rationale: A spiral approach returns to concepts repeatedly with increasing complexity, which strengthens retention and understanding through distributed practice.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to solve real-world problems that connect science, math, and writing. Which type of unit is most appropriate?
options: A unit of isolated worksheets
A lecture-only unit
A unit with no assessment
An interdisciplinary project-based unit with clear objectives from each subject
questions.rationale: Interdisciplinary projects integrate skills across content areas and give authentic purposes. Objectives from each subject ensure rigor and alignment.

questions.stem: A teacher plans for a class in which some students read two grade levels below and others above grade level. Which planning decision best supports all learners with the same learning objective?
options: Give all students the same grade-level text without support
Give advanced readers extra homework only
Provide texts at varied levels on the same topic and tasks that all lead to the same objective
Lower the objective for struggling readers
questions.rationale: Differentiating process and content while keeping the objective constant provides access and challenge. Lowering the objective limits opportunity.

questions.stem: What is the role of a closing activity in a lesson?
options: To give homework without explanation
To start a new topic
To help students summarize their learning and give the teacher evidence of understanding
To end the class early
questions.rationale: A closing activity brings the lesson to a purposeful end, reinforcing key ideas and providing a quick check on what students learned.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a pacing guide moves faster than her students can master the content. What is the best response?
options: Follow the pacing guide exactly regardless of results
Skip the content that is difficult
Stop using assessments
Adjust pacing based on evidence of student learning while keeping the essential standards in focus
questions.rationale: Pacing guides are tools. Teachers should use assessment data to adjust the pace and ensure students master the essential knowledge and skills.

questions.stem: After an observation, an administrator tells a teacher that questions asked were mostly recall-level. What is the most professional response?
options: Dismiss the feedback as subjective
Stop asking questions
Reflect on the feedback, review lesson questions, and plan higher-level questions for upcoming lessons
Argue that the administrator does not understand the class
questions.rationale: Reflective practitioners use feedback to adjust practice. Setting a specific improvement goal turns observation into growth.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to learn a new strategy for supporting English learners. Which professional development option is likely to lead to the greatest change in classroom practice?
options: Reading a brochure
Attending a conference without applying the ideas
Ongoing, job-embedded learning with modeling, classroom practice, and follow-up coaching
A one-time lecture with no follow-up
questions.rationale: Research shows that sustained, job-embedded professional development with coaching changes practice more than one-time events.

questions.stem: Texas teachers must renew a standard certificate periodically by completing continuing professional education. Which statement is accurate?
options: Educators renew by retaking the certification exam every year
Certificates never need renewal
Educators holding a standard certificate must complete continuing professional education hours on a five-year renewal cycle
Renewal is required only when changing districts
questions.rationale: Standard certificates in Texas are renewed every five years after completing the required CPE hours. Requirements are set by SBEC and can include specific topics.

questions.stem: A classroom teacher and a paraprofessional work together daily. The teacher wants to maximize the paraprofessional's contribution. Which practice is best?
options: Have the paraprofessional make grading decisions
Assign the paraprofessional to handle all instruction for struggling students
Share lesson plans in advance, define roles clearly, and communicate regularly about student needs
Keep communication minimal
questions.rationale: Teachers retain responsibility for instruction and assessment, and effective teams plan together and clarify roles. Paraprofessionals support under the teacher's direction.

questions.stem: Two colleagues disagree about how to handle a team project. Which action best reflects professional conflict resolution?
options: Complain about the colleague to other teachers
Refuse to work together
Meet privately, listen to each other's perspectives, and focus on shared goals for students
Post about the disagreement on social media
questions.rationale: Professional collaboration includes respectful communication and a focus on student outcomes. Gossip and public complaints damage trust.

questions.stem: A campus uses a data team protocol. Which sequence best reflects the cycle used by effective data teams?
options: Collect data, file it, and move on
Identify a focus, ignore data, and hope for improvement
Analyze data, identify a focus area, plan instructional strategies, implement, and monitor results
Implement strategies, collect data later, and then choose a focus
questions.rationale: Effective data teams follow a continuous improvement cycle: examine the data, set a goal, choose strategies, apply them, and measure again.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a small study in her own classroom to test whether a new vocabulary routine improves quiz scores. Which term describes this process?
options: Action research
Peer tutoring
Curriculum mapping
Norm referencing
questions.rationale: Action research is systematic inquiry conducted by teachers to improve their own practice by planning, acting, observing, and reflecting.

questions.stem: A teacher shares a successful lesson plan with team members who teach the same course. Which professional value does this reflect?
options: Avoidance of feedback
Isolation
Competition among colleagues
Collaboration for the benefit of all students
questions.rationale: Sharing resources builds a collaborative culture and benefits students across classrooms.

questions.stem: In Texas, teachers are evaluated using T-TESS. What is an important purpose of this system?
options: To support professional growth through observation, feedback, and goal setting
To replace all student assessments
To determine student grades
To rank teachers against each other publicly
questions.rationale: T-TESS is a teacher appraisal and growth system based on a rubric of effective practices. It uses goal setting, observations, and conferences.

questions.stem: A teacher is asked to serve on the campus improvement committee. Which contribution best reflects professional responsibility?
options: Pushing only for personal preferences
Using the meeting to criticize students
Sharing instructional insights and data from the classroom to help set priorities
Remaining silent to avoid conflict
questions.rationale: Participating in school improvement means offering informed perspectives and supporting shared goals for student learning.

questions.stem: A teacher has students use a tablet to look up the definition of a word and copy it into a notebook. According to the SAMR model, this is best described as
options: Augmentation with substantial new functionality
Redefinition, because the task could not exist without technology
Substitution, because the technology replaces a dictionary with no functional change
Modification, because the task is significantly redesigned
questions.rationale: SAMR describes levels of technology integration. Substitution replaces a traditional tool with a digital one with no functional change.

questions.stem: A teacher has students collaborate in real time on a shared document with peers from another school, adding comments and revisions. Which SAMR level is most likely reached?
options: Substitution
Augmentation with no benefit
No integration
Modification or redefinition, because the technology enables collaboration and feedback that would not be possible otherwise
questions.rationale: Real-time collaboration with a remote audience significantly redesigns the task and creates new learning possibilities.

questions.stem: A student who is blind uses a screen reader to access class materials. Which teacher action best supports accessibility?
options: Provide materials in paper only
Send only scanned images of documents
Rely on color alone to convey information
Provide digital materials with text descriptions for images and a logical heading structure
questions.rationale: Accessible design includes alt text, structure, and compatible formats. Images of text and color-only cues are not readable by screen readers.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to evaluate online sources for a research project. Which criterion is most important to teach?
options: Choosing the first search result
Using only the source with the most social media shares
Evaluating the author's expertise, purpose, evidence, and currency
Preferring sources with the most advertisements
questions.rationale: Information literacy includes checking credibility, bias, evidence, and timeliness. Ranking in search results does not guarantee reliability.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use a free online app that requires students under 13 to create accounts with their names and email addresses. What legal concern should the teacher consider first?
options: Whether the app has a mobile version
Whether the app is popular
Children's online privacy laws, such as COPPA, which limit collection of personal information from children under 13 without verifiable parental consent
Copyright of the app name
questions.rationale: COPPA regulates online services collecting personal data from children under 13. Schools should follow district approval processes and confirm privacy practices before using such tools.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to reduce the digital divide for students who lack home internet access. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Require all assignments to be completed online at home
Provide offline-accessible materials, allow time at school to complete digital work, and connect families with district resources
Penalize students without internet access
Assume all students can use a phone
questions.rationale: Equitable technology use means providing alternatives and supports for students with limited access. Penalizing students for lack of access is unfair.

questions.stem: A teacher teaches students not to share passwords, to think before posting, and to respect others online. Which concept is being taught?
options: Web design
Digital citizenship
Data mining
Keyboarding speed
questions.rationale: Digital citizenship teaches safe, ethical, and responsible technology use.

questions.stem: A teacher is deciding between two educational apps. One has more features, and the other is a better match for the learning objective and the students' needs. According to sound technology integration principles, which should the teacher choose?
options: The app that best supports the objective and the learners, regardless of the number of features
The app that costs more
The app with the most downloads
The app with more features
questions.rationale: Technology should serve learning goals. Selecting tools based on fit with objectives and student needs, not novelty or features, is the guiding principle.

questions.stem: A student with a physical disability that makes handwriting difficult uses speech-to-text software to complete essays. This is an example of
options: A violation of academic integrity
A modification that lowers expectations
A distraction from learning
Assistive technology that provides access without changing the learning goal
questions.rationale: Assistive technology helps students with disabilities participate in learning. Speech-to-text supports composition while the writing expectations remain the same.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to compare two solutions to a math problem and decide which is more efficient, explaining their reasoning. Which level of Bloom's revised taxonomy is primarily addressed?
options: Remember
Apply
Understand
Evaluate
questions.rationale: Evaluating involves making judgments based on criteria, such as efficiency, and justifying them.

questions.stem: A teacher poses an ill-structured problem with no single correct answer, such as designing a plan to reduce lunchroom waste. What is the main benefit of such tasks?
options: They avoid the need for evidence
They require students to define the problem, gather information, and weigh evidence to propose and justify solutions
They are easier to grade than multiple-choice items
They have a single correct answer
questions.rationale: Open-ended, real-world problems develop higher-order thinking and require judgment, reasoning, and communication.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to promote metacognition during reading. Which practice is most effective?
options: Teaching students to pause and ask themselves whether they understand and what strategies they can use when they do not
Asking students to memorize the text
Telling students to read faster
Assigning longer texts
questions.rationale: Metacognition is awareness and control of one's own thinking. Comprehension monitoring and fix-up strategies help students manage understanding.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a data table and asks them to identify a trend, make a prediction, and explain the reasoning. Which skill set is most clearly being developed?
options: Handwriting fluency
Rote memorization
Following oral directions
Analysis and inference using evidence
questions.rationale: Interpreting data, predicting, and explaining involve analyzing evidence and drawing conclusions.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to avoid confirmation bias when researching a controversial topic. Which assignment best supports this goal?
options: Require students to use one source
Have students vote and move on
Assign students only to research sources that agree with them
Ask students to find and evaluate credible sources representing multiple perspectives before forming a position
questions.rationale: Examining diverse perspectives helps students avoid selectively seeking only agreeing information and builds balanced reasoning.

questions.stem: A teacher uses the Socratic method in a lesson on a literary text. What is her primary role during the discussion?
options: To remain silent throughout
To grade responses in real time
To pose probing questions that push students to clarify, justify, and examine assumptions
To lecture and give the correct interpretation
questions.rationale: In Socratic discussion, the teacher guides with questions that provoke deeper analysis, while students construct meaning together.

questions.stem: Which student response shows the strongest critical thinking about a claim in a news article?
options: "I like the author's picture."
"I think this is true because it was on the internet."
"The article is long."
"The author states this as fact, but I looked for the source of the statistic and found it comes from a group with a stake in the outcome."
questions.rationale: Critical thinkers examine evidence, sources, and potential bias instead of accepting claims at face value.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to explain how two historical events are connected and to support their explanation with evidence from primary sources. Which depth-of-knowledge level is most likely?
options: Level 1, recall
Level 4 only, extended project
Level 3, strategic thinking
Level 2 only, skill application
questions.rationale: DOK 3 requires reasoning, planning, and using evidence to support conclusions. Linking events with sources fits strategic thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher notices students can solve routine problems but struggle when the context changes. Which instructional strategy best promotes transfer?
options: Teach only the procedure
Give more problems of the same type
Test only with familiar problems
Provide varied examples, ask students to identify underlying principles, and practice applying them in new contexts
questions.rationale: Transfer improves when students see multiple contexts and abstract the common structure. Repeating the same type builds procedural fluency but not flexible application.

questions.stem: During a science investigation, a teacher asks students to predict an outcome before testing it. What is the main benefit of requiring predictions?
options: The teacher can skip discussion
Students activate prior knowledge and can compare results to their expectations, which can reveal and revise misconceptions
The investigation will be shorter
Students will always predict correctly
questions.rationale: Predictions make students' thinking visible and create cognitive conflict when results differ, which fosters conceptual change.

questions.stem: A teacher presents a fifth grader with two identical glasses of water, then pours one into a tall, thin glass. The student insists the tall glass holds more. According to Piaget, this response most likely shows a lack of
options: Zone of proximal development, which Piaget defined
Formal operational reasoning, which develops in early childhood
Object permanence, characteristic of infancy
Conservation, characteristic of the preoperational and early concrete stages
questions.rationale: Conservation is the understanding that quantity stays the same despite changes in appearance. It develops during the concrete operational stage.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a struggling reader a partner who reads aloud with her, provides prompts, and gradually lets her read more independently. Which theorist's concept does this best illustrate?
options: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development with scaffolding
Piaget's equilibration
Erikson's identity versus role confusion
Skinner's operant conditioning
questions.rationale: Vygotsky emphasized learning through social interaction with a more knowledgeable other who provides support that is gradually withdrawn as competence grows.

questions.stem: Which type of learning activity is most developmentally appropriate for second graders studying plants?
options: Planting seeds, observing growth, and recording what they see
Listening to a 45-minute lecture
Taking a written essay test on plant biology
Reading a long abstract article without visuals
questions.rationale: Young learners benefit from concrete, hands-on experiences linked to real objects, with short reflective tasks.

questions.stem: A middle school teacher notices that students often care intensely about peer opinions and struggle to see consequences of risky choices. Which developmental explanation best fits this?
options: Adolescents are not influenced by peers
Adolescents think exactly like adults
Adolescents have completed cognitive development
Adolescents are developing abstract reasoning and executive function while social acceptance becomes especially important
questions.rationale: Early adolescence is marked by growth in abstract thought, still-developing prefrontal regulation, and heightened sensitivity to peer approval.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a concept map to help students connect new vocabulary to ideas they already know. This reflects which learning principle?
options: Prior knowledge has no effect on learning
New information should be kept separate from past knowledge
Meaningful learning occurs when new information is connected to existing schemas
Learning occurs best through isolated memorization
questions.rationale: Constructivist and cognitive theories hold that learners build understanding by linking new ideas to existing knowledge structures.
