questions.stem: A student who is anxious about a presentation freezes and cannot recall material he knows well. Which concept from information processing best explains this?
options: Long-term memory has a fixed capacity
Learning styles determine memory
Sensory memory is permanent
High stress can overload working memory and interfere with retrieval
questions.rationale: Anxiety consumes working memory resources, which can block access to stored information.

questions.stem: A teacher greets students at the door, learns about their interests, and checks in with those who seem upset. Which developmental principle is she supporting?
options: Emotional safety and positive relationships are foundational for learning
Students learn best when anxious
Relationships matter only in early childhood
Social development is separate from academic growth
questions.rationale: Learners who feel safe and connected are more able to engage cognitively. Relationships matter at every age.

questions.stem: A teacher knows that Isabel, a student identified as gifted, finishes tasks early and becomes bored. Which strategy best addresses her needs?
options: Assign more of the same worksheets
Move her to a lower grade
Provide extension tasks that deepen complexity and encourage independent inquiry
Ask her to tutor others all the time
questions.rationale: Gifted learners need greater depth and complexity, not more of the same. Occasional peer collaboration is fine, but constant tutoring does not meet her needs.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews her class data and notices that students from some groups are underrepresented in advanced-level activities despite similar test scores. Which action best addresses this equity issue?
options: Lower expectations for those students
Review referral and selection practices, use multiple measures, and provide supports and access to advanced opportunities
Make advanced activities more difficult to enter
Leave the practices as they are
questions.rationale: Equity requires examining how opportunities are distributed and removing barriers. Using multiple measures and supports promotes fair access.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a student's cultural background as a source of examples in a math lesson, such as using a local market in word problems. This reflects which approach?
options: Tracking
Rote learning
Behaviorism
Culturally responsive teaching
questions.rationale: Culturally responsive teaching connects instruction to students' cultural knowledge and experiences, making learning relevant and respectful.

questions.stem: A student with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder frequently leaves his seat. His 504 plan allows movement breaks. Which classroom practice best honors the plan while keeping instruction on track?
options: Provide scheduled brief movement tasks, such as delivering materials, and let him use a standing desk option
Remove him from group work
Require him to remain seated all period
Send him to the hallway whenever he moves
questions.rationale: Accommodations should be implemented in ways that support learning. Planned movement addresses the need without disrupting class.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to ensure all learners can access the lesson by providing multiple means of representation, expression, and engagement. Which framework is this?
options: Competency-based promotion
Universal Design for Learning
Behavior contracting
Response to Intervention
questions.rationale: UDL proactively designs flexible instruction so that diverse learners have options. It is guided by three principles: representation, action and expression, and engagement.

questions.stem: A student identified as an emergent bilingual speaks fluent social English but struggles with academic reading. Which concept explains this?
options: Academic language develops before social language
Language proficiency is the same in all contexts
Social language (BICS) develops sooner than academic language (CALP)
Fluent speakers cannot have academic difficulties
questions.rationale: Cummins distinguished conversational fluency (BICS) from the academic language proficiency (CALP) needed for school, which can take much longer.

questions.stem: A student in a general education class is performing well below grade level in reading and has not been formally evaluated. According to the Response to Intervention approach, what should the teacher do first?
options: Immediately place the student in special education
Wait until the end of the year
Retain the student without further data
Provide research-based interventions, monitor progress, and share data with the campus team
questions.rationale: RTI/MTSS uses tiered support and progress monitoring to determine whether instruction is effective. Data collected can inform decisions about further evaluation.

questions.stem: A teacher groups students for a reading activity based on current skills. After two weeks, she regroups them based on new assessment data. This is an example of
options: Random seating
Whole-class instruction only
Flexible grouping
Permanent ability grouping
questions.rationale: Flexible grouping changes group membership based on assessment data and learning goals, preventing students from being locked into a level.

questions.stem: A student's family recently experienced job loss, and the student has been arriving late and tired. Which response best reflects sensitivity to student diversity?
options: Mark the student tardy without comment
Approach with empathy, connect the family to school resources, and adjust expectations for logistics while maintaining learning goals
Tell the class about the family's situation
Lower the student's grades for tardiness
questions.rationale: Teachers should recognize the effects of circumstances on learning and respond supportively and confidentially while holding high expectations.

questions.stem: A teacher implements a station rotation with tasks at three readiness levels, each aligned to the same standard. During the rotation, he meets with a small group for targeted instruction. Which aspect of differentiation does this best illustrate?
options: Reducing standards for some students
Using ongoing assessment to match tasks and teacher support to readiness
Replacing assessment with observation only
Eliminating whole-class instruction forever
questions.rationale: Effective differentiation uses data to tailor tasks and support while keeping the same standard.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a lesson on persuasive writing and includes a graphic organizer, a word bank, and an exemplar for students who need extra support. These are best described as
options: Penalties
Standardized procedures
Distractions
Scaffolds
questions.rationale: Scaffolds provide temporary supports that help students reach the objective and are removed as proficiency grows.

questions.stem: A student who is deaf joins a class with an interpreter. How should the teacher address the student during instruction?
options: Talk very quickly
Speak only to the interpreter
Speak directly to the student, not the interpreter, and allow time for interpretation
Avoid asking the student questions
questions.rationale: Teachers should address the student directly and ensure pacing allows for interpretation. Treating the interpreter as the audience excludes the student.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a student from a culture that values quiet respect for adults does not volunteer answers. How should the teacher interpret this behavior?
options: As possibly reflecting cultural norms, and offer varied participation formats that value the student's contributions
As a reason to stop calling on the student
As a sign that the student is unintelligent
As disrespect for the teacher
questions.rationale: Understanding cultural differences helps teachers avoid misinterpretation. Small-group or written participation can give the student comfortable ways to contribute.

questions.stem: A teacher plans to use students' home languages as a resource, allowing bilingual students to discuss ideas in either language before writing in English. Which principle supports this?
options: Bilingualism is a disadvantage
English immersion with no home language is always best
Using home languages slows English learning
Students' home language knowledge can support learning in a second language
questions.rationale: Research on bilingual education indicates that leveraging first-language skills promotes concept understanding and transfer to English.

questions.stem: A teacher designs a task for a student with an IEP that includes modified grade-level content. Which statement about modifications is most accurate?
options: Modifications apply to all students
Teachers may modify expectations at will
A modification is the same as an accommodation
A modification changes what the student is expected to learn or demonstrate and must be authorized by the ARD committee
questions.rationale: Accommodations change how a student accesses learning; modifications change what is expected. Modifications for students receiving special education are decided by the ARD committee.

questions.stem: On the first day of class, a teacher asks students to help create classroom norms and then posts them. What is the main benefit of this approach?
options: Students gain ownership of expectations and are more likely to follow them
Students will never break the norms
The norms will be identical to those in other classes
The teacher avoids setting expectations
questions.rationale: Involving students in creating norms builds responsibility and community. Teachers still guide the process.

questions.stem: A student makes a joke that insults classmates' accents. Which teacher response best supports a positive climate?
options: Ignore it
Address the comment privately or briefly in class, reaffirm respect norms, and check in with affected students
Embarrass the student publicly
Laugh along with the joke
questions.rationale: Prompt, respectful responses that reaffirm norms and support affected students maintain an inclusive environment.

questions.stem: Which classroom arrangement best supports an inclusive learning environment?
options: Flexible seating that allows clear sightlines, access for all students, and spaces for collaboration
Seats fixed for the entire year
Seating based solely on test scores
Seating arranged to isolate students with disabilities
questions.rationale: Physical arrangement affects access and interaction. Inclusive layouts consider mobility, sightlines, and collaboration.

questions.stem: A teacher displays student work from all students over the course of the year and highlights different strengths. What is the primary effect of this practice?
options: It helps every student feel valued and see models of quality work
It replaces grading
It creates competition among students
It shames students with lower grades
questions.rationale: Showcasing varied work builds belonging and provides examples without ranking students.

questions.stem: A student calls out answers repeatedly during direct instruction. Which response best reflects a proactive approach?
options: Remind the class of the participation procedure, reinforce students who raise hands, and provide the student a private cue
Ignore the student for the rest of the year
Announce the student's name each time to the class
Send the student to the office the first time
questions.rationale: Proactive management teaches and reinforces expected behavior, with private redirection when needed.

questions.stem: Mr. Lopez notices two students off-task while he works with a small group. He moves closer to them without interrupting the group. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Time-out
Punishment
Extinction
Proximity control
questions.rationale: Proximity control uses physical closeness to redirect behavior with minimal disruption.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a student a choice between two ways to complete an assignment. Which motivation principle does this support?
options: Learned helplessness
Punishment
Extrinsic reward
Autonomy, a component of self-determination theory
questions.rationale: Providing meaningful choices supports autonomy, which increases intrinsic motivation.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to increase student engagement in a lesson on fractions. Which strategy is most likely to do so?
options: Lecture for the entire period
Assign extra worksheets
Include a hands-on task using fraction manipulatives with partner discussion
Have students copy notes silently
questions.rationale: Active, social, and concrete learning tasks increase engagement and understanding.

questions.stem: A teacher provides a student who has been sent out of class several times with a check-in/check-out routine, where the student meets an adult at the start and end of each day and receives feedback on goals. This is an example of
options: A tier 2 behavioral support
A tier 1 universal practice for all students
A tier 3 intensive intervention
A disciplinary consequence
questions.rationale: Check-in/check-out is a targeted, tier 2 intervention that provides structure, feedback, and positive adult contact.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that her class is calmer when she uses a consistent opening routine. What principle does this illustrate?
options: Students prefer chaos
Routines limit creativity
Predictable routines reduce anxiety and increase time on task
Routines are only for young students
questions.rationale: Predictable structures help students know what to do, which supports a positive learning climate.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to build a positive relationship with families at the start of the year. Which first step is most effective?
options: Communicate only when grades drop
Wait until a problem occurs to contact families
Send a list of rules only
Send a welcoming message sharing contact information and positive expectations for the year
questions.rationale: Early positive outreach establishes trust and opens communication before problems arise.

questions.stem: During a conference, a parent says she is worried because her child often says school is too hard. Which teacher response is best?
options: Blame the parent
Listen, acknowledge her concern, share specific evidence of the child's progress and needs, and discuss how to work together
Say the child is fine and change the subject
Tell her the child is lazy
questions.rationale: Effective conferences involve listening, using data, and collaborating on next steps.

questions.stem: A parent emails a teacher late at night with an angry message about a grade. What is the most professional response?
options: Respond calmly within a reasonable time, acknowledge the concern, and offer to discuss it in a conference
Reply immediately with an equally angry tone
Ignore the message
Forward the message to the class
questions.rationale: Professional communication stays respectful, timely, and solution oriented, and moves complex issues to a conversation.

questions.stem: A teacher shares a student's strengths and a specific goal during a parent conference. Why is it helpful to begin with strengths?
options: It builds trust and frames challenges as areas for growth rather than deficits
It avoids discussing the problem
It guarantees the parent will agree with the teacher
It is required by law
questions.rationale: Starting with strengths establishes a positive tone and shows the teacher knows the child well.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a family night to share how parents can support reading at home. Which feature would make the event most useful?
options: Hands-on demonstrations, take-home materials, and translation for families who need it
A long lecture with no materials
A presentation using only educational jargon
An event at the same time as other school events
questions.rationale: Practical, accessible events help families apply strategies at home.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to partner with the family of a student who is chronically absent. Which approach is most likely to be productive?
options: Assume the family does not value education
Ask about barriers in a nonjudgmental way, share the impact of absences, and collaborate on a plan with school supports
Threaten legal action in the first call
Report the family to authorities without a conversation
questions.rationale: Understanding barriers such as transportation, health, or work schedules and working together increases attendance more effectively than blame.

questions.stem: A student refuses to stand for the Pledge of Allegiance because of personal beliefs, and a teacher wants to require participation. Under West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, what is the legal position?
options: Schools may require participation if the policy is posted
Schools may require it if a majority of students agree
Schools cannot compel students to salute the flag or recite the pledge
Schools may require participation during state testing only
questions.rationale: In Barnette (1943), the Court held that compelling students to salute the flag violates the First Amendment. Texas law also lets a parent request that a child be excused from reciting the pledge.

questions.stem: A high school principal removes an article about teen pregnancy from a student newspaper produced in a journalism class as part of the curriculum. Which case most directly supports the principal's authority?
options: Plyler v. Doe, which governs school newspapers
Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier, which lets schools exercise editorial control over school-sponsored student expression for legitimate educational reasons
Tinker v. Des Moines, which prohibits any limit on student expression
Goss v. Lopez, which protects publication rights
questions.rationale: Hazelwood (1988) held that schools may regulate school-sponsored expression, such as a curricular newspaper, if the restriction is reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns.

questions.stem: A family living in a motel after losing their home tries to enroll their child, but the school asks for proof of residency and immunization records. Under the McKinney-Vento Act, what must the school do?
options: Send the child to a different district
Enroll the child immediately while the family works to obtain the documents, with help from the district homeless liaison
Enroll the child only after a thirty-day waiting period
Refuse enrollment until all documents are provided
questions.rationale: McKinney-Vento requires schools to enroll children experiencing homelessness immediately, even without documents, and to provide transportation to the school of origin when feasible.

questions.stem: A high school student becomes pregnant, and a teacher suggests she transfer to an alternative school. Which federal law most directly prohibits excluding her because of pregnancy?
options: The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act
The Every Student Succeeds Act
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act
Title IX of the Education Amendments, which prohibits sex discrimination in federally funded education programs
questions.rationale: Title IX protects students from discrimination based on sex, including pregnancy and parenting status. Schools must allow participation and provide reasonable accommodations such as excused absences for medical needs.

questions.stem: In Castañeda v. Pickard, a case from Texas, a federal court set a three-part test for evaluating programs serving English learners. Which of the following is one of the parts?
options: The program must teach in English only
The program must be based on sound educational theory, be implemented with adequate resources, and be evaluated to show that it works
The program must be offered only to students with disabilities
The program must exclude students from grade-level content
questions.rationale: Castañeda held that districts must adopt a program based on sound theory, implement it effectively with qualified staff and materials, and evaluate it, changing it if students are not overcoming language barriers.

questions.stem: In Endrew F. v. Douglas County School District, the Supreme Court addressed the standard for the educational benefit of an IEP. What did the Court hold?
options: An IEP must be reasonably calculated to enable a child to make progress appropriate in light of the child's circumstances
An IEP need only provide trivial educational benefit
An IEP must guarantee the child reaches the top of the class
An IEP is required only for students in high school
questions.rationale: Endrew F. (2017) raised the bar beyond merely more than de minimis benefit; IEP goals should be appropriately ambitious and reflect the child's circumstances.

questions.stem: A parent files for a due process hearing after disagreeing with a proposed change in the student's special education placement. While the dispute is pending, what does the IDEA stay-put provision generally require?
options: The student receives services only at home
The student is moved immediately to the proposed placement
The student remains in the current educational placement unless the parents and district agree otherwise
The student is removed from school until the dispute is resolved
questions.rationale: The stay-put rule protects continuity of services by keeping the child in the last agreed-upon placement during proceedings.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use images in a class presentation without risking copyright infringement. Which choice is safest?
options: Use any image found through a search engine
Use any image because the presentation is for school
Use any image if it is not watermarked
Use images that are in the public domain or licensed under Creative Commons terms that permit the intended use, and credit the source as required
questions.rationale: Public domain and openly licensed works can be used according to their terms. Educational purpose alone does not make every use lawful.

questions.stem: Under Section 504, which statement best describes who qualifies as a person with a disability?
options: Only students who score below grade level
Only students who qualify for special education under IDEA
An individual with a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities
Only students with physical disabilities
questions.rationale: Section 504 uses a broader definition than IDEA. A student may qualify without needing specially designed instruction, for example one with a condition requiring accommodations for equal access.

questions.stem: A Spanish-speaking parent will attend an ARD meeting. Which action best protects the parent's right to participate?
options: Ask the student to translate the meeting
Conduct the meeting in English and mail a summary later
Provide an interpreter and translated documents so the parent can understand and take part in decisions
Hold the meeting without the parent if the parent cannot understand English
questions.rationale: IDEA requires schools to take steps to ensure the parent understands the proceedings, including providing an interpreter when needed. Meaningful parent participation is a core safeguard.

questions.stem: Texas uses the T-TESS rubric to describe effective teaching. Which set lists the four domains?
options: Planning, Instruction, Learning Environment, and Professional Practices and Responsibilities
Assessment, Technology, Finance, and Facilities
Recruitment, Retention, Compensation, and Evaluation
Curriculum, Discipline, Athletics, and Fine Arts
questions.rationale: The T-TESS rubric organizes teaching practice into four domains. Observers use evidence in each domain to support growth conversations.

questions.stem: A group of teachers plan a lesson together, one teaches it while the others observe student learning, and then they revise the lesson based on what they saw. Which professional practice is this?
options: Curriculum compacting
Teacher-proof instruction
Norm-referenced evaluation
Lesson study
questions.rationale: Lesson study is a collaborative cycle of planning, teaching, observing student learning, and refining a lesson. It focuses attention on student thinking rather than teacher performance.

questions.stem: An elementary teacher notices that students who experience repeated success on tasks begin to feel capable and work harder, while those who experience repeated failure begin to say they are not smart. Which Erikson stage best fits these students?
options: Trust versus mistrust
Industry versus inferiority
Identity versus role confusion
Integrity versus despair
questions.rationale: Erikson proposed that children ages about 6 to 12 face the challenge of developing competence through mastering skills. Repeated failure can lead to feelings of inferiority.

questions.stem: A middle school student refuses to cheat because "rules keep society running and everyone has to follow them." According to Kohlberg, this reasoning reflects which level of moral development?
options: Preconventional morality, with a focus on avoiding punishment
Amoral reasoning
Conventional morality, with a focus on law and order
Postconventional morality, with a focus on universal principles
questions.rationale: Kohlberg's conventional level includes reasoning based on social expectations and maintaining order. Preconventional reasoning focuses on consequences, and postconventional reasoning focuses on abstract ethical principles.

questions.stem: A teacher has a respected older student demonstrate a science procedure while younger students watch, hoping they will see that people like them can succeed. This best applies which concept from Bandura?
options: Assimilation and accommodation
Object permanence
Operant conditioning through punishment
Observational learning and self-efficacy through modeling
questions.rationale: Bandura's social learning theory holds that people learn by watching models, and seeing similar others succeed can strengthen self-efficacy.

questions.stem: A teacher ends each week with a short, low-stakes quiz on material from the past four weeks rather than rereading notes. Cognitive research would describe the main benefit of this practice as
options: Students retain more when they avoid recalling material
Quizzing only measures learning and does not affect it
Cramming is the most effective way to retain information
Retrieval practice strengthens long-term retention more than rereading
questions.rationale: The testing effect shows that actively retrieving information from memory improves later recall compared with passive review.

questions.stem: A teacher plans practice on a skill by returning to it at increasing intervals over several weeks, mixing it with other problem types. Which two principles of learning does this reflect?
options: Spaced practice and interleaving
Rote repetition and cramming
Overlearning and isolation
Massed practice and blocking
questions.rationale: Distributing practice over time (spacing) and mixing problem types (interleaving) improve retention and the ability to choose appropriate strategies, even though they feel harder in the moment.

questions.stem: To support a child's development, a teacher considers the child's family, neighborhood, and cultural context in addition to the classroom. Which theory emphasizes these nested influences?
options: Piaget's stage theory
Skinner's operant conditioning
Kohlberg's moral development theory
Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory
questions.rationale: Bronfenbrenner described development as shaped by interacting systems, from the immediate microsystem of family and school to broader cultural influences.

questions.stem: A teacher is helping a student who frequently loses track of multi-step directions, forgets materials, and has difficulty planning long assignments. Which cognitive skills are most likely involved?
options: Phonological awareness
Sensory memory only
Visual acuity
Executive functions such as working memory, planning, and organization
questions.rationale: Executive functions are mental skills for planning, organizing, and holding information in mind. Explicit supports such as checklists, chunked tasks, and routines help students strengthen them.

questions.stem: A teacher presents a vocabulary word with a picture, a definition, and a short example sentence, and asks students to describe it aloud. This approach draws on which learning principle?
options: Dual coding, in which verbal and visual representations together strengthen memory
Extrinsic motivation
Operant conditioning
Learned helplessness
questions.rationale: Dual coding theory says information encoded both verbally and visually is easier to remember than information in one form alone.

questions.stem: According to Krashen's input hypothesis, English learners acquire language best when exposed to input that is
options: Slightly beyond their current level but still understandable (i+1)
Far above their level with no support
Below their level so they feel comfortable
Presented only in writing
questions.rationale: Krashen's i+1 describes comprehensible input that is one step beyond the learner's current competence, made understandable with context and support.

questions.stem: A second-grade student reads slowly, confuses similar sounds, spells unpredictably, and has trouble matching letters to sounds despite good listening comprehension and adequate instruction. Which concern should the teacher raise with the campus team?
options: A possible reading difficulty such as dyslexia, which involves difficulty with accurate and fluent word reading and spelling
A gift for visual learning
A hearing impairment only
A lack of effort
questions.rationale: Dyslexia is a neurobiological difference that affects word reading, decoding, and spelling, usually due to phonological processing difficulty. Texas requires screening and appropriate instruction.

questions.stem: A teacher assigns students tasks on the same concept at different levels of complexity, based on readiness, so each group works at a level that is challenging but achievable. Which differentiation strategy is this?
options: Jigsaw
Whole-class lecture
Tiered assignments
Learning centers with no readiness plan
questions.rationale: Tiered assignments adjust the complexity of a task while keeping the same essential understanding, matching challenge to readiness.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a four-square organizer that asks for the definition, characteristics, examples, and non-examples of a new term. Which strategy is this?
options: A KWL chart
The Frayer model
A cloze procedure
A running record
questions.rationale: The Frayer model deepens vocabulary understanding by having learners define a concept, list attributes, and distinguish examples from non-examples.

questions.stem: A teacher requires students to demonstrate at least 80 percent mastery on a unit before moving to the next, giving corrective instruction and another chance to those who do not. This reflects which approach?
options: Direct lecture
Mastery learning
Norm-referenced grading
Discovery learning
questions.rationale: Bloom's mastery learning holds that most students can reach mastery given enough time and appropriate instruction, with formative checks and corrective activities.

questions.stem: A teacher tells a class, "When you finish your math, you may spend ten minutes on the computer." Which principle is this?
options: Negative punishment
The Premack principle, in which a preferred activity reinforces completion of a less-preferred one
Learned helplessness
Extinction
questions.rationale: The Premack principle uses access to a preferred activity as a reinforcer for completing a less-preferred activity.

questions.stem: A teacher gives intermittent, unpredictable praise for participation. Compared with praising every response, which outcome is most likely?
options: Behavior stops sooner
Students become less motivated
Students stop noticing praise permanently
Behavior is more resistant to extinction because reinforcement is variable
questions.rationale: Intermittent or variable reinforcement schedules produce behaviors that persist longer once reinforcement slows or stops than continuous reinforcement does.

questions.stem: A teacher publicly corrects one student for talking, and nearby students immediately stop talking too. Kounin called this effect
options: Overlapping
Withitness
Momentum
The ripple effect
questions.rationale: Kounin's ripple effect describes how a teacher's response to one student's misbehavior influences the behavior of nearby students.

questions.stem: A teacher says privately to a student, "I feel frustrated when materials are left on the floor because someone could trip." Which communication technique is this?
options: A threat
An I-message, which describes the behavior, the feeling, and the effect without blaming
A You-message that assigns blame
A reward system
questions.rationale: I-messages express concern without accusing, preserving the relationship and opening the door to cooperation.

questions.stem: A student spills paint on the floor. The teacher has the student clean it up and then reflect on how to prevent it. According to Dreikurs, this is an example of
options: A natural reward
A logical consequence that is related to the behavior and respectful
Time-out
A punishment unrelated to the behavior
questions.rationale: Logical consequences connect directly to the misbehavior, are delivered respectfully, and teach responsibility, unlike arbitrary punishments.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students tokens for completing assignments and exchanges them for privileges at the end of the week. This is known as
options: A token economy
A norm-referenced system
Extinction
A negative reinforcement system
questions.rationale: A token economy provides tokens as secondary reinforcers for target behaviors, which students trade for backup reinforcers.

questions.stem: In a jigsaw activity, each student in a home group becomes an expert on one section of a text, then teaches it to the group. What is the main instructional benefit?
options: Students no longer need to read
Positive interdependence: every student must contribute and learn from others to master the whole text
Each student learns only one section
The teacher can leave the room
questions.rationale: Jigsaw builds individual accountability and interdependence because group members depend on each other for the missing pieces.

questions.stem: In reciprocal teaching, students take turns leading a discussion of a text using four strategies. Which list is correct?
options: Predicting, questioning, clarifying, and summarizing
Grading, ranking, sorting, and labeling
Scanning, skipping, guessing, and ignoring
Memorizing, copying, drilling, and testing
questions.rationale: Reciprocal teaching, developed by Palincsar and Brown, builds comprehension through the four strategies of predicting, questioning, clarifying, and summarizing.

questions.stem: A teacher reads a hard passage aloud and says, "I stopped here because this word confused me. I'm going to reread the sentence before and see if the context helps." Which instructional technique is this?
options: Silent sustained reading
Think-aloud modeling
Choral reading
Round-robin reading
questions.rationale: Think-alouds make a skilled reader's thinking visible so students can learn strategies for monitoring and repairing comprehension.

questions.stem: A teacher shows students a two-column note-taking format where the left column holds questions and key terms and the right column holds notes, with a summary at the bottom. Which note-taking system is this?
options: A KWL chart
A concept attainment chart
A cloze exercise
Cornell notes
questions.rationale: Cornell notes organize notes with cues and a summary to support review and retrieval.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to examine how a bat and a bird are similar and different and to classify the traits. Which research-based instructional strategy is she using?
options: Identifying similarities and differences
Extrinsic reinforcement
Choral response
Rote memorization
questions.rationale: Marzano's research identified comparing, classifying, and creating metaphors and analogies as high-yield strategies for deepening understanding.

questions.stem: A kindergarten teacher asks students to clap the syllables in the word "butterfly," then to say the word without "but." Which early literacy skill is being developed?
options: Reading fluency
Text comprehension
Phonological awareness
Phonics
questions.rationale: Phonological awareness is the ability to hear and manipulate the sounds of spoken language, such as syllables, without relying on print. Phonics links sounds to written letters.

questions.stem: A teacher receives an email that appears to be from the district technology office asking her to click a link and enter her password to avoid losing her account. What should she do?
options: Reply with her password
Avoid clicking, verify with the technology office through a known contact, and report the message as possible phishing
Click the link and enter the password quickly
Forward the email to all colleagues
questions.rationale: Phishing messages create urgency to steal credentials. Educators protect student data by verifying requests and reporting suspicious messages.

questions.stem: A teacher reviews a student's work and gives the comment, "Good, 8 out of 10." Which change would make this feedback more likely to improve future performance?
options: Add a smiley face
Replace the score with an exclamation mark
State which parts met the goal, where the work fell short, and one specific next step
Add the class average
questions.rationale: Feedback is most useful when it is goal-referenced, specific, and actionable, giving the learner information about the gap and how to close it.

questions.stem: A district reports that 70 percent of a campus's students "met grade level" on the state reading assessment. In this report, the standard is the cut score for meeting grade level. What type of interpretation is this?
options: An ipsative interpretation, because each student is compared with past performance
A criterion-referenced interpretation, because performance is compared with a defined standard
A diagnostic interpretation, because skills are identified
A norm-referenced interpretation, because students are ranked
questions.rationale: Criterion-referenced interpretations compare performance with a fixed standard, such as a cut score, rather than with other students.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to analyze the quality of their own writing against criteria and set goals. Which practice best supports this?
options: Have students score their drafts with the rubric, compare their scores with the teacher's, and write a goal for revision
Have students grade each other's papers anonymously with no criteria
Return papers with only grades
Skip drafts and assign final copies
questions.rationale: Self-assessment against clear criteria, followed by comparison with expert judgment and goal setting, builds students' ability to monitor and regulate learning.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to post a photograph of a student winning a school science fair on the class website. The district has designated photographs as directory information. What should the teacher check first?
options: Whether the photo is in color
Whether the parent has opted out of directory information disclosure or the district's media release requires consent
Whether the student likes the photograph
Whether the website has a mobile version
questions.rationale: FERPA permits districts to designate directory information but requires that parents be given the opportunity to opt out. Districts may also require separate media release forms.

questions.stem: A teacher notes that a parent seems upset during a conference and says, "No one here has ever listened to us." What is the best first response?
options: Defend the school's record
End the meeting
Acknowledge the frustration, ask what happened, and listen before problem solving
Change the subject to the student's grades
questions.rationale: Active listening and validation help rebuild trust. Understanding the parent's experience guides effective next steps.

questions.stem: A teacher in a professional learning community notices that her students' scores on a common assessment are lower than her teammates' on the same standard. What is the most productive approach?
options: Hide the results
Request a different team
Blame the test
Examine item-level results with teammates, learn how they taught the standard, and try their strategies while monitoring results
questions.rationale: PLCs rely on transparent use of common assessment data to learn from effective practice and improve results for students.

questions.stem: A toddler watches an adult hide a toy under a blanket and immediately lifts the blanket to find it. Which Piagetian achievement does this show?
options: Reversibility, the ability to mentally undo a sequence of actions in order
Hypothetical-deductive reasoning, the ability to test abstract possibilities mentally
Object permanence, the understanding that things continue to exist when out of sight
Conservation, the understanding that quantity stays the same when appearance changes
questions.rationale: Object permanence emerges late in the sensorimotor stage and underlies later symbolic thought.

questions.stem: A four-year-old tells her teacher that the moon follows her car and that her stuffed rabbit feels sad when left at home. This thinking is best described as
options: Abstract reasoning typical of the formal operational stage
Trial-and-error exploration typical of the sensorimotor stage
Animism and egocentrism typical of the preoperational stage
Logical classification typical of the concrete operational stage
questions.rationale: Preoperational children attribute life and feelings to objects and struggle to take other perspectives.

questions.stem: A fifth-grade teacher asks students to arrange ten rods from shortest to longest and to insert a new rod in the correct place. Which skill is being used?
options: Propositional logic, a pattern that develops in the formal operational stage
Deferred imitation, a pattern that develops in the sensorimotor stage
Egocentric speech, a pattern that develops in the preoperational stage
Seriation, a logical operation that develops during the concrete operational stage
questions.rationale: Ordering objects along a dimension and inserting new items is seriation, a hallmark of concrete operations.

questions.stem: A tenth-grade student can reason about a hypothetical situation such as, "If gravity were half as strong, how would sports change?" Which cognitive capacity does this reflect?
options: Centration, which focuses attention on one salient feature of a situation
Concrete reasoning, which depends on direct manipulation of physical materials
Assimilation of a new object into a sensorimotor scheme without any modification
Hypothetical-deductive reasoning, which allows systematic thinking about situations that are not real
questions.rationale: Formal operational thinkers can reason about possibilities, hypotheses, and abstract relationships without concrete referents.

questions.stem: A teacher observes a first grader quietly talking to himself while working through a puzzle: "This piece goes here... no, turn it." According to Vygotsky, this private speech most likely
options: Shows that the child is ignoring classroom expectations on purpose
Signals a language delay that requires immediate evaluation
Serves as a tool for guiding thinking and regulating behavior during a challenging task
Indicates that the child is too immature for independent work
questions.rationale: Vygotsky viewed private speech as a bridge between social speech and inner thought that helps children self-regulate.

questions.stem: A second-grade teacher notices that most of her students play side by side with similar materials but rarely share or interact. Parten would describe this play as
options: Solitary play, where children play alone and are unaware of peers
Parallel play, where children play near each other without coordinating
Onlooker play, where children only watch others and do not join
Cooperative play, where children share goals and roles in an organized activity
questions.rationale: Parallel play occurs when children use similar materials near each other without interacting directly.

questions.stem: A seventh grader becomes convinced that everyone will notice the pimple on her chin and refuses to present in class. Elkind's concept that best explains this belief is
options: The conservation error, in which adolescents misjudge quantities after transformation
Parallel play, in which adolescents work next to peers without interacting
The personal fable, in which adolescents believe their experiences are unique and invulnerable
The imaginary audience, in which adolescents believe others are constantly watching them
questions.rationale: Early adolescent egocentrism includes the imaginary audience, which heightens self-consciousness.

questions.stem: A student says, "I failed because the test was unfair," while another says, "I failed because I did not study." Weiner's attribution theory distinguishes these explanations by
options: Zone of development, since only the first is within the ZPD
Locus and controllability, since the second explanation is internal and controllable
Reinforcement schedule, since only the second is variable ratio
Stage and operation, since only the first is preoperational
questions.rationale: Attributions differ in locus (internal or external), stability, and controllability, which influence motivation.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students who fail a quiz to attribute the result to effort and strategy rather than to ability. Which teacher statement best supports this?
options: "Some people are just naturally better at this kind of problem than others."
"You did your best, so there is nothing you could have changed here."
"Don't worry about it. The test was probably harder than usual this time."
"You missed these because we haven't practiced this strategy yet. Here is a new way to check your work."
questions.rationale: Attributing outcomes to changeable strategies promotes persistence, while stable ability or luck attributions lower it.

questions.stem: Students in Ms. Alba's class focus on beating peers' scores and avoid challenging tasks that might expose mistakes. Which motivational pattern does this describe?
options: A mastery-goal orientation, in which the aim is to understand and improve skills
A performance-goal orientation, in which the aim is to demonstrate ability relative to others
A learning-goal orientation, in which errors are treated as information
An intrinsic orientation, in which activities are valued for their own sake
questions.rationale: Performance goals emphasize relative standing and can lead to avoiding challenge, unlike mastery goals.

questions.stem: A student states, "I can't do math" after failing several tests in a row despite having succeeded earlier in the year. Which concept best explains the pattern?
options: Egocentrism, in which perspective-taking is limited
Learned helplessness, in which repeated perceived failure leads to the belief that effort cannot change outcomes
Object permanence, in which hidden items are understood to still exist
Conservation, in which quantity is judged independently of appearance
questions.rationale: Learned helplessness develops when students conclude outcomes are beyond their control.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a lesson so that a challenge feels neither boring nor overwhelming and students lose track of time while working. Csikszentmihalyi would say the teacher is aiming to produce
options: Cognitive dissonance, a state of discomfort caused by contradictory beliefs
Extinction, a state in which a conditioned response fades
Learned helplessness, a state of passivity after repeated failure
Flow, a state of deep engagement when skill level matches task challenge
questions.rationale: Flow occurs when the difficulty of a task is balanced with a person's skills and the goals are clear.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to remember the planets by using the sentence "My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos." This memory technique is a
options: Metacognitive prompt that asks students to monitor understanding
Graphic organizer that shows hierarchical relationships
Mnemonic device that attaches arbitrary items to a memorable cue
Formative assessment that measures prior knowledge
questions.rationale: Mnemonics provide retrieval cues for lists and facts that lack inherent structure.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to explain how a new term relates to personal experiences instead of repeating its definition. According to levels-of-processing theory, why is this more effective?
options: Shallow repetition always creates more durable memory than elaboration
Personal experiences are stored in sensory memory for longer periods
Explanations reduce the capacity of working memory so less is forgotten
Deeper, meaning-based processing produces stronger memory traces than shallow repetition
questions.rationale: Craik and Lockhart proposed that deeper semantic processing leads to better retention than superficial rehearsal.

questions.stem: A teacher presents a new topic by first showing a brief overview that links to the unit's big ideas. Ausubel called such a tool a(n)
options: Reinforcer, which strengthens a behavior when it follows the behavior
Advance organizer, which provides a framework for connecting new information to existing knowledge
Scaffold, which is a temporary support to complete a task independently
Summative assessment, which measures achievement after instruction
questions.rationale: Advance organizers provide a conceptual structure before learning to help integrate new material.

questions.stem: A student learned to solve area problems with rectangles and later uses the same reasoning to find the area of an irregular room by splitting it into rectangles. This is an example of
options: Positive transfer of learning to a new situation
Negative transfer in which earlier learning interferes with new learning
Retroactive interference that erases earlier learning
Proactive interference that blocks retrieval of older information
questions.rationale: Positive transfer occurs when prior learning helps with a new task.

questions.stem: A student who learned to write the date as month/day/year while at school in the United States struggles to write day/month/year at a new school abroad and keeps writing the old order. This is best described as
options: Accommodation, in which schemes change to fit new information
Negative transfer, in which previously learned habits interfere with new learning
Scaffolding, in which a teacher gradually withdraws support
Positive transfer, in which earlier skills facilitate later skills
questions.rationale: Negative transfer occurs when old learning makes new learning more difficult.

questions.stem: A fourth grader is taught to use a checklist to plan, monitor, and evaluate each step of her own research project. This practice primarily develops
options: Self-regulated learning skills such as planning and self-monitoring
Egocentric speech through private talk
Operant conditioning through continuous reinforcement
Object permanence and early symbolic play
questions.rationale: Zimmerman described self-regulated learning as cycles of forethought, performance, and reflection.

questions.stem: A child hears a loud bell at the start of every fire drill and now feels a racing heart whenever the school bell rings. This is best explained by
options: Classical conditioning, in which a neutral stimulus becomes linked with an emotional response
Insight learning, in which a solution appears suddenly
Operant conditioning, in which behavior is shaped by consequences
Observational learning, in which behavior is copied from a model
questions.rationale: Pairing a neutral stimulus with an alarming one can produce a conditioned emotional response.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that students quickly forget facts taught in a single long lesson but remember better when the same facts are revisited over several weeks. Which principle explains this?
options: The recency effect, which holds that the final item in a list is recalled best
The spacing effect, which holds that distributed practice yields better retention than massed practice
The Zeigarnik effect, which holds that interrupted tasks are recalled better
The Flynn effect, which holds that test scores rise across generations
questions.rationale: Spaced review gives repeated retrieval opportunities that strengthen long-term memory.

questions.stem: A teacher presents complex diagrams with lengthy narration and on-screen text at the same time, and students struggle to follow. Cognitive load theory suggests the teacher should
options: Reduce extraneous load, such as by presenting text in smaller segments and removing redundant information
Increase intrinsic load by adding more elements to each diagram
Add decorative images so that students stay interested
Present all information at once so that students can organize it themselves
questions.rationale: Working memory is limited, so removing redundant or distracting elements frees capacity for learning.

questions.stem: Why does a teacher use worked examples before asking novice students to solve similar problems on their own?
options: Worked examples replace the need for later independent practice entirely
Worked examples are mainly useful for students who already know the content well
Studying solved examples reduces cognitive load and helps novices learn problem-solving structure
Worked examples prevent students from ever making an error on the topic
questions.rationale: Novices benefit from worked examples because they can focus on structure instead of search.

questions.stem: A kindergarten teacher notices that students attend best during activities lasting about ten minutes with movement. Which explanation is most consistent with development?
options: Young children can sustain attention for an hour if they are told to behave
Movement during learning reduces memory for all students at every age
Young children's attention span is limited and grows with age, so short, active tasks match their abilities
Attention span is fixed at birth and cannot change with instruction
questions.rationale: Attention span lengthens gradually, and active, varied tasks fit early childhood.

questions.stem: During the first week of school, a new student sits alone and does not speak. Considering Maslow's hierarchy, what should the teacher address first?
options: Cognitive needs, by assigning advanced reading beyond grade level
Belonging and safety needs, by welcoming the student and pairing the student with a friendly peer
Self-actualization needs, by assigning an open-ended creativity project
Esteem needs, by awarding the student a leadership role in the class
questions.rationale: Maslow proposed that needs for safety and belonging must be reasonably met before higher needs.

questions.stem: A teacher whose students are two years apart in reading achievement concludes that development in one domain does not always predict another. Which principle of development supports this?
options: Development proceeds at the same rate in all domains for typical children
Development depends only on heredity and not at all on environment
Development is uneven, so students may progress at different rates in cognitive, social, emotional, and physical domains
Development is complete by early childhood and then only declines
questions.rationale: Children develop unevenly across domains, so teachers cannot infer one area from another.

questions.stem: Research on adolescent brain development suggests that teens may take more risks when peers are present. Which instructional response is most consistent with this research?
options: Structure group tasks with clear roles and norms and teach decision-making strategies explicitly
Eliminate all collaborative tasks because teens cannot work together safely
Assume risk-taking disappears if teachers lower expectations
Rely entirely on rewards because teens do not respond to relationships
questions.rationale: The prefrontal cortex matures later, so supports such as structure and explicit strategy teaching help.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to build on students' background knowledge before reading a text about hurricanes. Which activity best does this?
options: Tell students to read silently and write one summary sentence
Show the final answers to the end-of-chapter questions first
Ask students to brainstorm what they know about storms and record it on a class chart
Give students a vocabulary test over words they have not yet seen
questions.rationale: Activating prior knowledge helps students connect new information to existing schemas.

questions.stem: A student learns that all four-legged animals are dogs, then calls a cow a dog. After the teacher explains the difference, the student creates a new category for cows. In Piagetian terms the creation of the new category is
options: Accommodation, in which existing schemes are changed or new ones created to fit new information
Assimilation, in which new information is fit into an existing scheme unchanged
Equilibrium, in which no new information challenges the existing scheme
Centration, in which attention is focused on only one aspect of a situation
questions.rationale: Accommodation involves restructuring schemes when assimilation fails.

questions.stem: A student reads, "Plants make their own food," and connects it to a garden she has grown. According to constructivism, what is happening?
options: The learner is being conditioned by repeated reinforcement of correct responses
The learner is passively absorbing knowledge transmitted by the text
The learner is actively building understanding by linking new information to prior experience
The learner is relying on innate knowledge that requires no experience
questions.rationale: Constructivism holds that learners construct knowledge through experience and reflection.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a K-W-L chart at the start of a unit. Which learning principle does the first two columns support?
options: Reducing the need for any direct instruction
Activating prior knowledge and setting purposes for learning
Evaluating final achievement at the end of the unit
Sorting students into permanent ability groups
questions.rationale: The K and W columns surface prior knowledge and questions, guiding learning.

questions.stem: A teacher gives each student a sticker for every correct answer on a drill, and the number of correct answers increases. Which concept explains the increase?
options: Positive reinforcement, in which a pleasant consequence increases the likelihood of behavior
Punishment, in which an unpleasant consequence reduces behavior
Negative reinforcement, in which removing an aversive stimulus increases behavior
Extinction, in which withholding reinforcement reduces behavior
questions.rationale: Adding a desired consequence that raises the behavior is positive reinforcement.

questions.stem: A student stops raising his hand after the teacher ignores his comments for several weeks. Which behavioral concept applies?
options: Shaping, in which successive approximations of behavior are reinforced
Modeling, in which behavior is learned by observation
Extinction, in which behavior declines when it is no longer reinforced
Generalization, in which a response appears in similar situations
questions.rationale: Extinction is the weakening of a behavior when reinforcement stops.

questions.stem: A physical education teacher wants a student to learn a full tennis serve. She first praises the toss, then the toss and swing, then the entire serve. This procedure is
options: Extinction through withdrawal of reinforcement
Latent learning through unreinforced exploration
Classical conditioning through stimulus pairing
Shaping through reinforcement of successive approximations
questions.rationale: Shaping reinforces progressively closer approximations to a target behavior.

questions.stem: A teacher models how to read a graph aloud, then students watch a classmate do the same before attempting it themselves. Which theorist's work best supports this approach?
options: Bandura, who emphasized learning through observation and modeling
Piaget, who emphasized learning through self-discovery in stages
Pavlov, who emphasized learning through stimulus association
Skinner, who emphasized learning through reinforcement of voluntary behavior
questions.rationale: Bandura's social cognitive theory highlights attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation in observational learning.

questions.stem: A student who has experienced success on similar tasks believes strongly that she can master an upcoming geometry unit. Bandura would say this belief is
options: Locus of control, which is a belief about the source of rewards
Learned optimism, which is a general positive outlook toward all events
Self-efficacy, which is strongly influenced by prior mastery experiences
Self-concept, which is a global evaluation of overall worth
questions.rationale: Self-efficacy is task-specific confidence, and mastery experiences are its strongest source.

questions.stem: A third-grade student with a speech sound disorder is often teased. Which action best supports the student's social-emotional development?
options: Ignore the teasing because children usually resolve it themselves
Teach classmates respectful communication norms and give the student opportunities to succeed in valued roles
Ask the student to stay silent in class to avoid teasing
Seat the student away from the class to protect the student from peers
questions.rationale: Teachers support healthy development by creating respectful norms and building competence.

questions.stem: In an upper elementary classroom, which activity best matches students' concrete operational thinking?
options: Debating an abstract hypothetical about ethics without examples
Listening to a long lecture on theoretical models without visuals
Using fraction strips to compare and order fractions and then explaining the results
Memorizing algebraic proofs without any concrete context
questions.rationale: Concrete operational learners reason logically about tangible objects and examples.

questions.stem: A teacher recognizes that eighth graders are working on identity. Which classroom practice best supports healthy identity development, as described by Erikson?
options: Reward only the students who conform most to the teacher's preferences
Offer choices in topics and roles and allow students to explore different interests safely
Discourage questions about values to avoid conflict
Assign all students identical roles to prevent comparison
questions.rationale: Adolescents navigate identity versus role confusion by exploring options and receiving support.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates a school-age child's growing sense of industry as described by Erikson?
options: A fourth grader proudly finishes a science fair project after weeks of work
A teenager questions family values and experiments with a new style
An infant cries when a caregiver leaves the room
A toddler refuses to share a toy during snack time
questions.rationale: Industry versus inferiority centers on mastering skills and finishing tasks in middle childhood.

questions.stem: A first-grade teacher notices that some students develop reading skills earlier than others despite similar instruction. Which principle of development best applies?
options: All students must read at the same level by the end of the semester
Individual differences exist in the rate of development, so teachers should plan for variability
Reading development is fixed and unaffected by instruction
Students who read later will never catch up to their peers
questions.rationale: Development varies, and instruction should support students at different points.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a short silent pause before taking student responses and notices that answers become more elaborate. Which cognitive principle best explains the improvement?
options: Silence conditions students to respond with a reflex
Silent periods prevent forgetting by suppressing long-term memory
Pausing activates sensory memory so that students remember every detail of the question
Students need processing time in working memory to retrieve information and organize a response
questions.rationale: Wait time allows working memory to retrieve and organize ideas before responding.

questions.stem: A teacher helps students sort animals into mammals, birds, and reptiles before introducing new species. Which learning principle is applied?
options: Categories prevent students from forming any misconceptions
Organizing information into categories helps learners store and retrieve it more efficiently
Random order is the best way to ensure long-term memory
Sorting tasks are useful only for assessment purposes
questions.rationale: Schemas and categories organize knowledge and support retrieval.

questions.stem: A student remembers a teacher's explanation of photosynthesis when she links it to a diagram, a gesture, and a rap the class created. Which concept best describes why multiple connections help?
options: Repeating the exact same sentence prevents forgetting
Elaboration and multiple retrieval cues strengthen memory traces
Using only auditory input is the most reliable path to learning
Overloading short-term memory ensures long-term retention
questions.rationale: Creating multiple associations gives more routes to retrieve information.

questions.stem: A teacher grants a student's request to redo a project and the student succeeds. The teacher's response reflects which view of intelligence?
options: Incremental, in which ability grows through effort and strategy
Behaviorist, in which ability is a response to rewards
Genetic, in which ability is determined only at birth
Entity, in which ability is a fixed trait
questions.rationale: Dweck's mindset research contrasts incremental views with entity views of ability.

questions.stem: A teacher explains to the class that the brain strengthens connections when they practice and make mistakes. This message primarily promotes
options: Learned helplessness based on unsuccessful experiences
A fixed mindset that ability is stable over time
Extrinsic motivation based on rewards for performance
A growth mindset that effort and strategies improve abilities
questions.rationale: Messages about neuroplasticity help students see ability as malleable.

questions.stem: A newly arrived student nods and points but does not yet speak English. In the Texas English Language Proficiency Standards, which proficiency level best describes this student?
options: Advanced high, because the student can produce grade-level academic language with little support
Beginning, because the student relies heavily on nonverbal communication and understands very little English
Advanced, because the student can discuss abstract topics in English independently
Intermediate, because the student can use extended sentences with moderate support
questions.rationale: Beginning-level English learners communicate with gestures, single words, or home language and need high support.

questions.stem: In Texas, which committee makes decisions about the identification, instruction, and exit of a student from an English learner program?
options: The Campus Improvement Committee (CIC)
The Admission, Review, and Dismissal (ARD) committee
The Section 504 evaluation committee
The Language Proficiency Assessment Committee (LPAC)
questions.rationale: The LPAC reviews home language surveys, assessments, and progress for English learners and decides placement, services, and reclassification.

questions.stem: A family enrolling a child in a Texas school completes a form that asks which language the child speaks at home. What is the primary purpose of this document?
options: To determine the child's eligibility for special education
To assign the child to a grade level based on age
To decide whether the child qualifies for gifted education
To identify students who may need an evaluation of English proficiency
questions.rationale: A home language survey flags possible English learners so that proficiency testing can follow.

questions.stem: A sixth-grade teacher gives English learners a word bank, sentence starters, and a picture-supported glossary for a science lab. These supports are best classified as
options: Linguistic accommodations that provide access to grade-level content while English develops
Enrichment activities designed for students who are already proficient
Modifications that reduce the science standards expected of English learners
Disciplinary consequences for students who fall behind in vocabulary
questions.rationale: Linguistic supports provide access without lowering the content expectations.

questions.stem: A teacher in a dual language program teaches half the day in Spanish and half in English so that native speakers of both languages become bilingual and biliterate. This is an example of
options: A transitional bilingual model that exits students after two years
A pull-out ESL model for beginning English learners only
A two-way dual language immersion model
A newcomer program that operates for a few weeks
questions.rationale: Two-way dual language programs serve both English and partner-language speakers with the goal of bilingualism and biliteracy.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a sheltered instruction approach in a science class. Which practice best reflects this approach?
options: Teaching English grammar rules separately and delaying all content instruction
Pairing clear content and language objectives with visuals, hands-on tasks, and structured academic talk
Slowing down the pace and removing all academic vocabulary from the lesson
Allowing English learners to leave the room during the lesson to avoid confusion
questions.rationale: Sheltered instruction makes grade-level content comprehensible while building English.

questions.stem: A teacher explains a new term to a newcomer by showing a photo, acting it out, and having the student draw it before reading a definition. Which principle of language acquisition does this reflect?
options: Strict immersion with no visual support
Error correction before any attempt at communication
Rote memorization of isolated vocabulary lists
Comprehensible input supported by context clues
questions.rationale: Context-rich input helps learners connect new words with meaning.

questions.stem: A teacher knows that Carlos speaks fluent conversational English on the playground but struggles with academic writing. According to Cummins, how long can academic language proficiency (CALP) typically take to develop?
options: Roughly two weeks, the same time conversational fluency requires
Roughly five to seven years, much longer than conversational fluency
It never develops if the home language is used in the classroom
Exactly one school year for all students regardless of background
questions.rationale: Research suggests CALP takes several years, longer than BICS.

questions.stem: Which student is most likely to need a gifted and talented evaluation in Texas?
options: A student who earns a perfect score on one spelling quiz
A student who consistently shows advanced reasoning and achievement far above grade-level peers in one or more areas
A student who finishes tasks early because the tasks are very easy
A student who is very well behaved and never talks in class
questions.rationale: Gifted identification considers evidence of high ability and achievement across multiple measures.

questions.stem: A student is identified as gifted in mathematics and also has dysgraphia that makes handwriting very difficult. This student is best described as
options: Twice-exceptional, requiring both enrichment and supports for the disability
A candidate for removal from the gifted program because of the disability
A student who should be given less demanding math tasks
Underachieving because of low motivation
questions.rationale: Twice-exceptional students need challenge in areas of strength and accommodations for areas of need.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to offer enrichment for students who have already mastered a unit's standards. Which option best provides depth rather than just more work?
options: An independent investigation that requires students to analyze a real-world problem and present original conclusions
A requirement to tutor classmates for the remainder of the unit
A packet of worksheets from the previous grade level
Twenty additional practice problems identical to those already completed
questions.rationale: Enrichment should increase complexity and thinking, not volume.

questions.stem: A student on the autism spectrum becomes anxious when the daily routine changes unexpectedly. Which support is most helpful?
options: A reprimand each time the student shows anxiety
A sudden change of routine to help the student learn flexibility quickly
A visual schedule that shows the day's activities and preview of any changes
Removal from all group activities until the student is calm all day
questions.rationale: Visual schedules increase predictability and reduce anxiety for many students with autism.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a student with ADHD a checklist for multi-step tasks and breaks long assignments into short segments. These supports are intended to
options: Lower the expectations for the student's grade-level standards
Replace the need for any behavior or academic support
Strengthen organization and sustained attention while keeping the learning goal the same
Reward the student for symptoms of inattention
questions.rationale: Chunking and checklists are common accommodations that support executive functioning.

questions.stem: A student with an emotional disturbance has a behavior intervention plan that calls for a quiet cool-down spot when the student feels overwhelmed. During a lesson the student asks to go there. What should the teacher do?
options: Allow the student to use the cool-down space as written in the plan and prepare for a smooth return to instruction
Tell the student to wait until the end of class so other students are not distracted
Send the student to the office every time the request occurs
Deny the request until the student finishes the assignment
questions.rationale: BIPs are part of the IEP and must be implemented as written to support appropriate behavior.

questions.stem: A student with a visual impairment is working in a group on a science lab. Which teacher action best supports participation?
options: Provide tactile or enlarged materials, describe visual information aloud, and assign the student a meaningful role
Hand the student a finished lab report to copy
Assign the student to observe quietly while peers perform the lab
Excuse the student from all lab tasks to avoid difficulty
questions.rationale: Access plus meaningful roles supports participation for students with visual impairments.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a student with a mild hearing loss often misses oral directions. Which classroom adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Raise your voice substantially during all instruction for the entire class
Seat the student at the back of the room to prevent distraction
Repeat each direction ten times until the student says that they understand
Face the student when speaking, reduce background noise, and provide written or visual directions
questions.rationale: Clear sightlines, quiet, and visual supports improve access for students with hearing loss.

questions.stem: A student with a physical disability uses a wheelchair, and the lab tables in the science room are too high. Which action best reflects legal and instructional responsibility?
options: Provide an accessible workstation so the student can participate in the same lab as peers
Excuse the student from lab activities and grade only on the written test
Allow the student to watch a video of the lab instead of participating
Ask the student to bring a table from home
questions.rationale: Schools must provide access and equal opportunity under IDEA, Section 504, and the ADA.

questions.stem: How does an accommodation differ from a modification?
options: An accommodation is a punishment, while a modification is a reward
An accommodation applies only to gifted students, while a modification applies to all students
An accommodation changes the grade-level standard, while a modification changes only the seating
An accommodation changes how a student accesses or shows learning, while a modification changes what the student is expected to learn
questions.rationale: Accommodations alter the means, while modifications alter the expectations.

questions.stem: A teacher provides a student with a calculator for a unit on multi-step word problems because the student has a documented math calculation disability, and the unit goal is problem solving. This is best classified as
options: An enrichment, because it adds challenge
A modification, because it lowers the learning goal
A consequence, because it penalizes the student
An accommodation, because it provides access without changing the targeted skill
questions.rationale: A calculator removes a calculation barrier while the student still demonstrates problem solving.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a 504 plan from an IEP?
options: A 504 plan provides accommodations for students with disabilities who need access, while an IEP provides specially designed instruction under IDEA
A 504 plan can be created only by the parent, while an IEP can be created only by the teacher
A 504 plan is a state-level plan, while an IEP is a federal-level plan
A 504 plan is for students with no disability, while an IEP is for students with a mild disability
questions.rationale: 504 plans ensure equal access, while IEPs provide specialized instruction and related services for eligible students.

questions.stem: A student in Tier 2 reading intervention for eight weeks shows little progress. According to Response to Intervention, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reduce the number of assessments to avoid discouragement
Retain the student in grade without additional data
Remove the student from intervention and wait another year
Review progress monitoring data and consider more intensive Tier 3 intervention or a referral for evaluation
questions.rationale: RTI uses data to adjust the intensity of support and determine whether evaluation is needed.

questions.stem: In a multi-tiered system of supports, what characterizes Tier 1?
options: Intensive, individualized intervention for a few students
Special education services only for identified students
Small-group intervention only for students who failed a screener
High-quality core instruction and universal supports for all students
questions.rationale: Tier 1 is the foundation of effective instruction available to everyone.

questions.stem: A student from a family experiencing poverty frequently arrives without supplies. Which response best reflects equitable practice?
options: Require the student to explain to the class why supplies are missing
Send a note home publicly shaming the family
Lower the student's grade each time the student lacks supplies
