Keep a classroom supply station available to all students without drawing attention to anyone
questions.rationale: Equitable practice removes barriers while protecting dignity.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that students from a high-context cultural background often rely on indirect communication and group harmony. How should this inform participation structures?
options: Assume that quiet students are unintelligent
Penalize indirect communication in all assignments
Require every student to debate directly in front of the class
Offer small-group and partner discussion formats and interpret communication styles without bias
questions.rationale: Cultural communication differences should inform flexible participation structures.

questions.stem: A teacher draws on students' families' knowledge, such as farming, construction, and cooking, to design math tasks. This reflects which concept?
options: Cognitive dissonance, which treats conflicting ideas as a source of discomfort
Tracking, which groups students by prior achievement
Funds of knowledge, which treats students' home and community experiences as academic resources
Operant conditioning, which uses reinforcement to shape behavior
questions.rationale: Funds of knowledge honors students' home expertise as a foundation for learning.

questions.stem: A teacher is aware that stereotypes about performance can influence outcomes. Which practice best reduces the effect of stereotype threat on students?
options: Seat students by group so that expectations are clear
Lower expectations for groups believed to underperform
Communicate high standards along with belief in each student's capacity to meet them and emphasize that ability can grow
Remind students of the stereotypes before each test to prepare them
questions.rationale: Wise feedback pairs high standards with assurance to counteract threat.

questions.stem: A teacher who grades a paper anonymously notices that her scores differ from when she knew the author's name. Which concept best explains the difference?
options: Negative transfer, in which earlier learning interferes with new learning
Implicit bias, in which unconscious attitudes can influence judgment
Shaping, in which closer approximations are reinforced
Conservation, in which quantity is understood to be constant
questions.rationale: Implicit biases operate outside awareness and can affect evaluation, so blind scoring helps.

questions.stem: A teacher learns that a student is living with a foster family after a recent move. Which action best supports the student?
options: Maintain consistent routines, build a trusting relationship, and coordinate with the counselor and caseworker while protecting privacy
Announce the situation to the class to generate sympathy
Avoid contact with the foster parents to prevent conflict
Reduce all expectations until the student completes a year with the family
questions.rationale: Foster students benefit from stability, relationships, and coordinated, confidential support.

questions.stem: A student who experienced a traumatic event becomes easily startled and has trouble concentrating. Which trauma-informed practice is most appropriate?
options: Require the student to retell the event to the class
Use public reprimands to teach the student to control reactions
Remove all structure so the student does not feel controlled
Provide predictable routines, offer choices, and respond calmly while connecting the student with the counselor
questions.rationale: Trauma-informed practice emphasizes safety, predictability, and supportive relationships.

questions.stem: A migrant student has attended four schools in two years and has gaps in math. Which action best supports the student?
options: Ignore the gaps and teach only grade-level content
Assume the student cannot learn because of frequent moves
Use diagnostic assessment to identify gaps and provide targeted instruction to connect missing concepts
Place the student in a lower grade based on the gaps
questions.rationale: Diagnostic assessment guides targeted support so students can catch up.

questions.stem: A teacher presents a concept using a short video, a hands-on model, and a text summary. Which UDL principle does this practice illustrate?
options: Multiple means of assessment security
Multiple means of engagement
Multiple means of expression
Multiple means of representation
questions.rationale: Providing information in several formats supports diverse learners.

questions.stem: A teacher assigns a RAFT task in which students write as a river (role) to city planners (audience) in a letter (format) arguing for protection (topic). What is the main purpose of the RAFT strategy?
options: To sort students permanently into creative or analytical tracks
To replace grade-level standards with creative tasks that have no criteria
To reduce the number of assessments needed during the unit
To differentiate product and engage students by varying role, audience, format, and topic around the same standard
questions.rationale: RAFT offers choice and authentic purpose while targeting the same learning goal.

questions.stem: While most of the class works on a station rotation, a teacher gives early finishers an anchor activity. Which choice is the best anchor activity?
options: Free time with no expectations
A worksheet from a different subject with no connection to learning goals
An ongoing independent task tied to the unit, such as a research inquiry or reading log
Cleaning the classroom for the rest of the period
questions.rationale: Anchor activities are meaningful, self-directed tasks that students can work on when finished.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a learning contract in which each student agrees to complete required tasks plus selected options by a date. What is the main benefit?
options: It guarantees equal achievement for every student
It builds ownership and self-management while ensuring that all students address essential standards
It allows students to skip any work they find hard
It removes the need for any teacher feedback during the unit
questions.rationale: Contracts balance choice and accountability.

questions.stem: A teacher compacts the curriculum for a student who demonstrates mastery of a unit on a pre-assessment. What should happen next?
options: Move the student to unrelated tasks that have no academic purpose
Require the student to complete every original assignment anyway
Excuse the student from all assignments for the unit
Replace the mastered content with extension activities that deepen or accelerate learning
questions.rationale: Compacting eliminates repetition and provides challenge in its place.

questions.stem: A teacher groups students by interest for a literature project rather than by reading level. This differentiates according to
options: Readiness, which depends on prior achievement
Interest, which can raise engagement while keeping the same learning goal
Behavior, which determines privileges
Intelligence quotient, which determines placement
questions.rationale: Tomlinson described readiness, interest, and learning profile as bases for differentiation.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to honor religious diversity during a December unit. Which approach is most appropriate in a public school?
options: Teach about multiple traditions objectively for educational purposes without promoting any one belief
Require students to participate in religious rituals
Ignore any student who mentions a religious holiday
Lead the class in prayer from the teacher's tradition
questions.rationale: Public schools may teach about religion neutrally but may not promote or require religious practice.

questions.stem: A teacher is planning a unit and realizes that all the texts feature characters of a single background. Which action best supports equity and engagement?
options: Keep the texts because they match the textbook order
Allow students to choose only texts about their own background
Remove all texts that mention cultural differences
Select texts that act as both mirrors and windows so students see themselves and learn about others
questions.rationale: Diverse texts affirm identity and build understanding of others.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that two students are frequently absent because they care for younger siblings. What is the best first step?
options: Talk privately with the students and family to understand constraints and connect them with campus supports
Mark them truant and refer to the district without a conversation
Assign extra homework as a consequence for absences
Ignore the absences because they are not the teacher's responsibility
questions.rationale: Understanding circumstances leads to supports such as flexible deadlines and counseling.

questions.stem: A teacher in a diverse class wants all students to feel comfortable sharing ideas. Which strategy best builds psychological safety?
options: Allow humor that targets other students' accents
Call only on students who are sure to answer correctly
Establish norms for respectful disagreement and respond to all contributions as valuable
Correct each error publicly and quickly
questions.rationale: Psychological safety increases risk taking and participation.

questions.stem: A district reviews data and finds that students of color are disproportionately referred for special education in the category of emotional disturbance. Which concern does this raise?
options: Disproportionality, which may reflect bias in referral, evaluation, or instruction
Reliability, because the referral forms are too long
Practicality, because the evaluation process takes too long
Content validity, because the forms include behavior descriptions
questions.rationale: IDEA requires monitoring of disproportionate representation and examining practices.

questions.stem: A student with dyslexia receives audiobooks for content-area reading. Why is this an appropriate accommodation?
options: It replaces the need for reading intervention
It excuses the student from developing any reading skill
It lowers the content standard for the student
It provides access to grade-level content while the student continues to build decoding skills through intervention
questions.rationale: Audiobooks give access to ideas without relying solely on decoding.

questions.stem: In Texas, when must schools screen students for dyslexia?
options: Only if parents request screening in writing
Only after students fail the state reading test twice
Only in high school, when students apply to college
Students are screened at the end of kindergarten and again in first grade, and evaluated when there are indicators of risk
questions.rationale: Texas law requires universal screening for dyslexia and related disorders in kindergarten and grade 1.

questions.stem: A student's records show repeated school changes, absences, and low scores, and the teacher considers referring the student for special education. What should the team consider before concluding that a disability exists?
options: Whether the learning problems are the result of lack of appropriate instruction or limited English proficiency rather than a disability
Whether the student likes the teacher
Whether the student has been absent at least once
Whether the student's family has a history of low scores
questions.rationale: IDEA requires ruling out lack of instruction and limited English proficiency as determinant factors.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to ensure that classroom materials do not reinforce stereotypes. Which practice best supports this goal?
options: Use only materials created before 1990
Avoid any mention of cultural groups
Review images, examples, and texts for diverse representation and discuss them critically with students
Select materials solely based on low cost
questions.rationale: Critical review of materials supports inclusive instruction.

questions.stem: In the Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills (TEKS), what does a student expectation describe?
options: A set of discipline rules for classrooms across the state
A specific statement of what students should know or be able to do at the end of a grade or course
A daily script that every teacher must follow at the same pace
A list of approved textbooks for each subject area
questions.rationale: Student expectations are the specific, assessable components of the knowledge and skills statements.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that the TEKS contain both content and process standards in math. How should the teacher plan instruction?
options: Teach the process standards only after all content is complete
Ignore the process standards because they are not assessed
Teach each process standard on a single day and move on
Integrate the process standards, such as problem solving and communication, with the content standards in every unit
questions.rationale: Process standards are meant to be integrated throughout instruction.

questions.stem: Texas teachers who serve English learners are expected to address the English Language Proficiency Standards (ELPS). How are the ELPS used in content classes?
options: Teachers use the ELPS only for students in special education
Teachers replace the content standards with the ELPS
Teachers apply the ELPS only in English language arts classes
Teachers incorporate language objectives that support students' language development while teaching grade-level content
questions.rationale: The ELPS are cross-curricular and must be used alongside content standards.

questions.stem: A teacher writes the objective: "Given a map, students will identify at least four major rivers of Texas with 80 percent accuracy." Which component is the condition?
options: "four major rivers of Texas"
"Given a map"
"identify"
"80 percent accuracy"
questions.rationale: Objectives with an ABCD format include audience, behavior, condition, and degree.

questions.stem: Which objective verb is most measurable?
options: Be aware of different genres
Appreciate the value of reading
Understand the author's purpose
Compare two characters using specific text evidence
questions.rationale: Measurable objectives use observable verbs such as compare, list, or solve.

questions.stem: In Understanding by Design, what are essential questions?
options: Questions that the teacher answers during direct instruction
Open-ended questions that provoke deeper inquiry and are revisited throughout a unit
Questions that review the previous day's content only
Questions that have one correct answer and are asked on the final test
questions.rationale: Essential questions guide inquiry into big ideas and have no single right answer.

questions.stem: A teacher follows the Hunter lesson design. After the anticipatory set and objective, she explains and models the skill. Which element is this?
options: Evaluation
Closure
Input and modeling
Independent practice
questions.rationale: Hunter's design includes anticipatory set, objective, input, modeling, checking for understanding, guided and independent practice, and closure.

questions.stem: A teacher circulates while students complete practice problems with a partner and gives immediate feedback. This stage of the lesson is best called
options: Guided practice
Independent practice
Summative evaluation
Anticipatory set
questions.rationale: Guided practice includes teacher monitoring and support while students apply the skill.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to complete a short task alone to show they can use the new skill without help. This is
options: Guided practice
Anticipatory set
Modeling
Independent practice
questions.rationale: Independent practice shows whether students can apply learning without assistance.

questions.stem: In the 5E model, a teacher asks students to apply the concept of buoyancy to design a boat that holds the most weight. Which phase is this?
options: Explore
Evaluate
Elaborate
Engage
questions.rationale: Elaborate extends understanding by applying concepts in new contexts.

questions.stem: A teacher begins a unit by displaying a discrepant event, such as a heavy object that floats, and asks students to explain what they observe. Which 5E phase is this?
options: Elaborate
Engage
Evaluate
Explain
questions.rationale: The Engage phase captures interest and elicits prior knowledge.

questions.stem: A teacher uses explicit instruction to teach a new math procedure. Which sequence best reflects this approach?
options: Independent practice, then explanation
Clear explanation, modeling with think-aloud, guided practice with feedback, then independent practice
A long lecture followed by homework only
Discovery with no instruction, then a quiz
questions.rationale: Explicit instruction is systematic and includes modeling, guided practice, and independent practice.

questions.stem: A teacher decides to teach the Tier 2 words "analyze," "contrast," and "evidence" explicitly. Which statement best describes Tier 2 words?
options: Rare words specific to one subject, such as isotope
Words that are never needed for school
High-utility academic words that appear across many content areas
Everyday words that students learn at home
questions.rationale: Beck's tiers distinguish common words (Tier 1), general academic words (Tier 2), and domain-specific words (Tier 3).

questions.stem: A teacher teaches the word "photosynthesis" in a science unit. According to Beck's tiers, this word is
options: Tier 1, because it is a basic everyday word
Tier 4, because it is the most advanced
Tier 3, because it is specific to a particular domain
Tier 2, because it appears in all subjects
questions.rationale: Tier 3 words are domain-specific and best taught within content.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a read-aloud where she pauses to model how she makes predictions and asks students to do the same. Which comprehension strategy is being taught?
options: Predicting, which engages students by using clues to anticipate what comes next
Decoding, which focuses on sounding out unfamiliar words
Spelling, which focuses on correct letter sequences
Fluency, which focuses on rate and expression
questions.rationale: Predicting activates prior knowledge and supports comprehension.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to learn to visualize while reading. Which instructional step best teaches this strategy?
options: Tell students to read faster to form pictures
Provide a worksheet with a list of definitions
Have students copy the passage three times
Model a think-aloud describing the mental images created by a passage and then have students sketch or describe their own
questions.rationale: Strategy instruction involves modeling and guided practice.

questions.stem: In the writing process, a student rereads a draft to add details and rearrange paragraphs. Which stage is this?
options: Publishing
Editing
Prewriting
Revising
questions.rationale: Revising focuses on ideas, organization, and clarity, while editing addresses conventions.

questions.stem: A teacher models how to write a topic sentence and then asks students to craft one for their own paragraph. This is an example of
options: Independent writing without instruction
Summative assessment of writing
Modeled writing followed by guided practice
Peer editing for conventions
questions.rationale: Modeling and guided practice build skill gradually.

questions.stem: A teacher introduces multiplication by having students build arrays with tiles, then draw arrays, and finally write equations. Which instructional sequence is this?
options: Concrete-representational-abstract
Lecture-quiz-review
Abstract-representational-concrete
Memorization-recall-test
questions.rationale: CRA moves from physical objects to pictures to symbols.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to explain why the algorithm for adding fractions works using drawings. What type of knowledge is she emphasizing?
options: Conceptual understanding, which explains why procedures work
Rote memory, which focuses on recall without meaning
Test-taking skills, which focus on format
Procedural fluency only, which focuses on speed
questions.rationale: Strong math instruction balances conceptual understanding and procedural fluency.

questions.stem: A science teacher plans a lesson where students collect data, create a graph, and draw a conclusion. Which scientific practice is being emphasized?
options: Reading a textbook chapter silently
Copying lab procedures verbatim
Memorizing a list of facts
Analyzing and interpreting data
questions.rationale: Science practices include planning investigations and analyzing data.

questions.stem: A social studies teacher gives students a letter written by a soldier and a government report on the same battle and asks them to compare perspectives. Which skill is targeted?
options: Memorizing dates of battles
Copying the textbook summary
Analyzing primary sources for point of view and bias
Locating battle sites on a map
questions.rationale: Comparing sources builds historical thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher in a second-grade classroom sets up three centers: one for fluency, one for vocabulary, and one for writing. What is a key factor for effective center management?
options: Allowing students to choose any center without limits
Teaching and practicing routines and providing meaningful, self-checking tasks
Assigning identical tasks at every center
Leaving students alone without any expectations
questions.rationale: Centers work when routines are clear and tasks are purposeful.

questions.stem: A teacher arranges students in heterogeneous groups for a science investigation and assigns roles such as recorder and materials manager. What is the main purpose of assigning roles?
options: To prevent students from talking
To rank students based on ability
To lower the difficulty of the task for everyone
To ensure each student has a meaningful responsibility and promotes accountability
questions.rationale: Roles support positive interdependence and individual accountability.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that students quickly lose focus during a 40-minute lecture and decides to restructure. Which plan best reflects effective lesson pacing?
options: Present information in short segments of about ten minutes alternated with active processing tasks
Add a long video at the end to fill time
Remove all direct instruction from the lesson
Extend the lecture to the full class period without breaks
questions.rationale: Chunking with active processing sustains attention.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a smooth transition by announcing the next activity, giving a one-minute warning, and posting directions. What is the primary benefit?
options: It increases the time students spend waiting
It saves instructional time and reduces behavior problems during changes between activities
It eliminates the need for classroom procedures
It makes assessment unnecessary
questions.rationale: Planned transitions maintain momentum.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a unit-planning calendar to map which standards to teach each week and when to assess. This is most closely related to
options: Student seating arrangement
Grade-level retention policy
Curriculum mapping and pacing
Disciplinary referral
questions.rationale: Maps and pacing guides organize instruction over time.

questions.stem: When planning with the TEKS in mind, why do teachers distinguish between readiness standards and supporting standards?
options: Readiness standards are prioritized because they are essential for success in the next grade or course, while supporting standards reinforce them
Readiness standards are optional, while supporting standards are required
Readiness standards apply only to tested subjects
Readiness standards are written by individual teachers
questions.rationale: Prioritizing essential standards helps teachers allocate time and depth.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use a graphic organizer to teach cause and effect. Which organizer is the best fit?
options: A timeline listing dates only
A flowchart or cause-and-effect chain showing linked events
A Venn diagram comparing two items
A KWL chart tracking what students know
questions.rationale: Matching the organizer to the thinking skill clarifies relationships.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to compare and contrast two characters. Which graphic organizer works best?
options: Pyramid
Flowchart
Timeline
Venn diagram
questions.rationale: A Venn diagram shows similarities and differences.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a unit on persuasive writing to teach standards from both ELA and social studies by having students argue for a historical decision. This is an example of
options: A pull-out intervention program
Test preparation using released items
Remedial instruction for students who are behind
Interdisciplinary instruction that integrates standards from multiple subjects
questions.rationale: Integrating standards deepens understanding and uses time efficiently.

questions.stem: A teacher selects a text with a Lexile measure far above the reading levels of most of her students for independent reading. What is the likely outcome?
options: Students will automatically accelerate to the higher level
Students will have no difficulty because of motivation
Students will read faster than before
Students may become frustrated and fail to comprehend, so supports or alternative texts are needed
questions.rationale: Matching text complexity to readers supports comprehension.

questions.stem: A kindergarten teacher is deciding between a play-based center and a worksheet for teaching letter sounds. Which choice is most developmentally appropriate?
options: A long lecture about phonics rules
An online quiz with timed responses
A page of repeated letter copying with no talk
A hands-on center where students match objects to beginning sounds and talk about them
questions.rationale: Developmentally appropriate practice is active, concrete, and social.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students an advance outline, key vocabulary, and a purpose for reading before a challenging article. This is best described as
options: Pre-reading supports that activate knowledge and set a purpose
Independent practice
Post-reading assessment
Summative evaluation
questions.rationale: Pre-reading supports prepare students for complex text.

questions.stem: In a unit on fractions, a teacher plans a pre-assessment, three weeks of instruction with formative checks, and a final project. Which element is the pre-assessment designed to inform?
options: Differentiation and starting points for instruction
The final grade for the unit
The number of homework assignments
The seating chart for the semester
questions.rationale: Pre-assessments identify readiness for planning.

questions.stem: A teacher is planning how to close a lesson on the causes of the Texas Revolution. Which closure activity best consolidates learning?
options: Students line up early with no activity
The teacher assigns an unrelated reading for homework
The teacher lectures for five more minutes with no student input
Students write a two-sentence summary and share one cause with a partner
questions.rationale: Effective closure involves students in summarizing.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a self-paced digital program for part of the math block while meeting with small groups. Which planning step is most important?
options: Ensure the program aligns with the TEKS and review its data regularly to adjust instruction
Assign the program for the entire period without monitoring
Allow students to choose any program without checking content
Replace all small-group instruction with the program
questions.rationale: Digital tools should align with standards and inform instruction.

questions.stem: Which planning decision best supports students who need more time to master a skill without holding back the entire class?
options: Use flexible grouping and station rotations with targeted small-group instruction
Assign extra homework without teaching
Skip the skill and move on
Hold the entire class until all students have mastered the skill
questions.rationale: Flexible structures differentiate time and support.

questions.stem: When planning a field trip tied to a science unit, which step is most important to ensure the trip supports learning goals?
options: Skip preparation to keep it a surprise
Plan no follow-up so that students can relax
Choose the destination based on lowest cost only
Define objectives, prepare students with background, and plan a follow-up activity
questions.rationale: Trips are most effective when integrated into instruction.

questions.stem: A teacher integrates music and movement into a lesson to teach patterns in math. Which rationale best supports this decision?
options: Students learn only when they are moving
Music replaces the need for any math instruction
Multiple modalities can strengthen understanding and memory for patterns
Movement ensures all students master patterns
questions.rationale: Using several senses supports memory and engagement.

questions.stem: A teacher wants her fifth-grade science unit to build on what students learned in fourth grade about ecosystems. Which planning action is most appropriate?
options: Assume all students remember everything from last year
Skip ecosystems because they were taught already
Review the previous grade's standards and assess prior knowledge to determine where to begin
Start with the highest-level standards without any review
questions.rationale: Vertical alignment guides planning from prior knowledge.

questions.stem: A teacher writes: "Students will use context clues to determine the meaning of unfamiliar words in a grade-level passage." Which assessment best matches this objective?
options: Students spell the words correctly
Students copy the words into sentences
Students define words from a list they memorized
Students read a new passage and explain the meaning of underlined words using clues
questions.rationale: Assessment should require using context clues in a new text.

questions.stem: A teacher is writing a true-false item. Which revision best improves the item?
options: Combine two ideas in one statement to save space
Remove absolute words such as "always" and "never" and test one clear idea
Add the phrase "all of the above" to the statement
Make the true statements longer than the false statements
questions.rationale: Absolute terms cue false answers, and double-barreled statements are ambiguous.

questions.stem: Which characteristic makes a multiple-choice stem effective?
options: It includes irrelevant details to test attention to detail
It poses a complete problem so students can answer before reading the options
It is as short as possible and leaves the question unfinished
It contains a grammatical clue that points to the correct option
questions.rationale: A clear, self-contained stem measures knowledge instead of reading guesswork.

questions.stem: A teacher builds a matching section with eight terms and eight definitions, each used exactly once. What is the main weakness of this format?
options: It cannot assess any recall of facts
It requires students to write extended explanations
Students can answer the last items by elimination, which reduces the information gained
It always produces lower reliability than essays
questions.rationale: Equal-length matching lists let students narrow choices by process of elimination.

questions.stem: A teacher keeps notes of what students say and do during a science lab, writing short, dated observations. This is called
options: A standardized test
Anecdotal records
A cut-score classification
A norm-referenced percentile report
questions.rationale: Anecdotal records document specific student behaviors and learning.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a strength of a rating scale used to assess a student presentation?
options: It allows the teacher to judge the degree to which each performance trait was demonstrated
It measures only memorized facts
It removes the need for any scoring criteria
It guarantees complete objectivity among scorers
questions.rationale: Rating scales capture degrees of quality on defined traits.

questions.stem: A distribution of test scores has a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 10. A student scores 90. What is the student's z-score and interpretation?
options: -2.0, meaning the score is two standard deviations below the mean
+0.2, meaning the score is slightly above the mean
+2.0, meaning the score is two standard deviations above the mean
+20, meaning the score is twenty percent above the mean

questions.stem: On a standardized test, a student is in the 5th stanine. How should the teacher interpret this?
options: The student ranks fifth in the class
The student answered five questions correctly
The student scored in the bottom 5 percent
The student's performance is in the average range
questions.rationale: Stanines divide scores into nine bands, with 5 at the center.

questions.stem: A parent sees a grade-equivalent score of 7.2 for her fourth grader's reading test and concludes the child should be in seventh grade. What is the best explanation?
options: The score is not a real score and can be ignored
The score means the child performed like the average seventh grader would on this fourth-grade test, not that the child is ready for seventh-grade work
The child has mastered all seventh-grade reading skills
The child should be promoted immediately
questions.rationale: Grade equivalents are easily misinterpreted and do not indicate mastery of higher-grade content.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to know whether a new reading test predicts students' later success on a state exam. Which type of validity evidence does she need?
options: Content validity, shown by comparing items to objectives
Test-retest reliability, shown by repeated administration
Face validity, shown by whether the test looks appropriate
Predictive validity, shown by correlating scores with later performance
questions.rationale: Predictive validity examines how well scores forecast future outcomes.

questions.stem: A new math screener is compared with a well-established math test given at the same time, and the scores are highly related. Which evidence does this provide?
options: Content validity
Predictive validity
Concurrent validity
Inter-rater reliability
questions.rationale: Concurrent validity compares scores with an established measure given at the same time.

questions.stem: A test designed to measure reading comprehension gives lower scores to students who are slower typists because it requires typed answers. This is a threat to
options: Internal consistency, because the items are too similar
Construct validity, because scores reflect typing skill in addition to reading comprehension
Face validity, because the test looks inappropriate
Predictive validity, because the test does not forecast outcomes
questions.rationale: Construct-irrelevant variance reduces the accuracy of inferences.

questions.stem: A teacher splits a 40-item test into odd and even items and correlates the two halves. Which type of reliability is she estimating?
options: Test-retest reliability
Alternate-form reliability
Inter-rater reliability
Internal consistency, using the split-half method
questions.rationale: Split-half reliability checks whether items measure the same construct.

questions.stem: A teacher gives two equivalent versions of a unit test to different class periods on the same day to reduce sharing of answers. Which reliability concern should she check?
options: Predictive validity, to ensure scores predict grades
Inter-rater reliability, to ensure scorers agree
Alternate-form reliability, to ensure both versions yield similar results
Face validity, to ensure the forms look the same
questions.rationale: Alternate forms should be equivalent in difficulty and content.

questions.stem: Which accommodation on a state assessment is most appropriate for a student with a documented visual impairment?
options: Reduced number of questions
Large-print or braille test materials
A different test measuring easier standards
Extra points on the final score
questions.rationale: Accommodations provide access without changing what is measured.

questions.stem: A teacher notes that students in one subgroup consistently underperform on the same items. Which analysis is most appropriate?
options: Remove all items from the test for every student
Check whether the items contain language or cultural references that introduce bias before drawing conclusions about the group
Raise the scores of the subgroup by a fixed amount
Conclude that the subgroup lacks ability in the content
questions.rationale: Differential item functioning may reveal bias.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a graphic organizer to complete during a lesson and collects them to see which students need support. This is
options: A placement test
A norm-referenced test
A summative assessment of mastery after instruction
A formative assessment of understanding during instruction
questions.rationale: Formative tools gather evidence in time to adjust teaching.

questions.stem: Why do some teachers give ungraded practice quizzes before the unit test?
options: To rank students for the grade book
To replace the unit test entirely
To provide feedback and let students identify what to study without grade pressure
To increase test anxiety
questions.rationale: Low-stakes practice supports learning.

questions.stem: A student frequently performs well on class activities but freezes on timed tests. Which action best addresses test anxiety?
options: Remove all tests from the student's course
Give extra homework about test-taking facts
Tell the student to stop worrying
Teach relaxation and test-taking strategies and provide low-stakes practice under timed conditions
questions.rationale: Strategy instruction and gradual exposure reduce anxiety.

questions.stem: A teacher observes that a student can answer questions orally with great detail but writes only short, simple responses. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The student may understand the content but face challenges with written expression, so additional methods of assessment are needed
The student does not understand the content
The student should receive a failing grade for writing only
The student is deliberately avoiding work
questions.rationale: Using multiple modes provides a fuller picture.

questions.stem: A teacher gives a performance task and provides students with the scoring guide in advance. A colleague argues this gives away the answer. Which response is most accurate?
options: The scoring guide should be kept secret so students cannot aim for the criteria
Criteria are unnecessary for performance tasks
Sharing criteria clarifies the target and supports learning without revealing the content of the answer
Students should guess the criteria so that they can show creativity
questions.rationale: Transparent criteria improve performance and fairness.

questions.stem: A class completes a pre-test, mid-unit quiz, and post-test. The teacher graphs the class average at each point. What is this data primarily showing?
options: Growth in class performance across the unit
The percentile ranks of the students
The reliability of the tests
The difficulty of individual items
questions.rationale: Comparing scores over time shows progress.

questions.stem: A teacher computes the p-value for an item and finds it is 0.15. How should she interpret this?
options: Only 15 percent of students answered correctly, so the item is very difficult and should be reviewed
Fifteen percent of students skipped the item
The item is highly reliable
The item should be kept because it is easy
questions.rationale: Item difficulty (p) is the proportion of students answering correctly.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to see whether an item distinguishes between high and low performers on the test. Which statistic should she examine?
options: The range of the scores
The mean of the whole class
The mode of the scores
The discrimination index
questions.rationale: Discrimination compares performance of high and low scorers on an item.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that on one multiple-choice item no students chose option C. What does this suggest?
options: The item is too easy and must be deleted from the bank forever
Option C is a perfect distractor
Option C is not functioning as a plausible distractor and should be revised
Option C is the correct answer
questions.rationale: Distractors that no one chooses add nothing.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a checklist during a lab to record whether each student labeled the diagram, measured accurately, and recorded data. What is the main advantage of a checklist?
options: It replaces the need for any teacher observation
It measures degrees of quality for every skill
It produces a norm-referenced score
It provides a quick way to document whether specific skills are present or absent
questions.rationale: Checklists record yes-or-no evidence of skills.

questions.stem: A teacher grades an essay but is influenced by the student's handwriting, which is neat. This is an example of
options: A leniency error, in which all students receive the highest scores
A central tendency error, in which all scores are in the middle
A halo effect, in which an unrelated positive trait influences scoring
A contrast effect, in which a preceding paper influences scoring
questions.rationale: The halo effect occurs when a general impression affects specific judgments.

questions.stem: A district compares campus-level performance using the percentage of students who passed a test without considering prior achievement. What is the main limitation of this approach?
options: It is too reliable to be useful
It does not account for differences in students' starting points and so may not reflect growth
It measures only attendance
It uses a norm-referenced standard
questions.rationale: Status measures do not show growth.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to track students' progress on the same skill across the semester in a way that is easy to understand. Which tool is most useful?
options: A seating chart
A pie chart showing the number of tests given
A list of the teacher's favorite questions
A line graph of each student's scores over time
questions.rationale: Graphs of repeated measures show growth.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use students' self-assessments to monitor learning. Which strategy makes the self-assessment most accurate?
options: Ask students to rate themselves without any criteria
Use the self-assessment as the only grade
Provide clear criteria and examples of work at different levels to compare against
Tell students that high ratings earn more points
questions.rationale: Criteria and examples improve accuracy.

questions.stem: A teacher compares a student's current writing sample to the student's earlier sample to describe progress. This is an example of
options: Criterion-referenced assessment against a standard only
Placement testing
Ipsative (self-referenced) assessment
Norm-referenced assessment
questions.rationale: Ipsative assessment compares a learner with their own earlier performance.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a short quiz at the start of class on yesterday's material and uses it to decide what to review. Which type of assessment use is this?
options: Summative use to assign final grades
Selection use to admit students
Accountability use to rank schools
Formative use to adjust instruction
questions.rationale: Using quiz data to plan review is formative.

questions.stem: A teacher wants parents to understand their child's progress on specific standards. Which report is most useful?
options: A single average without explanation
A list of rankings in the class
A report that shows only attendance
A standards-based progress report with descriptors of performance on each skill
questions.rationale: Specific descriptors communicate learning clearly.

questions.stem: A teacher administers an interim assessment aligned to the unit's standards midway through the unit. How should she use the results?
options: Use the scores only to rank students
Record the scores as the final unit grade
Identify which standards need reteaching and adjust groups and pacing before the unit ends
Wait until the next semester to analyze them
questions.rationale: Interim data support timely instructional decisions.

questions.stem: In a performance assessment, a teacher asks students to demonstrate a dance sequence and scores it with a rubric. Why is a performance task appropriate here?
options: Rubrics cannot be used in fine arts
The skill itself is a performance that can be observed directly
Multiple-choice items are always more valid
Performances cannot be scored reliably
questions.rationale: Direct observation of the skill gives valid evidence.

questions.stem: A teacher examines a student's work samples and notices that the student frequently reverses b and d. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ignore the pattern because reversals are always typical in older students
Penalize the student for each reversal
Retain the student in the grade
Document the pattern, provide targeted practice, and share with the campus team if it persists
questions.rationale: Documenting patterns supports data-based decisions.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a diagnostic assessment?
options: An assessment used to rank all students in a district
An assessment used only for students in special education
An assessment used to assign final grades at the end of the course
An assessment used to pinpoint specific strengths and weaknesses so instruction can target them
questions.rationale: Diagnostic tools inform planning.

questions.stem: A teacher conducts an error analysis of student work on a multi-digit subtraction test and finds that most errors involve regrouping across zeros. How should she use this finding?
options: Assume the students did not try
Reduce the number of subtraction problems on tests
Retest the same items without instruction
Design targeted instruction on regrouping across zeros using models and guided practice
questions.rationale: Error analysis reveals patterns of misunderstanding.

questions.stem: Which assessment practice is most consistent with the principle that assessment should support learning?
options: Withholding feedback until after the semester
Providing feedback that students can use to improve before a final grade is recorded
Giving only a final exam with no earlier checks
Using tests only to punish students
questions.rationale: Assessment for learning provides actionable information.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a quiz given on Friday afternoon before a holiday has lower scores than usual across all classes. What is the best interpretation?
options: The quiz is invalid for all future use
The students have permanently lost learning
The teacher is not effective
Conditions such as timing may have affected performance, so the teacher should use additional evidence before drawing conclusions
questions.rationale: Context influences scores, so multiple sources of evidence are needed.

questions.stem: On the first day, a teacher greets students by name at the door, shares a short personal story, and invites students to share something about themselves. What is the main purpose?
options: To collect data for the teacher's evaluation
To identify which students are likely to misbehave
To begin building relationships and a sense of belonging that supports learning
To avoid teaching any content for the first week
questions.rationale: Early relationship-building establishes a welcoming climate.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a morning meeting where students greet each other, share news, and discuss a message. Which outcome is the practice designed to promote?
options: Silent seat work
Separation of students by ability
Community, social skills, and readiness for learning
Faster completion of worksheets
questions.rationale: Morning meetings build belonging and communication.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to promote equitable participation when students share answers aloud. Which structure best distributes opportunities to respond?
options: Always calling on the first hand raised
Allowing the same students to answer all questions
Calling only on students seated near the front
Randomly selecting names with cards or sticks and giving think time first
questions.rationale: Random selection spreads opportunities and signals that everyone is expected to think.

questions.stem: A student makes a mistake on the board and classmates laugh. Which teacher response best protects the climate?
options: Join the laughter to lighten the mood
Reaffirm that mistakes are part of learning, redirect the laughter, and help the student revise the solution
Send the student back to the seat without feedback
Ignore the laughter and move on without comment
questions.rationale: Respectful norms keep risk taking safe.

questions.stem: A teacher displays a poster that reads, "In this room, we help each other learn." Which approach is the most effective way to make this norm real?
options: Replace the sign with a list of consequences
Punish students who do not follow the sign
Post the sign and assume students will follow it
Teach and model what helping looks like and recognize examples when they occur
questions.rationale: Norms need explicit teaching and reinforcement.

questions.stem: A teacher discovers that she gives more detailed feedback to students she perceives as high achievers. Which action best addresses this equity issue?
options: Create a feedback tracking sheet and ensure that all students receive specific, actionable comments
Continue because high achievers can use the feedback best
Give general praise to everyone
Reduce feedback to all students equally
questions.rationale: Differential feedback reinforces gaps.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that two students who are English learners are consistently left out of group work. What is the best response?
options: Assign the students to work alone to avoid conflict
Remove group work from the unit
Structure groups with roles and language supports so that all members contribute
Allow students to form groups freely every time
questions.rationale: Structured participation supports inclusion.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to create a classroom where students feel emotionally safe. Which practice is most important?
options: Comparing students publicly to motivate them
Responding consistently and respectfully to all students, including when they make mistakes
Using sarcasm to keep students alert
Allowing students to tease each other
questions.rationale: Consistent respect fosters safety.

questions.stem: A student shares that she feels unwelcome because classmates mimic her accent. Which sequence of teacher actions is most appropriate?
options: Move the student to a different class without a conversation
Tell the student to ignore the comments
Listen privately, address the behavior with the class using established norms, and follow up with the student and the counselor
Mention the student by name to the class while scolding
questions.rationale: Respond to harassment promptly and supportively.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to build a classroom community among students in a new class. Which activity best builds trust?
options: Competitive contests with a single winner
Cooperative team-building tasks that require each member's contribution
Silent seat work all week
Rankings of students on the board
questions.rationale: Collaboration builds trust and belonging.

questions.stem: Which student behavior best demonstrates the effects of a respectful classroom climate?
options: Students only speak when the teacher calls on them
Students disagree politely and build on each other's ideas
Students avoid speaking because they fear being wrong
Students interrupt each other to be heard
questions.rationale: Respectful climates encourage polite dialogue.

questions.stem: A student who identifies as LGBTQ+ confides in the teacher about being bullied. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Provide support, follow the district bullying policy and reporting procedures, and keep the student's disclosure confidential unless safety requires otherwise
Wait for the situation to resolve itself
Share the student's identity with other staff to raise awareness
Tell the student to avoid the bullies
questions.rationale: Teachers must act on bullying and protect privacy.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to ensure that classroom discussions about controversial topics remain respectful. Which step is best?
options: Avoid all discussion of controversial topics
Allow the loudest students to lead
Establish ground rules, require evidence for claims, and model neutral facilitation
Encourage students to shout down opposing views
questions.rationale: Structured discussion protects respect.

questions.stem: A teacher observes that boys dominate science lab roles, leaving girls with note-taking jobs. Which strategy best promotes equity?
options: Assign roles by gender to simplify planning
Rotate roles on a schedule so every student experiences each responsibility
Let students choose roles each day
Eliminate roles and let groups do whatever they wish
questions.rationale: Rotating roles ensures equitable access.

questions.stem: A teacher regularly asks students for feedback on classroom activities and uses it to make changes. How does this practice support classroom climate?
options: It eliminates the need for classroom norms
It makes lesson planning unnecessary
It gives students control over grading decisions
It shows students that their voices matter and increases ownership of the learning environment
questions.rationale: Student voice builds respect and trust.

questions.stem: A teacher celebrates both academic and personal accomplishments, such as persistence and kindness, on a class wall. Which message does this send?
options: Competition is the primary goal
Many forms of success are valued, which builds an inclusive climate
Students must be perfect to be recognized
Only the highest test scores are valued
questions.rationale: Broad recognition fosters belonging.

questions.stem: A teacher plans a lesson on a historical event involving a group that is represented in the class. Which approach shows cultural sensitivity?
options: Ask the students from that group to speak for the entire group
Present multiple perspectives from credible sources and invite, but not require, students to share family experiences
Skip the topic to avoid discomfort
Teach only the version in the textbook
questions.rationale: Sensitive teaching balances accuracy and respect.

questions.stem: A teacher seats students in groups of four and rotates the groups every few weeks. What is the purpose of rotation?
options: To reduce the amount of instruction
To allow students to work with different peers and strengthen the classroom community
To make it easier to rank students
To prevent students from making friends
questions.rationale: Rotating groups builds relationships.

questions.stem: A teacher decorates the classroom with images and quotes from people of diverse backgrounds. How does this contribute to the learning environment?
options: It is only for display during school visits
It distracts students from learning
It helps students see themselves and others as part of the learning community
It replaces the need for culturally relevant instruction
questions.rationale: Representation affirms identity.

questions.stem: A teacher uses restorative circles after a conflict between students. What is the primary goal?
options: To repair harm, restore relationships, and have students take responsibility
To identify the guilty student for punishment
To separate the students permanently
To avoid discussing the conflict
questions.rationale: Restorative practices focus on repairing relationships.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a nonverbal signal, such as raising a hand, to quiet the class. What is the main advantage?
options: It prevents students from learning any procedures
It stops the behavior without interrupting instruction or raising her voice
It increases the volume in the room
It requires no teaching of expectations
questions.rationale: Nonverbal cues are quick and calm.

questions.stem: A teacher tracks that a student calls out most often during math. Using ABC analysis, she finds the antecedent is difficult problems and the consequence is attention from peers. What is the best intervention?
options: Teach a hand-raising routine, provide support for difficult problems, and reinforce appropriate requests for help
Give the student more difficult problems
Ignore all behavior in math
Remove the student from math class
questions.rationale: Functional analysis points to the cause and function.

questions.stem: A student is rewarded with praise every time she raises her hand and waits to be called on. Over time hand raising increases. What is occurring?
options: Punishment of the undesired behavior
Extinction of the behavior
Positive reinforcement of the desired behavior
Negative reinforcement of the behavior
questions.rationale: Praise as a pleasant consequence increases the behavior.

questions.stem: A teacher reduces a student's homework after the student completes class tasks with high accuracy. If the student's accuracy continues to rise, which concept applies?
options: Shaping, because approximations are reinforced
Extinction, because reinforcement is withheld
Negative reinforcement, because removing an unpleasant task increases the behavior
Positive punishment, because adding a consequence decreases behavior
questions.rationale: Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior by removing an aversive stimulus.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the difference between punishment and negative reinforcement?
options: Both always increase behavior
Punishment increases behavior, while negative reinforcement decreases behavior
Both always decrease behavior
Punishment decreases behavior, while negative reinforcement increases behavior
questions.rationale: Reinforcement strengthens, punishment weakens.

questions.stem: A teacher provides a student with a sticker after every five minutes of on-task behavior. Which reinforcement schedule is this?
options: Fixed ratio
Fixed interval
Variable ratio
Variable interval
questions.rationale: Reinforcement after a set time is a fixed-interval schedule.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that praising students publicly makes one student uncomfortable. What should the teacher do?
options: Stop praising the student
Praise only other students
Increase the volume of public praise
Provide private praise through a note or quiet comment
questions.rationale: Praise should match the student's needs.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a class-wide system where the class earns points toward a reward when most students follow procedures. Which concept is being used?
options: Extinction
Individual punishment
Group contingency
Modeling
questions.rationale: Group contingencies tie rewards to group behavior.

questions.stem: Which response best reflects a logical approach to a student who repeatedly arrives late?
options: Lock the door to prevent entry
Lower the student's grades for each tardy
Meet privately to identify barriers and develop a plan with supports for on-time arrival
Publicly announce the student's tardiness each day
questions.rationale: Problem solving addresses the cause.

questions.stem: A student becomes verbally aggressive in class. Which de-escalation technique is most appropriate?
options: Physically block the student's path
Argue with the student about the behavior
Stay calm, use a low tone, give space, and offer choices to help the student regain control
Raise your voice to establish authority
questions.rationale: De-escalation reduces tension.

questions.stem: A teacher assigns jobs such as line leader and materials manager to students. How does this support classroom management?
options: It ranks students by importance
It allows the teacher to avoid planning
It gives students responsibility and helps the room run smoothly
It removes the need for any procedures
questions.rationale: Classroom jobs build ownership.

questions.stem: A teacher uses Kounin's concept of "overlapping" when she responds to a disruption in the back of the room while continuing to help a student at her desk. What does this demonstrate?
options: A failure to monitor the room
A plan to send students to the office
A strategy of ignoring misbehavior
The ability to attend to two events at once without stopping the lesson
questions.rationale: Overlapping means managing multiple activities simultaneously.

questions.stem: A teacher quickly moves from one activity to the next with little downtime. Which of Kounin's concepts does this describe?
options: Group alerting, keeping all students attentive
Withitness, knowing what is happening in the room
Momentum, maintaining the flow of the lesson without slowdowns
Ripple effect, the influence of corrections on others
questions.rationale: Momentum keeps lessons moving smoothly.

questions.stem: A teacher scans the room often and quickly addresses the correct student when misbehavior occurs. Which Kounin concept is evident?
options: Satiation, growing tired of an activity
Smoothness, avoiding abrupt transitions
Overlapping, handling two events simultaneously
Withitness, awareness of what is happening in all parts of the classroom
questions.rationale: Withitness is the teacher's ability to know what is happening and respond accurately.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a clear, consistent consequence system that is taught at the start of the year. What is the primary benefit?
options: Students know what to expect, which reduces misbehavior and perceptions of unfairness
Students will never misbehave
Students no longer need to follow routines
The teacher can change consequences daily
questions.rationale: Consistency builds fairness.

questions.stem: A teacher asks a talkative student to help distribute materials at the start of a task. Which principle does this illustrate?
options: Punishing talkativeness
Ignoring the student
Channeling energy into a productive role to prevent disruption
Removing the student from the class
questions.rationale: Positive roles can redirect behavior.

questions.stem: A teacher has a student with frequent outbursts and considers using a behavior contract. Which feature makes a contract more effective?
options: Clear, specific, measurable goals that the student helps develop, with agreed reinforcement
Punishments chosen only by the teacher
Vague goals about being good
A contract that cannot be reviewed
questions.rationale: Effective contracts are specific and collaborative.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that students are most disruptive during transitions between centers. Which proactive step is most helpful?
options: Skip centers to avoid transitions
Allow students to move whenever they want
Add more centers
Teach and rehearse the transition procedure, including a timer and signal
questions.rationale: Rehearsed transitions reduce disruptions.

questions.stem: A student frequently seeks attention by making jokes. The teacher chooses to praise on-task behavior and minimize attention for jokes. This strategy is
options: Punishment by removal
Negative reinforcement
Differential reinforcement of appropriate behavior
Time-out from reinforcement
questions.rationale: Reinforcing desired behavior while withholding attention for misbehavior reduces it.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a self-monitoring checklist for a student to record whether the student stayed on task during each ten-minute interval. What is the main benefit?
options: It builds self-awareness and responsibility for behavior
It punishes off-task behavior
It makes the teacher responsible for all behavior
It eliminates the need for feedback
questions.rationale: Self-monitoring increases self-regulation.

questions.stem: A teacher sees two students arguing about a game at recess. Which response best fosters conflict resolution skills?
options: Decide who is right and impose a punishment
Ignore them because arguments are normal
Guide the students to state their feelings, listen to each other, and propose a solution
Send both students to the office immediately
questions.rationale: Teaching problem solving builds skills.

questions.stem: A teacher says, "Today we will compare two ways to solve this equation, so watch for how the steps are alike and different." What communication practice is this?
options: Assessing prior knowledge with a quiz
Setting a purpose and focusing attention before instruction
Giving corrective feedback after an error
Closing the lesson with a summary
questions.rationale: Telling students what to look for focuses attention and guides processing.

questions.stem: Which statement is most effective for giving a clear instruction?
options: "Open your books to page 40 and read the first paragraph silently."
"Get started on whatever you need."
"Work on it until I say stop, and you should know what to do."
"Do the thing we did last time."
questions.rationale: Clear instructions are specific and observable.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that students misunderstand a key term she used. Which communication strategy best prevents this in the future?
options: Replace all technical terms with vague words
Assume students will infer meaning from context
Use the term more frequently without explanation
Define key terms with examples and have students restate them in their own words
questions.rationale: Explicit vocabulary instruction clarifies meaning.

questions.stem: A teacher asks, "Can you tell me more about why you think that?" after a student gives an answer. What is the purpose of this question?
options: To signal that the answer is incorrect
To end the discussion quickly
To encourage elaboration and reveal the student's reasoning
To avoid evaluating the answer
questions.rationale: Probing questions deepen thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher uses the Initiate-Respond-Evaluate pattern in most class discussions, calling on one student to answer and then saying whether it is right. How could she shift to promote more thinking?
options: Evaluate each response immediately and move on
Call only on students who are sure to be right
Follow responses with open prompts such as "Who sees it differently?" and invite students to respond to each other
End the discussion after a single answer
questions.rationale: Reducing evaluation encourages dialogue.

questions.stem: A teacher reads aloud to a class and adjusts her tone, pace, and gestures to make the story engaging. This illustrates
options: Testing students on vocabulary
Replacing the need for any discussion
Using expressive delivery to support comprehension and interest
Distracting students from the text
questions.rationale: Effective delivery enhances meaning.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to give feedback on a student's essay in a way that preserves motivation. Which comment pattern is best?
options: List every error in the paper
Name a specific strength, then identify one priority area with a concrete suggestion
Write only "needs work"
Compare the paper to a classmate's
questions.rationale: Balanced, focused feedback motivates revision.

questions.stem: A teacher notices that a student interprets sarcasm literally. Which communication adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Use direct, literal language and explicitly teach figurative language when it is used
Ignore the confusion
Remove the student from class discussions
Increase the use of sarcasm so the student learns
questions.rationale: Clear language supports students who interpret literally.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to assess student understanding of a spoken explanation. Which technique is most effective?
options: Have students copy the explanation verbatim
Ask students whether they were listening
Tell students the main idea again
Ask students to summarize the main idea to a partner
questions.rationale: Paraphrasing shows comprehension.

questions.stem: A teacher makes sure that the directions on assignments use the same format and language each time. What is the main benefit?
options: Students learn only one type of task
Students stop reading the directions
The teacher can avoid explaining expectations
Consistency reduces confusion and helps students focus on the task
questions.rationale: Predictable formats ease processing.

questions.stem: During a class discussion a student gives an answer that is partly correct. Which teacher response best supports learning?
options: Praise the whole answer to protect feelings
Ignore the response
Say "wrong" and call on another student
Acknowledge the correct part and ask a follow-up question to help the student refine the rest
questions.rationale: Responsive feedback builds on partial understanding.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a technique where students turn to a partner and explain what they just learned before whole-class sharing. What are two benefits of this strategy?
options: Greater participation and rehearsal of ideas before sharing publicly
Elimination of misconceptions and guaranteed mastery
Reduced need for any instruction and fewer assessments
Silence in the classroom and higher teacher talk time
questions.rationale: Partner talk increases engagement and clarifies thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher is aware that her tone of voice can affect students' emotions. Which approach best supports a positive climate?
options: Avoid speaking to students individually
Use sarcasm to be humorous
Use a calm, respectful tone, even when correcting behavior
Use a harsh tone to show seriousness
questions.rationale: Tone communicates respect.

questions.stem: A teacher gives directions in English only to a class with several students who recently arrived from another country. Which change best supports communication?
options: Assume the students will copy peers
Give directions only once
Pair spoken directions with gestures, visuals, and written steps
Speak louder and faster
questions.rationale: Multimodal directions aid comprehension.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a problem with an unfamiliar format and asks them to plan an approach before solving. Which skill is being developed?
options: Rote memorization of steps
Speed without understanding
Copying the teacher's solution
Problem-solving strategy selection and planning
questions.rationale: Planning is a key phase of problem solving.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to move beyond summarizing a news article to evaluating its argument. Which prompt best supports this?
options: "Does the author provide sufficient evidence for the claim? Explain what is missing or convincing."
"Underline the longest sentence."
"List the facts stated in the first paragraph."
"Copy the title and author's name."
questions.rationale: Evaluation requires judging evidence.

questions.stem: In a lesson on fractions, a teacher asks students to explain whether 3/4 is greater than 5/8 using a diagram. Which thinking skill is emphasized?
options: Recall of definitions
Speed of computation
Reasoning and justification using representations
Memorization of algorithms
questions.rationale: Explaining with diagrams builds reasoning.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a K-W-L chart and then asks students to generate questions they want to investigate. Which skill does this promote?
options: Inquiry and curiosity-driven research
Following a script
Memorizing teacher-provided facts
Passive listening
questions.rationale: Student-generated questions drive inquiry.

questions.stem: A teacher presents students with two conflicting explanations of a scientific phenomenon and asks them to design a test to decide which is better. Which skill does this promote?
options: Memorizing explanations
Scientific reasoning, including hypothesis testing and evaluating evidence
Choosing the explanation they like best
Accepting the explanation from the textbook
questions.rationale: Testing explanations develops reasoning.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to sort statements into facts and opinions and justify each choice. What skill is being practiced?
options: Following directions
Handwriting
Distinguishing fact from opinion using evidence
Rote recall
questions.rationale: Classifying statements requires criteria.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a data set and asks them to identify patterns and propose explanations. Which Bloom level is most targeted?
options: Remember
Apply
Analyze
Create
questions.rationale: Identifying patterns is analysis.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to design an original solution to reduce traffic near the school and justify the design. Which Bloom level is most targeted?
options: Apply
Remember
Understand
Create
questions.rationale: Designing a new solution is creating.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to learn how to ask higher-level questions. Which activity is most effective?
options: Provide question stems at different levels and have students write and answer their own questions
Have students copy questions from the textbook
Tell students to ask harder questions without examples
Prohibit student questions
questions.rationale: Modeling and practice build questioning skills.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a Socratic seminar to discuss a text. What is a key student responsibility?
options: Listen silently and repeat the teacher's view
Avoid referring to the text
Prepare by reading closely and supporting opinions with textual evidence
Speak as often as possible regardless of content
questions.rationale: Evidence-based dialogue is the focus.

questions.stem: A teacher encourages students to consider counterarguments when writing persuasive essays. What skill does this develop?
options: Evaluating multiple perspectives and strengthening arguments
Writing quickly without planning
Memorizing the teacher's opinion
Ignoring opposing views
questions.rationale: Considering counterarguments deepens reasoning.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to monitor their own thinking while solving a multistep problem. Which prompt supports metacognition?
options: "Hurry up and finish."
"Did you copy the answer?"
"Why are you not like the others?"
"What strategy are you using, and how do you know it is working?"
questions.rationale: Metacognitive prompts encourage reflection.

questions.stem: In a lesson on reading, a teacher asks students to "read like a detective," noting clues and questions. Which strategy is being taught?
options: Choral reading
Memorizing the text
Close reading with annotation and inference
Skimming for speed
questions.rationale: Close reading focuses on careful analysis.

questions.stem: A teacher gives students a model of a flawed argument and asks them to find the logical error. Which skill is promoted?
options: Rewriting spelling errors
Copying the argument
Evaluating reasoning and identifying fallacies
Memorizing the argument
questions.rationale: Critiquing arguments develops logical thinking.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to plan how they would test whether plants grow better with music. Which element is most important to include in the plan?
options: Giving the plants as much water as possible
Controlling variables so that only the music differs between groups
Changing several variables at once
Using different plants for each group with different soil
questions.rationale: A fair test changes only one variable.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a classroom response system to ask a multiple-choice question and sees a bar graph of answers. What is the main instructional benefit?
options: Eliminating the need for questioning
Replacing teacher feedback
Increasing homework
Immediate class-level data to inform the next teaching move
questions.rationale: Instant data supports responsive teaching.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to create short videos explaining a science concept to younger students. According to the SAMR model, this task most likely represents
options: Augmentation without any functional change
No technology integration
Substitution, because the video replaces a worksheet exactly
Modification or redefinition, because students create new content for an authentic audience
questions.rationale: Creating and sharing media transforms the task.

questions.stem: A teacher wants students to collaborate on a research project from different locations. Which tool is most appropriate?
options: A single printed copy passed between students
A shared online document or workspace with commenting features
A phone call with no record
Individual handwritten notes mailed to the teacher
questions.rationale: Cloud tools support collaboration.

questions.stem: A teacher teaches students to recognize that search results may be influenced by advertising and algorithms. Which skill is being developed?
options: Keyboarding
Coding
Digital and media literacy
Handwriting
questions.rationale: Understanding search influences builds critical evaluation.

questions.stem: A school asks teachers to use only tools that have been vetted for student privacy. A teacher finds a free app that asks students to create accounts with personal data. What should she do?
options: Request district review and approval before using it with students
Tell students to use it at home on their own
Ignore the privacy policy because the app is free
Use it with her own account on behalf of the class without telling anyone
questions.rationale: Districts must vet tools for compliance with student privacy laws.

questions.stem: A teacher uses a virtual simulation of a chemical reaction because the real experiment is unsafe. What is the main advantage?
options: The simulation is always more accurate than real experiments
The simulation replaces all hands-on work for all topics
The simulation requires no teacher guidance
Students can safely explore and manipulate variables that would be dangerous or costly in real life
questions.rationale: Simulations extend learning opportunities.

questions.stem: A teacher notices students copying text from websites into their essays. Which response best addresses academic integrity?
options: Teach how to paraphrase and cite sources, and use drafts and conferences to monitor original work
Give students zeros without any instruction
Ban all internet use for research
Ignore copying because it is common
questions.rationale: Instruction and process monitoring reduce plagiarism.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to use a spreadsheet to organize data from a science experiment and create a graph. Which skill is being developed?
options: Data analysis and representation using technology
Typing speed
Handwriting speed
Memorizing formulas
questions.rationale: Spreadsheets support data organization and analysis.

questions.stem: A teacher is concerned about students' screen time during class. Which approach best balances technology use?
options: Use devices all period every day
Use technology for purposeful tasks and include offline, hands-on, and discussion activities
Prohibit all technology use
Allow students to use devices for any purpose
questions.rationale: Purposeful use balances learning modalities.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to evaluate an educational app. Which criterion is most important?
options: Alignment with learning objectives and evidence that it supports student learning
Whether the app is free
The number of animations in the app
The popularity of the app on social media
